Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.

p.seg: Qín raised an army and approached Zhōu to demand the Nine Tripods.
The Lord of Zhōu was troubled by this,
and informed Yán Lǜ.
Yán Lǜ said:
"My lord, do not worry.
I request to go east and borrow aid from Qí."
Yán Lǜ arrived in Qí,
and said to the King of Qí:
"Now Qín's actions are without principle;
they wish to raise troops, approach Zhōu, and demand the Nine Tripods.
The ruler and ministers of Zhōu,
after thorough deliberation within,
believe that rather than giving them to Qín,
it would be better to return them to your great state.
To preserve a state in peril
is a fine reputation;
to obtain the Nine Tripods
is a substantial treasure.
I hope Your Majesty will consider this."
The King of Qí was greatly pleased,
dispatched an army of fifty thousand men,
and sent Chén Chénsī to lead them in rescuing Zhōu,
whereupon the Qín troops withdrew.
The Qí general then demanded the Nine Tripods,
and the Lord of Zhōu was troubled again.
Yán Lǜ said:
"My lord, do not worry.
I request to go east and resolve this."
Yán Lǜ arrived in Qí,
and said to the King of Qí:
"Zhōu, relying on the righteousness of your great state,
has been able to preserve its ruler, ministers, fathers, and sons.
We wish to present the Nine Tripods,
but we do not know by which route your great state will bring them to Qí?"
The King of Qí said:
"We shall take the route through Liáng."
Yán Lǜ said:
"That will not do.
The ruler and ministers of Liáng desire to obtain the Nine Tripods;
they have plotted for them beneath the Huī Terrace,
and above the Shǎo Sea,
for a long time now.
If the tripods enter Liáng,
they will certainly not come out."
The King of Qí said:
"We shall take the route through Chǔ."
Yán Lǜ replied:
"That will not do.
The ruler and ministers of Chǔ desire to obtain the Nine Tripods;
they have plotted for them within the Yè Court,
for a long time now.
If they enter Chǔ,
the tripods will certainly not come out."
The King said:
"Then by what route, after all,
shall we bring them to Qí?"
Yán Lǜ said:
"Our humble state has indeed been privately concerned for Your Majesty about this.
Now these tripods—
they are not like vinegar pots, sauce jars, or earthenware vessels
that can be carried under the arm or lifted by hand to bring to Qí;
nor are they like birds gathering, crows flying,
hares leaping, or horses galloping—
swiftly coming to a halt in Qí.
In the past, when Zhōu attacked Yīn,
and obtained the Nine Tripods,
for each single tripod, ninety thousand men were needed to haul it,
nine times nine being eight hundred and ten thousand men in total.
The soldiers and troops,
the equipment and gear
required for the task were proportionate to this.
Now even if Your Majesty had such men,
by what route could they bring them out?
I privately worry for Your Majesty about this."
The King of Qí said:
"Your repeated visits here
are as good as not giving them to us at all."
Yán Lǜ said:
"We dare not deceive your great state.
Hasten to decide the route by which they will be taken out,
and our humble state will move the tripods to await your command."
The King of Qí then desisted.
Qín attacked Yíyáng.
The Lord of Zhōu said to Zhào Lěi:
"What do you think will happen?"
He replied:
"Yíyáng will certainly be taken."
The Lord said:
"Yíyáng's city walls are eight lǐ square,
it has a hundred thousand skilled soldiers,
and grain supplies to last several years.
Gōng Zhòng's army numbers two hundred thousand,
and Jǐng Cuì, with the masses of Chǔ,
will come to the mountains and rescue it.
Qín will certainly achieve nothing."
He replied:
"Gān Mào
is a traveler from afar.
If he attacks Yíyáng and succeeds,
he will be like the Duke of Zhōu;
if he does not succeed,
he will be erased from Qín.
The King of Qín, disregarding the counsel of his ministers and elders, attacks Yíyáng.
If Yíyáng is not taken,
the King of Qín will be shamed.
Therefore I say it will be taken."
The Lord said:
"Plan for me, then—
what should we do?"
He replied:
"Tell Jǐng Cuì this:
'Your lordship's rank is that of Zhíguī,
your office is that of Zhùguó.
If you fight and win,
you cannot be further advanced;
if you do not win,
you will die.
It would be better to turn against Qín and aid Yíyáng.
If you advance your troops,
Qín, fearing that you will take advantage of their exhaustion,
will certainly offer you treasures to win your favor;
Gōng Zhòng, admiring your action of pressuring Qín on his behalf,
will also certainly offer all his treasures.'"
Qín took Yíyáng,
and Jǐng Cuì indeed advanced his troops.
Qín grew fearful,
and hastily offered Zhǔzǎo;
Hán indeed also offered heavy treasures.
Jǐng Cuì obtained a city from Qín,
received treasures from Hán,
and was grateful to Eastern Zhōu.
Eastern Zhōu and Western Zhōu went to war,
and Hán came to rescue Western Zhōu.
Someone spoke on behalf of Eastern Zhōu to the King of Hán, saying:
"Western Zhōu
is the former state of the Son of Heaven,
and possesses many precious vessels and heavy treasures.
If you hold your troops and do not send them out,
you can win the gratitude of Eastern Zhōu,
and the treasures of Western Zhōu can all be yours."
Eastern Zhōu and Western Zhōu were in conflict,
and Western Zhōu wished to make peace with Chǔ and Hán.
Qí Míng said to the Lord of Eastern Zhōu:
"I fear that Western Zhōu will give treasures to Chǔ and Hán,
ordering them to seek territory from Eastern Zhōu on its behalf.
It would be better to say to Chǔ and Hán:
'Western Zhōu wishes to offer treasures,
but it is playing a double game.
If the troops of Eastern Zhōu do not urgently press Western Zhōu,
then Western Zhōu's treasures will not enter Chǔ and Hán.
If Chǔ and Hán wish to obtain the treasures,
then they should promptly urge us to attack Western Zhōu.
When Western Zhōu's treasures come out,
it will be us obtaining the treasures for Chǔ and Hán,
and winning their gratitude,
while Western Zhōu is weakened.'"
Eastern Zhōu wished to plant rice,
but Western Zhōu would not release the water,
and Eastern Zhōu was troubled by this.
Sūzǐ said to the Lord of Eastern Zhōu:
"May I request to go and make Western Zhōu release the water?"
He then went to see the Lord of Western Zhōu and said:
"Your lordship's plan is mistaken!
Now, by not releasing the water,
you are enriching Eastern Zhōu.
At present, its people all plant wheat,
and have no other crops.
If you wish to harm them,
it would be better to release the water for a time,
to ruin what they have planted.
Release the water,
and Eastern Zhōu will certainly plant rice again;
then, when they plant rice, seize it again.
If you do this,
then the people of Eastern Zhōu can be made to rely entirely on Western Zhōu,
and accept orders from your lordship."
The Lord of Western Zhōu said:
"Good."
He then released the water.
Sūzǐ also obtained gold from both states.
Zhāo Xiàn was in Yángdí,
and the Lord of Zhōu intended to order his Prime Minister to go there,
but the Prime Minister was unwilling.
Sū Lì spoke on his behalf to the Lord of Zhōu, saying:
"When the King of Chǔ and the King of Wèi met,
our lord ordered Chén Fēng to go to Chǔ,
and ordered Xiàng Gōng to go to Wèi.
When Chǔ and Hán met,
our lord ordered Xǔ Gōng to go to Chǔ,
and ordered Xiàng Gōng to go to Hán.
Now, Zhāoxiàn is not a ruler of men,
yet Your Lordship ordered the chancellor to go;
if his king were in Yángzhái,
whom would Your Lordship order to go?"
The ruler of Zhōu said:
"Well said."
He then halted the journey.
Qín sought passage through Zhōu to attack Hán.
Zhōu feared that granting passage would incur Hán's hatred,
while not granting it would incur Qín's hatred.
Shǐ Yǎn said to the ruler of Zhōu:
"Why does Your Lordship not send someone to tell Hán's Gōngshū:
'The reason Qín dares to cut through the passes and attack Hán
is that it trusts Dōngzhōu.
Why does Your Excellency not give land to Zhōu,
dispatch a high-ranking envoy to Chǔ,
so that Qín will surely become suspicious
and cease to trust Zhōu?
Thus Hán will not be attacked.'
Then also tell the king of Qín:
'Hán forcibly gave land to Zhōu,
intending to make Qín suspicious of Zhōu.
I, your humble servant, dare not refuse to accept it.'
Qín will have no grounds to order Zhōu not to accept it,
thus gaining land from Hán while obeying Qín."
Chǔ attacked Yōngshì.
Zhōu supplied grain to Qín and Hán.
The king of Chǔ was angry with Zhōu,
and the ruler of Zhōu was troubled by this.
Someone spoke to the king of Chǔ on behalf of Zhōu, saying:
"With Your Majesty's strength, if you anger Zhōu,
Zhōu, in fear,
will surely ally with the states to which it gave grain,
thus strengthening Your Majesty's enemies.
Therefore, Your Majesty should quickly dispel Zhōu's fear.
Having first incurred offense and later gained relief,
it will surely serve Your Majesty diligently."
Zhōu Zuì said to Shí Lǐ:
"Why do you not use Qín to attack Qí?
I will request that Qí make you its chancellor.
You, serving Qín with Qí's resources,
will surely have no worries.
You can then have me, Zhōu Zuì, reside in Wèi to assist you,
thus putting the world under your control.
In the east, you will be esteemed by Qí;
in the west, honored by Qín.
When Qín and Qí unite,
you will always hold great weight."
The Zhōu chancellor Lǚ Cāng
introduced a guest to the ruler of Zhōu.
The former chancellor, Gōngshī Jí, fearing the guest would slander him,
sent someone to tell the ruler of Zhōu:
"The guest
is a skilled debater,
but the reason he is unsuitable
is his fondness for defaming others."
Zhōu Wénjūn dismissed the scholar Gōngshī Jí
and appointed Lǚ Cāng as chancellor.
The people of the state were displeased.
The ruler felt deeply troubled.
Someone said to Zhōu Wénjūn:
"A state must have both criticism and praise.
A loyal minister ensures criticism falls upon himself,
while praise goes to his ruler.
The ruler of Sòng seized the people's farming time to build a tower,
and the people criticized him,
for there was no loyal minister to cover for him.
Zǐ Hǎn resigned as chancellor to become Minister of Works,
so the people criticized Zǐ Hǎn and praised their ruler.
Duke Huán of Qí had seven markets in his palace
and seven hundred lanes of courtesans.
The people of the state criticized him.
Guǎn Zhòng therefore built a mansion with three returning terraces,
to cover for Duke Huán—
was this not harming himself before the people?
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* record hundreds of instances of ministers assassinating rulers,
all involving ministers who enjoyed praise.
Thus, when a minister gains praise,
it is not a blessing for the state.
For the masses form strength,
and accumulated earth becomes a mountain."
The ruler of Zhōu thus did not dismiss him.
A man from Wēn went to Zhōu,
but Zhōu did not admit him.
The visitor then replied:
"I am a host."
Asked about his alley, he did not know it,
so the officials imprisoned him.
The ruler sent someone to question him:
"You are not from Zhōu,
yet you claim not to be a visitor—why?"
He replied:
"Since youth, I have recited the *Book of Songs*.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'Under the vast sky,
all land is the king's;
along the shores of the land,
all are the king's subjects.'
Now the ruler of Zhōu rules the world,
so I am a subject of the Son of Heaven.
How then can I be a visitor?
Therefore, I said I am a host."
The ruler then ordered the officials to release him.
Someone spoke to Jīn Tóu on behalf of Zhōu Zuì, saying:
"Qín, due to Zhōu Zuì's going to Qí, suspects the world,
and moreover knows that Zhào finds it difficult to fight the people of Qí.
Fearing an alliance between Qí and Hán,
it will surely first ally with Qín.
If Qín and Qí unite,
then your state will be emptied.
You should instead rescue Qí,
while assisting Qín in attacking Hán and Wèi.
Shàngdǎng and Zhǎngzǐ will belong to Zhào
thereafter.
You will gain treasures from Qín in the east,
take land from Hán in the south,
and Wèi will thus be constrained.
Proceed slowly eastward,
and you will achieve an alliance."
Zhōu Zuì said to Jīn Tóu:
"You are burdening Qín with an order to fight powerful Qí.
If victorious,
Qín will take over Qí
and enfeoff it,
preventing excessive territorial cessions,
and then let the world fight;
if defeated,
your state will be greatly wounded,
and you will have to obey Qín.
Qín will take all of Shàngdǎng and Tàiyuán from Hán and Wèi,
and the west will cease to belong to Qín thereafter.
Qín's territory
is half the world.
It controls the fate of Qí, Chǔ, and the Three Jìn.
Your state and person will be endangered—
what kind of strategy is this?"
Shí Xíngqín said to Dàliáng Zào:
"To secure the name of hegemon-king,
it is best to prepare skilled debaters from the two Zhōu."
He said to the ruler of Zhōu:
"Your Lordship should have skilled debaters
strive on your behalf in Qín."
Someone said to Xuē Gōng:
"Zhōu Zuì was favored by the king of Qí,
yet was expelled.
Listening to Zhù Fú
and appointing Lǚ Lǐ as chancellor
aims to win over Qín.
If Qín and Qí unite,
Fú and Lǐ will gain importance.
With Zhōu and Qí aligned,
Qín will surely slight you.
You should urgently march troops northward toward Zhào to pressure Qín and Wèi,
recruit Zhōu Zuì for later action,
and moreover reverse the king of Qí's trust,
while preventing the world from following suit.
Without Qín,
the world will turn against Qí,
and Fú will surely flee.
With whom will the king of Qí govern his state?"
Qí listened to Zhù Fú
and alienated Zhōu Zuì.
Someone said to the king of Qí:
"Expelling Zhōu Zuì,
listening to Zhù Fú,
and appointing Lǚ Lǐ as chancellor
aim to deeply win over Qín.
If Qín gains the world,
it will attack Qí deeply.
If Qí unites,
Zhào will fear attack,
so it urgently mobilizes troops to show Qín.
Qín, using Zhào to attack,
and joining Qí to attack Zhào—
the actual reasoning is the same.
It will surely not settle.
Thus, employing Zhù Fú
aligns with the world's reasoning."
Sū Lì spoke to Sū Qín on behalf of Zhōu Zuì, saying:
"You should have the king listen to Zuì,
using land to ally with Wèi and Zhào.
Thus, Qí will surely angrily ally with them,
and you will thereby ally Qí with powerful Chǔ, producing results.
If you wish to capitalize on Zuì's affairs,
then the one uniting Qí
will be you;
the one ceding land
will be Zuì."
He said to Zhōu Zuì:
"When Chóu Hè becomes the prime minister of Sòng,
it will be to observe how Qín responds to Zhào and Sòng,
and to defeat the three states.
If the three states are not defeated,
then he will ally Zhào and Sòng with the eastern states to isolate Qín.
He will also observe the relations between Hán and Wèi with Qí.
If they are not firm,
then he will join Sòng to defeat the three states,
and thus betray Zhào and Sòng to the three states.
Why don't you, sir, send someone to tell the kings of Hán and Wèi:
'Do you want Qín and Zhào to betray each other?
Why not make Zhōu Zuì concurrently prime minister?
If they see that they cannot be separated,
then Qín and Zhào will certainly betray each other
and ally with Your Majesty.'"
On behalf of Zhōu Zuì, he said to the King of Wèi:
"Qín knows that Zhào finds it difficult to fight Qí,
and fears an alliance between Qí and Zhào,
so it will secretly strengthen Zhào.
Zhào dares not fight,
fearing that Qín will not support it,
so it will first ally with Qí.
Qín and Zhào will contend for Qí,
and Your Majesty will have no one there,
which is unacceptable.
If Your Majesty does not send Zhōu Zuì away,
to ally with and win over Qí,
and instead hastily attacks Qí with troops,
there will be no basis for such action."
He said to Zhōu Zuì:
"The King of Wèi entrusted the state to you, sir,
valuing an alliance with Qín to attack Qí.
Lord Xuē, your former lord,
lightly forgets his Xuē,
and disregards the tombs of his ancestors.
Yet you alone cultivate empty trust as a lofty conduct,
openly leading the ministers to rely on your former lord,
and refusing to join in attacking Qí.
This will provoke the powerful Qín to anger, which is unacceptable.
You would do better to say to the King of Wèi and Lord Xuē:
'I request to enter Qí on Your Majesty's behalf.
The world cannot harm Qí.
If there is a change,
I will request to rescue it;
if there is no change,
Your Majesty may then attack it.
Moreover, I am a servant of Qí.
If I hinder Your Majesty's relations with the world,
that is unacceptable.
Your Majesty has bestowed great favors upon me.
If I enter Qí,
then Your Majesty will also be free from the burden of Qí.'"
Zhào took Zhōu's sacrificial land,
and the Lord of Zhōu was troubled by it.
He informed Zhèng Cháo.
Zhèng Cháo said:
"Do not worry, my lord.
I request thirty pieces of gold to retrieve it."
The Lord of Zhōu gave it to him.
Zhèng Cháo presented it to Zhào's Grand Diviner,
and informed him of the matter of the sacrificial land.
When the king fell ill,
he had him perform divination.
The Grand Diviner reproached him, saying:
"Zhōu's sacrificial land is causing the affliction."
Zhào then returned it.
Dù Hè wanted to elevate Jǐng Cuì in Zhōu.
He said to the Lord of Zhōu:
"Your state is small.
If you exhaust your treasures, pearls, and jade to serve the feudal lords,
you must carefully consider it.
It is like setting a net:
if you set it where there are no birds,
you will gain nothing all day;
if you set it where there are many birds,
you will frighten the birds away;
you must set it where birds may or may not be,
only then can you catch many birds.
Now, if you bestow favors on great men,
they will look down on you;
if you bestow them on petty men,
they have nothing to offer in return,
and you will waste resources.
You must bestow favors on impoverished scholars of the present,
who are not yet but will become great men.
Only then can you achieve your desires."
The crown prince of Zhōu Gòng died,
leaving five sons by concubines.
He loved them all,
and had not designated an heir.
Sīmǎ Jiǎn said to the King of Chǔ:
"Why not enfeoff Prince Jiù,
and request that he be made crown prince?"
Zuǒ Chéng said to Sīmǎ Jiǎn:
"If the Lord of Zhōu does not listen,
your wisdom will be thwarted and your ties with Zhōu severed.
It would be better to say to the Lord of Zhōu:
'Whom do you wish to establish?
Secretly inform Jiǎn,
and Jiǎn will have the King of Chǔ grant him land.'
If you wish to become crown prince,
then have someone say to the Prime Minister's charioteer, Zhǎnzi, and the steward Kōng:
'The king seems to want you to do it.
This is a strong man,
and his presence in the court is inconvenient for the Prime Minister.'"
The Prime Minister then had him made crown prince.
The three states blocked Qín,
and Zhōu ordered its Prime Minister to go to Qín.
Because Qín was轻视,
he delayed his departure.
Someone said to the Prime Minister:
"Whether Qín轻视 or values us is unknown.
Qín wants to know the situation of the three states.
You should go and see the King of Qín, saying:
'I request to inform Your Majesty of the situation in the east.'
Qín will certainly value you.
This will elevate Zhōu,
and elevating Zhōu will win over Qín.
Qí valued us, so we had Zhōu,
and we won over Qí.
Thus, Zhōu never lost relations with a valued state."
Chāng Tā fled from Western Zhōu
to Eastern Zhōu,
disclosing all of Western Zhōu's secrets to Eastern Zhōu.
Eastern Zhōu was delighted,
while Western Zhōu was furious.
Féng Dàn said:
"I can kill him."
The lord gave him thirty catties of gold.
Féng Dàn had someone carry the gold and a letter,
secretly sending a letter to Chāng Tā, saying:
"Inform Chāng Tā:
if the matter can be accomplished,
strive to accomplish it;
if it cannot be accomplished,
flee quickly, flee quickly.
If the matter drags on, it will be exposed,
and you will bring about your own death."
He then had someone inform the scout of Eastern Zhōu:
"Tonight, a traitor will enter."
The scout captured him and presented him to Eastern Zhōu,
and Eastern Zhōu immediately killed Chāng Tā.
Zhāo Jiǎn was on bad terms with Eastern Zhōu.
Someone said to Zhāo Jiǎn:
"Let me devise a secret plan for you."
Zhāo Jiǎn said:
"What is it?"
"Western Zhōu deeply hates Eastern Zhōu.
It has long wanted Eastern Zhōu to fall out with Chǔ.
Western Zhōu will certainly have an assassin kill you,
and then declare it was Eastern Zhōu,
to win over the king through Western Zhōu."
Zhāo Jiǎn said:
"Good.
But I also fear that Eastern Zhōu will assassinate me
and then blame Western Zhōu to Chǔ to轻视 it."
He quickly made peace with Eastern Zhōu.
The Yán clan committed treason,
and Yáng Shù was involved.
Passing through Zhōu,
the Lord of Zhōu detained him for fourteen days,
then sent him off in a carriage with a team of four horses.
Hán sent someone to reprimand Zhōu,
and the Lord of Zhōu was troubled by it.
A visitor said to the Lord of Zhōu:
"Tell him directly:
'I knew the Yán clan committed treason,
and that Yáng Shù was involved,
so I detained him for fourteen days to await orders.
A small state is insufficient to harbor traitors,
and your envoy did not arrive,
so I sent him away.'"
Lord Xuē used Qí to attack Chǔ for Hán and Wèi,
and also attacked Qín with Hán and Wèi,
borrowing troops and provisions from Western Zhōu.
Hán Qìng, on behalf of Western Zhōu, said to Lord Xuē:
"You used Qí to attack Chǔ for Hán and Wèi,
and after nine years took the area north of Wǎn and Yè to strengthen Hán and Wèi.
Now you attack Qín to further benefit them.
Hán and Wèi have no worries from Chǔ in the south,
and no threats from Qín in the west.
Then their territory will expand and their power increase,
and Qí will certainly be轻视.
For the root and branches alternate in prosperity,
and emptiness and fullness have their times.
I secretly fear for you."
You would do better to have our state secretly ally with Qin while you refrain from attacking,
and also do not borrow troops or beg for provisions.
You approach Hángǔ Pass but do not attack,
and have our state inform the King of Qin of your intentions, saying:
'Lord Xuē will certainly defeat Qin to strengthen Hán and Wèi.
The reason he advances his troops
is to make Your Majesty order Chǔ to cede its eastern territories to Qí.'
The King of Qin will release the King of Chǔ to make peace.
If you have our state show loyalty to Qin in this manner,
Qin will avoid being defeated,
and will use Chǔ's eastern territories to extricate itself,
so it will certainly desire this.
Once the King of Chǔ is released,
he will certainly be grateful to Qí.
Qí will obtain the eastern territories and grow even stronger,
and the Xuē family will be free from trouble for generations.
Qin will not be greatly weakened,
and situated west of the Three Jìn,
the Three Jìn will certainly value Qí."
Lord Xuē said:
"Excellent."
Thereupon, he ordered Hán Qìng to enter Qin,
and made the three states cease attacking Qin,
and did not borrow troops or beg for provisions from Western Zhōu.
Qin attacked Wèi's general Mǐ Wǔ's army at Yīquē,
and advanced its troops to attack Zhōu.
Speaking to Lǐ Duì on behalf of Zhōu Zuì,
"You would do better to prevent Qin from attacking Zhōu.
The best strategy for Zhào
is to make Qin and Wèi fight again.
Now if Qin attacks Zhōu and captures it,
then its forces will certainly suffer many casualties.
If Qin wishes to wait until it captures Zhōu,
it will certainly not attack Wèi;
if Qin attacks Zhōu but fails to capture it,
having previously exhausted itself defeating Wèi,
and later failing to capture Zhōu,
it will also certainly not attack Wèi.
Now if you prevent it,
and Qin has not yet made peace with Wèi,
and with the full might of Zhào ordering it to stop,
it will certainly not dare to disobey.
This way, you will repel Qin and stabilize Zhōu.
Once Qin leaves Zhōu,
it will certainly attack Wèi again.
Wèi will be unable to withstand it,
and will certainly seek peace through you,
then your importance will increase.
If Wèi does not seek peace,
but urgently resists,
then you will have preserved Zhōu and made Qin and Wèi fight.
All importance will then lie with Zhào."
Qin ordered Chūlǐ Jí to enter Zhōu with a hundred chariots.
The Lord of Zhōu welcomed him with troops,
showing great respect.
The King of Chǔ was angry,
and reproached Zhōu,
for honoring the Qin guest.
Yóu Téng said to the King of Chǔ:
"Long ago, Zhì Bó wished to attack Qiúyóu.
He presented them with a large bell,
transporting it on a broad cart,
and then followed with troops.
Qiúyóu was ultimately destroyed,
because it was unprepared.
When Duke Huán attacked Cài,
he claimed he was attacking Chǔ,
but in fact he was surprising Cài.
Now Qin
is a state of tigers and wolves,
with the intention of devouring Zhōu.
Sending Chūlǐ Jí into Zhōu with a hundred chariots,
the Lord of Zhōu fears this,
and is warned by the examples of Cài and Qiúyóu.
Therefore, he placed long weapons in front,
and strong crossbows behind,
calling it 'guarding Jí,'
but in reality imprisoning him.
How could the Lord of Zhōu not love his state?
He fears that one day his state will perish,
and worries for Your Majesty."
The King of Chǔ was then pleased.
During the Yōngshì campaign,
Hán demanded armor and grain from Zhōu.
The Lord of Zhōu was troubled by this,
and told Sū Dài.
Sū Dài said:
"Why worry?
I can make Hán not demand armor and grain from Zhōu,
and also obtain Gāodū for you."
The Lord of Zhōu was greatly pleased and said:
"If you can do this,
I will entrust the state to you."
Sū Dài then went to see the Hán Chancellor Gōng Zhōng and said:
"Have you not heard of Chǔ's plan?
Zhāo Yìng said to the King of Chǔ:
'The Hán clan is exhausted from war,
its granaries are empty,
and it has nothing to defend the city.
If we attack them while they are starving,
we will certainly capture it within a month.'
Now they have besieged Yōngshì for five months and cannot capture it,
which shows Chǔ's weakness.
The King of Chǔ initially did not believe Zhāo Yìng's plan,
but now you are demanding armor and grain from Zhōu,
which announces Chǔ's weakness.
When Zhāo Yìng hears of this,
he will certainly urge the King of Chǔ to increase troops to defend Yōngshì,
and Yōngshì will certainly be captured."
Gōng Zhōng said:
"Good.
But my envoy has already been sent."
Sū Dài said:
"Why not give Gāodū to Zhōu?"
Gōng Zhōng angrily said:
"I have not demanded armor and grain from Zhōu,
which is already more than enough.
Why should I give Gāodū?"
Sū Dài said:
"If you give them Gāodū,
then Zhōu will certainly turn and join Hán.
When Qin hears of this, it will certainly be greatly angered,
and will burn Zhōu's credentials,
cutting off diplomatic relations.
This way, you will obtain a whole Zhōu in exchange for a ruined Gāodū.
Why not give it?"
Gōng Zhōng said:
"Good."
He did not demand armor and grain from Zhōu and instead gave them Gāodū.
Chǔ ultimately failed to capture Yōngshì and withdrew.
The Lord of Zhōu went to Qin.
Someone said to Zhōu Zuì:
"It would be better to praise the King of Qin's filial piety,
and then offer Yìng as a fief for the Queen Dowager.
The King of Qin and the Queen Dowager will certainly be pleased,
and then you will have Qin's support.
If relations are good,
the Lord of Zhōu will certainly consider it your achievement;
if relations turn sour,
the one who urged the Lord of Zhōu to enter Qin
will certainly be blamed."
Sū Lì said to the Lord of Zhōu:
"The one who defeated Hán and Wèi,
killed Wǔ,
attacked Zhào,
and captured Lìn, Líshí, and Qí,
was all Bái Qǐ.
He is skilled in employing troops,
and also has the Mandate of Heaven.
Now if he attacks Liáng,
Liáng will certainly be destroyed,
and if it is destroyed, Zhōu will be in danger.
You would do better to stop him.
Say to Bái Qǐ:
'In Chǔ, there was a man named Yǎng Yóujī,
skilled in archery.
He could shoot at willow leaves from a hundred paces away,
hitting them a hundred times out of a hundred.
Everyone around him said he was excellent.
One man passed by and said,
"You are skilled at shooting,
and can be taught archery."
Yǎng Yóujī said,
"Everyone says I am skilled,
but you say I can be taught archery.
Why don't you shoot in my place?"
The man said,
"I cannot teach you how to support the left and bend the right.
But shooting at willow leaves,
hitting a hundred times out of a hundred,
and not knowing when to stop and rest—
after a while, when your strength is exhausted,
your bow will waver and your arrow will curve,
and with one shot that misses,
all your previous achievements will be lost."
Now you have defeated Hán and Wèi,
killed Wǔ,
and attacked Zhào in the north,
capturing Lìn, Líshí, and Qí—
all this is your doing.
Your achievements are many.
Now you are leading Qin's troops out of the passes,
passing through the two Zhōu,
trampling Hán to attack Liáng.
If you attack once and fail,
all your previous achievements will be wiped out.
You would do better to claim illness and not go out.'"
Chǔ troops are south of the mountain,
and Wú Dé will vent the King of Chǔ's anger on Zhōu.
Someone said to the Lord of Zhōu:
"It would be better to have the Crown Prince lead the army to properly welcome Wú Dé at the border,
while you personally welcome him in the suburbs,
so that all under heaven will know that you honor Wú Dé."
Because it was leaked to Chǔ,
it was said:
'The vessel by which the Zhōu ruler serves Wú Dé,
must be named "Plot Against Chǔ."'
The king will certainly seek it,
and Wú Dé will have nothing to present,
so the king will certainly punish him."
Chǔ requested passage between the two Zhōu states,
in order to approach Hán and Wèi,
and the Zhōu ruler was troubled by this.
Sū Qín said to the Zhōu ruler:
"Clear the road and connect it to the river,
and Hán and Wèi will certainly resent it.
Qí and Qín, fearing that Chǔ would seize the Nine Tripods,
will certainly rescue Hán and Wèi and attack Chǔ.
If Chǔ cannot defend beyond Fāngchéng,
how could it secure passage between the two Zhōu states?
If the four states do not resent it,
even if you, my lord, do not wish to grant it,
Chǔ will certainly take it by force."
Sīkòu Bù spoke to the Zhōu ruler on behalf of Zhōu Zuì:
"My lord sent someone to tell the king of Qí that Zhōu Zuì refused to become crown prince;
I consider this unwise for you, my lord.
Hányě Shì bought a fine sword for the Grand Duke of Qí,
but the duke did not recognize its quality,
returned the sword, and demanded his money back.
A Yuè man offered a thousand pieces of gold to buy it,
but he broke it and refused to sell.
When about to die,
he instructed his son, saying:
'You must not keep knowledge to yourself alone.'
Now, my lord, having Zhōu Zuì made crown prince,
is a covenant known only to you,
and no one in the world will believe it.
I fear the king of Qí will actually establish Guǒ for you, my lord,
and then yield to Zhōu Zuì,
in order to shift the blame to Qí.
You, my lord, are full of schemes,
and Zhōu Zuì is full of deceit;
why does my lord not buy trustworthiness?
In terms of support and care, none is more beloved than Zhōu Zuì,
so let the world see it."
Qín summoned the Zhōu ruler,
and the Zhōu ruler found it difficult to go.
Someone spoke to the king of Wèi on behalf of the Zhōu ruler:
"Qín has summoned the Zhōu ruler,
intending to use him to attack Wèi's Nányáng.
Why does Your Majesty not make a show of force south of the river?
When the Zhōu ruler hears of this,
he will use it as an excuse to Qín and not go.
If the Zhōu ruler does not enter Qín,
Qín will certainly not dare to cross the river and attack Nányáng."
Wǔ was defeated at Yīquē,
and the Zhōu ruler went to Wèi to seek aid,
but the king of Wèi excused himself on account of the emergency in Shàngdǎng.
The Zhōu ruler returned,
and upon seeing the royal park of Liáng, he took delight in it.
Qímǔ Huī said to the Zhōu ruler:
"The Wēn park is no less than this,
and moreover, it is closer.
I can obtain it for you, my lord."
He went to see the king of Wèi,
and the king said:
"Does the Zhōu ruler resent me?"
He replied:
"He does not resent you.
Moreover, whom would he resent?
I am concerned for Your Majesty.
The Zhōu ruler
is a master strategist.
He has set up his state to defend against Qín for Your Majesty,
yet Your Majesty has no defense for him.
I foresee that he will certainly use his state to serve Qín;
if Qín mobilizes all its troops beyond the passes,
together with Zhōu's forces, to attack Nányáng,
then both Shàngdǎng regions will be cut off."
The king of Wèi said:
"What, then, is to be done?"
Qímǔ Huī said:
"The Zhōu ruler's disposition is not without petty gain,
and he serves Qín yet loves petty gain.
If Your Majesty now promises thirty thousand garrison troops and the Wēn park,
the Zhōu ruler will be able to justify himself to his kinsmen and the common people,
and, delighting in the benefit of the Wēn park,
he will certainly not ally with Qín.
I have heard that the profit from the Wēn park
is eighty pieces of gold per year.
If the Zhōu ruler obtains the Wēn park,
what he will offer in service to Your Majesty
will be one hundred and twenty pieces of gold per year,
so Shàngdǎng will be spared trouble and gain forty pieces of gold."
The king of Wèi then sent Mèng Mǎo to deliver the Wēn park to the Zhōu ruler and promised him the garrison troops.
Hán and Wèi exchanged territory,
and Western Zhōu was disadvantaged.
Fán Yú said to the king of Chǔ:
"Zhōu is certainly doomed.
Hán and Wèi's exchange of territory—
Hán gains two counties,
Wèi loses two counties.
The reason they are doing this
is to completely encircle the two Zhōu states,
which is worth more than two counties,
for the Nine Tripods are there.
Moreover, if Wèi possesses Nányáng, the territory of Zhèng, Sānchuān, and encircles the two Zhōu states,
then the area beyond Chǔ's Fāngchéng will be in danger;
if Hán annexes both Shàngdǎng regions and approaches Zhào,
then Zhào's territory above Yángcháng will be in danger.
Therefore, if the exchange is completed,
both Chǔ and Zhào will be weakened."
The king of Chǔ became alarmed,
and, through Zhào, stopped the exchange.
Qín wished to attack Zhōu,
and Zhōu Zuì said to the king of Qín:
"For the sake of Your Majesty's state's plans,
do not attack Zhōu.
Attacking Zhōu truly does not benefit the state,
yet the reputation will frighten the world.
If the world is frightened by Qín's reputation,
they will certainly ally in the east with Qí.
If troops are exhausted at Zhōu,
and the world unites with Qí,
then Qín will be isolated and unable to rule as king.
This is because the world wishes to exhaust Qín,
hence they urge Your Majesty to attack Zhōu.
If Qín and the world are both exhausted,
then orders will not be enforced in Zhōu."
Gōng Tuō said to the Zhōu ruler:
"Wǎn relied on Qín and despised Jìn,
and when Qín suffered famine, Wǎn perished.
Zhèng relied on Wèi and despised Hán,
and when Wèi attacked Cài, Zhèng perished.
Zhū and Jǔ perished because of Qí,
Chén and Cài perished because of Chǔ.
These all relied on distant allies and despised nearby enemies.
Now, my lord, you rely on Hán and Wèi and despise Qín;
I fear the state will suffer harm.
My lord should rather have Zhōu Zuì secretly ally with Zhào to prepare against Qín;
then you will not be destroyed."
Someone said to the king of Qí:
"Why does Your Majesty not grant territory to Zhōu Zuì to make him crown prince?"
The king of Qí ordered Sīmǎ Hàn to use bribes to advance Zhōu Zuì in Zhōu.
Zuǒ Shàng said to Sīmǎ Hàn:
"If Zhōu does not comply,
your wisdom will be thwarted and your ties with Zhōu severed.
You should rather say to the Zhōu ruler:
'What do you wish to arrange?
Have someone secretly inform Hàn,
and Hàn will request that the king advance him with territory.'"
Zuǒ Shàng thereby gained employment.
When the three states attacked Qín and returned,
Western Zhōu feared that Wèi would borrow its route.
Someone spoke to the king of Wèi on behalf of Western Zhōu:
"Chǔ and Sòng are displeased with Qín's favor to the three states;
they will attack Your Majesty's stores to benefit Qín."
The king of Wèi became afraid,
and ordered the army to set up camp and quickly march east.
Wǔ was defeated,
and Zhōu sent Zhōu Zú to Qín.
Someone said to Zhōu Zú:
"Why not say to the Zhōu ruler:
'If I go to Qín,
relations between Qín and Zhōu will certainly deteriorate.
Among your lordship's ministers,
there is one who is valued by Qín and wishes to become chancellor;
he will slander me to Qín,
and I will be unable to carry out my mission.
I wish to be dismissed and then go.
My lord should then make him chancellor;
once he obtains the chancellorship,
he will not cause Qín to bear ill will toward Zhōu.'
If my lord values Qín,
he will send the chancellor to go;
if I go and am dismissed,
it will show contempt for Qín,
and you, sir, will certainly not be spared.
If you speak thus and act accordingly,
relations with Qín will improve,
and it will be your accomplishment;
if relations with Qín deteriorate,
it will not be good for you, sir, and you will be punished."
Wèi Yāng fled Wèi and entered Qín,
and Duke Xiào made him chancellor,
enfeoffing him in Shāng,
with the title Lord Shāng.
Lord Shāng governed Qín,
laws and decrees were thoroughly implemented,
fair and without partiality,
punishing without sparing the powerful,
rewarding without favoring the close.
The law applied even to the crown prince,
and his tutor was tattooed and had his nose cut off.
After a year,
no one would pick up lost items on the road,
and the people did not take what was not theirs.
The military became greatly strengthened,
and the feudal lords feared it.
However, it was harsh and lacking in kindness,
merely subduing them by force.
Duke Xiào implemented it for eight years,
and when he fell ill and was near death,
he wanted to pass the throne to Lord Shāng,
but Lord Shāng declined and did not accept.
After Duke Xiào died,
King Huì succeeded him.
Upon taking office,
not long after,
Lord Shāng requested to return home.
Someone advised King Huì, saying:
"When ministers hold too much power, the state is endangered;
when those close to you are too intimate, your person is endangered.
Now, even the women and children of Qín speak of Lord Shāng's laws,
and none speak of Your Majesty's laws.
This means Lord Shāng has become the ruler,
and Your Majesty has become the subject.
Moreover, Lord Shāng
is indeed Your Majesty's enemy.
I hope Your Majesty will consider this."
When Lord Shāng returned,
King Huì had him torn apart by chariots,
and the people of Qín showed no pity.
Sū Qín first advocated the Horizontal Alliance
and persuaded King Huì of Qín, saying:
"Your Majesty's state
has the benefits of Bā, Shǔ, and Hànzhōng to the west,
the utility of the Hú and Mò tribes and Dài horses to the north,
the natural barriers of Wūshān and Qiánzhōng to the south,
and the strongholds of Yáo and Hán to the east.
The fields are fertile and beautiful,
the people are prosperous and wealthy,
there are ten thousand war chariots,
a million fierce warriors,
a thousand lǐ of fertile plains,
abundant reserves,
and a strategically advantageous terrain.
This is what is called the 'Heavenly Storehouse,'
a powerful state under heaven.
With Your Majesty's wisdom,
the multitude of scholars and people,
the use of chariots and cavalry,
and the teachings of military strategy,
you can annex the feudal lords,
devour the world,
proclaim yourself emperor, and govern.
I hope Your Majesty will give it some thought,
and allow me to present the results."
The King of Qín said:
"I have heard that
those whose feathers are not full cannot fly high,
those whose laws are not established cannot punish,
those whose virtue is not profound cannot command the people,
and those whose governance is not smooth cannot trouble their ministers.
Now, you, sir, have solemnly traveled a thousand lǐ
to instruct me at court,
but I would prefer to discuss this another day."
Sū Qín said:
"I had suspected that Your Majesty would not be able to employ this.
In ancient times, Shénnóng attacked Bǔsuì,
Huángdì attacked Zhuōlù and captured Chīyóu,
Yáo attacked Huāndōu,
Shùn attacked Sānmiáo,
Yǔ attacked Gònggōng,
Tāng attacked the Xià dynasty,
King Wén attacked Chóng,
King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
and Duke Huán of Qí relied on warfare to become hegemon of the world.
From this perspective,
how can there be those who do not wage war?
In ancient times, envoys' chariots raced with hubs clashing,
and alliances were formed through words,
uniting the world as one;
with vertical and horizontal alliances,
weapons were never stored away;
scholars competed in rhetoric, and the
feudal lords were confused and misled;
countless troubles arose,
impossible to fully manage;
laws and regulations were established,
but the people became deceitful;
documents and policies were dense and muddled,
and the common people were left wanting;
rulers and subjects worried together,
and the people had nothing to rely on;
clear words and principles were proclaimed,
yet warfare only increased;
eloquent speech and grand attire
did not cease attacks and battles;
excessive rhetoric and ornate language
left the world ungoverned;
tongues grew weary and ears deaf,
yet no success was seen;
righteous conduct and sworn trust
did not bring the world closer.
Therefore,
they abandoned culture and embraced force,
generously nurturing warriors willing to die,
mending armor and sharpening weapons,
to achieve victory on the battlefield.
To gain benefits by merely staying put,
or to expand territory by sitting idly—
even the ancient Five Emperors, Three Kings, and Five Hegemons,
wise rulers and virtuous lords,
often wished to achieve this by sitting still,
but circumstances did not allow it,
so they continued with war.
In open terrain, two armies would attack each other,
in close quarters, they would clash with halberds and spears,
and only then could great achievements be made.
Thus, victory is won abroad through force,
and righteousness is strengthened at home;
authority is established above,
and the people submit below.
Now, to unite the world,
overwhelm the ten thousand chariots,
subdue enemy states,
control the realm within the seas,
treat the common people as one's children,
and make the feudal lords submit—
without force, it is impossible!
Today's successors to the throne
neglect the ultimate way,
are confused by teachings,
disordered in governance,
bewildered by words,
misled by speech,
sunk in argument,
and drowned in rhetoric.
Judging from this,
Your Majesty certainly cannot carry it out."
Sū Qín submitted his persuasion to the King of Qín ten times, but his advice was not heeded.
His sable fur coat wore out,
his hundred catties of gold were exhausted,
his resources were depleted,
and he left Qín to return home.
He bound his legs with cloth and wore straw sandals,
carrying his books on his back and a bag on his shoulder,
his appearance haggard,
his face dark and sallow,
with a look of dejection.
When he returned home,
his wife did not leave her loom,
his sister-in-law did not cook for him,
and his parents did not speak to him.
Sū Qín sighed and said:
"My wife does not regard me as her husband,
my sister-in-law does not regard me as her brother-in-law,
and my parents do not regard me as their son.
This is all Qín's fault."
So that night, he took out his books,
laid out several dozen boxes,
and found the strategies of *The Grand Duke's Secret Talisman*,
bent over and recited them,
selecting and refining them to form his theories.
When he grew drowsy while reading,
he would take an awl and stab his thigh,
until blood flowed down to his feet.
He said:
"How could there be one who persuades a ruler
and cannot obtain his gold, jade, brocade, and embroidery,
or attain the high rank of minister or chancellor?"
After a year, his theories were perfected,
and he said:
"Now I can truly persuade the rulers of this age!"
Then he went to the Yānwūjí Gate,
met and persuaded the King of Zhào beneath a magnificent hall,
and talked with him, clapping his hands.
The King of Zhào was greatly pleased,
and enfeoffed him as Lord Wǔ'ān.
He received the seal of chancellor,
a hundred armored chariots,
a thousand bolts of brocade,
a hundred pairs of white jade discs,
ten thousand yì of gold,
to follow behind him,
forming vertical alliances to break up horizontal ones,
and to suppress powerful Qín.
Thus, when Sū Qín served as prime minister of Zhào,
the passes were closed and communication ceased.
At that time,
with the vastness of all under heaven,
the multitude of the myriad people,
the awe of kings and marquises,
and the authority of strategic ministers,
all sought to determine policy through Sū Qín's strategies.
Not a peck of grain was expended,
not a single soldier was troubled,
not a single officer was engaged in battle,
not a single bowstring was snapped,
not a single arrow was broken,
yet the feudal lords became close to one another,
more intimate than brothers.
When a worthy man is present, all under heaven submit;
when one man is employed, all under heaven follow.
Therefore it is said:
Rely on governance,
not on valor;
rely on deliberations within the court and temple,
not on efforts beyond the four borders.
At the peak of Sū Qín's influence,
tens of thousands of yi of gold were at his disposal,
carriages with linked teams of horses turned their wheels,
shining brilliantly along the roads.
The states east of the mountains
submitted as if blown by the wind,
making Zhào greatly esteemed.
Moreover, Sū Qín was merely a scholar from a poor alley, with a dug-out door, mulberry-wood door, and bent-wood hinge.
Yet, leaning on his carriage rail and gripping the reins,
he traversed all under heaven horizontally,
persuading the kings of the feudal lords at their courts,
silencing the mouths of those to their left and right,
with none in all under heaven able to oppose him.
When he was about to persuade the King of Chǔ,
passing through Luòyáng on the way,
his parents, hearing of it,
cleaned the house and swept the road,
set out music and prepared drinks,
and went thirty li out to the suburbs to welcome him.
His wife watched him sidelong,
listening with tilted ear;
his sister-in-law crawled like a snake, prostrating herself,
bowing four times, kneeling of her own accord, and apologizing.
Sū Qín said:
"Sister-in-law,
why were you so arrogant before and so humble now?"
The sister-in-law said:
"Because Jìzǐ's position is now exalted
and he possesses much gold."
Sū Qín said:
"Alas!
In poverty, even one's parents do not treat one as a son;
in wealth and honor, even relatives are fearful.
In human life in this world,
power, position, wealth, and honor—
how can they be neglected!"
King Huì of Qín said to Hánquánzǐ:
"Sū Qín deceived me,
wishing to use the wisdom of one man
to sway the lords east of the mountains back and forth,
forming an alliance to deceive Qín.
Zhào indeed relied on its multitude,
thus first sending Sū Qín with silks and silken fabrics to make pacts with the feudal lords.
That the feudal lords cannot be unified
is as clear as tethered chickens that cannot all roost together.
I am indignant,
holding anger for many days.
I wish to send Wǔ'ānzǐ Qǐ to go and convey my intent."
Hánquánzǐ said:
"That will not do.
For attacking cities and destroying towns,
send Wǔ'ānzǐ.
For benefiting our state and dealing with the feudal lords,
send the guest minister Zhāng Yí."
King Huì of Qín said:
"I respectfully accept your command."
Líng Xiàng said to the King of Qín:
"Xiàng wished to use Qí to serve Your Majesty,
by having it attack Sòng.
If Sòng is destroyed,
the state of Jìn will be endangered,
and Ānyì will be yours, O King.
Yān and Zhào, detesting the alliance of Qí and Qín,
will surely cede territory to ally with Your Majesty.
Qí will then surely esteem Your Majesty highly.
Thus, Xiàng's plan to attack Sòng
is also to intimidate Qí and increase Your Majesty's importance.
Why, O King, should you dislike Xiàng's plan to attack Sòng?
Xiàng, considering Your Majesty's wisdom as foreknowing,
therefore did not speak of it earlier."
Zhāng Yí persuaded the King of Qín, saying:
"Your servant has heard that
to speak without knowing is unwise,
and to know yet not speak is disloyal.
As a subject, disloyalty deserves death;
speaking without due consideration also deserves death.
Nevertheless,
your servant wishes to fully relate all he has heard,
and let Your Majesty judge his crime.
Your servant has heard that
all under heaven, with Yān in the north and Wèi in the south,
linking Chǔ and securing Qí,
gathering the remnant Hán to complete the alliance,
intend to face southwest and make trouble for Qín.
Your servant privately laughs at this.
There are three ways to perish in the world,
and all under heaven have obtained them—
is this not what is meant?
Your servant has heard it said:
'Those who attack order with disorder perish;
those who attack righteousness with wickedness perish;
those who attack compliance with defiance perish.'
Now, the treasuries and storehouses of all under heaven are not full,
granaries are empty.
Mobilizing all their officers and people,
deploying armies numbering in the hundreds of thousands or millions,
with naked blades before them
and axes and execution blocks behind them,
yet they all flee and run away,
unable to face death.
To blame the common people for not being able to face death
is because their superiors cannot enforce killing.
When rewards are promised, they are not given;
when punishments are declared, they are not carried out.
When rewards and punishments are not implemented,
the people do not face death.
Now, when Qín issues commands and implements rewards and punishments,
whether to attack or not attack depends on the circumstances.
Our men emerge from the bosoms of their parents,
having never in their lives seen an enemy,
yet upon hearing of battle, they stamp their feet, bare their bodies,
confront naked blades,
tread on hot coals,
and those resolved to die in the front ranks are all like this.
Now, to resolve to die and to resolve to live are not the same,
yet the people do this because they value fervor.
One can overcome ten,
ten can overcome a hundred,
a hundred can overcome a thousand,
a thousand can overcome ten thousand,
and ten thousand can overcome all under heaven.
Now, as for Qín's territorial shape,
cutting the long and supplementing the short,
it extends several thousand li square,
with renowned armies numbering in the millions.
Qín's commands, rewards, and punishments,
and the advantages and disadvantages of its terrain,
are unmatched in all under heaven.
With this to confront all under heaven,
all under heaven are insufficient to be annexed and possessed.
Thus it is known that when Qín fights, it has never not been victorious;
when it attacks, it has never not taken;
what it confronts, it has never not shattered.
It has opened up territory for several thousand li—
this is a very great achievement.
Yet armor and weapons are blunted,
officers and people are weary,
stores and accumulations are exhausted,
fields lie fallow,
granaries are empty,
the feudal lords of the four neighboring regions do not submit,
and the name of Hegemon and King is not achieved.
This is for no other reason
than that your strategic ministers have not fully devoted their loyalty.
Your servant dares to speak of the past.
In the past, Qí in the south crushed Chǔ,
in the center crushed Sòng,
in the west subdued Qín,
in the north crushed Yān,
and in the center commanded the rulers of Hán and Wèi.
Its territory was vast and its soldiers strong;
it was victorious in battle and successful in attack.
Its decrees commanded all under heaven.
The clear Jì River and the turbid Huáng Hé
were sufficient to serve as its boundaries;
the Long Wall and the great fortifications
were sufficient to serve as its barriers.
Qí
was a state that fought five battles;
losing one battle, it lost Qí.
Thus, from this perspective,
warfare determines the survival or destruction of a state of ten thousand chariots.
Moreover, I have heard it said:
'Uproot the tree and dig out the roots;
do not dwell near calamity,
and calamity will not exist.'
When Qín fought against the people of Jīng,
it crushed Jīng,
captured Yǐng,
and seized Dòngtíng, Wǔdū, and Jiāngnán.
The king of Jīng fled in exile,
and hid east in Chén.
At that time,
had we followed Jīng with troops,
Jīng could have been conquered.
Conquering Jīng,
its people would have been ample for plunder,
its land ample for profit.
To the east, it would have strengthened Qí and Yān,
and in the central regions, overawed the Three Jìn.
Then, with this one move, the name of Hegemon-King could have been achieved,
and the neighboring feudal lords could have been made to pay court.
Yet your strategists did not act,
led the army back,
and made peace with Jīng.
Now the people of Jīng have gathered their ruined state,
assembled their scattered people,
raised their altars of soil and grain,
and established their ancestral temples,
ordering them to lead the world westward to oppose Qín.
This, then, was the first instance of losing the way to become Hegemon-King.
The world united in purpose
and stationed troops at Huàxià,
but Your Majesty defeated them by stratagem.
The troops reached the outer walls of Liáng,
besieged Liáng for several weeks,
and Liáng could have been taken.
Taking Liáng,
then Wèi could have been conquered.
Conquering Wèi,
then the resolve of Jīng and Zhào would have been severed.
With the resolve of Jīng and Zhào severed,
Zhào would have been endangered.
With Zhào endangered, Jīng would have been isolated.
To the east, it would have strengthened Qí and Yān,
and in the central regions, overawed the Three Jìn.
Then, with this one move, the name of Hegemon-King could have been achieved,
and the neighboring feudal lords could have been made to pay court.
Yet your strategists did not act,
led the army back,
and made peace with the house of Wèi,
allowing the house of Wèi to gather its ruined state,
assemble its scattered people,
raise its altars of soil and grain,
and establish its ancestral temples.
This, then, was the second instance of losing the way to become Hegemon-King.
Previously, when the Marquis of Ráng governed Qín,
he used the troops of one state
but sought to achieve the merit of two states.
Thus, the troops were constantly exposed to hardship abroad,
while officers and people grew weary and sick at home.
The name of Hegemon-King was not achieved.
This, then, was the third instance of losing the way to become Hegemon-King.
The house of Zhào
is a central state,
a place where mixed peoples dwell.
Its people are fickle and difficult to employ,
its commands and orders are not well-regulated,
its rewards and punishments are not trustworthy,
its terrain is not advantageous,
and its rulers cannot fully utilize the strength of its people.
It inherently possesses the form of a doomed state.
Yet, not concerned for its populace,
it mustered all its officers and people
and stationed troops below Chángpíng,
to contend for Hán's Shàngdǎng.
Your Majesty defeated them by stratagem,
and captured Wǔ'ān.
At that time,
the high and low of the house of Zhào were not close,
the noble and base did not trust each other.
Thus, Hándān could not be defended.
Had we taken Hándān,
secured Héjiān,
led the army away,
marched west to attack Xiūwǔ,
crossed Yángcháng,
and subdued Dài and Shàngdǎng—
Dài's thirty-six counties,
Shàngdǎng's seventeen counties—
without using a single suit of armor,
without troubling a single commoner,
all would have become Qín's possession.
Dài and Shàngdǎng
would have become Qín's without a fight,
Dōngyáng and Héwài would have turned back to Qí without a fight,
and the area north of Zhōnghūchí would have become Yān's without a fight.
Thus, conquering Zhào would have meant Hán's inevitable demise.
With Hán gone, Jīng and Wèi could not stand independently.
With Jīng and Wèi unable to stand independently,
then with one move we could have destroyed Hán,
undermined Wèi,
and controlled Jīng,
weakening Qí and Yān in the east,
breaching the mouth of Báimǎ,
to flood the house of Wèi.
With one move, the Three Jìn would have perished,
and the Vertical Alliance would have been defeated.
Your Majesty could have simply waited with folded hands,
the whole world would have followed in submission,
and the name of Hegemon-King could have been achieved.
Yet your strategists did not act,
led the army back,
and made peace with the house of Zhào.
With Your Majesty's wisdom,
and the strength of Qín's troops,
the enterprise of Hegemon-King,
and the exalted position that should have been attained—
instead, you were deceived by a doomed state.
This is the ineptitude of your strategists.
Moreover, Zhào, which should have perished, did not perish;
Qín, which should have become Hegemon, did not become Hegemon.
The world thus measured Qín's strategists—first instance.
Then you again mustered all troops to attack Hándān,
but could not take it.
Discarding armor and weapons in anger,
trembling, you retreated.
The world thus measured Qín's strength—second instance.
The army then withdrew,
and assembled at Lǐxià.
Your Majesty again concentrated forces to engage them in battle,
but could not achieve a decisive victory.
Again, both sides wearily retreated.
The world thus measured Qín's strength—third instance.
Internally, they gauge our strategists;
externally, they probe our military strength.
From this perspective,
I believe that for the world to form a Vertical Alliance
is hardly difficult.
Internally, our armor and weapons are blunted,
officers and people are weary,
stores are depleted,
fields lie fallow,
granaries are empty;
externally, the world's united resolve is very firm.
I hope Your Majesty will give this due consideration.
Moreover, I have heard it said:
'Tremble with fear,
and be cautious day by day.
If you are cautious in your way,
you can possess the world.'
How do we know this is so?
In the past, when Zhòu was Son of Heaven,
he led the world's million armored troops,
drinking on the left from the Qígǔ,
and on the right from the Huánshuǐ,
until the Qí River dried up and the Huán River ceased to flow,
as he opposed King Wǔ of Zhōu.
King Wǔ led three thousand plain-armored troops,
fought for one day,
shattered Zhòu's state,
captured his person,
seized his land,
and possessed his people,
and none in the world did not grieve.
Zhì Bó led the masses of three states
to attack Lord Xiāng of Zhào at Jìnyáng,
breached the waters to flood it.
After three years,
the city was about to fall.
Lord Xiāng consulted the tortoise shell,
counted the stalks and interpreted the omens,
to see advantage and harm,
and which state could be turned.
He then sent Zhāng Mèngtán,
who secretly went forth,
overturned Zhì Bó's covenant,
won over the masses of two states,
attacked Zhì Bó's state,
captured his person,
and thus achieved Lord Xiāng's merit.
Now the land of Qín, cutting long and supplementing short,
extends several thousand lǐ square,
with renowned troops numbering in the millions.
Qín's commands and orders, rewards and punishments,
and the advantages and disadvantages of its terrain,
are unmatched in the world.
With this to confront the world,
the world can be annexed and possessed.
I risk death hoping to see Your Majesty,
to speak on the means to crush the world's Vertical Alliance,
conquer Zhào and destroy Hán,
subjugate Jīng and Wèi,
befriend Qí and Yān,
to achieve the name of Hegemon-King,
and the way to make the neighboring feudal lords pay court.
Your Majesty, please hear my proposal.
If, with one move, the alliance of the world is not broken,
Zhào not subdued,
Hán not destroyed,
Jīng and Wèi not submitting as vassals,
Qí and Yān not drawing close,
the name of Hegemon-King not achieved,
and the feudal lords of the four borders not coming to court,
then may Your Majesty behead me and parade my corpse through the state,
to serve as a warning to those whose counsel to their lord is disloyal."
Zhāng Yí wanted to borrow Qín troops to rescue Wèi.
Zuǒ Chéng said to Gān Mào:
"Do not give them to him.
If Wèi does not return the Qín troops,
then Master Zhāng will not return to Qín.
If Wèi does return the Qín troops,
and Master Zhāng achieves his ambitions in Wèi,
he will not dare return to Qín.
If Master Zhāng does not leave Qín,
he will certainly hold you in high esteem."
Sīmǎ Cuò and Zhāng Yí debated before King Huì of Qín.
Sīmǎ Cuò wished to attack Shǔ.
Zhāng Yí said:
"It would be better to attack Hán."
The King said:
"I ask to hear your reasoning."
He replied:
"Be friendly with Wèi and treat Chǔ well,
send troops down to Sānchuān,
block the passes of Huányuán and Gōushì,
hold the road at Túnliú,
have Wèi cut off Nányáng,
have Chǔ press upon Nánzhèng,
while Qín attacks Xīnchéng and Yíyáng,
thereby approaching the outskirts of the Two Zhōu,
punishing the Zhōu ruler for his crimes,
and encroaching upon the territories of Chǔ and Wèi.
When Zhōu realizes it cannot save itself,
the Nine Tripods and precious vessels will surely be yielded.
Seize the Nine Tripods,
examine the maps and registers,
hold the Son of Heaven hostage to command the world,
and none in the world will dare disobey.
This is the way of a true king.
Now as for Shǔ,
it is a remote western state,
the leader of the Róng and Dí barbarians.
Exhausting troops and wearying the masses would not suffice to achieve fame,
and gaining its land would not be profitable.
I have heard it said:
'Those who contend for fame do so at court;
those who contend for profit do so in the marketplace.'
Now Sānchuān and the Zhōu house
are the marketplace and court of the world,
yet Your Majesty does not contend there,
but instead contends with the Róng and Dí.
This is far removed from the way of a true king."
Sīmǎ Cuò said:
"Not so.
I have heard that
he who wishes to enrich the state
must strive to broaden its territory;
he who wishes to strengthen the army
must strive to enrich his people;
he who wishes to be king
must strive to broaden his virtue.
When these three resources are complete,
kingship follows.
Now Your Majesty's territory is small and the people poor,
therefore I wish to undertake what is easy.
Now Shǔ
is a remote western state,
the leader of the Róng and Dí,
and it has the turmoil of a Jié or Zhòu.
For Qín to attack it
is like sending a wolf or jackal to chase a flock of sheep.
Taking its land
is sufficient to broaden the state;
obtaining its wealth
repairing weapons without harming the masses,
and they will already be subdued.
Thus, conquering one state,
the world will not consider it tyrannical;
exhausting the profits of the Western Sea,
the feudal lords will not consider it greedy.
Thus, with one move we gain both name and substance,
and furthermore have the name of suppressing tyranny and rectifying disorder.
Now, to attack Hán and seize the Son of Heaven—
seizing the Son of Heaven
is an evil name,
and may not necessarily be profitable.
Furthermore, it bears the name of unrighteousness,
and attacks what the world does not desire—
Dangerous!
I beg to explain the reason:
Zhōu is the ancestral house of the world;
Qí is an ally of Hán and Zhōu.
When Zhōu realizes it will lose the Nine Tripods,
and Hán realizes it will lose Sānchuān,
they will certainly unite the strength and plans of both states,
relying on Qí and Zhào,
and seek a resolution with Chǔ and Wèi.
Giving the tripods to Chǔ,
and territory to Wèi,
Your Majesty would be unable to stop it.
This is what I call 'dangerous'.
It is not as complete as attacking Shǔ."
King Huì said:
"Excellent! I will heed you."
He finally raised troops to attack Shǔ,
captured it in the tenth month,
and thus pacified Shǔ.
The ruler of Shǔ had his title changed to Marquis,
and Chén Zhuāng was made Chancellor of Shǔ.
Once Shǔ was subjugated,
Qín grew increasingly strong, wealthy, and substantial,
and looked down upon the feudal lords.
Zhāng Yí slandered Chūlǐ Jí,
honored him and sent him to Chǔ.
He then had the King of Chǔ
request for him to be made Chancellor in Qín.
Master Zhāng said to the King of Qín:
"I honored Chūlǐ Jí and sent him
intending to foster interstate relations.
Now he is in Chǔ,
and the King of Chǔ requests for him to be made Chancellor in Qín.
I have heard his words:
'Does the King wish to corner Yí in Qín?
I beg to assist the King.'
The King of Chǔ considered this true,
hence he made the request for the chancellorship.
If Your Majesty now truly listens to him,
he will certainly use state affairs to serve the King of Chǔ."
The King of Qín was greatly enraged,
and Chūlǐ Jí fled.
Zhāng Yí wished to give Hànzhōng to Chǔ.
He petitioned the King of Qín, saying:
"Having Hànzhōng
is like a moth. If one plants trees in the wrong place,
people will certainly harm them;
if a household possesses wealth it should not have,
it injures its foundation.
Hànzhōng borders Chǔ to the south, benefiting Chǔ;
it is a burden to the state."
Gān Mào said to the King:
"Those with vast territories
surely have many worries!
If there is a change in the world,
and Your Majesty cedes Hànzhōng to make peace with Chǔ,
Chǔ will certainly turn against the world and ally with Your Majesty.
If Your Majesty now gives Hànzhōng to Chǔ,
then when there is a change in the world,
with what will Your Majesty bargain with Chǔ?"
Chǔ attacked Wèi.
Zhāng Yí said to the King of Qín:
"It would be better to aid Wèi to strengthen it.
If Wèi is victorious in battle,
it will again heed Qín,
and will certainly cede the lands west of the [Yellow] River;
if it is not victorious,
Wèi will be unable to defend itself,
and Your Majesty will certainly seize it."
The King followed Yí's advice,
took ten thousand soldiers from Píshì,
and a hundred chariots,
and gave them to Wèi.
Xī Shǒu defeated King Wēi,
the Wèi troops were exhausted and worn out,
they feared Qín,
and indeed offered the lands west of the [Yellow] River.
Tián Xīn spoke to King Huì of Qín on behalf of Chén Zhěn, saying:
"I fear Your Majesty is like the Lord of Guó.
Now, Duke Xiàn of Jìn wished to attack Guó,
but feared Zhōu Zhī Qiáo remained.
Xún Xī said:
'The Zhōu Shū has a saying,
"A beautiful woman breaks the tongue."'
So he sent him female musicians
to disorder his governance.
Zhōu Zhī Qiáo remonstrated but was not heeded,
and so left.
Thereupon he attacked Guó,
and destroyed it.
He also wished to attack Yú,
but feared Gōng Zhī Qí remained.
Xún Xī said:
'The Zhōu Shū has a saying,
"A beautiful man breaks the old."'
So he sent him a beautiful man,
who taught him to slander Gōng Zhī Qí.
Gōng Zhī Qí remonstrated but was not heeded,
and so fled.
Thus he attacked Yú,
and captured it.
Now Qín considers itself a kingly state,
and the state that can harm a kingly state
is Chǔ.
Chǔ knows that Lord Héng is skilled in using troops,
and in employing troops and Chén Zhěn’s wisdom,
so it flatters Zhāng Yí with five states.
When he comes,
he will certainly malign these two men.
I hope Your Majesty will not listen to him.”
Zhāng Yí indeed came to take leave,
and spoke against Zhěn,
so the king was angry and would not listen.
Zhāng Yí again maligned Chén Zhěn to the King of Qín,
saying:
“Zhěn travels between Chǔ and Qín,
and now Chǔ does not treat Qín well but treats Zhěn well.
This means Zhěn acts for himself and not for the state.
Moreover, Zhěn wishes to leave Qín and go to Chǔ.
Why does Your Majesty not investigate this?”
The king said to Chén Zhěn:
“I hear you wish to leave Qín and go to Chǔ.
Is it true?”
Chén Zhěn said:
“Yes.”
The king said:
“Yí’s words are indeed true.”
Chén Zhěn said:
“It is not only Yí who knows this;
every traveler on the road knows it.
They say:
‘Xiàojǐ loved his parents,
so all under heaven wished to have him as a son;
Wǔ Zǐxū was loyal to his lord,
so all under heaven wished to have him as a minister.
A male or female servant sold within the neighborhood
is a good servant;
a divorced woman married within the village
is a good woman.’
If I am not loyal to my lord,
why would Chǔ consider me loyal?
If one is loyal and yet is cast aside,
if I do not go to Chǔ,
where else should I go?”
The King of Qín said:
“Well said.”
So he was determined to go.
Chén Zhěn left Chǔ and went to Qín.
Zhāng Yí said to the King of Qín:
“Chén Zhěn is Your Majesty’s minister,
yet he often leaks state secrets to Chǔ.
I cannot work with him;
I hope Your Majesty will expel him.
If he goes back to Chǔ again,
I hope Your Majesty will kill him.”
The king said:
“How would Zhěn dare go to Chǔ?”
The king summoned Chén Zhěn and told him:
“I am willing to listen to your words.
Where do you wish to go?
I will prepare a carriage for you.”
He replied:
“Your servant wishes to go to Chǔ.”
The king said:
“Yí said you would go to Chǔ,
and I myself also know you will go to Chǔ.
If you are not going to Chǔ,
then where will you go?”
Zhěn said:
“When I leave,
I must deliberately go to Chǔ,
to comply with Your Majesty and Yí’s plan,
and to prove whether I am going to Chǔ or not.
There was a man of Chǔ who had two wives.
A man flirted with the elder wife,
and she scolded him;
he flirted with the younger wife,
and she consented.
Not long after,
the man with two wives died.
A friend asked the flirtatious man:
‘Will you marry the elder wife
or the younger wife?’
‘I will marry the elder wife.’
The friend said:
‘The elder wife scolded you,
the younger wife consented to you.
Why do you marry the elder wife?’
He said:
‘When she was another man’s wife,
I wished her to consent to me.
Now as my wife,
I wish her to scold others for me.’
Now the King of Chǔ is an enlightened ruler,
and Zhāo Yáng is a worthy minister.
If I, as a minister,
often leak state secrets to the King of Chǔ,
the king certainly will not keep me,
and Zhāo Yáng will not work with me.
This proves whether I am going to Chǔ or not.”
Zhěn left,
and Zhāng Yí entered.
He asked the king:
“Where is Chén Zhěn really going?”
The king said:
“That Zhěn is the most eloquent debater in the world.
He looked intently at me and said:
‘Zhěn must go to Chǔ.’
I had no choice then.
So I asked him:
‘If you must go to Chǔ,
then Yí’s words are indeed true!’
Zhěn said:
‘It is not only Yí’s words;
every traveler on the road knows it.
In the past, Wǔ Zǐxū was loyal to his lord,
so all under heaven wished to have him as a minister;
Xiàojǐ loved his parents,
so all under heaven wished to have him as a son.
Therefore, a male or female servant sold within the neighborhood and taken
is a good servant;
a divorced woman married within the village
is a good woman.
If I am not loyal to Your Majesty,
what would Chǔ want with me?
If one is loyal and yet is cast aside,
if I do not go to Chǔ,
where else should I go?’”
The king thought this reasonable,
and so treated him well.
Qí assisted Chǔ in attacking Qín,
and captured Qūwò.
Afterward,
Qín wished to attack Qí,
but Qí and Chǔ had friendly relations,
so King Huì was troubled.
He said to Zhāng Yí:
“I wish to attack Qí,
but Qí and Chǔ are currently friendly.
Consider this for me—
what should I do?”
Zhāng Yí said:
“Your Majesty should prepare carriages
and gifts for me,
and I will try.”
Zhāng Yí went south to see the King of Chǔ,
and said:
“The one my humble state’s king admires most
is none greater than Your Majesty;
the one I most wish to serve as minister
is also none greater than Your Majesty.
The one my humble state’s king hates most
is also none before the King of Qí;
the one I hate most
is also none greater than the King of Qí.
Now the King of Qí’s crimes
against my humble state’s king are very grave.
My humble state wishes to attack him,
but your great state is friendly with him.
Therefore, my humble state’s king cannot follow your command,
and I cannot serve as your minister.
If Your Majesty can close the passes and sever relations with Qí,
I will ask the King of Qín to present the land of Shāngwū,
six hundred li square.
If so,
Qí will certainly weaken.
If Qí weakens, it will certainly serve Your Majesty.
Then you will weaken Qí in the north,
gain virtue from Qí in the west,
and privately gain the land of Shāngwū for profit.
Thus, with one plan, three benefits will arrive together.”
The King of Chǔ was greatly pleased.
He announced it in the court,
saying:
“I have obtained the fields of Shāngwū, six hundred li square.”
All the ministers who heard it congratulated him.
Chén Zhěn came later
and alone did not congratulate.
The King of Chǔ said:
“I have not troubled a single soldier,
nor injured a single person,
and have obtained the land of Shāngwū, six hundred li square.
I consider myself wise!
All the officials congratulate me;
you alone do not congratulate.
Why?”
Chén Zhěn replied:
“Your servant sees that the land of Shāngwū cannot be obtained,
and disaster will certainly arrive.
Therefore, I dare not rashly congratulate.”
The king said:
“Why?”
He replied:
"The reason why Qin values Your Majesty
is because Your Majesty has Qí as an ally.
Now, before obtaining the land,
if you first sever ties with Qí,
then Chǔ will be isolated.
Why would Qin then value an isolated state?
Moreover, if you first cede land and then break with Qí,
Qin would certainly not agree to such a plan.
If you first break with Qí and then demand the land,
you will surely be deceived by Zhāng Yí.
If you are deceived by Zhāng Yí,
Your Majesty will certainly regret it.
This would create trouble from Qin in the west,
and sever relations with Qí in the north.
Then the armies of both states will surely come."
The King of Chǔ did not listen
and said:
"My plan is sound!
You should keep silent
and await the outcome of my affairs."
The King of Chǔ sent an envoy to break off relations with Qí.
Before the envoy returned,
he sent another to reinforce the break.
Zhāng Yí returned,
and Qin sent an envoy to Qí.
Qí and Qin secretly formed an alliance.
Chǔ then sent a general to receive the land from Qin.
When Zhāng Yí arrived,
he claimed illness and did not attend court.
The King of Chǔ said:
"Does Master Zhāng think I have not broken with Qí?"
He then sent a brave warrior to go and curse the King of Qí.
When Zhāng Yí knew that Chǔ had broken with Qí,
he came out to see the envoy and said:
"From such-and-such place to such-and-such place,
it is six lǐ in length and breadth."
The envoy said:
"I heard it was six hundred lǐ,
not six lǐ."
Yí said:
"I, Yí, am but a petty man.
How could I offer six hundred lǐ?"
The envoy returned and reported to the King of Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ was greatly angered
and wished to raise an army to attack Qin.
Chén Zhěn said:
"May I speak now?"
The king said:
"You may."
Zhěn said:
"Attacking Qin is not a good plan.
Your Majesty would do better to bribe Qin with a major city
and join them in attacking Qí.
Thus, what we lose to Qin we will recover from Qí.
The state of Chǔ will still remain intact.
Now that Your Majesty has already broken with Qí
and demands redress from Qin for the deception,
this will cause Qí and Qin to unite against us,
and we will surely suffer great harm."
The King of Chǔ did not listen
and raised an army to attack Qin.
Qin allied with Qí,
and Hán joined them.
The Chǔ army was badly defeated at Dùlíng.
Thus, although the territory and people of Chǔ were not weakened,
they barely managed to survive.
This was due to failing to heed Chén Zhěn's strategy
and mistakenly trusting Zhāng Yí.
Chǔ broke with Qí,
and Qí raised an army to attack Chǔ.
Chén Zhěn said to the King of Chǔ:
"Your Majesty should cede land to make peace with Qí in the east
and seek reconciliation with Qin in the west."
The King of Chǔ sent Chén Zhěn to Qin.
The King of Qin said to Zhěn:
"You are a man of Qin,
and I have known you for a long time.
I am not talented,
and cannot personally attend to state affairs,
so you left me to serve the King of Chǔ.
Now Qí and Chǔ are attacking each other.
Some say it is advantageous to rescue them,
others say it is not.
Can you not only loyally plan for your lord
but also spare some thought for me?"
Chén Zhěn said:
"Has Your Majesty not heard of the man from Wú who traveled to Chǔ?
The King of Chǔ was very fond of him.
When he fell ill,
the king sent someone to ask him,
saying:
'Are you truly ill,
or are you homesick?'
His attendants said:
'We do not know whether he is homesick or not,
but if he truly is, he will sing in the Wú style.'
Now I, Zhěn, will sing in the Wú style for Your Majesty.
Has Your Majesty not heard the story of Guǎn Yǔ?
Two tigers
were fighting over a man.
Guǎn Zhuāngzǐ was about to stab them,
but Guǎn Yǔ stopped him, saying:
'The tiger
is a fierce beast;
man
is sweet bait.
Now two tigers are fighting over a man.
The smaller will surely die,
and the larger will surely be injured.
If you wait for the tiger to be injured and then stab it,
you will kill both tigers with one move.
Without the toil of stabbing one tiger,
you will gain the fame of having stabbed two.'
Now Qí and Chǔ are at war.
They will surely be defeated.
When they are defeated,
Your Majesty can raise an army to rescue them.
This will bring the benefit of rescuing Qí
without the harm of attacking Chǔ.
To devise strategies, heed advice, and foresee outcomes—
only Your Majesty is capable of this.
Strategy
is the foundation of affairs;
heeding advice
is the key to survival or ruin.
If strategy is flawed and advice is misguided,
few can maintain their state.
Therefore it is said:
'A strategy that considers both sides
is hard to subvert;
advice that does not miss the essence
is hard to mislead.'"
When King Huì of Qin died,
Gōngsūn Yǎn wanted to ruin Zhāng Yí.
Lǐ Chóu said to Gōngsūn Yǎn:
"It would be better to summon Gān Mào from Wèi,
summon Gōngsūn Xiǎn from Hán,
and promote Chūlǐzǐ within the state.
These three men
are all enemies of Zhāng Yí.
If you employ them,
then the feudal lords will surely see that Zhāng Yí has lost favor in Qin!"
The Lord of Yìqú went to Wèi.
Gōngsūn Yǎn said to the Lord of Yìqú:
"The road is long,
and I may not see you again.
Let me tell you something important."
The Lord of Yìqú said:
"I wish to hear it."
He replied:
"If the central states have no conflict with Qin,
then Qin will burn and plunder your state.
If the central states are in conflict with Qin,
then Qin will send envoys with generous gifts
to seek your state's favor."
The Lord of Yìqú said:
"I shall heed your words."
Not long after,
five states attacked Qin.
Chén Zhěn said to the King of Qin:
"The Lord of Yìqú
is a worthy ruler among the barbarians.
Your Majesty should bribe him to pacify his heart."
The King of Qin said:
"Good."
He then sent a thousand bolts of embroidered silk
and a hundred beautiful women
to the Lord of Yìqú.
The Lord of Yìqú gathered his ministers and plotted, saying:
"This is exactly what Gōngsūn Yǎn spoke of."
He then raised an army to attack Qin by surprise,
and heavily defeated the Qin army below Lǐbó.
Physician Biǎn Què visited King Wǔ of Qin.
King Wǔ showed him his ailment,
and Biǎn Què requested to remove it.
His attendants said:
"Your ailment
is in front of the ear,
below the eye.
Removing it may not cure it,
and it may cause deafness
and blindness."
The king told this to Biǎn Què.
Biǎn Què angrily threw down his stone needle:
"You consult with those who know,
but are ruined by those who do not.
If this is how Qin's government is run,
then with one move you could ruin the state."
King Wǔ of Qín said to Gān Mào:
"I wish to open a road for carriages to the Sānchuān region,
so that I may spy on the royal house of Zhōu.
Will I then die without regret?"
Gān Mào replied:
"I request to go to Wèi,
to make a pact to attack Hán."
The king ordered Xiàng Shòu to accompany him.
Gān Mào arrived in Wèi
and said to Xiàng Shòu:
"You return and tell the king:
'Wèi has agreed to my proposal,
but I hope the king will not attack.'
When the matter is accomplished,
all credit shall be given to you."
Xiàng Shòu returned and reported this to the king.
The king welcomed Gān Mào at Xìrǎng.
When Gān Mào arrived,
the king asked him the reason.
He replied:
"Yíyáng
is a large district.
Shàngdǎng and Nányáng have stored supplies there for a long time.
It is called a district,
but in reality it is a commandery.
