Now, Your Majesty, facing multiple perils,
marching a thousand lǐ to attack it
is difficult.
I have heard that Zhāng Yí annexed the lands of Bā and Shǔ in the west,
seized the territory beyond the Xīhé in the north,
and took Shàngyōng in the south.
Yet the world did not praise Zhāng Yí more, but considered the former king wise.
Marquis Wén of Wèi ordered Yuè Yáng to lead troops
and attack Zhōngshān.
After three years he captured it.
Yuè Yáng returned and spoke of his achievements.
Marquis Wén showed him a chest full of slanderous letters.
Yuè Yáng bowed twice and touched his head to the ground, saying:
'This was not my achievement,
but the strength of my lord.'
Now I am a minister who is a traveler from another state.
If Chūlǐ Jí and Gōngsūn Yǎn,
relying on Hán, speak against me,
Your Majesty will surely listen to them.
This would mean Your Majesty deceiving Wèi,
and I would incur the resentment of Gōng Zhòng Chǐ.
Long ago, Zēngzǐ lived in Bì.
In Bì there was a man who shared Zēngzǐ's name and clan
and killed someone.
Someone told Zēngzǐ's mother:
'Zēng Shēn has killed a man.'
Zēngzǐ's mother said:
'My son does not kill people.'
And she continued weaving calmly.
After a while,
someone else said:
'Zēng Shēn has killed a man.'
His mother still continued weaving calmly.
A short time later,
another person came and told her:
'Zēng Shēn has killed a man.'
His mother became afraid,
threw down her shuttle, climbed over the wall, and fled.
Now, with Zēngzǐ's virtue
and his mother's trust in him,
when three people cast doubt,
even a loving mother could not keep her faith.
Now, my virtue does not match Zēngzǐ's,
and Your Majesty's trust in me
is not like that of Zēngzǐ's mother.
Those who doubt me
are not fewer than three.
I fear Your Majesty will throw down the shuttle for my sake."
The king said:
"I will not listen to them.
Let me make a covenant with you."
Thereupon he made a covenant with him at Xìrǎng.
They indeed attacked Yíyáng,
but for five months could not capture it.
Chūlǐ Jí and Gōngsūn Yǎn were at court
and argued before the king.
The king was about to listen to them
and summoned Gān Mào to inform him.
Gān Mào replied:
"Xìrǎng is over there."
The king said:
"It is so."
He then mobilized all his troops
and again sent Gān Mào to attack.
Thus they captured Yíyáng.
During the Yíyáng campaign,
Féng Zhāng said to the King of Qín:
"If we do not capture Yíyáng,
Hán and Chǔ will take advantage of our exhaustion,
and the state will surely be in danger!
It would be better to promise Chǔ the Hànzhōng region to please them.
If Chǔ is pleased and does not advance,
Hán will be isolated
and can do nothing against Qín!"The king said:
"Good."
They indeed sent Féng Zhāng to promise Chǔ the Hànzhōng region,
and captured Yíyáng.
The King of Chǔ, based on these words, demanded Hànzhōng from Féng Zhāng.
Féng Zhāng said to the King of Qín:
"Your Majesty should then disown me
and firmly tell the King of Chǔ:
'I originally had no land to promise the King of Chǔ.'"
Gān Mào attacked Yíyáng.
After three drum rolls, the troops still did not advance.
A commandant of Qín's right army said to him:
"If you, sir, do not discuss military tactics,
you will surely be in great distress."
Gān Mào said:
"I am a traveler who has become chancellor of Qín.
I used Yíyáng as bait for the king.
Now, if we attack Yíyáng and do not capture it,
Gōngsūn Yǎn and Chūlǐ Jí will undermine me at court,
and Gōng Zhòng will press me from Hán abroad.
Then my days of campaigning are over!
I request that tomorrow, if the drums roll and we cannot take it,
we shall make the outer walls of Yíyáng our tomb."
Thereupon he brought out his private gold
to increase the public rewards.
The next day the drums rolled,
and Yíyáng was captured.
Before Yíyáng was taken,
with many Qín casualties,
Gān Mào wanted to cease hostilities.
Zuǒ Chéng said to Gān Mào:
"You, sir, are attacked internally by Chūlǐ Jí and Gōngsūn Yǎn,
and abroad you have incurred the resentment of Hán Chǐ.
Now if you, sir, use troops without success,
you will surely be cornered.
It would be better for you, sir, to advance the troops and attack Yíyáng.
If Yíyáng is captured,
then your achievements will be great.
Then Chūlǐ Jí and Gōngsūn Yǎn will have no grounds for action,
and the Qín populace will deeply resent them."
During the Yíyáng campaign,
Chǔ betrayed Qín and allied with Hán.
The King of Qín was afraid.
Gān Mào said:
"Although Chǔ has allied with Hán,
it will not fight first for Hán's sake.
Hán also fears that if it fights,
Chǔ may change its stance behind its back.
Hán and Chǔ are sure to guard against each other.
Chǔ speaks of alliance with Hán,
but harbors no additional resentment against Qín.
Therefore, I know they are guarding against each other."
The King of Qín said to Gān Mào:
"The envoys sent by Chǔ are often forceful.
They contend with me in argument,
and I am often at a loss.
What should I do about it?"
Gān Mào replied:
"Your Majesty, do not worry!
If forceful men come as envoys,
then Your Majesty should not heed their business.
If timid and weak men come as envoys,
then Your Majesty must heed them.
Thus the timid and weak will be employed,
and the forceful will not!
Your Majesty can thereby control them."
Gān Mào fled from Qín
and was about to go to Qí.
As he exited the pass, he met Master Sū
and said:
"Have you, sir, heard of the maidens by the river?"
Master Sū said:
"I have not."
He said:
"The maidens by the river
included one whose family was poor and had no candle.
The maidens discussed among themselves
and wanted to send her away.
The poor maiden without a candle was about to leave
and said to the maidens:
'Because I have no candle,
I have always come early
to sweep the room and lay out the mats.
Why begrudge the leftover light that illuminates the four walls?
If you would kindly bestow it on me,
what harm would it do to the maidens?
I consider myself beneficial to the maidens.
Why send me away?'"
The maidens spoke among themselves
and, thinking it reasonable, kept him.
Now I am unworthy,
cast out by Qín and leaving the pass,
I wish to sweep your rooms and lay out your mats,
and hope you will not drive me away."
Sūzǐ said:
"Good.
I shall have you honored in Qí."
Then he went west to persuade the King of Qín, saying:
"Gān Mào
is a worthy man,
no ordinary person.
He has served Qín for generations and been greatly esteemed;
from the Xiáo Pass
to the Xīgǔ, he knows all the terrain, treacherous or easy.
If he allies Qí with Hán and Wèi,
turning to plot against Qín,
that would not benefit Qín."
The King of Qín said:
"Then what should be done?"
Sū Dài said:
"Better to increase his ceremonial gifts,
enrich his stipend to welcome him.
If he comes, place him in Huáigǔ,
never let him leave for life,
and how could the world then scheme against Qín?"
The King of Qín said:
"Good."
He granted him the rank of Shàngqīng
and sent a minister to welcome him in Qí.
Gān Mào declined and did not go.
Sū Qín falsely told the King:
"Gān Mào
is a worthy man.
Now Qín has granted him Shàngqīng
and sent a minister to welcome him.
Mào is grateful for Your Majesty's favor,
so he does not go,
wishing to be Your Majesty's servant.
How will Your Majesty treat him with courtesy?
If Your Majesty does not keep him,
he surely will not feel grateful.
With Gān Mào's worthiness,
if he gains free use of mighty Qín's masses,
then he will be hard to deal with!"
The King of Qí said:
"Good."
He granted him the rank of Shàngqīng
and commanded him to stay.
Gān Mào served as Qín's minister.
The King of Qín favored Gōngsūn Yǎn,
and privately intended to appoint him,
thus saying to him personally:
"I shall make you my minister."
An official of Gān Mào overheard this on the road
and reported it to Gān Mào.
Gān Mào then entered to see the King, saying:
"Your Majesty has obtained a worthy minister;
I dare to bow twice in congratulations."
The King said:
"I entrust the state to you;
how could I obtain another worthy minister?"
He replied:
"Your Majesty is about to make Xīshǒu your minister."
The King said:
"How did you hear this?"
He replied:
"Xīshǒu told me."
The King was angry that Xīshǒu had leaked it,
and expelled him.
Gān Mào allied Qín and Wèi to attack Chǔ.
Chǔ's minister in Qín, Qū Gài,
made peace between Chǔ and Qín,
and Qín opened its passes to receive the Chǔ envoy.
Gān Mào said to the King of Qín:
"If alarmed by Chǔ
and not letting Wèi control the peace,
Chǔ will surely say
'Qín has sold out Wèi.'
Wèi, displeased, will ally with Chǔ,
and with Chǔ and Wèi united,
our state will likely suffer harm.
Your Majesty should let Wèi control the peace;
Wèi will surely be pleased.
If Your Majesty avoids offending Wèi,
then the land gained will surely be much."
Regarding the affair at Xíngshān,
Zhào was about to join Qín in attacking Qí.
Qí, afraid,
ordered Tián Zhāng to cede Yángwǔ to Zhào,
and sent Shùnzǐ as a hostage.
The King of Zhào was pleased,
then halted troops and informed Qín, saying:
"Qí has granted Yángwǔ to our humble state
and sent Shùnzǐ,
wishing to avert the attack.
I dare inform your subordinate officials."
The King of Qín sent Prince Tā to Zhào,
to tell the King of Zhào:
"Qí joined your great state in rescuing Wèi but broke the pact,
untrustworthy and unreliable.
Your great state, finding this unrighteous,
informed our humble state
and granted it two shè of land
for sacrificial offerings.
Now you halt troops again,
intending to ally with Qí and receive its land;
this is beyond what your envoy can comprehend.
We request to add forty thousand armored troops;
your great state may decide."
Sū Dài presented a letter to Ránghóu on behalf of Qí, saying:
"I hear from those coming and going:
'Qín will add forty thousand armored troops to Zhào to attack Qí.'
I privately assured the king of our humble state:
'The King of Qín is clear-sighted and skilled in strategy,
Ránghóu is wise and experienced in affairs;
surely they will not add forty thousand armored troops to Zhào to attack Qí.'
Why is this?
The alliance of the Three Jìn
is Qín's deep-seated enemy.
The Three Jìn have betrayed Qín a hundred times,
deceived Qín a hundred times,
yet are not considered untrustworthy,
not considered without conduct.
Now to crush Qí and fatten Zhào,
Zhào, Qín's deep-seated enemy,
does not benefit Qín.
This is the first reason.
Qín's strategists must say:
'Crush Qí, weaken Jìn,
then control victory over Jìn and Chǔ.'
But Qí
is a weary state;
for all under heaven to attack it
is like bursting a boil with a thousand-jūn crossbow.
How could the King of Qín then control Jìn and Chǔ!
This is the second reason.
If Qín sends few troops,
Jìn and Chǔ will not trust it;
if it sends many troops,
then Jìn and Chǔ will be controlled by Qín.
Qí, afraid,
will surely not flee to Qín
but flee to Jìn and Chǔ.
This is the third reason.
If Qí cedes land to enrich Jìn and Chǔ,
then Jìn and Chǔ will be pacified.
If Qí raises troops
and they turn their swords,
then Qín will instead suffer attack.
This is the fourth reason.
Thus Jìn and Chǔ use Qín to crush Qí,
and use Qí to crush Qín;
how wise are Jìn and Chǔ,
and how foolish Qí and Qín!
This is the fifth reason.
If Qín obtains Ānyì,
treats Qí well to pacify it,
it will surely have no troubles.
With Qín holding Ānyì,
then Hán and Wèi will surely not have Shàngdǎng.
To seize the vitals of the Three Jìn
compared to sending troops and fearing their non-return,
which is more beneficial?
Therefore I privately assured the king of our humble state:
'The King of Qín is clear-sighted and skilled in strategy,
Ránghóu is wise and experienced in affairs;
surely they will not add Zhào's armored troops
of forty thousand men
to attack Qí.'"
The Qín Dowager Xuān loved Wèi Chǒufū.
The Dowager fell ill and was about to die,
issuing an order:
"For my burial,
Wèizi must be buried with me."
Wèizi was troubled by this.
Yōng Ruì spoke to the Dowager on Wèizi's behalf, saying:
"Do you consider the dead to have consciousness?"
The Dowager said:
"They have no consciousness."
He said:
"With Your Majesty's divine intelligence,
you clearly know the dead have no consciousness;
why vainly bury one loved in life
with the unconscious dead!
If the dead have consciousness,
the late king's accumulated anger has lasted long;
Your Majesty would lack means to atone for faults,
how could you spare time to favor Wèi Chǒufū privately?"
The Dowager said:
"Good."
Then she stopped.
Lord Xuē spoke to Wèi Rǎn on behalf of Wèi, saying:
"I have heard that the King of Qín intends to use Lǚ Lǐ to win over Qí,
in order to dominate the world.
You will certainly be diminished.
If Qí and Qín join forces to confront the Three Jìn,
Lǚ Lǐ will inevitably serve as chancellor to both,
which means you would be helping Qí
to elevate Lǚ Lǐ.
Once Qí is spared from the military conflicts of the world,
its enmity toward you will surely deepen.
You would do better to urge the King of Qín to have my state complete the campaign against Qí.
If Qí is defeated,
I will request that the lands gained be enfeoffed to you.
With Qí broken and Jìn strengthened,
the King of Qín, fearing Jìn's might,
will certainly value you to win over Jìn.
Qí, having given territory to Jìn and my state,
will be unable to withstand Qín,
and Jìn will certainly value you to serve Qín.
Thus, by destroying Qí you will achieve merit,
and by controlling Jìn you will gain weight.
Destroy Qí, secure your fief,
and both Qín and Jìn will value you.
If Qí is not destroyed,
and Lǚ Lǐ is employed again,
you will surely be in great distress."
The Qín guest minister Zào said to the Marquis of Rǎng:
"Qín enfeoffed you with Táo,
and has relied on you to dominate the world for several years.
If the campaign against Qí succeeds,
Táo will become a state of ten thousand chariots,
leading the minor states,
and guiding them to pay homage to the Son of Heaven.
The world will surely obey,
achieving the work of the Five Hegemons.
If the campaign against Qí fails,
Táo will become a neighboring concern,
with no one to rely on.
Therefore, the campaign against Qí is for Táo
a matter of survival or extinction.
"If you wish to accomplish this,
why not send someone to say to the Chancellor of Yān:
'A sage cannot create the opportunity,
but when the opportunity comes, he does not lose it.
Shùn, though worthy,
had he not encountered Yáo,
would not have become the Son of Heaven.
Tāng and Wǔ, though worthy,
would not have become kings had they not faced Jié and Zhòu.
Thus, with the worthiness of Shùn, Tāng, and Wǔ,
without encountering the right time, they could not have become emperors or kings.
Now to attack Qí
is your great opportunity.
By leveraging the strength of the world,
to attack the enemy state of Qí,
to avenge the disgrace of King Huì,
to accomplish the achievements of King Zhāo,
and to eliminate the harm for ten thousand generations—
this is Yān's lasting benefit,
and your great fame.
The *Shū* says:
"In cultivating virtue, nothing is better than making it abundant;
in eliminating harm, nothing is better than making it thorough."
Wú did not destroy Yuè,
so Yuè consequently destroyed Wú.
Qí did not destroy Yān,
so Yān should consequently destroy Qí.
If Qí is not destroyed by Yān,
as Wú was destroyed by Yuè,
this is because the disease was not eradicated thoroughly.
If you do not seize this moment
to accomplish your merit,
and eliminate your harm,
when Qín eventually has other matters and allies with Qí,
and Qí and Zhào unite,
their enmity toward you will surely deepen.
Holding your enemy to punish Yān,
later even if you regret it,
it will be impossible.
Mobilize all Yān's troops and swiftly attack them.
The world's support for you
will be like avenging a father's or son's enemy.
If you can truly destroy Qí,
you will be enfeoffed south of the river,
becoming a state of ten thousand chariots,
with roads extending throughout the central states,
bordering Táo to the south,
free from worry for generations.
I hope you will focus your will on attacking Qí,
with no other considerations.'"
Someone said to Wèi Rǎn:
"Have you heard the talk from the east?"
He replied:
"I have not."
The speaker said:
"Xīn, Zhāng Yáng,
and Wú Zé advised the King of Wèi,
Lord Xuē, and Gōngshū, saying:
'We, in war,
carry the ancestral tablets and pledge the state to make a covenant with the king,
ensuring there will certainly be no trouble.
If there is anyone who defeats us,
we request to be beheaded.
However, we have a concern.
The King of Chǔ,
relying on his state to depend on Rǎn,
yet serving our lord—
this is our great concern.'
Now if you go east and thereby speak to Chǔ,
you would be making Zhāng Yí's words like those of Yǔ,
and ensuring the ruin of your affairs.
You would do better to return to your state,
show favor to Chǔ, and observe what Lord Xuē does for you.
Observe what the three states seek from Qín but cannot obtain,
and request to call upon the three states to gain their trust.
Observe what Zhāng Yí and Zé cannot obtain from Lord Xuē,
and you request it to enhance your own weight."
Someone said to Wèi Rǎn:
"If peace is not achieved,
troops will certainly be dispatched.
Bái Qǐ
will again take command.
If victorious,
he will surely bring you to distress.
If not victorious,
he will surely serve Zhào and follow you.
You will again be diminished.
You would do better not to act much,
then swiftly arrive."
Someone said to the Marquis of Rǎng:
"Considering your enfeoffment for you,
it would be as if removing
Sòng's crime, increasing
Qí's anger; wait
to devastate and attack the chaotic Sòng,
show favor to strong Qí,
and secure your own enfeoffment.
This is also an opportunity for a hundred generations!"
Someone said to Wèi Rǎn:
"If Chǔ defeats Qín,
it cannot balance with Qí as equals.
Qín for three generations has accumulated grievances with Hán and Wèi,
while Qí's favor has newly been added.
If Qí and Qín contend with each other,
and Hán and Wèi listen to the east,
then Qín will be attacked.
Qí possesses the lands of the eastern state,
a thousand *li* square.
Chǔ encompasses the Jiǔyí,
also a thousand *li* square,
with the Fúlí fortress to the south,
and the Gānyú pass to the north.
It holds authority over Sòng and Wèi,
so Sòng and Wèi are merely like Ā and Zhēn.
Benefiting from two thousand *li*,
rich and controlling Yuè's subjects,
how can Qín balance with Qí as equals?
Hán and Wèi, dividing the fertile lands of Fāngchéng to approach Zhèng?
If troops rest and rise again,
it will be enough to harm Qín,
without necessarily waiting for Qí."
When the five states withdrew from Chénggāo,
the King of Qín wanted to seek the chancellorship of Hán and Wèi for Lord Chéngyáng,
but Hán
and Wèi would not agree.
The Queen Dowager of Qín spoke to the King of Qín on behalf of Wèi Rǎn, saying:
"Lord Chéngyáng, because of your sake,
was in distress and resided in Qí.
Now that you see his success and take him in,
can you also win his heart?"
The King said:
"Not yet."
The Queen Dowager said:
"If you do not take him in when he is in distress,
but take him in when he is successful,
I fear he will not be used by you.
Moreover, taking in Lord Chéngyáng
is the way to lose Hán and Wèi."
Fàn Zǐ, through Wáng Jǐ, entered Qín
and presented a letter to King Zhāo, saying:
"I have heard that an enlightened ruler governs correctly:
those with merit must be rewarded,
those with ability must be given office.
Those with great labor have generous emoluments,
those with many achievements have noble ranks,
those who can govern the masses hold high office.
Therefore, those without ability dare not assume their posts,
and those with ability cannot be hidden."
If you deem my words worthy,
then act upon them to further benefit your path;
if you are unwilling to implement them,
then keeping me here long serves no purpose.
As the saying goes:
'A ruler rewards those he favors,
and punishes those he despises.
An enlightened ruler, however, does not act thus;
he rewards only the meritorious,
and metes out punishment only to the guilty.'
Now, my chest is not sturdy enough to serve as a chopping block,
nor is my waist fit to await the axe and halberd—
how would I dare to test Your Majesty with dubious matters?
Even if you consider me lowly
and treat me with contempt and humiliation,
surely you would not disregard that those who recommended me
might later face repercussions before you!"
"I have heard that Zhōu possessed Dǐ'è,
Sòng possessed Jiélǜ,
Liáng possessed Xuánlí,
and Chǔ possessed Hépú.
These four treasures
were overlooked by craftsmen,
yet became renowned vessels of the realm.
If so, then what a sage king discards—
can it truly be insufficient to enrich the state?"
"I have heard that those skilled at enriching their families
draw resources from the state;
those skilled at enriching the state
draw resources from the feudal lords.
When the realm has an enlightened ruler,
the feudal lords cannot monopolize wealth.
Why is this so?
Because it withers prosperity.
A good physician knows whether a patient will live or die;
a sage ruler discerns the outcomes of success and failure.
If beneficial, he acts;
if harmful, he desists;
if uncertain, he tests it cautiously.
Even if Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, and Tāng were reborn,
they could not alter this!
The most profound words, I dare not commit to writing;
the shallow ones are not worth hearing either.
Perhaps
I am foolish and fail to grasp Your Majesty's heart?
Or perhaps those who speak of me
are deemed lowly and unworthy of being heeded?
If it is not so,
then my wish,
is to beg a little leisure for observation,
to see Your Majesty and enter your presence."
The letter was presented;
the King of Qín was pleased.
He then thanked Wáng Jī for his recommendation
and sent a carriage to summon him.
When Fàn Jū arrived in Qín,
the king welcomed him in the courtyard,
saying to Fàn Jū:
"I ought to have received your instruction in person long ago.
Recently, the matter of Yìqú was urgent,
and I had to attend to the Queen Mother daily.
Now that the Yìqú affair is settled,
I am finally able to receive your counsel in person.
I am privately ashamed of my dullness,
and respectfully observe the rites of host and guest."
Fàn Jū declined modestly.
On that day, when Fàn Jū was presented,
all who saw him changed countenance.
The King of Qín dismissed his attendants;
the palace was empty, with no one else present.
The king knelt and pleaded:
"How would you deign to instruct me, sir?"
Fàn Jū replied:
"Yes, yes."
After a while,
the king pleaded again,
and Fàn Jū said:
"Yes, yes."
This happened three times.
The king rose to his knees and said:
"Will you not instruct me, sir?"
Fàn Jū apologized:
"I dare not be thus.
I have heard that when Lǚ Shàng first met King Wén,
he was but a fisherman
angling on the banks of the Wèi River's north shore.
In such a case,
their acquaintance was distant.
Yet after one conversation,
he was made Grand Tutor,
taken in the same carriage back—
because his words were profound.
Thus, King Wén indeed achieved success through Lǚ Shàng,
and eventually ruled the realm and established himself as emperor.
Had King Wén kept Lǚ Wàng at a distance and not spoken deeply with him,
then Zhōu would have lacked the virtue of the Son of Heaven,
and King Wén and King Wǔ would have had none to aid their royal cause.
Now I am a minister from afar,
acquainted with you only distantly.
Yet what I wish to present
concerns rectifying the ruler's affairs,
intervening between flesh and blood.
I wish to present my humble loyalty,
but do not yet know Your Majesty's heart.
That is why I did not answer despite your three inquiries.
It is not that I fear something and dare not speak;
I know that if I speak today,
I may be executed tomorrow.
Yet I do not dare to fear.
If Your Majesty trusts and acts upon my words,
death would not be a worry for me,
exile would not be a sorrow.
To lacquer my body and become a leper,
to dishevel my hair and become a madman—
these would not shame me.
The Five Emperors, sages though they were, died;
the Three Kings, benevolent though they were, died;
the Five Hegemons, worthy though they were, died;
Wū Huò, strong though he was, died;
Bēn and Yù, brave though they were, died.
Death
is something no man can avoid.
Facing an inevitable fate,
if I can bring even slight benefit to Qín,
that is my greatest wish.
What have I to fear?
Wǔ Zǐxū, hidden in a sack, fled Zhāoguān,
traveling by night and hiding by day,
until he reached Língshuǐ.
With nothing to feed himself,
he crawled on hands and knees,
begging for food in the markets of Wú,
yet ultimately revived the state of Wú,
and Hé Lǘ became hegemon.
If I could offer counsel like Wǔ Zǐxū,
even if imprisoned thereafter,
never to see the light again,
and my advice were implemented,
what would I have to grieve?
Jīzǐ and Jiēyú
lacquered their bodies and became lepers,
disheveled their hair and became madmen,
yet brought no benefit to Yīn or Chǔ.
If I could act like Jīzǐ and Jiēyú,
and lacquering my body could benefit a worthy ruler,
that would be my greatest honor.
What shame would I have?
What I fear
is only that after my death,
the world, seeing my utter loyalty end in downfall,
would shut their mouths and bind their feet,
and none would approach Qín.
You, above, fear the sternness of the Queen Mother;
below, you are confused by the posturing of treacherous ministers.
Dwelling deep within the palace,
never leaving the hands of guardians and tutors;
lifelong benighted and deluded,
with none to expose treachery—
at worst, the ancestral temples may be destroyed and overturned;
at least, you yourself may be isolated and endangered.
This is what I fear!
As for hardship and disgrace,
the peril of death,
I dare not fear them.
If my death brings order to Qín,
it is better than living."
The king rose to his knees and said:
"What words are these, sir!
Qín is remote and isolated,
and I am foolish and unworthy.
That you, sir, have deigned to come here—
this is Heaven using me to trouble you, sir,
to preserve the temples of the former kings.
That I may receive instruction from you, sir—
this is Heaven favoring the former kings and not abandoning their orphan.
How can you speak thus, sir!
Matters great and small,
from the Queen Mother above
to the ministers below—
I wish you to instruct me fully on all,
without doubting me."
Fàn Jū bowed twice;
the King of Qín also bowed twice.
Fàn Jū said:
"Your Majesty's state—
to the north, there are Gānquán and Gǔkǒu;
to the south, it is girded by the Jīng and Wèi rivers;
to the west, there are Lǒng and Shǔ;
to the east, there are passes and slopes.
With a thousand war chariots
and a million fierce warriors,
given the bravery of Qín's soldiers
and the multitude of its chariots and cavalry,
to face the feudal lords
is like unleashing Hán Lú
to chase a lame hare—
hegemonic and royal achievement is within reach."
Now, the reason you turn inward and dare not look toward military action east of the mountains
is that the Marquis of Ráng has not been loyal in planning for the state,
and Your Majesty's strategy has its flaws."
The King said:
"I wish to hear about these flawed strategies."
Sūi said:
"Your Majesty crossing over Hán and Wèi to attack the strong state of Qí
is not a sound strategy.
Sending too few troops
would be insufficient to harm Qí;
sending too many would harm Qín.
I suspect Your Majesty's plan is to send a small force
and rely entirely on the armies of Hán and Wèi, but that would be unrighteous.
Now, seeing that an allied state cannot be trusted,
is it permissible to cross another state's territory to attack?
This is a flaw in strategy!
In the past,
the men of Qí attacked Chǔ,
won the battle,
shattered their army and killed their generals,
and expanded their territory by a thousand *lǐ*,
yet gained not an inch of land for themselves.
Was it that Qí did not desire land?
The situation made it impossible for them to hold it.
When the other feudal lords saw Qí exhausted and exposed,
its ruler and ministers estranged,
they raised armies and attacked it,
resulting in the ruler's humiliation and the army's defeat,
making them the laughingstock of the world.
The reason for this
was that by attacking Chǔ, they enriched Hán and Wèi.
This is what is called lending weapons to bandits and supplying food to thieves.
Your Majesty would do better to befriend the distant and attack the near.
Gaining an inch of land would then be Your Majesty's inch,
gaining a foot would be Your Majesty's foot.
Now, to abandon this and attack afar,
is that not mistaken?
Moreover, in the past,
the territory of Zhōngshān,
five hundred *lǐ* square,
was exclusively controlled by Zhào.
Achievement accomplished, fame established, and benefits secured,
then no one in the world could harm them.
Now, Hán and Wèi,
located in the central states,
are the pivot of the world.
If Your Majesty wishes to become hegemon,
you must befriend the central states
and use them as the pivot of the world,
to intimidate Chǔ and Zhào.
If Zhào is strong, then Chǔ will submit;
if Chǔ is strong, then Zhào will submit.
If Chǔ and Zhào submit, then Qí will surely fear,
and in fear will surely use humble words and generous gifts to serve Qín.
Once Qí submits, Hán and Wèi can be rendered empty."
The King said:
"I wish to befriend Wèi,
but Wèi is a state of many changes,
I cannot befriend it.
May I ask how to befriend Wèi?"
Fàn Sūi said:
"Use humble words and generous gifts to serve it.
If that does not work,
cede territory and bribe it.
If that does not work,
raise an army and attack it."
Thereupon he raised an army and attacked Xíngqiū.
Xíngqiū was captured
and Wèi requested to submit.
He said:
"The territories of Qín and Hán
are interwoven like embroidery.
Qín's possession of Hán
is like a tree having borers,
or a man having a disease in his heart and belly.
If change occurs in the world,
none will harm Qín more than Hán.
Your Majesty should subdue Hán."
The King said:
"I wish to subdue Hán,
but if it does not comply,
what should be done?"
Fàn Sūi said:
"Raise an army and attack Xíngyáng,
then the road to Chénggāo will be blocked;
cut the Tàiháng road to the north
and the troops from Shàngdǎng will not be able to descend;
with one move to attack Xíngyáng,
their state will be severed into three.
When Wèi and Hán see they are sure to perish,
how can they not comply?
If Hán complies, the task of hegemony can be achieved."
The King said:
"Good."
Fàn Sūi said:
"When I lived east of the mountains,
I heard that within Qí there was Tián Dān,
but did not hear of its king.
I hear that in Qín there are the Queen Dowager, the Marquis of Ráng,
the Lord of Jīngyáng, and the Lord of Huáyáng,
but do not hear that there is a king.
He who controls the state is called king,
he who can monopolize benefits and harms is called king,
he who holds the power of life and death is called king.
Now the Queen Dowager acts arbitrarily without regard,
the Marquis of Ráng goes on missions without reporting,
the Lords of Jīngyáng and Huáyáng make judgments without restraint,
with these four nobles in place, for the state not to be in peril
has never happened.
Because of these four,
those below are said to have no king.
If so, how can authority not be overturned,
and how can orders issue from the King?
I have heard:
'He who is skilled at governing a state
secures his authority internally,
and emphasizes his power externally.'
The Marquis of Ráng's envoys wield the King's weighty authority,
tear apart the feudal lords,
divide tallies across the world,
attack enemies and invade states,
and none dare disobey.
Victories in battle and captures of land
bring benefits to Táo;
when the state is exhausted,
it is controlled by the feudal lords;
when battles are lost,
resentment accumulates among the common people,
and disaster returns to the altars of soil and grain.
The *Book of Songs* says:
'When the fruit of a tree is abundant,
its branches break;
when its branches break,
its heart is injured.
Enlarging one's capital endangers the state;
honoring one's ministers debases the ruler.'
Nào Chǐ controlled the power of Qí,
pulled out King Mǐn's tendons,
hung him from a temple beam,
and he died overnight.
Lǐ Duì held power in Zhào,
reduced the food for Lord Fù,
and he starved to death in a hundred days.
Now in Qín,
the Queen Dowager and the Marquis of Ráng wield power,
assisted by the Lords of Gāolíng and Jīngyáng,
ultimately there is no King of Qín.
These are also of the same kind as Nào Chǐ and Lǐ Duì.
I now see Your Majesty standing alone in the court and temple,
and moreover, I fear that those who will possess the state of Qín in later generations
will not be Your Majesty's sons and grandsons."
The King of Qín was afraid,
thereupon he deposed the Queen Dowager,
expelled the Marquis of Ráng,
sent out the Lord of Gāolíng,
and drove the Lord of Jīngyáng beyond the pass.
King Zhāo said to Fàn Sūi:
"In the past,
Duke Huán of Qí obtained Guǎn Zhòng,
and called him 'Uncle Zhòng.'
Now I have obtained you,
I also regard you as a father."
Marquis Yìng said to King Zhāo:
"Have you also heard of the sacred grove in Héngsī?
In Héngsī there was a fierce youth
who asked to gamble with the grove,
saying:
'If I defeat the grove,
the grove will lend me its spirit for three days;
if I do not defeat the grove,
the grove may constrain me.'
Then with his left hand he cast for the grove,
with his right hand he cast for himself,
defeated the grove,
and the grove lent him its spirit.
After three days,
the grove went to seek it back,
but he did not return it.
After five days the grove withered,
after seven days the grove perished.
Now the state
is Your Majesty's grove;
power
is Your Majesty's spirit.
To lend these to others,
is that not perilous?
I have never heard of a finger larger than an arm,
or an arm larger than a thigh.
If such exists,
A hundred men carrying a gourd and hurrying along
cannot match one man holding it and running swiftly.
If a hundred men truly carry a gourd,
the gourd is bound to split.
Now in the state of Qín,
Huáyáng uses it,
Ránghóu uses it,
the Queen Dowager uses it,
and the King also uses it.
If it is not called a vessel, then so be it;
but once it is called a vessel,
the state is bound to split.
I have heard it said:
'When the fruit of a tree is abundant, its branches will break;
when its branches break, the heart of the tree is injured.
When a capital is large, it endangers the state;
when ministers are strong, they endanger their lord.'
Now, from those in the city who receive a peck of grain or more,
up to the Commandants, the Interior Minister, and the King's attendants,
is there anyone who is not a man of the Chancellor?
If the state has no troubles, then so be it;
but if the state has troubles,
I am certain to see the King standing alone in the court.
I privately fear for the King,
fearing that for ten thousand generations to come, the rulers of the state
will not be the King's descendants."
"I have heard
that in ancient times, those skilled at governance
kept their authority within and spread their support abroad,
so that the four quarters were governed without disorder or rebellion,
and envoys traveled the straight path,
not daring to do wrong.
Now the Queen Dowager's envoys
divide and split the feudal lords,
and their tallies are spread throughout the world.
Wielding the power of a great state,
they forcibly conscript troops
to attack the feudal lords.
When battles are won and cities captured,
all the profits go to Táo;
the state's silks and coins
are exhausted into the Queen Dowager's household;
and the benefits within the borders
are divided and transferred to Huáyáng.
What ancient times called
'the way to endanger the ruler and destroy the state'
must arise from this.
These three nobles exhaust the state for their own safety.
If so, how can orders issue from the King?
How can power not be divided?
Thus, our King truly occupies only one-third of the position."
Qín attacked Hán
and besieged Xíng.
Fàn Jū said to King Zhāo of Qín:
"There are those who attack men,
and there are those who attack territory.
Ránghóu attacked Wèi ten times without inflicting damage,
not because Qín was weak and Wèi strong,
but because what he attacked
was territory.
Territory is what a ruler loves dearly.
A ruler is what his ministers are willing to die for.
Attacking what a ruler loves,
and fighting with those willing to die for him,
that is why ten attacks could not bring victory.
Now the King is about to attack Hán and besiege Xíng.
I wish the King would not attack only their territory,
but attack their men.
If the King attacks Hán and besieges Xíng,
use Zhāng Yí as a pretext.
If Zhāng Yí has great influence,
he will cede territory to redeem himself before the King.
He will cede land until Hán is nearly exhausted.
If Zhāng Yí has little influence,
then the King can expel Zhāng Yí
and instead trade with someone inferior to Zhāng Yí.
Thus, what the King seeks from Hán
can be obtained through words."
Yìnghóu said:
"The people of Zhèng call uncut jade 'pú';
the people of Zhōu call un-dried rats 'pǔ.'
A man of Zhōu, carrying his 'pú,' passed by a merchant of Zhèng and said,
'Do you wish to buy a pǔ?'
The merchant of Zhèng said,
'I do.'
He took out his 'pǔ,'
looked at it,
and it was a rat.
He then declined and did not take it.
Now Lord Píngyuán considers himself worthy and is renowned throughout the world,
yet he degraded his lord's father at Shāqiū and made him a subject.
The kings of the world still honor him.
This shows that the kings of the world
are not as wise as the merchant of Zhèng.
They are dazzled by reputation
and do not know the reality."
The scholars of the world,
forming a vertical alliance, gathered in Zhào
and intended to attack Qín.
The Chancellor of Qín, Yìnghóu, said:
"Do not worry, my King.
Allow me to have them disbanded.
Qín bears no grudge against the scholars of the world.
They gather to attack Qín
only because they themselves desire wealth and honor.
Observe the great King's dogs:
those lying down lie down,
those rising rise,
those walking walk,
those stopping stop,
with no fighting among them.
But throw them a single bone,
and they lightly rise and bare their teeth at each other.
Why is that?
Because they have the intent to fight."
Thereupon, Táng Jū loaded music and instruments,
gave them five hundred gold pieces,
resided in Wǔ'ān,
held grand banquets and drank together,
saying,
"Who from Hándān will come to take it?"
Thus, those who were plotting certainly could not be given,
but those who could be given
became as brothers with them.
"You, sir, when calculating merit with Qín,
do not ask where the gold goes.
Those who exhaust the gold have the most merit.
Now I shall have someone load another five hundred gold pieces to follow you."
Táng Jū set out,
traveled to Wǔ'ān,
and distributed no more than three thousand gold pieces.
The scholars of the world
greatly fought among themselves.
Someone said to Yìnghóu:
"Did you capture Mǎfú?"
He said,
"Yes."
"And then besieged Hándān?"
He said,
"Yes."
"If Zhào perishes,
the King of Qín will rule as king,
and Wǔ'ānjūn will become one of the Three Dukes.
Wǔ'ānjūn has fought for Qín, winning battles and capturing over seventy cities for Qín,
destroying Yān, Yǐng, and Hànzhōng in the south,
capturing Mǎfú's army
without losing a single armored soldier.
Even the achievements of Lǚ Wàng of Zhōu
were no greater than this.
If Zhào perishes,
the King of Qín rules as king,
and Wǔ'ānjūn becomes one of the Three Dukes,
can you serve beneath him?
Even if you wish not to serve beneath him,
you certainly will have no choice.
Qín once attacked Xíng in Hán
and was trapped in Shàngdǎng.
The people of Shàngdǎng all returned to Zhào.
The people of the world
have long been unwilling to be subjects of Qín.
Now if you attack Zhào,
the northern territories will go to Yān,
the eastern territories to Qí,
the southern territories to Chǔ and Wèi.
Then what Qín gains will be almost nothing.
Therefore, it is better to seize the opportunity to partition it
and thereby make it a merit for Wǔ'ānjūn."
Yìnghóu lost Rǔnán of Hán.
King Zhāo of Qín said to Yìnghóu:
"You have lost your fiefdom.
Are you worried?"
Yìnghóu said:
"I am not worried."
The King said:
"Why not?"
He said:
"There was a man from Liáng named Dōngmén Wú.
His son died, yet he did not grieve.
His steward said:
'Your love for your son
was unmatched in the world.
Now your son is dead, yet you do not grieve.
Why is this?'
Dōngmén Wú replied:
'I once had no son.
When I had no son, I did not grieve.
Now my son is dead,
it is just the same as when I had no son.
Why should I grieve?'
I, your servant, was also once a son.
When I was a son, I did not grieve.
Now I have lost Rǔnán,
it is just the same as when I was an extra son in Liáng.
Why should I grieve?'"
The King of Qín did not think this was so.
He told Méng Ào, saying:
"Now,
when a single city of mine is besieged,
food loses its flavor for me,
and I find no ease upon my mat.
Now the Marquis of Yìng has lost territory,
yet he says he does not grieve.
Is this his true feeling?"
Méng Ào said:
"I beg to ascertain his true feelings."
Méng Ào then went to see the Marquis of Yìng,
and said:
"Ào wishes to die."
The Marquis of Yìng said:
"What do you mean?"
He said:
"The King of Qín regards you as his teacher,
there is no one under heaven who has not heard of it,
how much more so within the state of Qín!
Now, by virtue of my position, I have gained the role of general for the king,
commanding troops. I, your servant, consider Hán to be insignificant,
yet it has openly defied and attacked,
seizing your territory.
How then can Ào still live?
It would be better to die."
The Marquis of Yìng bowed to Méng Ào and said:
"I wish to entrust this matter to you, my lord."
Méng Ào reported this to King Zhāo.
From this time onward,
whenever the Marquis of Yìng spoke on matters concerning Hán,
the King of Qín would not listen,
because he considered him a captive of Rǔnán.
Qín attacked Hándān,
but for seventeen months could not take it.
Zhuāng said to Wáng Jī:
"Why do you not bestow rewards upon the army officers?"
Wáng Jī said:
"My relationship with the king
does not involve listening to the words of others."
Zhuāng said:
"That is not so.
Between father and son,
there are orders that will certainly be carried out,
and those that certainly will not.
Saying, 'Dismiss your noble wife,
sell your beloved concubine'—
this is an order that will certainly be carried out.
But then saying, 'Dare not think of them'—
this is an order that certainly will not be carried out.
An old woman guarding the village gate said,
'That evening,
so-and-so's young lady received such-and-such a gentleman inside.'
The noble wife had been dismissed,
the beloved concubine had been sold,
yet the heart could not forget them.
To wish to instruct someone,
the human heart inherently possesses [such desires].
Now, although you are favored by the king,
it does not surpass the closeness of father and son.
Although the army officers are lowly,
they are not inferior to an old woman guarding a village gate.
Moreover, you have long been accustomed to relying solely on the ruler and treating your subordinates with contempt.
I have heard it said:
'Three men create a tiger,
ten men can bend an iron pestle.
What many mouths shift,
flies without wings.'
Therefore I say,
it would be better to bestow rewards upon the army officers and treat them with courtesy."
Wáng Jī did not listen.
The army officers, in dire straits,
indeed maligned Wáng Jī and Dù Zhì,
accusing them of rebellion.
The King of Qín was greatly enraged,
and wished to execute Fàn Suī as well.
Fàn Suī said:
"I, your servant,
am a lowly man from the eastern borderlands.
Having offended Chǔ and Wèi,
I fled and came here seeking refuge.
I, your servant, had no support from the feudal lords,
nor any old acquaintances among your intimates.
Your Majesty raised me up from among the travelers and sojourners,
entrusting me with official duties.
All under heaven have heard of my person and Your Majesty's promotion of me.
Now, if by mischance or error I am deemed to share the heart of a criminal,
and Your Majesty openly executes me,
this would make Your Majesty's mistaken promotion manifest to all under heaven,
and become a subject of discussion among the feudal lords.
I beg to request poison and be granted death.
Bestow the favor of burying me with the honors of a minister of state.
Thus, Your Majesty will certainly not fail to punish my crime,
yet avoid the name of a mistaken promotion."
The King said:
"So be it."
He then did not kill him, but treated him well.
Cài Zé, having been driven out of Zhào,
entered Hán and Wèi.
On the road, he encountered robbers who seized his cooking pots and tripods.
Hearing that the Marquis of Yìng had employed Zhèng Ānpíng
and Wáng Jī,
both of whom had committed grave crimes,
and that the Marquis of Yìng felt ashamed within,
he then went west and entered Qín.
About to see King Zhāo,
he had someone spread declarations to provoke and anger the Marquis of Yìng, saying:
"The Yān guest Cài Zé
is a man of heroic prowess and great eloquence under heaven.
Once he sees the King of Qín,
the King of Qín will certainly make him chancellor and take away your position."
The Marquis of Yìng, hearing this,
sent someone to summon Cài Zé.
Cài Zé entered,
and merely bowed to the Marquis of Yìng.
The Marquis of Yìng was already displeased,
and when he saw him,
his manner was also arrogant.
The Marquis of Yìng therefore reproached him, saying:
"You have often declared
you would replace me as chancellor of Qín.
Is there such a thing?"
He replied:
"Yes."
The Marquis of Yìng said:
"I beg to hear your explanation."
Cài Zé said:
"Alas!
How late you are in seeing this.
Now the sequence of the four seasons
is that when one completes its task, it departs.
For a man to have strong hands and feet,
keen ears and eyes, and sagely wisdom—
is this not what a gentleman desires?"
The Marquis of Yìng said:
"Yes."
Cài Zé said:
To be steadfast in benevolence and uphold righteousness,
to practice the Way and bestow virtue upon all under heaven,
so that all under heaven cherish, delight in, respect, and love him,
and wish to make him their sovereign king—
is this not the hope of the eloquent and wise?"
The Marquis of Yìng said:
"Yes."
Cài Zé spoke again:
"Wealth, honor, prominence, and glory;
bringing order to the myriad things,
so that the myriad things each attain their proper place;
life, vitality, longevity, and long life,
ending one's years without premature death or injury;
all under heaven inheriting his tradition,
preserving his achievements,
transmitting them without end; name and substance pure and perfect,
his beneficent influence flowing for a thousand generations,
praised without cease,
lasting as long as all under heaven.
Is this not the fulfillment of the Way,
and what the sages call auspicious and good affairs?"
The Marquis of Yìng said:
"Yes."
Zé said:
"Such as Shāng Jūn of Qín,
Wú Qǐ of Chǔ,
and the Great Officer Zhǒng of Yuè—
their ends—were they also desirable?"
The Marquis of Yìng, knowing that Cài Zé wished to corner him with argument,
replied again:
"Why should they not be?
Now Gōngsūn Yāng served Duke Xiào,
exerting himself to the utmost without a second thought,
exhausting himself for the public good without turning to private gain.
He faithfully enforced rewards and punishments to achieve good governance,
expended all his wisdom and ability,
revealed his true feelings and sincerity,
bore resentment and blame,
deceived old friends,
and captured the Wèi prince Áng.
He ultimately became a general captured by Qin,
defeated the enemy army,
and expanded territory by a thousand li.
Wú Qǐ served King Dào of Chǔ,
ensuring that private interests did not harm public affairs,
slander did not obscure loyalty,
words were not spoken merely to curry favor,
actions were not taken just to gain acceptance,
and in upholding righteousness, he did not waver due to praise or slander.
He was certain to make his lord a hegemon and his state strong,
and did not shun misfortune or peril.
Minister Wén Zhǒng served the King of Yuè.
Though his lord faced hardship and disgrace,
he remained utterly loyal without slackening.
Even when his lord was on the verge of ruin,
he exhausted his abilities without abandoning him,
achieved many merits without boasting,
and despite wealth and honor, remained neither arrogant nor negligent.
These three men
reached the pinnacle of righteousness,
the utmost degree of loyalty.
Thus, a noble man may sacrifice his life to establish his name.
Where righteousness lies,
even if he dies,
there is no regret.
Why should this not be permissible?"
Cài Zé said:
"When the ruler is sage and the ministers are worthy,
it is the blessing of the world;
when the lord is enlightened and the ministers are loyal,
it is the blessing of the state;
when the father is kind and the son filial,
the husband trustworthy and the wife chaste,
it is the blessing of the family.
Thus, though Bǐgān was loyal,
he could not preserve Yīn;
though Wǔ Zǐxū was wise,
he could not preserve Wú;
though Shēnshēng was filial,
Jìn fell into confusion and chaos.
Having loyal ministers and filial sons,
yet the state perishes and falls into chaos—
why is this?
Because there were no enlightened rulers or worthy fathers to heed them.
Therefore, the world condemns their rulers and fathers,
and pities their ministers and sons.
If one must await death to establish loyalty and fame,
then Wēizǐ would be insufficiently benevolent,
Confucius insufficiently sage,
and Guǎn Zhòng insufficiently great."
Then Yìnghóu acknowledged this as good.
Seizing a brief opportunity,
Cài Zé then said:
"Shāng Jūn, Wú Qǐ, and Minister Wén Zhǒng—
as subjects,
they were utterly loyal and achieved merit—
this is indeed admirable.
Hóng Yāo served King Wén,
and the Duke of Zhōu assisted King Chéng—
were they not also loyal?
Judging by the relationship between ruler and minister,
between Shāng Jūn, Wú Qǐ, and Minister Wén Zhǒng,
and Hóng Yāo and the Duke of Zhōu,
which is more admirable?"
Yìnghóu said:
"Shāng Jūn, Wú Qǐ, and Minister Wén Zhǒng
are not their equals."
Cài Zé said:
"Then, your lord—
in kindness, benevolence, and trust in loyalty,
and in not betraying old acquaintances—
how does he compare to Duke Xiào of Qín, King Dào of Chǔ,
and the King of Yuè?"
Yìnghóu said:
"It is hard to say."
Cài Zé said:
"Your lord's closeness to loyal ministers
does not surpass that of Duke Xiào of Qín, the King of Yuè, or King Dào of Chǔ.
As for you, in serving your lord—
rectifying chaos, averting disasters, resolving crises,
expanding territory, increasing grain production,
enriching the state, satisfying the people, strengthening the ruler,
and spreading awe across the realm—
your achievements are renowned far and wide,
yet they do not surpass those of Shāng Jūn, Wú Qǐ, and Minister Wén Zhǒng.
But your rank, position, honor, and influence,
and the wealth of your private household exceed those three men.
Yet you do not retire—
I secretly fear for your peril.
As the saying goes:
'When the sun reaches its zenith, it must decline;
when the moon is full, it must wane.'
When things reach their peak, they decline—
this is the constant law of heaven.
Advancing and retreating, expanding and contracting, changing and transforming—
this is the constant way of the sage.
In the past,
Duke Huán of Qí assembled the feudal lords nine times,
bringing order to the world.
But at the meeting at Kuíqiū,
he showed an arrogant and complacent demeanor,
and nine states rebelled.
King Fūchāi of Wú, unmatched in the world,
looked down on the feudal lords,
bullied Qí and Jìn,
and thus met his death and the ruin of his state.
Xià Yù and Tàishǐ Qǐ could terrify three armies with their shouts,
yet they died at the hands of common men.
These all rode the crest of
supreme prosperity but failed to understand
the proper principles.
Now, Shāng Jūn, for Duke Xiào,
standardized weights,
regulated measures,
adjusted the light and heavy,
abolished the field boundaries,
taught the people farming and warfare.
Thus, when the army moved, territory expanded;
when the army rested, the state grew rich.
Therefore, Qín became invincible under heaven,
establishing its awe among the feudal lords.
But once his achievements were complete,
he was torn apart by chariots.
The land of Chǔ had a million spearmen,
yet Bái Qǐ led a force of tens of thousands
to battle Chǔ.
In one campaign, he took Yān and Yǐng;
in a second, he burned Yílíng.
To the south, he annexed Shǔ and Hàn;
crossing Hán and Wèi, he attacked powerful Zhào.
To the north, he buried the Mǎfú army,
slaughtering over four hundred thousand men.
Blood flowed into rivers,
the roar of boiling blood was like thunder,
enabling Qín to lay the foundation for empire.
From then on,
Zhào and Chǔ were cowed into submission,
daring not to attack Qín—
all due to Bái Qǐ's might.
The cities he personally subdued
numbered over seventy.
Yet once his achievements were complete,
he was ordered to die at Dùyóu.
Wú Qǐ, for King Dào of Chǔ, dismissed the incompetent,
abolished the useless,
cut redundant offices,
blocked private solicitations,
unified the customs of Chǔ,
attacked Yángyuè to the south,
annexed Chén and Cài to the north,
shattered the horizontal and dispersed the vertical alliances,
leaving itinerant persuaders with no opening for their words.
Once his achievements were complete,
he was ultimately torn limb from limb.
Minister Wén Zhǒng, for the King of Yuè,
cleared wilderness, founded settlements,
opened land, and increased grain production.
Leading men from all quarters,
harnessing the strength of high and low,
he captured strong Wú
and achieved hegemonic success.
Yet Gōu Jiàn finally forced him to suicide.
These four men,
having achieved success but not withdrawing,
met disaster as a result.
This is what is called being able to stretch but not contract,
able to go forward but not turn back.
Fàn Lǐ understood this,
transcended worldly affairs to avoid the age,
and lived long as Táo Zhūgōng.
Have you not observed gamblers?
Some want to stake everything on a big throw,
others want to share the winnings.
These are things you clearly know.
Now, as prime minister of Qín,
your plans are made without leaving your mat,
your strategies formed without leaving the court.
Sitting, you control the feudal lords.
Benefits extend to Sānchuān,
enriching Yíyáng.
You have opened the perilous Yángcháng pass,
blocked the mouth of Tàiháng,
cut the roads of Fàn and Zhōngháng,
built a thousand li of plank roads in Shǔ and Hàn,
making all under heaven fear Qín.
Qín's desires are fulfilled,
your achievements have reached their peak.
This is also the time for Qín to share the winnings!
If you do not retire now,
you will end up like Shāng Jūn, Lord Bái,
Wú Qǐ, and Minister Wén Zhǒng.
Why not return the prime minister's seal at this time,
yielding it to a worthy to receive?
You will surely have the integrity of Bóyí;
remaining Yìnghóu for life,
called 'the solitary one' for generations,
and enjoy the longevity of Wáng Qiáo and Chīsōngzǐ.
How does this compare to ending in disaster?
Which will you choose?"
Yìnghóu said:
"Excellent."
He then invited him in to sit as an honored guest.
Several days later,
he entered the court,
and spoke to King Zhāo of Qín:
"There is a newly arrived guest from east of the mountains,
Cài Zé.
This man is a skilled debater.
I have seen many people,
but none compare to him;
I am not his equal."
King Zhāo of Qín summoned him for an audience,
spoke with him,
was greatly pleased with him,
and appointed him as an "guest minister."
Yìnghóu then pleaded illness,
requesting to return his ministerial seal.
King Zhāo urged Yìnghóu to remain,
but Yìnghóu claimed his illness was severe,
and was thus relieved of his duties as chancellor.
King Zhāo, newly pleased with Cài Zé's strategies,
then appointed him as chancellor of Qín,
and to the east, annexed the Zhōu royal house.
Cài Zé served as chancellor to the King of Qín for several months.
Some people slandered him;
fearing execution,
he pleaded illness and returned the ministerial seal.
He was granted the title Gāngchéng Jūn.
He remained in Qín for over ten years,
serving King Zhāo,
King Xiàowén, and King Zhuāngxiāng,
and finally served the First Emperor.
He was sent by Qín as an envoy to Yān,
and within three years, Yān sent Crown Prince Dān to Qín as a hostage.
Qín captured Hànzhōng from Chǔ,
fought again at Lántián,
and heavily defeated the Chǔ army.
Hán and Wèi, hearing of Chǔ's distress,
then launched a southern raid, reaching Dèng.
The King of Chǔ withdrew his forces and returned.
Later, the three states plotted to attack Chǔ,
but feared Qín would come to its rescue.
Someone advised Xuē Gōng:
"You could send an envoy to inform Chǔ, saying:
'Now the armies of the three states are about to leave Chǔ.
If Chǔ can respond and join us in attacking Qín,
then even Lántián would not be hard to obtain!
How much more so Chǔ's former territories?'
Chǔ will doubt that Qín will necessarily rescue it,
and now that the three states speak of withdrawing,
Chǔ's response will certainly be vigorous.
Thus, Chǔ and the three states will plot to draw out Qín's troops.
If Qín learns of this,
it will certainly not send rescue.
If the three states swiftly attack Chǔ,
Chǔ will certainly flee to Qín in desperation;
Qín will then be even more afraid to send out troops.
Then we will have separated Qín from Chǔ and attacked Chǔ;
our military action will surely succeed."
Xuē Gōng said:
"Excellent."
He then sent an important envoy to Chǔ,
and Chǔ's response was indeed vigorous.
Thereupon, the three states joined forces to attack Chǔ.
Chǔ indeed appealed to Qín for urgent help,
but Qín then did not dare to send out troops.
The great minister achieved merit.
Xuē Gōng entered Wèi
and expelled the woman from Qí.
Hán Chūn said to the King of Qín:
"Why not take her as your wife,
and use Qí and Qín to pressure Wèi?
Then Shàngdǎng
will belong to Qín.
If Qí and Qín join forces and install Fùchú,
once Fùchú is installed,
with his mother in Qín,
then Wèi will be a county of Qín.
Wěn wishes to use Qí and Qín to pressure Wèi and distress Xuē Gōng;
Zuǒ wishes to secure his younger brother's position.
I ask to act for Your Majesty through Wěn and Zuǒ.
Wèi, in fear, will restore her,
and Fùchú will certainly have Wèi serve Qín for generations.
The woman from Qí, having entered Wèi, will resent Xuē Gōng,
and will in the end use Qí to serve Your Majesty."
Three states attacked Qín
and entered Hángǔ.
The King of Qín said to Lóu Huǎn:
"The armies of the three states have penetrated deep.
I wish to cede Hédōng and seek peace."
He replied:
"To cede Hédōng
is a great cost;
but to be spared from a national calamity
is a great benefit.
This is a matter for the elders of the state.
Why does Your Majesty not summon Gōngzǐ Chí and ask him?"
The king summoned Gōngzǐ Chí and asked him.
He replied:
"To make peace, you will regret it;
not to make peace, you will also regret it."
The king said:
"Why is that?"
He replied:
"If Your Majesty cedes Hédōng and makes peace,
though the three states will withdraw,
Your Majesty will certainly say:
'What a pity!
The three states were about to leave,
and I specifically gave them three cities.'
This is the regret of making peace.
If Your Majesty does not make peace,
and the three states enter Hángǔ,
Xiányáng will certainly be in danger.
Your Majesty will then say:
'What a pity!
I cherished three cities and did not make peace.'
This is the regret of not making peace."
The king said:
"Since I will regret it either way,
I would rather regret losing three cities
than regret endangering Xiányáng.
I have decided to make peace."
He finally sent Gōngzǐ Chí to negotiate peace with the three states using three cities,
and their armies then withdrew.
King Zhāo of Qín said to his attendants:
"Today's Hán and Wèi,
compared to their beginnings, which is stronger?"
They replied:
"They are not as strong."
The king said:
"Today's Rú'ěr and Wèi Qí,
compared to Mèngcháng
and Máng Mǎo in worthiness?"
They replied:
"They are not as worthy."
The king said:
"With the worthiness of Mèngcháng and Máng Mǎo,
leading the strong armies of Hán and Wèi to attack Qín,
they still could do nothing to me!
Now with the incompetent Rú'ěr and Wèi Qí,
leading the weak Hán and Wèi to attack Qín,
their inability to do anything to me
is even clearer!"
The attendants all said:
"Very much so."
Zhōngqī pushed aside his qín and replied:
"Your Majesty's assessment of the world
is mistaken.
In the past, during the time of the six Jìn families,
the Zhì clan was the strongest.
It destroyed and defeated the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans,
and led Hán and Wèi to besiege Zhào Xiāngzǐ in Jìnyáng.
They diverted the Jìn River to flood Jìnyáng,
and the city walls were only three planks from being submerged.
Zhì Bó went out to inspect the water,
with Hán Kāngzǐ driving his chariot,
and Wèi Huánzǐ riding as attendant.
Zhì Bó said:
'At first, I did not know that water could destroy a state;
now I know it.
The Fén River could easily flood Ānyì,
the Jiàng River could easily flood Píngyáng.'
Wèi Huánzǐ nudged Hán Kāngzǐ with his elbow,
Hán Kāngzǐ stepped on Wèi Huánzǐ's foot,
treading on his heel.
Elbow and foot connected on the chariot,
and the Zhì clan was divided.
He died, his state perished,
and became the laughingstock of the world.
Now the strength of Qín
cannot surpass that of Zhì Bó;
Hán and Wèi, though weak,
are still more worthy than they were under Jìnyáng.
This is precisely the time when they are using their elbows and feet.
I hope Your Majesty will not take it lightly."
Chǔ and Wèi fought at Xíngshān.
Wèi promised Qín Shàngluò,
to sever Qín from Chǔ.
Wèi was victorious in battle,
and Chǔ was defeated at Nányáng.
Qín demanded the promised reward from Wèi,
but Wèi did not give it.
Yíng Qiǎn said to the King of Qín:
"Why doesn't Your Majesty say to the King of Chǔ:
'Wèi promised me land,
but now that they have won the battle,
the King of Wèi has betrayed me.
Why doesn't Your Majesty meet with me?
Wèi fears an alliance between Qín and Chǔ,
and will surely give land to Qín.
Thus, Wèi will have defeated Chǔ but lost land to Qín;
this means Your Majesty is using Wèi's land to show favor to me,
and Qín will gain much wealth from Chǔ.
If Wèi is weak,
and does not cede land,
then Your Majesty can attack from the south,
and I will cut off their west,
and Wèi will surely be in danger.'"
The King of Qín said:
"Excellent."
He then relayed this to Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ publicly announced a meeting with Qín,
and the King of Wèi, hearing this, became fearful,
and offered Shàngluò to Qín.
The Chǔ envoy Jǐng Lǐ was in Qín,
and accompanied the King of Qín to meet the King of Wèi at the border.
Chǔ was angered by Qín's alliance,
and Zhōu Zuì said to the King of Chǔ:
"Wèi requested not to meet with Chǔ
and instead allied with Qín,
which is why Jǐng Lǐ met with them.
Our humble state is favorable to such meetings,
so Qí did not join the alliance."
The King of Chǔ thus did not punish Jǐng Lǐ
and felt grateful to Zhōu and Qín.
The King of Chǔ sent Jǐng Lǐ to Qín.
A guest said to the King of Qín:
"Jǐng Lǐ
is someone the King of Chǔ loves dearly,
so Your Majesty should detain him to bargain for land.
If the King of Chǔ agrees,
then we can obtain land without using troops;
if the King of Chǔ does not agree,
then kill Jǐng Lǐ,
and replace him with someone
less capable than Jǐng Lǐ.
This is a convenient plan."
The King of Qín then detained Jǐng Lǐ.
Jǐng Lǐ sent someone to persuade the King of Qín, saying:
"I see that Your Majesty's authority is slighted by the world,
and land cannot be obtained.
When I came as an envoy,
I heard that both Qí and Wèi are about to cede land to serve Qín.
The reason for this
is that Qín and Chǔ are brotherly states.
Now if Your Majesty detains me,
it will show the world that Qín has no Chǔ,
and why would Qí and Wèi value an isolated state?
If Chǔ knows that Qín is isolated,
they will not cede land,
and will instead form alliances with other states to plot against Qín,
and then the state will surely be in danger.
It would be better to release me."
The King of Qín then released him.
The King of Qín wanted to see Dùn Ruò,
but Dùn Ruò said:
"My principles do not allow me to bow in audience.
If Your Majesty can permit me not to bow,
then I will come.
If not,
then I will not see you."
The King of Qín agreed.
Then Dùn Zǐ said:
"In the world, there are those
who have the substance but not the name,
those who lack the substance but have the name,
and those who have neither the name nor the substance.
Does Your Majesty know of them?"
The King said:
"I do not."
Dùn Zǐ said:
"Those who have the substance but not the name
are merchants.
They lack the labor of plowing and weeding,
yet they have the substance of accumulated grain.
These are those who have the substance but not the name.
Those who lack the substance but have the name
are farmers.
They plow when the ground thaws,
and weed under the scorching sun,
yet they lack the substance of accumulated grain.
These are those who lack the substance but have the name.
Those who have neither the name nor the substance
are like Your Majesty.
You have been established as the ruler of ten thousand chariots,
yet you lack the name of filial piety;
you are supported by a thousand miles of land,
yet you lack the substance of filial piety."
The King of Qín became furious.
Dùn Ruò said:
"There are six warring states east of the mountains,
yet Your Majesty's authority does not extend over them,
but is instead suppressed by your mother.
I privately think this is not something Your Majesty should accept."
The King of Qín said:
"Can the states east of the mountains
be annexed?"
Dùn Zǐ said:
"Hán
is the throat of the world;
Wèi,
the chest and abdomen of the world.
If Your Majesty provides me with ten thousand gold
to travel,
and let me go to Hán and Wèi,
I will bring their key ministers to Qín,
and then Hán and Wèi will submit.
Once Hán and Wèi submit,
the world can be taken."
The King of Qín said:
"My state is poor,
and I fear I cannot provide it."
Dùn Zǐ said:
"The world is never without events,
and it is either vertical or horizontal alliances.
If the horizontal alliance succeeds,
then Qín will become emperor;
if the vertical alliance succeeds,
then Chǔ will become king.
If Qín becomes emperor,
the whole world will support and nourish you;
if Chǔ becomes king,
even if Your Majesty has ten thousand gold,
you will not be able to keep it for yourself."
The King of Qín said:
"Excellent."
He then provided ten thousand gold,
and sent Dùn Zǐ east to travel to Hán and Wèi,
to win over their generals and ministers.
He traveled north to Yān and Zhào,
and caused Lǐ Mù to be killed.
The King of Qí came to court,
and the four states submitted.
This was due to Dùn Zǐ's persuasion.
In the twentieth year of King Qǐngxiāng,
Bái Qǐ of Qín captured Chǔ's Xīlíng,
and also captured Yān, Yǐng, and Yílíng,
burning the tombs of the former kings.
The king moved northeast,
and took refuge in Chénchéng.
Chǔ was thus weakened,
and was looked down upon by Qín.
Then Bái Qǐ again led troops to attack.
There was a man from Chǔ named Huáng Xiē,
who was widely learned and well-informed,
and King Xiāng considered him eloquent,
so he sent him as an envoy to Qín.
He persuaded King Zhāo, saying:
"No state in the world is stronger than Qín and Chǔ.
Now I hear that Your Majesty intends to attack Chǔ.
This is like two tigers fighting
while a mangy dog benefits from their exhaustion.
It would be better to treat Chǔ well.
Allow me to explain.
I have heard:
'Things reach an extreme and then reverse,
as with winter and summer.
Reaching the extreme brings danger,
as with piling up chess pieces.'
Now Your Majesty's state occupies half the world,
with two borders,
something that has never existed
since the beginning of humanity for a state of ten thousand chariots.
The former kings, King Wén and King Zhuāng,
and Your Majesty yourself,
for three generations have not connected territory with Qí,
in order to cut off the key to vertical alliances.
Now Your Majesty has three times sent Shèng Qiáo to oversee affairs in Hán,
and Chéng Qiáo entered Yān from the north.
This shows that without using armor,
without extending military might,
you have gained a hundred miles of land.
Your Majesty can be said to be capable.
Your Majesty also raised troops to attack Wèi,
blockaded the gates of Dàliáng,
took Hénèi,
captured Yān, Suānzǎo, Xū, and Táorén.
The troops of Chǔ and Yān hovered but did not dare to confront you.
Your Majesty's achievements are also great."
The king rested his troops for two years,
then resumed the campaign,
capturing Pú, Yǎn, and Shǒuyuán,
bringing troops to the borders of Rén and Píng,
with Xiǎohuáng and Jìyáng fortifying their walls,
and the state of Wèi submitted.
The king further cut off the northern parts of Pú and Mò, attaching them to Yān,
severed the vital routes between Qí and Qín,
and broke the backbone of Chǔ and Wèi.
The five alliances and six gatherings of the world dared not come to their rescue,
and the king's might was thus feared.
If the king can maintain his achievements and uphold his authority,
reduce the desire for aggression and enrich the sincerity of benevolence and righteousness,
ensuring no future calamities,
then the Three Kings would not be enough to make four,
and the Five Hegemons would not be enough to make six.
"If the king relies on the multitude of his people,
the strength of his weapons and armor,
and seeks to destroy the might of Wèi in one blow,
desiring to subdue the lords of the world by force,
I fear there will be future calamities.
The Book of Songs says:
'Nothing is without a beginning,
but few things reach their end.'
The Book of Changes says:
'The fox wets its tail.'
This means that beginnings are easy,
but endings are difficult.
How do we know this is so?
The Zhì clan saw the benefit of attacking Zhào,
but did not foresee the disaster at Yúcì;
Wú saw the advantage of attacking Qí,
but did not know
of the defeat at Gānsuì.
These two states,
though not without great achievements,
were lured by profit in the front,
only to exchange it for calamity in the rear.
Wú trusted Yuè,
and thus attacked Qí,
and though they defeated the people of Qí at Àilíng,
upon returning, the king of Wú was captured by the king of Yuè at the banks of the Sānjiāng.
The Zhì clan trusted Hán and Wèi,
and thus attacked Zhào,
besieging the city of Jìnyáng,
and victory seemed imminent,
but Hán and Wèi turned against them,
killing Zhì Bó Yáo
atop the Zāotái.
Now the king resents that Chǔ has not been destroyed,
but forgets that destroying Chǔ will strengthen Wèi.
I consider this unwise for Your Majesty.
The Book of Songs says:
'The great warrior does not venture far from his home.'
From this perspective,
Chǔ is
an ally;
neighboring states are
enemies.
The Book of Songs says:
'Others have intentions,
which I can surmise.
The leaping hare,
meets the hound and is caught.'
Now the king midway
trusts that Hán and Wèi are well-disposed toward the king,
this is exactly like Wú trusting Yuè.
I have heard,
enemies cannot be taken lightly,
and opportunities cannot be lost.
I fear that Hán and Wèi's humble words and concerns are
actually deceiving the great state.
Why is this?
The king has neither accumulated virtue
toward Hán and Wèi over generations,
but rather generations of resentment.
Fathers, sons, and brothers of Hán and Wèi have fallen
in succession to Qín,
for a hundred generations.
Their states are ruined,
their altars of soil and grain destroyed,
their ancestral temples collapsed,
their bellies slit and jaws broken,
heads and bodies separated,
bones exposed in the marshes,
skulls fallen,
scattered across the borders;
fathers, sons, the old and weak taken captive,
following one another on the roads;
ghosts and spirits wander with no offerings,
the people have no means to live,
clans are scattered,
exiles become servants and concubines,
filling the land.
If Hán and Wèi do not perish,
they will be a worry for Qín's altars of soil and grain.
Now the king's attack on Chǔ,
is this not a mistake!
When the king attacks Chǔ,
then how will the troops be dispatched?
Will the king borrow the road
from the hostile Hán and Wèi!
On the day the troops set out
the king will worry they do not return,
for the king is lending troops
to the hostile Hán and Wèi.
If the king does not borrow the road from the hostile Hán and Wèi,
he must attack Yáng and Yòurǎng.
But Yáng and Yòurǎng,
these are vast rivers and great waters,
mountains, forests, streams, and valleys, barren lands,
even if the king possesses them,
it is not gaining territory.
Thus the king gains the reputation of destroying Chǔ,
but not the reality of gaining land.
Moreover, when the king attacks Chǔ,
the four states will surely rise in response to aid the king.
When Qín and Chǔ are locked in conflict and do not separate,
Wèi will send troops to attack Liú,
Fāngyǔ, Zhì, Húlíng,
Dàng, Xiāo, and Xiàng,
and the former Sòng will be entirely taken.
The people of Qí facing south,
the north of Sì will surely be seized.
These are all flat plains accessible in all directions,
fertile lands,
yet the king lets them attack alone.
The king destroys Chǔ only to enrich Hán and Wèi in the central states and strengthen Qí,
Hán and Wèi's strength will be enough
to rival Qín.
Qí, with Sì as its southern border,
the sea to the east,
the Hé River to the north,
and no future calamities,
among the states of the world,
none is stronger than Qí.
Qí and Wèi, gaining land and preserving advantages,
and pretending to serve the lower officials,
within a year,
if they cannot become emperors themselves,
they will have more than enough
to prevent the king from becoming emperor.
With the king's vast territory,
multitude of people,
and strength of arms,
once the masses are mobilized and focused on Chǔ,
forcing Hán and Wèi to submit,
and ceding imperial authority to Qí,
this is the king's miscalculation.
"I consider for the king,
nothing is better than befriending Chǔ.
If Qín and Chǔ unite as one,
and press upon Hán,
Hán will surely surrender.
The king, with the perilous terrain east of the mountains as his lapels,
and the advantages of the Hé River's bends as his belt,
Hán will surely become the sentinel within the passes.
If so,
the king with ten thousand troops at Zhèng,
Liáng will be terrified,
Xǔ and Líng will fortify their walls,
and Shàngcài and Zhàolíng will cease communication.
Thus,
Wèi too will become a sentinel within the passes.
Once the king befriends Chǔ,
and the two lords of ten thousand chariots within the passes focus on Qí,
Qí's right territory can be taken with folded hands.
Thus the king's land will stretch from one sea to the other,
controlling the vital points of the world.
Then Yān and Zhào will have no Qí and Chǔ,
and Qí and Chǔ will have no Yān and Zhào.
Then threatening Yān and Zhào,
and controlling Qí and Chǔ,
these four states
will submit without needing to be pained."
Someone argued for the six states to persuade the king of Qín, saying:
"Vast territory does not ensure safety,
nor does a large population ensure strength.
If vast territory meant safety,
and a large population meant strength,
then the descendants of Jié and Zhòu would still exist.
In the past,
the Zhào clan was also once strong.
What was Zhào's strength like?
Raising the left hand subdued Qí,
raising the right hand subdued Wèi,
suppressing the states of ten thousand chariots,
these two states,
were like the thousand-chariot state of Sòng.
They built Gāngpíng,
and Wèi had no eastern fields;
no one dared to even glance at the eastern gate while gathering firewood or grazing animals.
At that time,
Wèi was in more danger than a stack of eggs,
and the scholars of the world followed one another in planning, saying:
'Shall we return our pledges of allegiance
and pay court to the lord of Hándān!'
Thus, when anyone in the world spoke of attacking Hándān,
none failed to have the order carried out at dawn.
When Wèi attacked Hándān,
they subsequently retreated and held a meeting at Féngzé,
riding in summer carriages,
calling themselves the Summer Kings,
and paying court to the Son of Heaven,
so that all under heaven followed them.
When Tàigōng of Qí heard of this,
he raised troops and attacked Wèi,
splitting its territory in two,
and putting the state in great peril.
The King of Liáng personally embraced the jade tablet and held the jade disc,
begging to become a subject of Lord Chén,
and only then did the world release Liáng.
When King Wēi of Yǐng heard of this,
he could not sleep at night,
and had no appetite for food;
he led the common people of the world
to meet Shēn Zhuó at the banks of the Sìshuǐ,
and greatly defeated Shēn Zhuó.
When the people of Zhào heard of it, they advanced to Zhīsāng;
when the people of Yān heard of it, they advanced to Gédào.
Gédào was blocked,
and peaceful relations were severed.
Qí was defeated in battle and could not win,
and in planning could gain nothing,
so they sent Chén Máo to lay down his sword and shield,
submit to the south and accept blame,
persuade Zhào in the west,
and persuade Yān in the north,
explaining to their own people within,
and only then did the world release Qí together.
Thus, by accumulating the thin
to make it thick,
and gathering the little to make it much,
they spoke with one voice of King Wēi of Yǐng
in the narrow spaces between the weft threads.
How could I say that King Wēi of Yǐng's governance declined
and his plans fell into chaos, leading to this?
It was because Yǐng was strong,
and loomed over the feudal lords of the world,
that the world took pleasure in attacking it!"
He said to the King of Qín:
"I am privately puzzled that Your Majesty belittles Qí, takes Chǔ lightly,
and treats Hán with contempt.
I have heard that
a king whose troops are victorious does not become arrogant,
and a hegemon who makes covenants does not become resentful.
Victorious without arrogance,
thus he can subdue the age;
covenanting without resentment,
thus he can win over his neighbors.
Now Your Majesty extends virtue to Wèi and Zhào,
but lightly loses Qí—
this is arrogance;
victorious at Yíyáng,
you do not cherish the friendship with Chǔ—
this is resentment.
Arrogance and resentment are not the enterprise of a hegemon.
I privately worry for Your Majesty
and do not consider this acceptable."
"The Book of Songs says:
'There is none that does not have a beginning,
but few are able to have an end.'
Thus what the former kings valued
was precisely the beginning and the end.
How do we know this is so?
Long ago, Zhì Bóyáo destroyed Fàn and Zhōngháng,
besieged and pressed Jīnyáng,
and in the end became the laughingstock of the three families;
King Fūchāi of Wú cornered Yuè at Kuàijī,
defeated Qí at Àilíng,
held a meeting at Huángchí,
showed disrespect to Sòng,
and was subsequently captured by Gōujiàn,
dying at Gānsuì;
Lord Liáng attacked Chǔ and defeated Qí,
controlled the troops of Zhào and Hán,
drove the twelve feudal lords to pay court to the Son of Heaven at Méngjīn,
but later his son died,
and he himself wore a cloth cap and was detained in Qín.
These three were not without achievements,
but they could begin and could not end.
Now Your Majesty has broken Yíyáng,
devastated Sānchuān,
and made the scholars of the world dare not speak;
you have blocked the states of the world,
shifted the borders of the two Zhōu,
and the rulers of the age dare not communicate at the pass of Yánghóu;
you have taken Huángjí,
and the troops of Hán and Chǔ dare not advance.
If Your Majesty can carry this to the end,
then the Three Kings would be insufficient to make four,
and the Five Hegemons insufficient to make six.
If Your Majesty cannot carry this to the end,
and there are later troubles,
then I fear the lords of the feudal states,
and the scholars of the Hé and Jì rivers,
will regard Your Majesty as doing what Wú and Zhì did.
"The Book of Songs says:
'One who travels a hundred li regards ninety as half.'
This speaks of the difficulty of the final stretch.
Now Your Majesty shows signs of arrogance,
and in my heart, observing it,
