in the affairs of the world,
according to the hearts of the rulers of the age,
if it is not Chǔ that suffers attack,
it will surely be Qín.
How do we know this is so?
The people of Qín aid Wèi to resist Chǔ,
the people of Chǔ aid Hán to resist Qín;
the troops of the four states are matched,
and they have not yet been able to fight again.
Qí and Sòng are outside the inked line, acting as a counterweight;
thus it is said that whoever first gains Qí and Sòng will attack Qín.
If Qín first gains Qí and Sòng,
then the Hán clan will be weakened;
if the Hán clan is weakened,
then Chǔ will be isolated and suffer attack.
If Chǔ first gains Qí,
then the Wèi clan will be weakened;
if the Wèi clan is weakened,
then Qín will be isolated and suffer attack.
If you follow this plan and act accordingly,
then these two states will surely become the laughingstock of the world."
The King of Qín and Zhōng Qí were arguing,
and he could not win.
The King of Qín was greatly angered,
and Zhōng Qí walked slowly away.
Someone spoke to the King of Qín on Zhōng Qí's behalf, saying:
"He is a fierce man.
It is because Zhōng Qí happened to encounter an enlightened ruler;
if he had encountered a Jié or Zhòu,
he would surely have been killed."
The King of Qín therefore did not punish him.
Xiàn Zé said to Gōngsūn Xiāo:
"You, sir, are honored among the great ministers,
and have repeatedly campaigned with merit.
The reason you have not become chancellor
is that the Queen Dowager does not favor you.
As for Xīn Róng,
he is someone the Queen Dowager is close to.
Now he has fled to Chǔ,
and is in Eastern Zhōu.
Why don't you, with the weight of Qín and Chǔ behind you,
support him and make him chancellor in Zhōu?
Chǔ will surely find it convenient.
Thus Xīn Róng will have the weight of Qín and Chǔ,
the Queen Dowager will surely be pleased with you,
and you will surely become chancellor."
Lóu made a covenant between Qín and Wèi,
with the crown prince of Wèi as a hostage,
and Fēn Qiáng wanted to ruin it.
He said to the Queen Dowager:
"States are about reciprocity;
if we ruin Qín and benefit Wèi,
Wèi is sure to betray us.
On the day Wèi betrays Qín,
the crown prince will be as dung."
The Queen Dowager sat with the king and wept.
The king therefore became suspicious of the crown prince,
and ordered him to remain at Suānzǎo.
Lóu was troubled by this.
Zhāo Yǎn was going to Liáng for Zhōu,
and Lóu told him about it.
Zhāo Yǎn had an audience with the King of Liáng,
and the King of Liáng said:
"What news have you heard?"
He said:
"I have heard that Qín is about to attack Wèi."
The king said:
"We have set a date
and made a covenant with me."
He said:
"Qín suspects Your Majesty's covenant,
and because the crown prince remains in Suānzǎo
and does not go to Qín.
The King of Qín's plan is:
'If Wèi does not ally with me,
it will certainly attack me;
rather than staying here
and waiting to be attacked,
it would be better to strike first.'
With Qín's strength, if it humbles itself to ally with other states,
I fear it will harm Eastern Zhōu."
Lǚ Bùwéi of Púyáng, trading in Hándān,
saw the Qín hostage Yìrén,
and upon returning said to his father:
"How many times greater is the profit from farming?"
He said:
"Ten times."
"How many times greater is the profit from pearls and jade?"
He said:
"A hundred times."
"How many times greater is the profit from establishing a ruler of a state?"
He said:
"Countless."
He said:
"Now, toiling strenuously in the fields,
one cannot obtain warm clothes and surplus food;
now, establishing a state and setting up a ruler,
the benefits can be passed down for generations.
I wish to devote myself to this."
The Qín prince Yìrén was a hostage in Zhào,
residing in the city.
So he went to persuade him, saying:
"Zǐxī has the inheritance of the state,
and also has his mother at court.
Now you have no mother at court,
and are entrusted abroad
to an unpredictable state.
If one day the covenant is broken,
your body will become dust.
Now if you heed my plan,
seek to return,
you can possess Qín.
I will go to Qín on your behalf,
and they will certainly come to request you."
Then he persuaded Yángquán Jūn, the brother of the Queen of Qín, saying:
"Your crime is punishable by death,
do you know it?
All under your gate hold high and noble positions,
while none under the crown prince are honored.
Your treasury is filled with pearls and precious jades,
your fine horses fill the outer stables,
and beautiful women fill the rear chambers.
The King is advanced in years;
one day when the mountain crumbles,
and the crown prince takes power,
your danger
will be like piled eggs,
and your life shorter than a morning bloom.
I have a plan that can, in one stroke,
make you wealthy and noble for ten thousand years,
as secure as Mount Tài supported on four sides,
and certainly free from the peril of ruin."
Yángquán Jūn rose from his mat,
and requested to hear his plan.
Bùwéi said:
"The King is advanced in years,
and the Queen has no son.
Zǐxī has the inheritance of the state,
and Shì Cāng assists him.
When one day the mountain crumbles,
and Zǐxī ascends,
with Shì Cāng in power,
the Queen's gate
will surely grow wild grasses.
Zǐ Yìrén is a man of worthy talent,
abandoned in Zhào,
with no mother at court,
craning his neck to gaze west,
longing to return just once.
If the Queen sincerely requests
and establishes him,
then Zǐ Yìrén will gain a state though he had none,
and the Queen will gain a son though she had none."
Yángquán Jūn said:
"Indeed."
He entered and persuaded
the Queen,
and the Queen then requested Zhào to send him back.
Zhào had not yet sent him,
so Bùwéi persuaded Zhào, saying:
"Zǐ Yìrén
is a favored son of Qín,
with no mother at court.
The Queen wishes to take him as her son.
If Qín intended to slaughter Zhào,
it would not spare a single son to maintain strategy;
this is holding an empty hostage.
If Zǐ Yìrén returns and is established,
and Zhào sends him off with generous gifts,
he will not dare to betray virtue and reject kindness;
this will create goodwill on its own.
The King of Qín is old;
one day when his carriage rests,
even with Zǐ Yìrén,
it will not suffice to bind Qín."
Zhào then sent him.
When Yìrén arrived,
Bùwéi had him dress in Chǔ attire for the audience.
The Queen was pleased with his appearance,
and admired his wisdom, saying:
"I am from Chǔ."
And she took him as her son,
changing his name to Chǔ.
The King had him recite,
and he said:
"I was abandoned abroad from a young age,
and never had a tutor for instruction;
I am not practiced in recitation."
The King dismissed it,
and let him stay.
On another occasion, he said:
"Your Majesty once halted your carriage in Zhào;
the heroes of Zhào,
those who became known were not few.
Now that Your Majesty has returned to the state,
they all gaze westward in hope.
If Your Majesty does not send a single envoy to inquire after them,
I fear they will all bear resentment.
They might cause the borders to close early and open late."
The King thought this reasonable,
and marveled at his plan.
The Queen urged his establishment.
The King then summoned the chancellor,
and ordered him, saying:
"Among my sons, none compares to Chǔ."
He was established as crown prince.
When Zǐ Chǔ ascended,
he made Bùwéi his chancellor,
bestowing the title Marquis Wénxìn,
with the fief of twelve counties in Lántián.
The Queen became Queen Dowager Huáyáng,
and the feudal lords all sent cities to Qín.
Marquis Wénxìn wished to attack Zhào
to expand Héjiān,
so he sent Gāngchéng Jūn Cài Zé to serve Yān
for three years,
and the crown prince of Yān became a hostage in Qín.
Marquis Wénxìn then requested Zhāng Táng
to be chancellor of Yān,
intending to join Yān in attacking Zhào,
to expand the territory of Héjiān.
Zhāng Táng declined, saying:
"To go to Yān, one must pass through Zhào;
if the people of Zhào capture me,
they will receive a hundred lǐ of land."
Marquis Wénxìn left displeased.
The young attendant Gān Luó said:
"Why is Your Lordship so displeased?"
Marquis Wénxìn said:
"I sent Gāngchéng Jūn Cài Zé to serve Yān for three years,
and the crown prince of Yān has already entered as a hostage.
Now I personally requested Zhāng Qīng to be chancellor of Yān,
but he refuses to go."
Gān Luó said:
"I will make him go."
Marquis Wénxìn scolded him away, saying:
"I tried myself and he refused;
how can you make him go?"
Gān Luó said:
"Xiàng Tuó was only seven years old
when he became Confucius's teacher;
now I am already twelve years old!
Your Lordship should try me;
why immediately scold me?"
Gān Luó went to see Zhāng Táng and said:
"Your achievements,
how do they compare to Wǔ'ān Jūn's?"
Táng said:
"Wǔ'ān Jūn's victories in battle and conquests,
are beyond count;
cities attacked and towns destroyed,
are beyond count.
My achievements are not equal to Wǔ'ān Jūn's."
Gān Luó said:
"Do you clearly know
that your achievements are not equal to Wǔ'ān Jūn's?"
He said:
"I know it."
"When Yìnghóu was employed by Qín,
how did his authority compare to that of Wénxìn Hóu?"
He replied:
"Yìnghóu was not as authoritative as Wénxìn Hóu."
He said:
"Do you clearly know
that he was not as authoritative as Wénxìn Hóu?"
He replied:
"I know it."
Gān Luó said:
"When Yìnghóu wanted to attack Zhào,
Wǔ'ān Jūn opposed it,
and seven lǐ from Xiányáng,
he was strangled and killed.
Now Wénxìn Hóu personally requests you to become minister of Yān,
yet you are unwilling to go.
I do not know where you will meet your death!"
Táng said:
"I ask to follow the young man's advice and go!"
He ordered the treasury to prepare carriages,
the stables to prepare horses,
and the storehouse to prepare gifts.
The departure date was set.
Gān Luó said to Wénxìn Hóu:
"Lend me five chariots,
and allow me to first report to Zhào on behalf of Zhāng Táng."
He met the King of Zhào,
and the King of Zhào welcomed him outside the city.
He said to the King of Zhào:
"Have you heard that Crown Prince Dān of Yān has entered Qín?"
He replied:
"I have heard of it."
"Have you heard that Zhāng Táng is becoming minister of Yān?"
He replied:
"I have heard of it."
"Crown Prince Dān of Yān entering Qín
means Yān does not deceive Qín.
Zhāng Táng becoming minister of Yān
means Qín does not deceive Yān.
If Qín and Yān do not deceive each other,
then attacking Zhào
would be perilous. The reason Qín and Yān do not deceive each other
is no other than
their desire to attack Zhào and expand Héjiān.
Now if Your Majesty grants me five cities to expand Héjiān,
I will request the return of Crown Prince Dān of Yān,
and ally with strong Zhào to attack weak Yān."
The King of Zhào immediately ceded five cities
to expand Héjiān,
and Crown Prince Dān of Yān was returned.
Zhào attacked Yān,
capturing thirty-six counties of Shànggǔ,
and gave one-tenth to Qín.
Wénxìn Hóu fled,
and went to Zhào with Sīkōng Mǎ,
who was appointed as Shǒuxiàng by Zhào.
Qín dispatched troops to attack Zhào.
Sīkōng Mǎ advised the King of Zhào:
"When Wénxìn Hóu was chancellor of Qín,
I served him,
as a Shàngshū,
and became familiar with Qín affairs.
Now Your Majesty has appointed me to a minor post,
and I have become familiar with Zhào affairs.
Allow me to outline for Your Majesty the war between Qín and Zhào,
and personally observe which side will win.
Which is larger, Zhào or Qín?"
He replied:
"Zhào is not as large."
"Which has more people?"
He replied:
"Zhào does not."
"Which is wealthier in money and grain?"
He replied:
"Zhào is not."
"Which state is better governed?"
He replied:
"Zhào is not."
"Which chancellor is more virtuous?"
He replied:
"Zhào's is not."
"Which generals are more martial?"
He replied:
"Zhào's are not."
"Which has clearer laws and decrees?"
He replied:
"Zhào does not." Sīkōng Mǎ said:
"If so, then in a hundred comparisons, Your Majesty's state
does not match Qín in any,
and Your Majesty's state will perish."
The King of Zhào said:
"You, sir, have not distanced yourself from Zhào,
and have fully instructed me in state affairs.
I wish to follow your plan."
Sīkōng Mǎ said:
"If Your Majesty cedes half of Zhào to bribe Qín,
Qín will obtain half of Zhào without drawing a blade,
and will surely be pleased.
Internally, Qín will fear Zhào's defenses,
and externally, it will fear rescue from the other states.
Qín will certainly accept it.
Once Qín accepts the land and withdraws its troops,
Zhào can preserve itself with the remaining half of the state.
Qín, emboldened by the bribe, will grow stronger,
and the states east of the mountains will surely fear;
the loss of Zhào will endanger them,
and the other states will certainly be alarmed.
Alarmed, they will rescue each other,
and then the alliance can be formed.
I ask Your Majesty to form a vertical alliance.
If the alliance succeeds,
then Your Majesty will nominally lose half of Zhào,
but in reality gain the support of the states east of the mountains to oppose Qín.
Qín will not be enough to cause Zhào's destruction."
The King of Zhào said:
"Previously, when Qín dispatched troops to attack Zhào,
Zhào bribed them with twelve counties of Héjiān,
yet our territory was reduced, our military weakened,
and we still could not avoid Qín's threats.
Now if we cede half of Zhào to strengthen Qín,
we will lack the strength to preserve ourselves and will perish as a result.
I wish you would propose another plan."
Sīkōng Mǎ said:
"I was once a minor clerk in Qín,
holding a lowly post despite my seniority,
and have never commanded troops.
I ask to lead all of Zhào's troops to confront Qín for Your Majesty."
The King of Zhào would not appoint him as general.
Sīkōng Mǎ said:
"I have offered my humble plan,
but Your Majesty does not adopt it.
This means I have no way to serve Your Majesty,
and I ask to take my leave."
Sīkōng Mǎ left Zhào,
crossing Píngyuán.
The official at Píngyuán Ford, Guō Yí, greeted him and asked:
"Qín troops are attacking Zhào,
and you, honored guest, have come from Zhào.
How are things in Zhào?"
Sīkōng Mǎ told him that he had advised the King of Zhào
but was not heeded,
and Zhào would surely perish.
The official of Píngyuán said:
"In your estimation, honored guest,
when will Zhào perish?"
Sīkōng Mǎ said:
"If Zhào appoints Wǔ'ān Jūn as general,
it will perish within a year;
if it kills Wǔ'ān Jūn,
it will perish within half a year.
Among the King of Zhào's ministers is a man named Hán Cāng,
who flatters
and ingratiates himself with the King of Zhào.
Their relationship is very close,
and he is a man who envies the worthy and resents meritorious ministers.
Now that the state is in peril and facing destruction,
the king will certainly follow his advice,
and Wǔ'ān Jūn will surely die."
Hán Cāng indeed slandered him,
and the king sent someone to replace him.
When Wǔ'ān Jūn arrived,
he had Hán Cāng enumerate his crimes, saying:
"General, after your victory,
the king toasted you.
When you offered a toast before him,
you held a dagger in your hand,
which is a capital offense."
Wǔ'ān Jūn said:
"I suffer from a hunched back,
with a large body and short arms,
unable to reach the ground.
When rising or bowing, I cannot show proper respect,
and I feared committing a capital offense before the king,
so I had a craftsman make a wooden support
to extend my arm.
If His Majesty does not believe me,
I ask to show it."
He took it from his sleeve,
and showed it to Hán Cāng.
It looked like a wooden armrest,
wrapped in cloth.
"I ask you, sir,
to explain this clearly to the king."
Hán Cāng said:
"I have received orders from the king
to grant you death, General.
There is no pardon.
I dare not speak further."
The Lord of Wu'an faced north, bowed twice, and accepted the death sentence.
He drew his sword to take his own life,
then said:
"A subject may not commit suicide within the palace."
He passed by Sīkōng Mǎ's gate,
moving with great haste,
and exited through the Chù Gate.
Raising his sword with his right hand to kill himself,
his arm was too short to reach,
so he held the sword in his mouth, pressed it against a pillar, and stabbed himself.
The Lord of Wu'an died.
In the fifth month, Zhào perished.
The Magistrate of Píngyuán, whenever he met the various lords,
would invariably say to them:
"Alas,
Sīkōng Mǎ!"
He also believed that Sīkōng Mǎ's expulsion from Qín
was not due to ignorance;
his departure from Zhào,
was not due to incompetence.
Zhào lost Sīkōng Mǎ and the state perished.
A state that perishes
does so not because it lacks worthy men,
but because it cannot employ them.
Four states united as one,
intending to attack Qín.
The King of Qín summoned sixty of his ministers and guests
and questioned them, saying:
"Four states have united as one,
intending to plot against Qín.
I am distressed within,
and the common people are exhausted without.
What should be done about this?"
None of the ministers responded. Yáo Jiǎ replied:
"I, Jiǎ, am willing to go on a mission to these four states.
I will certainly thwart their schemes,
and pacify their armies."
Thereupon, he was provided with a hundred chariots,
a thousand catties of gold,
clothed in the king's own garments,
and crowned and danced with the king's own sword.
Yáo Jiǎ took his leave and departed.
He thwarted their schemes,
halted their armies,
and established friendly relations with them, reporting this to Qín.
The King of Qín was greatly pleased.
Jiǎ was enfeoffed with a thousand households
and appointed as a senior minister.
Hán Fēi learned of this
and said:
"Jiǎ used pearls and precious treasures,
traveling south as an envoy to Jīng and Wú,
and north as an envoy between Yān and Dài.
For three years,
the alliance of the four states may not have been solidly formed,
yet the pearls and precious treasures were all exhausted within.
This shows that Jiǎ used Your Majesty's authority
and the state's treasures
to privately forge alliances with the feudal lords abroad.
I hope Your Majesty will investigate this.
Moreover, he is the son of a gatekeeper from Liáng,
who once stole in Liáng,
served in Zhào and was expelled.
To employ the son of a generation of gatekeepers,
a great thief of Liáng,
an expelled minister of Zhào,
and to share with him plans for the altars of state,
is not the way to encourage the ministers."
The king summoned Yáo Jiǎ and asked him:
"I have heard that you used my wealth
to form alliances with the feudal lords.
Is this true?"
He replied:
"It is true."
The king said:
"What face do you have to see me again?"
He replied:
"Zēng Shēn was filial to his parents,
and all under heaven wished him to be their son;
Wǔ Zǐxū was loyal to his lord,
and all under heaven wished him to be their minister;
a chaste woman skilled in crafts,
and all under heaven wished her to be their consort.
Now I, Jiǎ, am loyal to the king, but the king does not know it.
If I, Jiǎ, had not returned from the four states,
where else would I go?
If I, Jiǎ, were not loyal to my lord,
why would the kings of the four states still employ my person?
Jié listened to slander and executed his good generals;
Zhòu heard slander and killed his loyal ministers,
leading to their own deaths and the destruction of their states.
Now if Your Majesty listens to slander,
then there will be no loyal ministers left."
The king said:
"You are the son of a gatekeeper,
a great thief of Liáng,
an expelled minister of Zhào."
Yáo Jiǎ said:
"Tàigōng Wàng [Lǚ Shàng]
was a man expelled from Qí,
a failed butcher of Zhāogē,
a minister expelled by Zǐliáng,
an enemy at Jíjīn who found no employment,
yet King Wén employed him and became king.
Guǎn Zhòng,
was a merchant from the outskirts,
a destitute recluse of Nányáng,
a prisoner released from Lǔ,
yet Duke Huán employed him and became hegemon. Bǎilǐ Xī,
a beggar from Yú,
was bought and sold for the price of five sheepskins,
yet Duke Mú made him minister
and made the Western Róng pay homage.
Duke Wén employed a thief from Zhōngshān,
and was victorious at Chéngpú.
These four men
all had disgrace and shame,
were greatly slandered under heaven,
yet enlightened rulers employed them,
knowing they could achieve merit.
If they had been like Biàn Suí, Wù Guāng, and Shēntú Dí,
how could a ruler have employed them!
Therefore, an enlightened ruler does not take their污点,
does not listen to their faults,
but examines whether they can be used for himself.
Thus, those who can preserve the altars of state—
even if there is external slander, he does not listen;
even if they have a lofty reputation in the world,
if they have not an inch of merit, he does not reward them.
Therefore, none of the ministers dare harbor empty hopes before their superior."
The King of Qín said:
"So it is."
He then reinstated Yáo Jiǎ and executed Hán Fēi.
King Wēi of Chǔ was victorious in battle at Xúzhōu,
and wished to expel Yīngzǐ from Qí.
Yīngzǐ was afraid.
Zhāng Chǒu said to the King of Chǔ:
"When Your Majesty was victorious at Xúzhōu,
Pànzǐ was not employed.
Pànzǐ had rendered service to the state,
and the common people were willing to be used by him.
Yīngzǐ was not good,
and employed Shēn Juàn.
Shēn Juàn—
the great ministers and the common people were unwilling to be used by him,
therefore Your Majesty defeated him.
Now if Yīngzǐ is expelled,
Pànzǐ will certainly be employed.
He will reorganize his officers and men to confront Your Majesty,
which will certainly not be to Your Majesty's advantage."
The King of Chǔ therefore did not expel him.
Qí was about to enfeoff Tián Yīng at Xuē.
The King of Chǔ heard of this,
became greatly angry,
and intended to attack Qí.
The King of Qí had thoughts of desisting.
Gōngsūn Hàn said:
"Whether the enfeoffment succeeds or not
does not lie with Qí,
but will again lie with Chǔ.
I, Hàn, will persuade the King of Chǔ,
making him desire Your Lordship's enfeoffment
even more than Qí does."
Yīngzǐ said:
"I wish to entrust this matter to you."
Gōngsūn Hàn spoke on his behalf to the King of Chǔ, saying:
"Lǔ and Sòng serve Chǔ, but Qí does not,
because Qí is large and Lǔ and Sòng are small.
Your Majesty only benefits from the smallness of Lǔ and Sòng,
but does not dislike the largeness of Qí—why is this?
Now Qí is ceding territory to enfeoff Tián Yīng;
this is the means by which it weakens itself.
I hope you will not stop it."
The King of Chǔ said:
"Good."
He therefore did not stop it.
Lord Jìngguō was about to fortify Xuē.
Many guests advised against it.
Lord Jìngguō told his receptionist
not to admit any more guests.
A man from Qí requested an audience, saying:
"I ask only to speak three words!
If I speak one word more,
I ask to be boiled."
Lord Jìngguō therefore granted him an audience.
The guest hurried forward and said:
"The sea's great fish."
Then he turned and ran away.
The lord said:
"The guest is still here."
The guest said:
"Your humble servant dares not treat death as a jest."
The lord said:
"No,
speak further."
He replied:
"Has my lord not heard of the great fish?
Nets cannot stop it,
hooks cannot pull it,
but if it flounders and loses the water,
then ants and crickets can take their pleasure with it.
Now this Qí,
is also your water.
If you long possess the protection of Qí,
what use is Xuē to you?
Even if you raise Xuē's walls up to the sky,
it would still be of no benefit."
The lord said:
"Good."
Then he stopped building the walls of Xuē.
Jìngguō Jūn said to the King of Qí:
"The accounts of the five offices,
one must not only listen to them daily
but also review them frequently."
The king said:
"I tire of hearing about the five."
And now he gave them to Jìngguō Jūn.
Jìngguō Jūn was fond of Qí Màobiàn.
Qí Màobiàn's character had many flaws,
and the disciples were displeased.
Shìwèi admonished Jìngguō Jūn about this,
but Jìngguō Jūn would not listen,
so Shìwèi took his leave and departed.
Mèngcháng Jūn also secretly tried to remonstrate,
but Jìngguō Jūn became greatly angry and said:
"Even if it means wiping out your kind,
and ruining my household,
if it can please Qí Màobiàn,
I would not refuse to do it."
Thereupon he housed him in the best quarters,
ordered his eldest son to serve him,
and had food brought morning and evening.
After several years,
King Wēi passed away,
and King Xuān ascended the throne.
Jìngguō Jūn's relations
were very poor with King Xuān,
so he took his leave and went to Xuē,
staying there together with Qí Màobiàn.
Not long after,
Qí Màobiàn bid farewell and set out,
requesting an audience with King Xuān.
Jìngguō Jūn said:
"The king is extremely displeased with Yīng,
if you go, you will surely meet your death there."
Qí Màobiàn said:
"I certainly do not seek to preserve my life,
I beg to go without fail."
Jìngguō Jūn could not stop him.
Qí Màobiàn traveled to Qí,
and when King Xuān heard of it,
he concealed his anger and waited for him.
Qí Màobiàn had an audience with King Xuān,
and the king said:
"You,
are the one whom Jìngguō Jūn listens to and loves!"
Qí Màobiàn said:
"Love, that he has,
but listening, that he does not.
When Your Majesty was still the crown prince,
I said to Jìngguō Jūn:
'The crown prince's appearance is unkind,
with a protruding chin and a pig-like gaze,
one like this will surely rebel.
It would be better to depose the crown prince,
and instead establish Jiāoshī, the infant son of Consort Wèi.'
Jìngguō Jūn wept and said:
'It cannot be,
I cannot bear it.'
If he had listened to me and done it,
he would certainly not have today's troubles.
This is the first instance.
As for Xuē,
Zhāoyáng requested
to exchange several times its land for Xuē,
and I also said:
'You must agree to it.'
Jìngguō Jūn said:
'I received Xuē from the former king,
even if I am disliked by the later king,
what would I alone say
to the former king!
Moreover, the former king's temple is in Xuē,
how could I give the former king's temple
to Chǔ!'
Again he would not listen to me.
This is the second instance."
King Xuān heaved a deep sigh,
moved in his countenance,
and said:
"Has Jìngguō Jūn's regard for me reached such an extent!
I was young,
and truly did not know this.
Will you, sir, for my sake,
bring Jìngguō Jūn here?"
Qí Màobiàn replied:
"I respectfully accept."
Jìngguō Jūn donned King Wēi's robes,
wore his sword and danced with it,
and King Xuān personally welcomed Jìngguō Jūn at the outskirts,
weeping at the sight of him.
When Jìngguō Jūn arrived,
he then requested that he become chancellor.
Jìngguō Jūn declined,
but with no alternative, he accepted.
After seven days,
he pleaded illness and firmly resigned.
Jìngguō Jūn could not refuse the resignation,
and after three days he consented.
At that time,
Jìngguō Jūn could truly be said to know how to judge men!
Because he knew how to judge men,
even when others criticized him
he was not deterred.
This is why Qí Màobiàn disregarded his own life,
took pleasure in hardship,
and hastened toward difficulty.
During the crisis at Hándān,
Zhào sought aid from Qí.
Lord Tián summoned his ministers
and consulted them, saying:
"Is it better to save Zhào
or not to save it?"
Zōuzǐ said:
"It is better not to save it."
Duàngān Lún said:
"If we do not save it,
then it will not be to our advantage."
Lord Tián said:
"Why is that?"
"If the Wèi clan annexes Hándān,
what advantage is that for Qí!"
Lord Tián said:
"Good."
Then he raised troops,
saying:
"Station the army in the outskirts of Hándān."
Duàngān Lún said:
"What I seek, whether advantageous or not,
is not this.
To save Hándān
by stationing the army in its outskirts
means Zhào will not be taken and Wèi will remain intact.
Therefore, it would be better to attack Xiānglíng to the south to exhaust Wèi.
Once Hándān is taken, we can take advantage of Wèi's exhaustion,
thus Zhào will be broken and Wèi weakened."
Lord Tián said:
"Good."
Then he raised troops and attacked Xiānglíng to the south.
In the seventh month,
Hándān was taken.
Qí then took advantage of Wèi's exhaustion,
and greatly defeated them at Guìlíng.
During the crisis at Nánliáng,
the Hán clan sought aid from Qí.
Lord Tián summoned his ministers
and consulted them, saying:
"Is it more expedient to save them early,
or to save them late?"
Zhāng Gài replied:
"If we save them late,
Hán will be broken and absorbed into Wèi,
so it is better to save them early."
Tián Chénsī said:
"That will not do.
Before the troops of Hán and Wèi are exhausted,
if we save them,
we will replace Hán and bear the brunt of Wèi's army,
only to end up taking orders from Hán instead.
Moreover, Wèi has the intention to crush Hán,
and when Hán sees it is about to perish,
it will surely appeal to Qí in the east."
If we secretly ally with the state of Hán,
and later take advantage of Wèi's decline,
then our state can be strengthened,
benefits can be gained,
and our reputation can be exalted."
Marquis Tián said:
"Excellent."
He then secretly informed the envoy from Hán and sent him back.
Hán, believing it had secured the exclusive support of Qí,
fought five battles and lost all five,
then turned east to plead with Qí for help.
Qí thereupon raised an army to attack Wèi,
decisively defeating them at Mǎlíng.
With Wèi broken and Hán weakened,
the rulers of Hán and Wèi, through Tián Yīng,
faced north and paid homage to Marquis Tián.
Chéng Hóu Zōu Jì was the chancellor of Qí,
while Tián Jì was the general.
They did not get along.
Gōngsūn Hàn said to Zōu Jì:
"Why don't you advise the king to campaign against Wèi?
If victorious,
it will be due to your strategy,
and you can claim the merit;
if the war is not won,
and Tián Jì fails to advance,
or survives the battle without fighting to the death,
he can be prosecuted for cowardice and executed."
Zōu Jì thought this reasonable,
so he persuaded the king to send Tián Jì to attack Wèi.
Tián Jì fought three battles and won all three.
Zōu Jì reported this to Gōngsūn Hàn,
who then sent a man carrying ten jin of gold
to go and consult a diviner in the marketplace,
saying:
"I am a man of Tián Jì.
He has fought three battles and won all three,
his prestige shakes the world.
He wishes to undertake a great enterprise—
is this auspicious or not?"
Once the diviner came out,
they had the man who posed as the diviner arrested,
and verified his words before the king.
Tián Jì then fled.
Tián Jì, as a general of Qí,
captured the crown prince Shēn of Liáng (Wèi),
and took Páng Juān prisoner.
Sūnzǐ said to Tián Jì:
"General, can you undertake a great enterprise?"
Tián Jì said:
"How so?"
Sūnzǐ said:
"General, do not disband your troops when you enter Qí.
Have your weary and weakened troops take the lead in guarding
the main passes.
The main passes are
narrow, winding paths,
where chariots can barely scrape past each other.
If you have your weary, weakened troops take the lead in guarding the main passes,
they will surely fight one against ten,
ten against a hundred,
and a hundred against a thousand.
Then, with Mount Tài at your back,
the Jǐ River to your left,
and Tiāntáng to your right,
have your heavy troops advance to Gāowǎn,
and send light chariots and swift cavalry to charge the Yōng Gate. If you do this,
then the ruler of Qí can be corrected,
and Chéng Hóu can be driven out.
Otherwise,
you will not be able to enter Qí."
Tián Jì did not listen,
and indeed did not enter Qí.
Tián Jì fled from Qí and went to Chǔ.
Zōu Jì replaced him as chancellor.
Qí feared that Tián Jì would use Chǔ's power to return to Qí.
Dù Hè said:
"I beg to remain in Chǔ."
He said to the King of Chǔ:
"The reason Zōu Jì is unfriendly toward Chǔ
is that he fears Tián Jì will use Chǔ's power to return to Qí.
Your Majesty should enfeoff Tián Jì south of the Yangtze River,
to show that Tián Jì will not return to Qí.
Then Zōu Jì will serve Chǔ diligently with the resources of Qí.
Tián Jì is a fugitive;
if he receives a fief,
he will certainly be grateful to Your Majesty.
If he returns to Qí,
he will surely use Qí to serve Chǔ.
This is the way to make use of both Jìs."
Chǔ indeed enfeoffed him south of the Yangtze.
Zōu Jì served King Xuān.
He recommended many people for office,
which displeased the king.
Yàn Shǒu was noble yet recommended few people,
and the king was pleased with him.
Zōu Jì said to King Xuān:
"Jì has heard that having one filial son
is not as good as having five filial sons.
Now, how many people has Shǒu recommended for office?"
King Xuān then considered Yàn Shǒu to be obstructing talent.
Zōu Jì was over eight chǐ tall,
with a handsome and striking appearance.
One morning, he dressed in his court robes and looked in the mirror,
asking his wife:
"Who is more handsome, I or Lord Xú of the north city?"
His wife said:
"You are extremely handsome.
How could Lord Xú compare to you!"
Lord Xú of the north city
was renowned as the most handsome man in the state of Qí.
Jì did not believe it himself,
so he asked his concubine:
"Who is more handsome, I or Lord Xú?"
The concubine said:
"How could Lord Xú compare to you!"
The next day, a guest came from outside,
and as they sat talking,
he asked the guest:
"Who is more handsome, I or Lord Xú?"
The guest said:
"Lord Xú is not as handsome as you!"
The following day,
Lord Xú came.
Jì looked at him closely
and thought himself inferior;
he looked in the mirror at himself
and felt he was far from comparable.
That evening,
he lay in bed pondering and said:
"My wife finds me handsome because she is partial to me;
my concubine finds me handsome because she fears me;
my guest finds me handsome because he seeks something from me."
Thereupon, he went to court to see King Wēi and said:
"I truly know I am not as handsome as Lord Xú.
Yet my wife is partial to me,
my concubine fears me,
and my guest seeks something from me—
all said I am more handsome than Lord Xú.
Now, the territory of Qí spans a thousand lǐ,
with one hundred and twenty cities.
The palace ladies and attendants
are all partial to Your Majesty;
the court ministers
all fear Your Majesty;
within the four borders,
there is none who does not seek something from Your Majesty.
From this perspective,
Your Majesty is greatly obscured!"
The king said:
"Well said."
He then issued an order:
"All ministers, officials, and commoners
who can point out my faults to my face
shall receive the highest reward;
those who submit written remonstrances to me
shall receive the middle reward;
those who criticize and discuss in public places,
and whose words reach my ears,
shall receive the lowest reward."
When the order was first issued,
ministers came forward to remonstrate,
and the courtyard was as crowded as a marketplace.
After several months,
they occasionally came forward intermittently.
After a full year,
even if they wished to speak,
there was nothing left to say.
When Yān, Zhào, Hán, and Wèi heard of this,
they all came to pay homage to Qí.
This is what is called winning victories in the court.
Qín sought passage through Hán and Wèi to attack Qí.
King Wēi of Qí sent Zhāngzǐ to lead troops and respond.
He confronted Qín's army
and encamped,
with envoys frequently passing between them.
Zhāngzǐ changed his army's flags and insignia
to mix with the Qín troops.
A scout reported
that Zhāngzǐ had defected to Qín with the Qí army,
but King Wēi did not respond.
Shortly thereafter,
the scout reported again
that Zhāngzǐ had surrendered the Qí army to Qín,
but King Wēi did not respond.
This happened three times.
An official requested:
"Those who report Zhāngzǐ's defeat
are different people but all say the same thing.
Why does Your Majesty not send generals to attack him?"
The king said:
"It is clear that he is not betraying me—
why should I attack him!"
After a short while,
news came that the Qí army had won a great victory,
and the Qín army was utterly defeated.
Thereupon, the King of Qín acknowledged himself as a vassal of the western border
and apologized to Qí.
The attendants asked:
"How did you know this would happen?"
He replied:
"Zhāngzǐ's mother, Qǐ, offended his father,
and his father killed her
and buried her beneath the horse stable.
When I appointed Zhāngzǐ as commander,
I encouraged him, saying:
'With your strength,
if you return with the army intact,
I will surely rebury your mother, the general's mother.'
He replied:
'It is not that I am unable to rebury my late mother.
My mother, Qǐ, offended my father.
My father died without giving me instruction.
To rebury my mother without my father's instruction
would be to deceive my deceased father.
Therefore, I dare not do so.'
If as a son he would not deceive his deceased father,
how could he as a minister deceive his living lord?"
Chǔ was about to attack Qí,
and Lǔ was allied with Chǔ,
which troubled the King of Qí.
Zhāng Gài said:
"I request to make Lǔ remain neutral."
He then went to see the Lord of Lǔ on behalf of Qí.
The Lord of Lǔ said:
"Is the King of Qí afraid?"
He replied:
"That is not something I know.
I have come to offer condolences to you."
The Lord of Lǔ said:
"Why condolences?"
He replied:
"Your strategy is mistaken.
You are not siding with the victor but with the one who will not win—
why is that?"
The Lord of Lǔ said:
"In your view, which will win, Qí or Chǔ?"
He replied:
"Even ghosts would not know."
"Then why are you offering condolences to me?"
He said:
"Qí
and Chǔ are evenly matched rivals.
Whether Lǔ joins or not makes no difference.
Why not instead order your troops
to join the side of the victor after the two states have fought?
If Chǔ wins a great victory over Qí,
its elite soldiers and selected troops will surely be decimated,
but its remaining forces will be enough to face the rest of the world.
If Qí wins,
its elite soldiers and selected troops will also be decimated.
If you then join your Lǔ troops with the victor after the battle,
the favor you confer will be immense,
and the gratitude you receive will also be immense."
The Lord of Lǔ agreed,
and personally withdrew his army.
Qín attacked Wèi,
and Chén Zhěn united the Three Jìn
and went east to tell the King of Qí:
"When the kings of ancient times waged war,
it was to rectify the world
and establish merit and fame,
for the sake of posterity.
Now, the mutual attacks among Qí, Chǔ, Yān, Zhào, Hán, and Liáng
—these six states—are excessive.
They are insufficient to establish merit and fame,
but are just enough to strengthen Qín and weaken themselves.
This is not the best strategy for the states east of the mountains.
What can endanger the states east of the mountains
is a strong Qín.
Instead of worrying about a strong Qín,
you exhaust and weaken each other in turn,
delivering both sides into Qín's hands.
This is what I consider the calamity for the states east of the mountains.
The world cuts itself up for Qín,
yet Qín does not even expend effort;
the world cooks itself for Qín,
yet Qín does not even provide the firewood.
How can Qín be so wise and the states east of the mountains so foolish?
I hope Your Majesty will consider this.
"The wars waged by the Five Emperors, Three Kings,
and Five Hegemons of ancient times
were against those without virtue.
Now, when Qín attacks the world, it is not so.
It inevitably seeks the opposite:
rulers must die in disgrace,
and the people must die as captives.
Now, the tears of Hán and Liáng have not yet dried,
but the people of Qí alone are not weeping.
It is not because Qí is dear
and Hán and Liáng distant,
but because Qí is far from Qín
while Hán and Liáng are near.
Now Qí is about to become near!
Now Qín intends to attack Liáng's Jiàng and Ānyì.
If Qín obtains Jiàng and Ānyì and advances east down the river,
it will surely use the river as its inner and outer line and attack Qí eastward,
seizing Qí all the way to the sea.
Facing south, it will isolate Chǔ, Hán, and Liáng;
facing north, it will isolate Yān and Zhào.
Qí will have no way to devise a strategy.
I hope Your Majesty will consider this carefully!
"Now the Three Jìn have already united,
renewing their brotherly covenant,
and have dispatched elite troops
to garrison Liáng's Jiàng and Ānyì.
This is a plan for ten thousand generations.
If Qí does not urgently send elite troops
to join the Three Jìn,
it will surely face future troubles.
If the Three Jìn unite,
Qín will certainly not dare to attack Liáng,
but will instead attack Chǔ to the south.
When Chǔ and Qín become entangled in conflict,
the Three Jìn, angered that Qí did not join them,
will surely attack Qí to the east.
This is what I mean by Qí certainly facing great troubles.
It would be better to urgently join forces with the Three Jìn."
The King of Qí respectfully agreed
and indeed joined forces with the Three Jìn.
Sū Qín formed a vertical alliance for Zhào
and persuaded King Xuān of Qí, saying:
"Qí has Tàishān to the south,
Lángyá to the east,
Qīnghé to the west,
and Bóhǎi to the north.
This is what is called a state fortified on all sides.
The territory of Qí spans two thousand lǐ,
with armored troops numbering several hundred thousand,
and grain piled high like hills.
Qí's chariots are excellent,
its five-family military system,
swift as arrows from a crossbow,
fierce as thunder and lightning in battle,
and dispersing like wind and rain.
Even when there is military service,
they have never crossed Tàishān,
traversed Qīnghé,
or ventured into Bóhǎi.
Línzī alone has seventy thousand households.
I have privately estimated that
even the lower households have three men each.
Three times seven is two hundred ten thousand—
without needing to conscript from distant counties,
the soldiers from Línzī
already number two hundred ten thousand.
Línzī is extremely wealthy and prosperous.
Its people all play the yú,
strum the sè,
strike the zhù, pluck the qín,
engage in cockfighting and dog racing,
play liùbó and kickballs;
on the roads of Línzī,
chariot hubs collide,
people's shoulders rub together,
connected lapels form curtains,
raised sleeves create canopies,
and sweat flung off becomes rain;
households are diligent and wealthy,
ambitions high and soaring.
With Your Majesty's wisdom and Qí's strength,
no one in the world can match you.
Yet now you face west and serve Qín—
I am privately ashamed for Your Majesty.
"Moreover, the reason Hán and Wèi fear Qín
is because they share borders with Qín.
When troops are deployed and confront each other,
within ten days at most,
the outcome of survival or destruction is decided.
If Hán and Wèi fight and defeat Qín,
their own troops will be half destroyed,
and their borders will be indefensible;
if they fight and do not defeat Qín,
destruction follows immediately.
This is why Hán and Wèi take fighting Qín seriously but readily become its vassals."
"Now, if Qin attacks Qí, it is not so.
It must pass through the lands of Hán and Wèi,
travel the road to Yángjìn,
and traverse the perilous path of Gāngfù,
where chariots cannot travel abreast,
nor horses run side by side.
With a hundred men guarding the pass,
a thousand cannot get through.
Even if Qin desires to advance deep,
it will look back like a wolf,
fearing that Hán and Wèi will plot against its rear.
Thus, it will be hesitant and fearful,
leaping high but not daring to advance.
That Qin cannot harm Qí is already clear.
If you do not deeply consider that Qin can do nothing to us,
yet wish to serve Qin facing west,
this is an error in the strategies of your ministers.
Now, without the reputation of serving Qin,
you can have the reality of a strong state.
I sincerely hope Your Majesty will give this some thought."
The King of Qí said:
"I am not clever,
but now you, my lord,
have instructed me with the teachings of the King of Zhào.
I respectfully offer my state to follow."
Zhāng Yí, advocating the Horizontal Alliance for Qin,
said to the King of Qí:
"Among the powerful states under heaven, none surpasses Qí.
Ministers, elders, and clans are prosperous, numerous, and joyful;
none surpasses Qí.
Yet those who strategize for Your Majesty
all speak for the moment
without considering the benefits for ten thousand generations.
Those who persuade Your Majesty to join the Vertical Alliance
must say that Qí has the strong Zhào to the west,
Hán and Wèi to the south,
and is a state backed by the sea,
with vast land and numerous people,
strong soldiers and brave warriors,
so even if there were a hundred Qins,
what could they do to us!
Your Majesty listens to their arguments
but does not examine their ultimate reality.
"Those advocating the Vertical Alliance form cliques and collude,
all claiming the Vertical Alliance is feasible.
I have heard that
Qí fought Lǔ three times,
and Lǔ won three times,
yet the state was endangered,
and ruin followed thereafter.
Although it had the name of victory,
it had the reality of ruin.
Why is this?
Because Qí was large and Lǔ was small.
Now, Zhào compared to Qin
is like Qí compared to Lǔ.
Qin and Zhào fought above the Hé and Zhāng rivers,
and Zhào fought twice and won twice against Qin;
they fought beneath Pānwú,
and Zhào fought twice and won twice against Qin.
After four battles,
Zhào lost several hundred thousand troops,
and Hándān barely remained.
Although it had the name of defeating Qin,
the state was ruined!
Why is this?
Because Qin was strong and Zhào was weak.
Now, Qin and Chǔ exchange marriages,
becoming brotherly states;
Hán presents Yíyáng,
Wèi offers Héwài,
Zhào comes to court at Miǎnchí,
ceding Héjiān to serve Qin.
If Your Majesty does not serve Qin,
Qin will drive Hán and Wèi to attack the southern lands of Qí,
order Zhào to cross the Héguān,
point to Bóguan,
and then Línzī and Jímò will not belong to Your Majesty.
Once the state is attacked,
even if you wish to serve Qin,
it will be impossible.
Therefore, I hope
Your Majesty will carefully consider this."
The King of Qí said:
"Qí is remote and secluded,
perched upon the Eastern Sea,
and has never heard of the long-term benefits for the state.
Now, our great guest has kindly instructed us,
and I offer my state to serve Qin."
He presented three hundred lǐ of fish and salt lands to Qin.
Hán and Qí were allied states.
Zhāng Yí, with Qin and Wèi, attacked Hán.
The King of Qí said:
"Hán
is our allied state.
If Qin attacks it,
we will rescue it."
Tián Chénsī said:
"Your Majesty's plan is mistaken;
it would be better to let it be.
Zǐ Kuài gave the state to Zǐ Zhī,
but the people did not support him,
and the feudal lords did not ally with him.
If Qin attacks Hán,
Chǔ and Zhào will surely rescue it,
and this will be heaven granting Yān to us."
The King said:
"Good."
He then promised the Hán envoy and sent him away.
Hán, believing it had secured an alliance with Qí,
then engaged Qin in battle.
Chǔ and Zhào indeed hastily raised troops
to rescue Hán,
and Qí took the opportunity to raise troops and attack Yān,
conquering the state of Yān in thirty days.
Zhāng Yí served King Huì of Qin.
When King Huì died,
King Wǔ ascended the throne.
The courtiers disliked Zhāng Yí,
saying:
"Yí served the former king disloyally."
Before the words ceased,
a reproach from Qí also arrived.
Zhāng Yí heard of this,
and said to King Wǔ:
"I have a foolish plan,
which I wish to offer to the king."
The King said:
"What is it?"
He said:
"For the sake of the state's strategy,
if there is a great upheaval in the east,
then the king can seize much land.
Now, the King of Qí deeply hates me, Zhāng Yí.
Wherever I am,
he will surely raise troops to attack it.
Therefore, I wish to offer my unworthy self to go to Liáng,
and Qí will surely raise troops to attack it.
When the troops of Qí and Liáng are entangled beneath the city walls,
unable to disengage,
the king can take the opportunity to attack Hán,
enter Sānchuān,
send troops through Hángǔ
without being attacked,
approach Zhōu,
and the ritual vessels will surely be presented.
Then, holding the Son of Heaven,
and examining the maps and registers,
this is the kingly enterprise."
The King said:
"Good."
He then prepared thirty chariots
and sent him to Liáng.
Qí indeed raised troops to attack it.
The King of Liáng was greatly frightened.
Zhāng Yí said:
"Your Majesty, do not worry;
allow me to make the Qí troops withdraw."
He then sent his retainer Féng Xǐ to Chǔ,
borrowing an envoy to go to Qí.
When matters with Qí and Chǔ were concluded,
he then said to the King of Qí:
"Your Majesty deeply hates Zhāng Yí,
yet,
how greatly Your Majesty has entrusted Yí
to the King of Qin."
The King of Qí said:
"I deeply hate Yí;
wherever he is,
I will surely raise troops to attack it.
How have I entrusted Yí?"
He replied:
"This is precisely how Your Majesty has entrusted Yí.
When Yí left Qin,
he made an agreement with the King of Qin, saying:
'For the king's strategy,
if there is a great upheaval in the east,
then the king can seize much land.
The King of Qí deeply hates me,
and wherever I am,
he will surely raise troops to attack it.
Therefore, I wish to offer my unworthy self to go to Liáng,
and Qí will surely raise troops to attack Liáng.
When the troops of Liáng and Qí are entangled beneath the city walls and cannot withdraw,
the king can take the opportunity to attack Hán,
enter Sānchuān,
send troops through Hángǔ without being attacked,
approach Zhōu,
and the ritual vessels will surely be presented.
Then, holding the Son of Heaven,
and examining the maps and registers,
this is the kingly enterprise.'"
The King of Qin considered this reasonable,
and with thirty war chariots, he escorted Zhang Yí to Wei.
As expected, he attacked it,
which meant that Your Majesty internally exhausted yourself and attacked an allied state,
expanded neighboring enemies to bring peril upon yourself,
and trusted Zhang Yí in the service of the King of Qin.
This is what I meant by entrusting matters to Zhang Yí."
The King said:
"Well said."
He then stopped the plan.
Xī Shǒu, using Wei’s forces, fought against Qí at Chéngkuāng
but was not victorious.
Zhang Yí told the King of Wei that not following his advice had endangered the state.
The King of Wei then made Zhang Yí his chancellor,
and Zhang Yí used the alliance of Qín and Wei to form a horizontal alliance with Qí.
Xī Shǒu, wishing to undermine this,
said to the Lord of Wèi:
"I, Yǎn, bear no grudge against Zhang Yí;
it is only that our methods for serving the state differ.
You must reconcile me with him."
The Lord of Wèi conveyed this to Zhang Yí,
who agreed,
and thus they sat together before the Lord of Wèi.
Xī Shǒu knelt and moved forward,
offering Zhang Yí a toast for a thousand autumns.
The next day, when Master Zhang departed,
Xī Shǒu escorted him all the way to the border of Qí.
The King of Qí heard of this,
became angry with Zhang Yí,
and said:
"Yǎn is my enemy,
yet Zhang Yí associates with him;
this surely means he and Yǎn are scheming to sell out my state."
He then refused to listen.
Zhāo Yáng, attacking Wèi for Chǔ,
destroyed armies, killed generals, and captured eight cities,
then shifted his troops to attack Qí.
Chén Zhěn, as an envoy of the King of Qí,
met Zhāo Yáng,
bowed twice
to congratulate him on his victory,
rose and asked:
"According to Chǔ’s laws,
for destroying armies and killing generals,
what office and rank are granted?"
Zhāo Yáng said:
"The office is Shàngzhùguó,
the rank is Shàngzhíguī."
Chén Zhěn said:
"What is more noble than this?"
He replied:
"Only the Lìngyǐn."
Chén Zhěn said:
"The Lìngyǐn is indeed noble!
But the king does not appoint two Lìngyǐn.
Allow me to offer you an analogy.
In Chǔ, there was a person making sacrifices,
who gave his retainer a goblet of wine.
The retainers said to each other:
'Several people drinking it would not be enough,
one person drinking it would have some left.
Let us draw snakes on the ground,
and whoever finishes first drinks the wine.'
One person finished his snake first,
took the wine and was about to drink it,
but then, holding the goblet in his left hand, he drew with his right hand,
saying:
'I can add feet to it.'
Before he finished,
another person completed his snake,
snatched the goblet and said:
'Snakes naturally have no feet;
how can you add feet to it?'
He then drank the wine.
The one who added feet to the snake
ultimately lost his wine.
Now you serve as chancellor of Chǔ and attacked Wèi,
destroyed armies, killed generals, and captured eight cities without weakening your troops.
If you then attack Qí,
though Qí greatly fears you,
with this achievement your reputation is already sufficient;
your office cannot be further elevated.
To be ever-victorious in war and not know when to stop—
you may lose your life,
and your rank may later be taken away—
is like adding feet to the snake."
Zhāo Yáng considered this reasonable,
withdrew his army and left.
Qín attacked Zhào.
Zhào ordered Lóu Huǎn to offer five cities to seek peace with Qín,
and to join them in attacking Qí.
The King of Qí, alarmed,
sent someone to offer ten cities to seek peace with Qín.
Master Lóu, fearing this,
then promised the King of Qín twenty-four counties of Shàngdǎng.
Zhào Zú went to Qí
and said to the King of Qí:
"Does Your Majesty wish for Qín and Zhào to break their alliance?
It would be better to form a vertical alliance with Zhào.
Zhào will certainly betray Qín.
If Zhào betrays Qín, then Qí will have no worries."
During the conflict at Quán,
Qí and Yān fought.
Qín sent Wèi Rǎn to Zhào,
to send troops to aid Yān in attacking Qí.
Lord Xuē sent Wèi Chǔ to Zhào,
who said to Lǐ Xiàng:
"If you aid Yān in attacking Qí,
Qí will certainly be hard-pressed.
Hard-pressed, it will surely cede territory to make peace with Yān,
and then turn to fight Zhào.
Thus, you would be raising troops for Yān in the east,
gaining territory for Yān.
Therefore, for your sake,
it would be better to hold your troops and not send them out.
Qí will certainly ease its pressure,
and once eased, it will again fight Yān.
If they fight and win,
their troops will be exhausted,
and Zhào can seize Táng and Qūnì;
if they fight and lose,
their fate will hang on Zhào.
Thus, by remaining neutral, you can take territory from both the exhausted Qí and the weary Yān.
The power over both states
will then rest with you."
Qín attacked Zhào at Chángpíng,
and Qí and Chǔ came to its rescue.
Qín’s strategists said:
"If Qí and Chǔ rescue Zhào
and are close allies,
then we should withdraw our troops;
if they are not close allies,
then we should press the attack."
Zhào had no food supplies,
and requested grain from Qí,
but Qí refused.
Sū Qín said to the King of Qí:
"It would be better to grant the request to make the Qín troops withdraw;
if you refuse, the Qín troops will not withdraw,
which would mean Qín’s plan succeeds,
while the plans of Qí and Yān fail.
Moreover, Zhào is to Yān and Qí
a protective screen,
like lips to teeth:
if the lips are gone, the teeth will be cold.
If Zhào falls today,
then tomorrow it will be the turn of Qí and Chǔ.
Furthermore, the task of rescuing Zhào
should be like holding a leaking jar
to pour water on a burning pot.
To rescue Zhào
is a noble act of righteousness;
to make the Qín troops withdraw
brings illustrious fame.
To righteously rescue a perishing Zhào,
and with authority make the strong Qín troops withdraw—
if you do not devote yourself to this,
but instead cling to your grain,
then those planning for the state are mistaken."
Someone said to the King of Qí:
"Zhōu and Hán have the strong Qín to their west,
and Zhào and Wèi to their east.
When Qín attacks the west of Zhōu and Hán,
if Zhào and Wèi do not attack,
Zhōu and Hán will be forced to cede territory,
and Hán will retreat, harming Zhōu.
By the time Hán retreats and Zhōu cedes territory,
Zhào and Wèi will also inevitably face trouble with Qín.
Now if Qí and Qín attack Zhào and Wèi,
it will be no different from Zhào and Wèi
responding to Qín by attacking Zhōu and Hán.
If you ally with Qín to attack Zhào and Wèi,
after Zhào and Wèi are destroyed,
Qín will turn east to attack Qí.
How then will Qí be able to seek help from the world!"
When the King of Chǔ died,
the crown prince was a hostage in Qí.
Sū Qín said to Lord Xuē:
"Why not detain the crown prince of Chǔ,
to bargain for the lower eastern territories?"
Lord Xuē said:
"That cannot be done.
If I detain the crown prince,
Yǐng will set up another king,
and then I would be holding an empty hostage
and acting unjustly toward the world."
Sū Qín said:
"Not so.
In Yǐng, a new king is being established.
You should therefore say to this new king:
'Give me Lower Dōngguó,
and I will kill the crown prince for you.
If not,
I will join the three states in installing him.'
In that case, Lower Dōngguó will certainly be obtainable."
Regarding Sū Qín's affairs,
one can request to undertake them;
one can cause the King of Chǔ to promptly hand over Lower Dōngguó;
one can secure additional territory from Chǔ;
one can feign loyalty to the crown prince and thereby cause Chǔ to cede even more land;
one can make the King of Chǔ drive away the crown prince;
one can feign loyalty to the crown prince and cause him to leave quickly;
one can make Sū Qín hated by Lord Xuē;
one can request a fief for Sū Qín from Chǔ;
one can have someone persuade Lord Xuē to treat Master Sū well;
one can have Master Sū clear himself with Lord Xuē.
Sū Qín said to Lord Xuē:
"Your servant has heard that when a plan is leaked, the affair achieves no success;
when a decision is not made, a name is not established.
Now, the reason you detain the crown prince
is to bargain for Lower Dōngguó.
If Lower Dōngguó is not obtained quickly,
then Chǔ's plans will change.
If they change, then you will be holding an empty hostage
and bear a bad name throughout the world."
Lord Xuē said:
"Good.
What should be done about it?"
He replied:
"I ask to go to Chǔ on your behalf,
to make them promptly hand over the land of Lower Dōngguó.
If Chǔ agrees,
then you will not fail."
Lord Xuē said:
"Good."
He therefore sent him.
(Sū Qín) said to the King of Chǔ:
"Qí intends to support the crown prince and install him.
In my observation, the reason Lord Xuē detains the crown prince
is to bargain for Lower Dōngguó.
If Your Majesty does not promptly hand over Lower Dōngguó,
then the crown prince will double the territory you have ceded
and have Qí support him."
The King of Chǔ said:
"I respectfully accept your instruction."
He therefore presented Lower Dōngguó.
Hence it is said
that one can cause Chǔ to promptly hand over land.
(Sū Qín) said to Lord Xuē:
"The situation in Chǔ allows for extracting more territory."
Lord Xuē said:
"How?"
"Please inform the crown prince of the reason,
have the crown prince petition you,
feigning loyalty to the crown prince,
and let the King of Chǔ hear of it.
Then more land can be obtained."
Hence it is said that one can secure additional territory from Chǔ.
(Sū Qín) said to the crown prince:
"Qí supports you and intends to install you.
The King of Chǔ requested to cede territory to keep you detained,
but Qí considers the land insufficient.
Why doesn't the crown prince double the territory Chǔ has ceded and offer it to Qí?
Qí will certainly support you."
The crown prince said:
"Good."
He doubled Chǔ's ceded territory and extended the offer to Qí.
The King of Chǔ heard this and was alarmed.
He increased the ceded territory and presented it,
still fearing the affair might not succeed.
Hence it is said that one can cause Chǔ to cede even more land.
(Sū Qín) said to the King of Chǔ:
"The reason Qí dares to demand so much territory
is because it holds the crown prince.
Now that they have obtained land, yet their demands do not cease,
it is because the crown prince is used as leverage against you.
Therefore, I can make the crown prince leave.
Once the crown prince leaves,
Qí will have no pretext,
and certainly will not double-cross you.
You can then swiftly ally with powerful Qí,
and when Qí responds,
it will certainly heed you.
In that case, you will have removed an enemy and gained Qí's alliance."
The King of Chǔ was greatly pleased,
and said:
"I ask to entrust the state to you."
Hence it is said
that one can make the King of Chǔ cause the crown prince to leave quickly.
(Sū Qín) said to the crown prince:
"The one who controls Chǔ is the king.
The one who trades on an empty title is you, the crown prince.
Qí may not necessarily believe your words,
yet Chǔ's achievement will be evident.
Once Chǔ's alliance is formed,
you, the crown prince, will certainly be in danger.
You, the crown prince, should consider this."
The crown prince said:
"I respectfully accept your instruction."
He then prepared a carriage and left that evening.
Hence it is said that one can cause the crown prince to leave urgently.
Sū Qín had someone request of Lord Xuē:
"The one who urged the detention of the crown prince was Sū Qín.
Sū Qín was not sincerely acting for you,
but rather to benefit Chǔ.
Sū Qín feared you would realize this,
so he demanded much territory from Chǔ to cover his tracks.
Now the one urging the crown prince is again Sū Qín,
yet you are unaware.
I privately suspect this for you."
Lord Xuē became greatly angry at Sū Qín.
Hence it is said
that one can have someone make Sū Qín hated by Lord Xuē.
(Sū Qín) also had someone say to the King of Chǔ:
"The one who caused Lord Xuē to detain the crown prince
was Sū Qín.
The one who supported you and sought to replace the Chǔ crown prince
was also Sū Qín.
The one who secured the cession of territory and solidified the agreement was also Sū Qín.
The one who was loyal to you and made the crown prince flee was also Sū Qín.
Now someone has made Sū Qín hated by Lord Xuē,
because he acted thinly for Qí and thickly for Chǔ.
I hope Your Majesty is aware of this."
The King of Chǔ said:
"I respectfully accept your instruction."
He therefore enfeoffed Sū Qín as Lord Wǔzhēn.
Hence it is said that one can request a fief for Sū Qín from Chǔ.
(Sū Qín) also had Jǐng Lǐ
request of Lord Xuē:
"The reason you are esteemed throughout the world
is because you can attract the world's scholars and hold power in Qí.
Now Sū Qín is a master debater of the world,
rarely seen in any generation.
If you therefore treat Sū Qín poorly,
then you are blocking the world's scholars and harming the paths of persuasion.
Those who are not well-disposed toward you will support Sū Qín,
and your affairs will be endangered.
Now Sū Qín is on good terms with the King of Chǔ,
yet you do not quickly befriend him.
This means you personally make an enemy of Chǔ.
Therefore, you should instead befriend him,
honor and esteem him.
Then you will have Chǔ's support."
Lord Xuē therefore treated Sū Qín well.
Hence it is said that one can
persuade Lord Xuē to treat Sū Qín well.
The King of Qí's wife died.
There were seven favored concubines all close to him.
Lord Xuē wished to know which one the king desired to establish,
so he presented seven earrings,
making one of them especially beautiful.
The next day, he observed where the beautiful earring was,
and urged the king to establish that one as his wife.
Lord Mèngcháng was about to go to Qín.
Thousands tried to stop him, but he would not listen.
Sū Qín wished to stop him.
Lord Mèngcháng said:
"Regarding human affairs,
I already know them all thoroughly.
What I have not yet heard
are solely ghostly
affairs."
Sū Qín said:
"When your servant came,
I certainly did not dare speak of human affairs.
I certainly intended to see you regarding ghostly affairs."
Lord Mèngcháng received him.
(Sū Qín) said to Lord Mèngcháng:
"Just now as I came,
passing by the Zī River,
I saw an earthen figurine
conversing with a peach-wood doll.
The peach-wood doll said to the earthen figurine:
'You,
are clay from the western bank,
molded into human form.
When the eighth month of the year arrives,
the rains fall,
the Zī River rises,
and then you will be destroyed.'"
The clay figurine said:
"Not so.
I am clay from the western bank,
and clay will simply return to the western bank.
Now you are a peachwood figurine from the eastern state,
carved and whittled into human form.
When the rains fall,
and the Zī River rises,
it will carry you away.
Then, drifting and floating, what will become of you?"
Now Qín is a state fortified on all sides,
like a tiger's mouth.
If you enter it,
I do not know how you will get out."
Mèngcháng Jūn then stopped.
When Mèngcháng Jūn was in Xuē,
the people of Jīng attacked it.
Chúnyú Kūn was on a mission from Qí to Jīng,
and on his return, he passed through Xuē.
Mèngcháng had someone observe his appearance
and personally went to the outskirts to welcome him.
He said to Chúnyú Kūn:
"The people of Jīng are attacking Xuē.
If you, Master, are not concerned,
I, Wén, will have no means to serve you again."
Chúnyú Kūn said:
"I respectfully heed your command."
When he reached Qí, he completed his report.
The King said:
"What did you see in Jīng?"
He replied:
"Jīng is very stubborn,
and Xuē also does not measure its own strength."
The King said:
"What do you mean?"
He replied:
"Xuē does not measure its strength
and built a pure temple for the former king.
Jīng, being stubborn, attacked it,
and the pure temple is sure to be endangered.
Therefore, I said Xuē does not measure its strength,
and Jīng is also very stubborn."
The King of Qí softened his expression and said:
"Ah!
The temple of my late lord is there!"
He quickly raised troops to rescue it.
Pleading with stumbling steps,
paying respects with hopeful bows,
even if successful, is meager.
A skilled persuader
lays out the situation,
speaks of the method,
and when others are in dire straits,
it is as if he himself is in a narrow and desperate spot.
How could forceful effort be needed then!
Mèngcháng Jūn provided Xiàhóu Zhāng
with food for four horses and a hundred men,
treating him with great joy.
Yet Xiàhóu Zhāng often spoke,
and never failed to slander Mèngcháng Jūn.
Someone reported this to Mèngcháng Jūn,
who said:
"I, Wén, have a way of serving Lord Xiàhóu.
Do not speak of it;
let it be."
Fán Jīng asked Xiàhóu Gong about this,
and Xiàhóu Gong said:
"Mèngcháng Jūn, though not a feudal lord, is esteemed,
yet he provides me with food for four horses and a hundred men.
I have not the slightest merit to deserve this,
so I slander him to create merit for him.
The reason he can be considered a man of honor
is because I slander him.
I devote myself to Mèngcháng Jūn;
how could I merely hold to words?"
Mèngcháng Jūn was sitting at a banquet
and said to three gentlemen:
"I wish to hear how you gentlemen would remedy my shortcomings."
One said:
"Should any ruler in the world
invade you, my lord,
I request
to stain his lapel with my blood."
Tián Mào said:
"Wherever chariot tracks can reach,
I will cover your shortcomings
and proclaim your strengths.
Whether it is a lord of a thousand chariots or a minister of ten thousand chariots,
if they desire to have you as lord,
it will be as if they could not reach you even if sent."
Shèng said:
"I wish to use the wealth and goods from your treasury
to gather talented men from the world,
who can resolve
doubts and respond to emergencies for you, like how Marquis Wén of Wèi
had Tián Zǐfāng
and Duàngān Mù.
This is what I would do for you, my lord."
A retainer of Mèngcháng Jūn
was in love with the lord's wife.
Someone informed Mèngcháng Jūn, saying:
"As your retainer,
to be involved in love with your wife inside
is extremely unfitting.
You should kill him."
The lord said:
"To see beauty and feel affection
is human nature.
Let it be; do not speak of it."
After a year had passed,
the lord summoned the man who loved his wife
and said to him:
"You have associated with me, Wén, for a long time,
yet no high office has been attainable,
and you do not desire minor offices.
The lord of Wèi and I are friends from commoner days.
I ask to prepare carriages, horses, leather, and silk,
and I hope you will follow the lord of Wèi with these."
In Wèi, he was highly regarded.
When relations between Qí and Wèi soured,
the lord of Wèi strongly desired
to rally troops from the world to attack Qí.
This man said to the lord of Wèi:
"Mèngcháng Jūn did not know I was unworthy
and used me to deceive you.
Moreover, I have heard that the former lords of Qí and Wèi
slaughtered horses and pressed down sheep,
swearing an oath:
'Later generations of Qí and Wèi shall not attack each other.
If any attack each other,
may their fate be like this.'
Now you rally troops from the world to attack Qí.
This is you betraying the oath of the former lords and deceiving Mèngcháng Jūn.
I hope you will not set your mind against Qí.
If you heed me, it is acceptable;
if you do not heed me,
though I am unworthy,
I will immediately stain your lapel with the blood from my neck."
The lord of Wèi then stopped.
When the people of Qí heard of this, they said:
"Mèngcháng Jūn can indeed be said to excel at handling affairs,
turning calamity into achievement."
Mèngcháng Jūn had a retainer he disliked
and wanted to dismiss him.
Lǔ Lián said to Mèngcháng Jūn:
"If an ape or macaque leaves the trees and takes to the water,
it is not as good as fish or turtles.
In traversing dangers and scaling heights,
a fine steed is not as good as a fox.
When Cáo Mò brandished his three-foot sword,
an entire army could not withstand him.
But if Cáo Mò laid down his three-foot sword
and took up a spade or hoe to dwell in the fields with farmers,
he would not be as good as a farmer.
Thus, if things abandon their strengths
and go to their weaknesses,
even Yáo would have shortcomings.
Now, if you assign someone a task and he cannot do it,
you call him unworthy.
If you teach someone and he cannot learn,
you call him clumsy.
If clumsy, you dismiss him;
if unworthy, you abandon him.
To have people abandoned and dismissed,
not associating with each other,
and then coming to harm and seek revenge
—is this not the foremost lesson established in the world?"
Mèngcháng Jūn said:
"Well said."
And he did not dismiss him.
Mèngcháng Jūn traveled
through the states
and reached Chǔ,
where an ivory bed was presented.
The Dēngtú of Yǐng
was ordered to deliver it,
but he did not wish to go.
He saw Mèng Chángjūn's retainer Gōngsūn Shù
and said:
a Dēngtú from Yǐng,
am to deliver an ivory bed.
The ivory bed is worth a thousand pieces of gold.
If it is damaged even by a hair's breadth,
selling my wife and children would not suffice to repay it.
If you, sir, can cause me not to go,
I have an ancestral sword,
which I wish to present to you."
Gōngsūn said:
"Agreed."
He entered to see Mèng Chángjūn and said:
"Do you intend to accept
the ivory bed from Chǔ?"
Mèng Chángjūn said:
"Yes."
Gōngsūn Shù said:
"I wish you would not accept it."
Mèng Chángjūn said:
"Why?"
Gōngsūn Shù said:
"The reason all the small states have sent you their ministerial seals is
because they have heard that in Qí you are able to uplift the poor and destitute,
and possess the righteousness to preserve the perishing and continue the severed lines.
The outstanding and heroic men of the small states
all entrust their state affairs to you,
truly admiring your righteousness,
and revering your integrity.
Now, if you go to Chǔ and accept an ivory bed,
for the states you have not yet reached,
how will they treat you?
I, Shù, wish you would not accept it."
Mèng Chángjūn said:
"Agreed."
Gōngsūn Shù hurried away.
Before he had gone out,
reaching the middle gate,
Mèng Chángjūn summoned him back,
and said:
"You advised Wén not to accept the ivory bed,
which is very good.
But now why do you lift your feet so high,
and your spirit appear so elated?"
Gōngsūn Shù said:
"I have three great joys,
and in addition, a precious sword."
Mèng Chángjūn said:
"What do you mean?"
Gōngsūn Shù said:
"Among the hundreds at your gate,
none dared to enter and remonstrate.
I alone entered to remonstrate—
this is my first joy;
my remonstrance was heeded—
this is my second joy;
my remonstrance stopped your error—
this is my third joy.
Regarding the delivery of the ivory bed,
the Dēngtú from Yǐng did not wish to go,
and promised Shù his ancestral sword."
Mèng Chángjūn said:
"Good.
Did you accept it?"
Gōngsūn Shù said:
"I did not dare."
Mèng Chángjūn said:
"Quickly accept it."
Thereupon, he wrote on the gate board:
"Whoever can promote Wén's reputation,
stop Wén's errors,
and privately obtain treasures from outside,
let him swiftly enter to remonstrate."
Chúnyú Kūn recommended seven men to King Xuān in a single day.
The King said:
"You come.
I have heard that
for a thousand lǐ, there is one scholar—
this is like standing shoulder to shoulder;
for a hundred generations, there is one sage—
it is as if they arrive following on each other's heels.
Now you, in one morning, recommend seven scholars;
are scholars not then too numerous?"
Chúnyú Kūn said:
"Not so.
Birds of the same wing flock together,
beasts of the same foot travel together.
If you seek chái hú and jú gěng in marshy wetlands,
you will not find a single one in generations.
But if you go to the shady sides of Gāo Shǔ and Liáng Fù,
you can load cart after cart.
All things have their kind.
Now, Kūn is of the kind of the worthy.
For the King to seek scholars through Kūn is like dipping water from a river,
or taking fire from a flint.
Kūn will recommend more to you;
how could it be limited to seven scholars?"
Qí wanted to attack Wèi. Chúnyú Kūn said to the King of Qí:
"Hánzǐ Lú
is the swiftest dog in the world.
Dōngguō Qūn
is the craftiest rabbit within the seas.
Hánzǐ Lú chased Dōngguō Qūn;
three times around the mountains,
five times leaping over the hills.
The rabbit was exhausted in front,
the dog gave out behind;
both dog and rabbit were utterly spent,
and each died where it was.
An old farmer saw them,
without the toil of weariness,
and took the prize for himself.
Now Qí and Wèi have long been locked in stalemate,
wearing down their troops,
exhausting their masses.
I fear that powerful Qín and great Chǔ, following behind,
will have the old farmer's success."
The King of Qí was alarmed,
dismissed his generals, and rested his troops.
Guózǐ said:
"Qín defeated the army of Mǎfú Jūn,
and besieged Hándān.
Qí and Wèi also assisted Qín in attacking Hándān;
Qí took Zī Shǔ,
and Wèi took Yī Shì.
Lord Wújì,
devising a convenient plan for all under heaven,
killed Jìn Bǐ,
led the Wèi troops to rescue the siege of Hándān,
causing Qín to lose possession and forfeit the world.
This was Qí entering Wèi
and the merit of rescuing Hándān.
Ānyì
is the pillar-state of Wèi;
Jìnyáng
is the pillar-state of Zhào;
Yān Yǐng
is the pillar-state of Chǔ.
Therefore, these three states wished to share borders with Qín.
Qín attacked Wèi and took Ānyì,
attacked Zhào and took Jìnyáng,
attacked Chǔ and took Yān Yǐng.
It blessed the lords of the three states,
annexed the lands of the two Zhōu,
raised Hán and took its territory,
amounting to half of the world.
Now it again coerces Zhào and Wèi,
alienates the central states,
enfeoffs the eastern wilds of Wèi,
annexes Wèi's Hénán,
severs Zhào's Dōngyáng—
then Zhào and Wèi are also endangered.
If Zhào and Wèi are endangered,
it is not to Qí's advantage.
The intent of Hán, Wèi, Zhào, and Chǔ
fears that Qín will unite the world
and make their lords its subjects,
therefore they concentrate their troops and unify their will to oppose Qín.
The three states share borders with Qín and their peril is urgent;
Qí does not share a border with Qín and its peril is slight.
Therefore, given the situation in the world,
they cannot but serve Qí.
So if Qín gains Qí,
its power in the central states becomes weighty;
if Zhào, Wèi, and Chǔ gain Qí,
they are sufficient to oppose Qín.
Therefore, for Qín, Zhào, and Wèi, gaining Qí makes them weighty,
losing Qí makes them light.
Qí possesses this position,
yet is unable to be weighty in the world—why is that?
Its employment of it is mistaken."
In Qí there was a man named Féng Xuān,
poor and destitute, unable to support himself.
He had someone recommend him to Mèng Chángjūn,
wishing to find sustenance at his gate.
Mèng Chángjūn said:
"What does the guest enjoy?"
He replied:
"The guest enjoys nothing."
Mèng Chángjūn said:
"What is the guest able to do?"
He replied:
"The guest is able to do nothing."
Mèng Chángjūn laughed and accepted him, saying:
"Agreed."
His attendants, because their lord held him in low esteem,
fed him coarse fare.
After a while,
he leaned against a pillar and plucked his sword,
singing:
"Long sword, let's go back!
I have no fish to eat."
His attendants reported this.
Mèng Chángjūn said:
"Give him fish to eat,
treat him like the other guests."
After a while,
he plucked his sword again,
singing:
"Long sword, let's go back!
I have no carriage to ride."
The attendants all laughed at him,
and reported it.
Mèng Chángjūn said:
"Prepare a carriage for him,
treat him like the carriage-riding guests."
Thereupon, he rode in his carriage,
raised his sword,
and visited his friend, saying:
"Mèng Chángjūn treats me as a guest."
Later, after a while,
he plucked his sword again,
singing:
"Long sword, let's go back!
I have no means to support my family."
The attendants all disliked him,
thinking him greedy and insatiable.
Mèng Chángjūn asked:
"Does Lord Féng have any relatives?"
They replied:
"He has an elderly mother."
Mèng Chángjūn sent someone to supply her with food and provisions,
so that she would lack nothing.
Thereupon, Féng Xuān no longer sang.
Later, Mèng Chángjūn issued a notice,
asking the guests in his household:
"Who is skilled in accounting,
and can collect debts from Xuē for me?"
Féng Xuān signed his name, saying:
"I can."
Mèng Chángjūn found this strange,
and said:
"Who is this?"
The attendants said:
"He is the one who sang 'Long sword, let's go back!'"
Mèng Chángjūn laughed and said:
"This guest truly has ability,
I have failed him,
never having met him."
He requested to see him,
and apologized, saying:
"I am weary with affairs,
confused with worries,
and by nature dull and foolish,
immersed in state matters,
I have offended you, sir.
If you are not ashamed,
do you intend to collect debts from Xuē for me?"
Féng Xuān said:
"I am willing."
Thereupon, he prepared a carriage and packed his luggage, loaded the debt contracts, and set off.
He bid farewell, saying:
"After the debts are fully collected,
what should I buy to bring back?"
Mèng Chángjūn said:
"Look at what my household lacks."
He drove to Xuē,
had the officials summon all the people who owed debts,
and all came to match their contracts.
When the contracts were all matched,
he rose and, feigning Mèng Chángjūn's order, bestowed the debts upon the people,
then burned the contracts.
The people shouted, "Long live!"
He drove straight back to Qí,
and sought an audience in the morning.
Mèng Chángjūn was surprised at his speed,
dressed formally to see him,
and said:
"Have the debts been fully collected?
How quickly you have returned!"
He said:
"They have been fully collected."
"What did you buy to bring back?"
Féng Xuān said:
"You said,
'Look at what my household lacks.'
I privately considered that
your palace is filled with treasures,
dogs and horses fill the outer stables,
and beautiful women crowd the lower chambers.
What your household lacks is righteousness!
I privately thought to buy righteousness for you."
Mèng Chángjūn said:
"How does one buy righteousness?"
He said:
"Now you have the small territory of Xuē,
yet you do not cherish and treat its people as your children,
but instead profit from them like a merchant.
I privately feigned your order,
bestowing the debts upon the people,
then burned the contracts.
The people shouted, 'Long live!'
This is how I bought righteousness for you."
Mèng Chángjūn was displeased,
and said:
"Alright,
sir, that is enough!"
A year later,
the King of Qí said to Mèng Chángjūn:
"I dare not use a minister of the former king as my minister."
Mèng Chángjūn went to his fief in Xuē.
When he was still a hundred lǐ away,
the people, supporting the elderly and carrying the young,
came to meet him on the road.
Mèng Chángjūn turned to Féng Xuān and said:
"The righteousness you bought for me,
I see it today."
Féng Xuān said:
"A cunning rabbit has three burrows,
only then can it avoid death.
Now you have one burrow,
you cannot yet rest easy on your pillow.
Allow me to dig two more burrows for you."
Mèng Chángjūn gave him fifty carriages,
five hundred jīn of gold,
and he traveled west to Liáng.
He said to King Huì:
"Qí has dismissed its great minister Mèng Chángjūn to the other states.
The state that welcomes him first
will become wealthy and militarily strong."
Thereupon, the King of Liáng vacated the highest position,
made the former chancellor the senior general,
and sent an envoy,
with a thousand jīn of gold,
and a hundred carriages,
to invite Mèng Chángjūn.
