Féng Xuān went ahead and advised Mèng Chángjūn, saying:
"A thousand jīn is a heavy gift;
a hundred carriages is a prominent envoy.
Qí will surely hear of this."
The Liáng envoy returned three times,
but Mèng Chángjūn firmly declined and did not go.
The King of Qí heard of this,
and the ruler and ministers became fearful.
He sent the Grand Tutor with a thousand jīn of gold,
two teams of four ornamented carriages,
a ceremonial sword,
and a sealed letter apologizing to Mèng Chángjūn, saying:
"I am unfortunate,
afflicted by the ancestral temple's curse,
misled by flattering ministers,
and have offended you.
I am not worthy.
I hope you will consider the ancestral temple of the former king,
and temporarily return to govern the myriad people?"
Féng Xuān advised Mèng Chángjūn, saying:
"I hope you will request the sacrificial vessels of the former king,
and establish an ancestral temple in Xuē."
When the temple was completed,
he returned and reported to Mèng Chángjūn, saying:
"The three burrows are now ready,
you may rest easy and enjoy yourself."
Mèng Chángjūn served as chancellor for several decades,
without the slightest misfortune,
all due to Féng Xuān's schemes.
Mèng Chángjūn formed a vertical alliance.
Gōngsūn Hóng said to Mèng Chángjūn:
"Why not send someone first to observe the King of Qín?
If the King of Qín is a ruler fit for an emperor,
you may fear you cannot even be his minister,
how would you have leisure to form an alliance to oppose him?
If the King of Qín is an unworthy ruler,
then forming an alliance to oppose him
would not be too late."
Mèng Chángjūn said:
"Good,
I hope you will go for me."
Gōngsūn Hóng respectfully assented,
and went to Qín with ten carriages.
King Zhāo heard of this,
and wanted to shame him with words.
When Gōngsūn Hóng had an audience,
King Zhāo said:
"How large is Lord Xuē's territory,
in size?"
Gōngsūn Hóng replied:
"A hundred lǐ."
King Zhāo laughed and said:
"My land extends several thousand lǐ,
yet I dare not cause trouble.
Now Lord Mèngcháng's territory is only a hundred lǐ square,
and yet he intends to cause trouble for me—
is that feasible?"
Gōngsūn Hóng replied:
"Lord Mèngcháng esteems men of worth,
while Your Majesty does not."
King Zhāo said:
"How does Lord Mèngcháng
esteem men of worth?"
Gōngsūn Hóng said:
"Those who, upholding righteousness, will not serve the Son of Heaven as ministers,
nor befriend the feudal lords,
who, when achieving their ambitions, feel no shame to be rulers themselves,
and when not achieving them, refuse to serve others as ministers—
such men number three;
those who in governance could serve as teachers to Guǎn Zhòng and
Shāng Yāng,
whose persuasive arguments are heeded and acted upon,
and who can bring about such results—
such men number five;
even if a stern ruler of ten thousand chariots
were to insult his envoy,
he would retreat and slit his own throat,
ensuring his blood stains his garments—
men like me number ten."
King Zhāo laughed and apologized,
saying:
"Why must you be like this, sir?
I was merely discussing with you!
I am well-disposed toward Lord Mèngcháng,
and I wish you would convey my sincere intentions to him!"
Gōngsūn Hóng said:
"I respectfully assent."
Gōngsūn Hóng can indeed be said to be unyielding.
King Zhāo
ruled a great state.
Mèngcháng
commanded a thousand chariots.
To uphold the righteousness of a thousand-chariot state and not be humiliated—
he can truly be called a fully capable envoy.
Lǚ Zhònglián said to Mèngcháng:
"My lord, you esteem men of worth!
Yōngmén Yǎng supported Jiāo Yì,
and Yángdézǐ supported others,
sharing with them the same food and drink,
clothing and furs,
and they all died for him.
Now your household is wealthier than those two lords,
yet no scholar has exhausted his travels for you."
The lord said:
"It is because I have not obtained such two men.
If I could obtain two such men,
how could I alone fail to have them exhaust themselves?"
He replied:
"In your stables are a hundred teams of horses,
all clad in embroidered trappings and fed beans and grain—
but are there any Qílín or Lù'ěr among them?
In your rear palace are ten consorts,
all dressed in fine white silk and hemp,
fed fine grain and meat—
but are there any Máo Qiáng or
Xī Shī among them?
Beauty and horses are sought from the present age—
why must scholars be awaited from antiquity?
Therefore it is said that your esteem for scholars is not yet genuine."
Lord Mèngcháng, having been expelled from Qí, returned again.
Tán Shízi met him at the border,
and said to Lord Mèngcháng:
"Do you not harbor resentment toward the officials and gentlemen of Qí?"
Lord Mèngcháng said:
"I do."
"Would you be satisfied to kill them?"
Lord Mèngcháng said:
"Yes."
Tán Shízi said:
"Events have inevitable outcomes,
principles have inherent logic—
do you understand this?"
Lord Mèngcháng said:
"I do not."
Tán Shízi said:
"The inevitable outcome of events
is death;
the inherent logic of principles
is that people flock to wealth and honor,
and shun poverty and lowliness.
This is the inevitable outcome of events,
the inherent logic of principles.
Let me use the market as an analogy.
The market is full in the morning,
empty by evening—
not because people love the market in the morning and hate it in the evening,
but because they go where goods are available,
and leave where they are gone.
I hope you will not resent them."
Lord Mèngcháng then took the five hundred tablets recording his resentments and erased them,
not daring to speak of them again.
King Xuān of Qí saw Yán Chù and said:
"Chù, come forward!"
Chù likewise said: "Your Majesty, come forward!"
King Xuān was displeased.
His attendants said:
"The king
is the ruler of men.
Chù
is a subject.
The king says 'Chù, come forward,'
yet he also says
'Your Majesty, come forward'—
is that permissible?"
Chù replied: "If Chù comes forward,
it is from admiration for power;
if the king comes forward, it is from esteem for scholars.
Rather than have Chù admire power,
it is better to have the king esteem scholars."
The king, angered, changed countenance and said:
"Which is nobler: the king, or the scholar?"
He replied: "The scholar is noble;
the king is not."
The king said:
"Is there an explanation?"
Chù said:
"There is.
In the past, when Qín attacked Qí,
it issued an order:
'Whoever dares to gather firewood within fifty paces of Liǔxià Huì's grave mound,
shall die without pardon.'
Another order said:
'Whoever can obtain the head of the King of Qí
shall be enfeoffed as a marquis with ten thousand households,
and rewarded with a thousand yì of gold.'
From this we see that
the head of a living king
is not worth as much as the grave mound of a dead scholar."
King Xuān fell silent, displeased.
All the attendants said: "Chù, come here, Chù, come here!
Our great king rules over a land of a thousand chariots,
and has erected bells weighing a thousand shí,
and ten thousand shí.
Scholars from all under heaven,
those devoted to benevolence and righteousness, all come to serve and reside here;
the eloquent and wise advance together,
none failing to offer counsel;
east, west, south, and north,
none dare not submit.
He seeks all things, and none are not fully provided;
and the hundred clans all draw near and adhere to him.
Now the so-called lofty scholars
are but commoners,
walking on foot and dwelling in farm fields,
or lower still, in rustic villages, as gatekeepers or neighborhood elders—
the lowliness of scholars
is extreme indeed!"
Chù replied:
"Not so.
I have heard that in ancient times, during the era of Great Yǔ,
there were ten thousand feudal states.
Why was this?
Because the way of abundant virtue
gained the strength of esteemed scholars.
Thus Shùn arose from the farm fields,
from a rustic village,
and became the Son of Heaven.
By the time of Tāng,
there were three thousand feudal lords.
In the present age,
those who face south and call themselves 'the solitary one'
number only twenty-four.
From this we see,
is it not a matter of policy, of gain and loss?
Gradually they are punished and destroyed,
until, when they are annihilated and
their clans extinguished,
even wishing to be a gatekeeper or neighborhood elder—
how could that be obtained?"
Therefore, does not the *Yì Zhuàn*
say:
'One who occupies a high position,
yet lacks the substance [for it],
and delights in the reputation [it brings],
will inevitably conduct himself
with arrogance and extravagance.
Arrogance, contempt, pride, and extravagance—
then misfortune follows them.
Therefore, one who lacks the substance yet delights in the reputation will be diminished;
one who lacks virtue yet hopes for blessings will meet with distress;
one who lacks merit yet receives emolument will be disgraced;
calamity is sure to be grasped.'
Hence it is said:
'Boasting of merit does not establish it;
empty wishes do not attain it.'
These are all cases of taking pleasure in their reputation,
splendid yet lacking the substance and virtue thereof.
Thus, Yáo had nine assistants,
Shùn had seven friends,
Yǔ had five aides,
Tāng had three supporters.
From ancient times to the present,
there has never been
one who could achieve an empty reputation throughout the world.
Therefore, a true king is not ashamed to inquire repeatedly,
nor feels ashamed to learn from those below.
It is for this reason that they perfected their moral virtue and spread their merit and fame to later generations—
Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, and King Wén of Zhōu were such.
Hence it is said:
'The formless is
the ruler of form.
The beginningless is
the root of affairs.'
To perceive its source above,
and comprehend its course below,
arriving at the sage's understanding of learning—
how could there be anything inauspicious!
Lǎozi said:
'Although noble,
one must take the humble as the root;
although high,
one must take the low as the foundation.
Therefore, lords and kings style themselves "the solitary one," "the few," "the unworthy"—
is this not taking the humble as the root?'
It is not that "solitary" and "few"
refer to people in distress, humble, and lowly positions,
yet lords and kings use them to refer to themselves.
Is this not humbling oneself and honoring the shì?
Yáo passed [the throne] to Shùn,
Shùn passed it to Yǔ,
King Chéng of Zhōu entrusted [the regency] to the Duke of Zhōu, Dàn,
and they are praised through the ages as enlightened rulers.
This shows they understood the worth of the shì."
King Xuān said:
"Alas!
How can a gentleman be insulted?
I have brought this humiliation upon myself!
Now that I have heard your words, sir,
I now understand the conduct of petty men.
I wish to ask to be accepted as your disciple.
Moreover, if you, Master Yán, associate with me,
your meals shall always be of the grand sacrifice,
when you go out you shall ride in a carriage,
and your wife and children shall have fine and elegant clothes."
Yán Chù declined and prepared to leave, saying:
"Jade is born in the mountains.
When worked, it is broken—
not that it is not precious,
but the uncarved jade is no longer whole.
A shì is born in the rustic wilds.
When recommended and selected, he receives emolument—
not that he does not attain honor and success,
but his form and spirit are no longer whole.
Chù wishes to return,
to eat late and consider it as meat,
to walk leisurely and consider it as a carriage,
to be without fault and consider it as nobility,
to be pure, tranquil, upright, and correct, and thereby find contentment for myself.
The one who decides on words is the king;
the one who exhausts loyalty and speaks directly is Chù.
The essential Way has been fully stated.
I wish to be granted leave to return,
to go peacefully back to
my humble village home."
Then he bowed twice and took his leave.
Chù knew contentment.
Returning to simplicity,
he was never disgraced for the rest of his life.
Master Wáng Dǒu went to the gate and wished to see King Xuān of Qí.
King Xuān sent a receptionist to usher him in.
Wáng Dǒu said:
"If Dǒu hastens to see the king, it shows he is fond of power;
if the king hastens to see Dǒu, it shows he is fond of shì.
What does the king think?"
The messenger went back and reported.
The king said:
"Let the master proceed slowly;
I request to follow."
King Xuān then hastened to meet him at the gate,
entered with him,
and said:
"I, who have received the ancestral temple of my late father,
and guard the altars of soil and grain,
have heard that you, sir, speak directly and remonstrate correctly without concealment."
Wáng Dǒu replied:
"What the king has heard is mistaken.
Dǒu was born in a time of disorder,
and serves a ruler of disorder.
How would I dare to speak directly and remonstrate correctly?"
King Xuān flushed with anger,
unpleased.
After a while,
Wáng Dǒu said:
"What our former lord, Duke Huán, delighted in was
nine times assembling the feudal lords,
once rectifying the world,
the Son of Heaven granting him the register,
and establishing him as the senior uncle.
Now the king has four of these."
King Xuān was pleased,
and said:
"I am foolish and uncultured,
guarding the state of Qí,
and only fear losing it.
How could I have four of these?"
Wáng Dǒu said:
"No.
Our former lord was fond of horses;
the king is also fond of horses.
Our former lord was fond of dogs;
the king is also fond of dogs.
Our former lord was fond of wine;
the king is also fond of wine.
Our former lord was fond of women;
the king is also fond of women.
Our former lord was fond of shì—
in this the king is not fond of shì."
King Xuān said:
"In the present age there are no shì;
what is there for me to be fond of?"
Wáng Dǒu said:
"There are no Qílín or Lù'ěr horses in the world,
yet the king's team of four is already complete.
There are no fine dogs like those of Dōngguō or the Lú clan in the world,
yet the king's hunting dogs are already provided.
There are no Máoqiáng or Xīshī in the world,
yet the king's palace is already filled.
The king is simply not fond of shì;
why worry that there are no shì?"
The king said:
"I am concerned for the state and love the people,
and certainly wish to obtain shì to govern them."
Wáng Dǒu said:
"The king's concern for the state and love for the people
is not equal to the king's love for a foot of fine silk."
The king said:
"What do you mean?"
Wáng Dǒu said:
"When the king has someone make a cap,
he does not use his close attendants and flatterers, but uses artisans.
Why is that?
Because they are capable.
Now when the king governs Qí,
he uses none but his close attendants and flatterers.
Therefore I say it is not equal to loving a foot of fine silk."
King Xuān apologized, saying:
"I am guilty before the state."
Thereupon he promoted five shì to official posts,
and the state of Qí was greatly well-governed.
The King of Qí sent an envoy to inquire after Queen Wēi of Zhào.
The letter had not yet been opened,
when Queen Wēi asked the envoy:
"Is the harvest also without ailment?
Are the people also without ailment?
Is the king also without ailment?"
The envoy was displeased,
and said:
"Your servant was sent as an envoy to you, Queen Wēi.
Now you do not ask after the king first,
but first ask after the harvest and the people.
Is this putting the lowly first and the noble last?"
Queen Wēi said: "Not so.
If there is no harvest,
how can there be people?
If there are no people,
how can there be a ruler?
How could there be one who asks, abandoning the root and asking about the branch?"
Then he advanced and asked him, saying:
"In Qí there is a recluse named Zhōnglí Zǐ,
is he well?
His way of being is such that
those who have grain he also feeds,
and those without grain he also feeds;
those who have clothes he also clothes,
and those without clothes he also clothes.
This is to assist the king
in nurturing his people,
why has he not been employed to this day?
Is Yèyáng Zǐ well?
His way of being is such that
he pities the widowed and solitary,
sympathizes with the orphaned and alone,
relieves the distressed and impoverished,
and supplements those who are lacking.
This is to assist the king in bringing peace to his people,
why has he not been employed to this day?
Is the daughter of Běigōng, Yīng'ér Zǐ, well?
She removed her
earrings and jades,
and remained unmarried until old age,
in order to care for her parents.
These are all examples of leading the people through filial sentiment,
why has she not been received at court to this day?
These two gentlemen are not employed,
and this one woman is not received at court,
how can you rule the state of Qí,
and treat the myriad people as your children?
Is Yúlíng Zǐzhòng still alive?
His way of being is such that
above he does not serve the king as a minister,
below he does not manage his household,
and in between he does not seek to associate with the feudal lords.
This is leading the people
toward uselessness,
why has he not been executed to this day?"
A man of Qí went to see Tián Pián,
and said: "I have heard of your lofty principles,
that you have set yourself not to take office,
and wish to serve as a laborer."
Tián Pián said: "How did you hear this?"
He replied:
"I heard it from my neighbor's daughter."
Tián Pián said:
"What do you mean?"
He replied:
"My neighbor's daughter
set herself not to marry,
yet by the age of thirty she had seven sons.
Not marrying is not marrying,
but she has surpassed marriage in its fullness.
Now you, sir, have set yourself not to take office,
yet you receive a stipend of a thousand zhōng,
and have a retinue of a hundred followers.
Not taking office is indeed so,
but your wealth surpasses that of office."
Tián Zǐ was at a loss for words.
Guǎn Yān offended the King of Qí,
and said to his attendants:
"Which of you will go with me to the feudal lords?"
His attendants were silent and none replied.
Guǎn Yān, with a pained expression, shed tears and said:
"Alas! How easy it is to obtain gentlemen, yet how difficult to employ them!"
Tián Xū replied:
"Gentlemen cannot get enough to eat even with three meals,
yet your geese and ducks have food to spare;
the women in your inner chambers wear fine silks and gauzes,
and trail damasks and crepes,
yet gentlemen cannot even obtain these for trimmings. Moreover, wealth is what you, my lord, regard lightly,
while death is what gentlemen regard heavily.
You, my lord, are unwilling to give what you regard lightly to gentlemen,
yet demand that gentlemen serve you with what they regard heavily—
it is not that gentlemen are easy to obtain and difficult to employ."
Sū Qín went from Yān to Qí,
and had an audience at the south gate of Huázhāng.
The King of Qí said:
"Ah! You have come.
Qín has sent Wèi Rǎn to propose the title of 'Emperor,'
what do you think of it?"
He replied:
"Your Majesty's question to me is sudden,
and the source of trouble is subtle.
If you do not agree,
you will incur Qín's resentment;
if you agree,
you will incur the resentment of all under heaven.
It would be better to agree in order to satisfy Qín,
but not to actually adopt the title, to satisfy all under heaven.
If Qín adopts the title,
and all under heaven accept it,
then Your Majesty may also adopt it.
The matter of precedence
does no harm to the title of Emperor.
If Qín adopts the title,
but all under heaven do not accept it,
then Your Majesty should not adopt it.
In this way, to win over all under heaven
is a great advantage."
Sū Qín said to the King of Qí:
"If Qí and Qín both establish themselves as two Emperors,
does Your Majesty think all under heaven will honor Qín,
or honor Qí?"
The King said:
"They will honor Qín."
"If you abandon the title of Emperor, will all under heaven favor Qí,
or favor Qín?"
The King said:
"They will favor Qí and despise Qín."
"With two Emperors established,
and an agreement to attack Zhào,
how does that compare in advantage to attacking Sòng?"
He replied:
"Indeed, by agreeing with Qín to become Emperor,
all under heaven will honor Qín alone and slight Qí. If Qí abandons the title of Emperor,
then all under heaven will favor Qí and despise Qín.
Attacking Zhào is not as advantageous as attacking Sòng.
Therefore, I wish Your Majesty would clearly abandon the title of Emperor,
to align with all under heaven;
break the agreement and reject Qín,
not allowing it to contend for supremacy;
and in the meantime, Your Majesty can seize Sòng.
With Sòng in hand, then Yángchéng of Wèi is endangered;
with Huáiběi in hand, then the eastern territories of Chǔ are endangered;
with Jìxī in hand, then Hédōng of Zhào is endangered;
with Yīn and Pínglù in hand, then the gates of Liáng will not open.
Therefore, abandon the title of Emperor and focus instead on the matter of attacking Sòng;
then the state will be weighty and its name honored.
Yān and Chǔ will submit due to the circumstances,
and all under heaven will not dare disobey.
This is the action of Tāng and Wǔ.
Respect Qín in name,
and later make all under heaven despise it—
this is what is called exchanging humility for honor!
I hope Your Majesty will consider this carefully!"
Sū Qín persuaded King Mǐn of Qí, saying:
"I have heard that those who delight in being the first under heaven to use arms invite worry,
and those who delight in taking the lead in forming alliances that incur resentment end up isolated.
Those who arise later rely on circumstances,
and those who avoid resentment await the right time.
Therefore, when a sage undertakes affairs,
he must rely on authority and act in accordance with the times.
Authority and circumstance
are the guides of all things;
and timing and situation
are the leaders of all affairs.
Thus, without authority and circumstance,
and going against timing and situation,
few can accomplish their affairs.
"Now even with swords like Gānjiàng and Mòyé,
without human strength,
they cannot cut or wound.
Strong arrows and sharp metal,
without the advantage of bowstring and trigger,
cannot kill from afar.
It is not that the arrows are not sharp,
nor the swords not keen,
so why?
Because authority and circumstance are not present.
How do we know this is so?
In the past, Zhào attacked Wèi by surprise,
its chariots and men did not rest or relay,
Wèi's city walls were leveled and its territory divided,
eight gates of Wèi were defended but two gates were destroyed—
this was the appearance of a doomed state.
The Lord of Wèi went barefoot
and sought help from Wèi.
The King of Wèi donned armor and girded his sword,
challenging Zhào and demanding battle.
Within Hándān there was panic,
and between the
Yellow River and the mountains, chaos.
Wèi, having this reliance,
also gathered its remaining armor and turned north,
destroyed Gāngpíng,
and razed the outer walls of Zhōngmóu.
Wèi was not stronger than Zhào,
it was like Wèi being the arrow and Wèi the bowstring and trigger—
relying on Wèi's strength, it gained territory east of the river.
Zhào grew fearful,
Chǔ came to Zhào's aid and attacked Wèi,
battling west of Zhōu,
exiting through Liáng's gates,
encamping in Línzhōng,
with horses drinking from the Great River.
Zhào, having this reliance,
also attacked Wèi north of the river, burning the Jí trenches,
and destroying Huángchéng.
Thus, the devastation of Gāngpíng,
the destruction of Zhōngmóu,
the fall of Huángchéng,
and the burning of Jígōu—
these were none of them desired by Zhào and Wèi.
Yet both states urged their execution.
Why was this?
Because Wèi understood the advantage of seizing the opportune moment.
Nowadays, those who govern states are not like this.
Weak in military strength, yet fond of confronting the strong;
exhausted as a state, yet fond of provoking widespread resentment;
affairs having failed, yet fond of persisting in them;
weak in military strength, yet hating to defer to others;
narrow in territory, yet fond of confronting the great;
affairs having failed, yet fond of prolonged deceit.
To practice these six things and yet seek hegemony—
that is far from the mark.
"I have heard that those skilled at governing a state
follow the will of the people
and assess the capabilities of their military,
and only then act in accordance with the world.
Thus, in forming alliances, they do not incur resentment on behalf of others;
in launching campaigns, they do not weaken the strong on behalf of others.
If this is done,
then military forces are not wasted,
authority is not diminished,
territory can be expanded,
and desires can be fulfilled.
In the past,
when Qí joined Hán and Wèi in attacking Qín and Chǔ,
its fighting was not particularly fierce,
nor did it gain more territory than Hán and Wèi.
Yet the world alone blamed Qí.
Why was this?
Because it incurred resentment on behalf of Hán and Wèi.
Moreover, the world was universally employing arms:
Qí and Yān fought,
while Zhào annexed Zhōngshān;
Qín and Chǔ fought, and Hán and Wèi knew no rest;
while Sòng and Yuè used their forces exclusively.
These ten states
all had their minds set on opposing one another,
yet the world's resentment was focused solely on Qí.
Why was this?
Because in alliances, it was fond of incurring resentment on behalf of others,
and in campaigns, it was fond of weakening the strong.
"Moreover, the calamity of the powerful and great
often lies in their intent to lord it over others;
the disaster of the weak and small
often lies in their seeking advantage by scheming against others.
Thus, great states are endangered,
and small states are destroyed.
The strategy for a great state
is none other than to act later and heavily punish the unrighteous.
For by acting later, it gains many allies and its troops are strong;
then it uses the strength of the many to confront the exhausted few—
military success is assured.
If its actions do not run counter to the world's sentiments,
then benefits will surely follow.
If a great state practices this,
then fame and titles will come unbidden,
and hegemony and kingship will be established without effort.
The principle for a small state
is to remain quiet and cautious and place little trust in other lords.
If quiet and cautious,
then neighboring states will not turn against it;
if it places little trust in other lords,
then the world will not betray it.
If externally it is not betrayed,
and internally there is no rebellion,
then weapons and armor will decay unused,
and silks and cloths will mold in storehouses unworn.
If a small state follows this way,
then without sacrifices, it will have blessings;
without borrowing, it will find sufficiency.
Thus it is said:
He who bases himself on benevolence becomes king;
he who establishes righteousness becomes hegemon;
he who exhausts military force perishes.
How do we know this is so?
In the past, King Fūchāi of Wú, taking advantage of his great strength, put himself at the forefront of the world.
He forcefully attacked Yǐng and subjugated Yuè,
personally leading the feudal lords,
yet in the end he died and his state was destroyed,
becoming an object of ridicule for the world.
Why was this?
Because this Fūchāi, in his ordinary conduct, plotted to be king,
and, relying on his strength, delighted in being the first to bring calamity upon the world.
In the past, Lái and Jǔ were fond of scheming,
Chén and Cài were fond of deceit.
Jǔ relied on Yuè and perished;
Cài relied on Jìn and was destroyed.
These all suffered disaster because internally they cultivated deceit,
and externally they trusted in other lords.
From this we can see
that the calamities of strength and weakness, greatness and smallness
are visible in past events.
"There is a saying:
'When the fine steed weakens,
the nag outruns it;
when Mèng Bēn grows weary,
a woman can overcome him.'
Now the nag and the woman,
in sinew, bone, and strength,
are not superior to the fine steed or Mèng Bēn.
Why then?
Because of the advantage of acting later.
Now, if the states of the world do not all perish together,
but one possesses strength and holds back its troops to act later,
storing up resentment to punish the unrighteous,
using military action subtly and cloaking it in righteousness,
then the conquest of the world can be achieved in a single stride.
Those who understand the affairs of the feudal lords
and discern the principles of terrain
do not need to form close alliances,
nor exchange hostages to secure relations;
they do not need to rush, yet affairs proceed swiftly;
they engage in many undertakings without opposition,
exchange territories without mutual hatred,
and when both are strong, they grow closer.
Why is this?
Because their circumstances share common concerns, and their military actions pursue advantage.
How do we know this is so?
In the past, Qí and Yān fought at the bend of Huán.
Yān was defeated,
and a host of a hundred thousand was entirely lost.
The Hú people attacked Yān's counties of Lóufán,
seizing their oxen and horses.
Now, the Hú and Qí were not ordinarily close,
nor did they have any treaty or hostage agreement to plot against Yān.
Yet they acted in concert more than if they had rushed to each other's aid.
Why was this?
It is because their circumstances shared common concerns, and their military actions pursued advantage.
From this we can see
that forming alliances based on shared circumstances yields long-term benefit,
and acting later allows one to make the feudal lords rush to do one's bidding.
Thus, an enlightened ruler or perceptive minister,
if truly intent on aiming for hegemony and kingship,
should not give priority to warfare and attack.
Warfare
is the mutilation of the state
and the expense of its cities and counties.
Once mutilation and expense have taken the lead,
few can gain the allegiance of the feudal lords.
As for warfare being mutilation:
When soldiers hear of war, they contribute private wealth to enrich the army markets,
contribute food and drink to feed daring warriors,
break their carriage poles to use as firewood,
slaughter oxen to toast the troops—
this is the way to exhaust a ruler.
Commoners offer prayers and sacrifices;
the ruler provides wine and ale;
in large cities and small towns, altars are set up;
in every market town, none fail to cease their affairs and serve the king—
this is the plan to empty the center.
On the day after battle,
with corpses strewn and the wounded supported,
even if there seems to be achievement,
the army has expended its resources,
the center is filled with weeping,
and the ruler's heart is wounded.
Those who died bankrupt their families for burial;
the wounded exhaust their wealth for medicine;
the survivors feast and revel within—
thus the expense equals that of the dead and wounded.
Hence, what the people expend
cannot be repaid by ten years of farming.
What the army expends—
spears and halberds broken,
rings and bowstrings snapped,
crossbows damaged,
chariots wrecked,
horses exhausted,
more than half the arrows lost.
The equipment of armor and weapons
is privately provided by the officials,
hidden away by the officers and grandees,
stolen by the servants and retainers—
cannot be repaid by ten years of farming.
When a state in the world suffers these twin expenses,
few can gain the allegiance of the feudal lords.
The expense of attacking a city:
the common people prepare protective screens,
raise assault shelters and shields,
each household gathers supplies,
each person digs tunnels,
exhausted by the labor of metal and blades.
The soldiers are worn out by earthworks,
the generals do not remove their armor;
if they can take the city within the expected time, it is considered swift.
Superiors grow weary of instruction,
soldiers are broken by warfare;
hence, few who attack three cities can overcome the enemy.
Therefore it is said:
Those who engage in warfare and attack
are not putting first what should be first.
How do we know this is so?
In the past, Zhì Bó Yáo attacked the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans,
killed their lords,
and destroyed their states.
He then besieged Jìnyáng to the west,
annexed two states,
and brought worry to one ruler.
This was the height of military action.
Yet Zhì Bó ultimately met his death and his state perished,
becoming a laughingstock for all under heaven.
Why is this said?
Because he gave priority to warfare and attack,
and brought about the calamity of destroying two lords.
In the past,
Zhōngshān mustered all its forces to confront Yān and Zhào,
fought to the south at Chángzǐ,
and defeated the Zhào forces;
fought to the north at Zhōngshān,
overcame the Yān army,
and killed its general.
Now Zhōngshān was a state of a thousand chariots,
yet it opposed two states of ten thousand chariots,
and in two battles achieved northern victories.
This was the pinnacle of military action.
Yet the state ultimately perished,
and its ruler and ministers became subjects of Qí.
Why?
Because they did not spare themselves the calamity of warfare and attack.
From this we can see,
the failures of warfare and attack
can be observed in past events.
"Those in the present age who are called skilled in using troops,
who end battles with successive victories,
and whose defenses cannot be breached,
are praised by all under heaven as excellent.
If a state obtains and preserves such,
it is not to the state's benefit.
Your servant has heard that those who achieve great victories in battle
see their officers mostly die and their troops grow weaker;
those whose defenses cannot be breached
see their common people exhausted and their city walls exposed.
When officers die abroad,
the people are worn out at home,
and the city walls are exposed along the borders,
this is not a joy for the king.
Now, when shooting at a target, one does not blame the target;
if one hits it, it is considered skillful;
if one misses, one feels ashamed.
Whether young or old, noble or humble,
all are of one mind in wishing to pierce it.
Why?
Because they dislike showing others that it is difficult.
Now, to exhaust oneself in battle for successive victories,
and to insist that defenses must not be breached,
is not only showing others that it is difficult,
but also harming others.
Thus, all under heaven will certainly become its enemies.
To exhaust officers and expose the state,
and to make many enemies in all under heaven,
is not something an enlightened ruler would abide.
To habitually use strong troops and weaken them,
is not something a perceptive minister would undertake.
Those enlightened rulers and perceptive ministers
achieve the submission of the feudal lords without moving the five weapons;
through polite refusal and generous gifts, they attain their goals.
Thus, when an enlightened ruler wages war,
he conquers enemy states without sending out armored troops;
enemy border cities surrender without deploying battering rams;
the officers and people remain unaware, yet the kingly enterprise arrives.
That enlightened ruler in his undertakings
uses little wealth,
takes long days and distant time, yet brings lasting benefit.
Therefore it is said:
If arms are raised later, the feudal lords can be made to hasten to serve.
"What your servant has heard
is that the way of attack and warfare does not lie in armies.
Even with a million troops,
they can be matched in the hall;
even with generals like Hélǘ or Wú Qǐ,
they can be captured within the doors;
a city wall a thousand zhàng high
can be taken from between the wine vessels;
a hundred-chǐ battering ram
can be broken upon the mats.
Thus, with the sounds of bells, drums, pipes, and zithers never ceasing,
territory can be expanded and desires fulfilled;
with the laughter of harmonious musicians, actors, and dwarfs never ending,
the feudal lords can be made to arrive on the same day.
Thus, a name matching heaven and earth is not considered noble;
benefits controlling all within the seas are not considered ample.
Therefore, those skilled at establishing the kingly enterprise
toil all under heaven while they themselves are at ease,
throw all under heaven into chaos while they themselves are secure.
If the feudal lords have no settled plans,
then their state has no lingering worries.
How do we know this is so?
Ease and order lie with me,
toil and chaos lie with all under heaven:
this is the way of kings.
When sharp troops come, resist them;
when calamity arrives, hasten to it.
If the feudal lords have no settled plans,
then their state has no lingering worries.
How do we know this is so?
In the past, the King of Wèi held a thousand lǐ of territory,
led three hundred sixty thousand armored troops.
In his strength, he captured Hándān,
besieged Dìngyáng to the west,
and further led twelve feudal lords to pay court to the Son of Heaven,
planning against Qín to the west.
The King of Qín feared this,
slept uneasily on his mat,
ate without tasting his food.
He issued orders throughout his realm,
preparing all battle equipment within the walls,
completing defensive preparations,
appointing generals for death-defying warriors,
awaiting the Wèi forces.
Wèi Yāng counseled the King of Qín, saying:
'The achievements of Wèi are great,
and its commands are heeded throughout all under heaven.
It has twelve feudal lords paying court to the Son of Heaven;
its allies are certainly many.
Thus, for a single Qín to oppose a great Wèi
is, I fear, not equal to the task.
Why does Your Majesty not send your servant to see the King of Wèi?
Then your servant requests to certainly defeat Wèi.'
The King of Qín assented.
Wèi Yāng saw the King of Wèi and said:
'Your Majesty's achievements are great indeed,
and your commands are heeded throughout all under heaven.
Now, the twelve feudal lords following Your Majesty
are none other than Sòng and Wèi,
or Zōu, Lǔ, Chén, and Cài.
These are indeed those whom Your Majesty can drive with whip and crop;
they are insufficient to make you king over all under heaven.
Your Majesty would do better to take Yān to the north,
attack Qí to the east;
then Zhào will certainly submit.
Take Qín to the west,
attack Chǔ to the south;
then Hán will certainly submit.
If Your Majesty has the heart to attack Qí and Chǔ,
and the will to make all under heaven follow,
then the kingly enterprise will appear.
Your Majesty should first adopt kingly attire,
and then plan against Qí and Chǔ.'
The King of Wèi was pleased with Wèi Yāng's words.
Therefore, he enlarged his palace,
made vermilion clothes and pillars,
set up nine streamers, and followed the banner with seven stars.
This is the position of the Son of Heaven, and the King of Wèi occupied it.
Thereupon, Qí and Chǔ grew angry.
The feudal lords fled to Qí.
The men of Qí attacked Wèi,
killed its crown prince,
and destroyed its army of a hundred thousand.
The King of Wèi was greatly terrified.
Barefoot, he marched his troops within his state,
and then encamped to the east of Qí;
only then did all under heaven let him be.
At that time,
the King of Qín, with folded hands, received the land west of the Yellow River,
and did not feel grateful to the King of Wèi.
Therefore it is said: from the beginning when Wèi Yāng plotted with the King of Qín,
their strategic agreement did not leave the mat;
their words were spoken between the wine vessels;
their plan was formed in the hall,
and yet the generals of Wèi were captured by Qí;
battering rams were not deployed,
and yet the land west of the Yellow River entered Qín.
This is what your servant means by matching them in the hall,
capturing generals within the doors,
taking cities from between the wine vessels,
and breaking rams upon the mats."
Among the people living near the outer wall of Qí's capital was one Gū Hú Xuǎn, who criticized King Mǐn directly.
He was executed at Tán Qú,
and the common people did not adhere.
Chén Jǔ, a scion of Qí's ruling Sūn family, spoke straightforwardly.
He was killed at the Eastern Gate,
and the clan and relatives became disaffected.
Sīmǎ Rángjū was a man of governance.
He was killed,
and the great ministers did not feel close.
For these reasons, Yān raised troops,
sending Lord Chāngguó to command and attack.
Qí sent Xiàngzǐ to command and respond.
The Qí army was defeated.
Xiàngzǐ escaped with a single carriage.
Dázǐ gathered the remaining troops,
rallied them again, and fought Yān.
He sought funds for rewards,
but King Mǐn refused to give them.
The army was defeated and fled.
The king fled to Jǔ.
Nào Chǐ enumerated his faults, saying:
"Between Qiānshèng and Bóchāng,
spanning several hundred li,
blood rained and soaked people's clothes.
Did Your Majesty know of this?"
The king said:
"I did not know."
"Between Yíng and Bó,
the earth split open down to the springs.
Did Your Majesty know of this?"
The king said:
"I did not know."
"There was a man who wept at the palace gate.
When sought, he could not be found;
when left alone, his cries were heard.
Did Your Majesty know of this?"
The king said:
"I did not know."
Nào Chǐ said:
"The raining of blood that soaked clothes—
this was Heaven giving warning.
The earth splitting open to the springs—
this was Earth giving warning.
The man weeping at the gate—
this was Man giving warning.
Heaven, Earth, and Man have all given warning,
yet Your Majesty did not take heed.
How could you escape execution?"
Thereupon, he killed King Mǐn at Gǔlǐ.
The crown prince then removed his royal garments
and fled to the home of the Grand Scribe, working as a gardener.
Jūnwánghòu,
the daughter of the Grand Scribe clan,
recognizing him as a noble man,
treated him well.
Tián Dān, with the city of Jímò
and the remnants of the defeated army,
defeated the Yān troops,
deceived Qí Jié,
and thus restored Qí.
He hastily welcomed the crown prince from Jǔ
and established him as king.
When King Xiāng ascended the throne,
he made Jūnwánghòu his queen,
and she gave birth to King Jiàn of Qí.
Serving King Mǐn,
Wángsūn Jiǎ was fifteen years old
and served King Mǐn. When the king fled,
he lost track of the king's whereabouts.
His mother said:
"When you go out in the morning and return late,
I lean against the gate and watch for you;
when you go out at dusk and do not return,
I lean against the village gate and watch for you.
Now you serve the king.
The king has fled,
and you do not know his whereabouts.
Where else should you go?"
Wángsūn Jiǎ then entered the marketplace,
saying:
"Nào Chǐ has thrown Qí into chaos
and killed King Mǐn.
Whoever wishes to join me in punishing him,
bare your right arm!"
Four hundred people in the marketplace followed him,
and together they punished Nào Chǐ,
stabbing and killing him.
Yān attacked Qí and captured over seventy cities,
leaving only Jǔ and Jímò undefeated.
Tián Dān of Qí used Jímò to defeat Yān,
killing Qí Jié.
Earlier, a Yān general had captured Liáochéng,
but someone slandered him.
Fearing execution,
he held and defended Liáochéng,
not daring to return.
Tián Dān attacked it for over a year,
with many soldiers dying,
yet Liáochéng did not fall.
Lǔ Lián then wrote a letter,
tied it to an arrow, and shot it into the city,
sending it to the Yān general, saying:
"I have heard that
a wise man does not oppose the times and abandon advantage,
a brave man does not fear death and ruin his name,
and a loyal minister does not put himself before his lord."
Now you act on momentary anger,
disregarding that the King of Yān is left without a minister—
this is not loyalty.
To lose your life and let Liáochéng fall,
while your might gains no trust in Qí—
this is not courage.
Your achievements ruined, your name destroyed,
with no praise from later generations—
this is not wisdom.
Thus, the wise do not hesitate,
and the brave do not fear death.
Now life and death, honor and disgrace,
high and low, noble and base—
all hinge on this moment.
I hope you will consider carefully and not follow vulgar ways.
Moreover, Chǔ attacked Nányáng,
and Wèi attacked Pínglù.
Qí had no intention to face south,
believing that the harm of losing Nányáng
was less than the benefit of gaining Jìběi.
Thus, they made their plan and held firm.
Now the Qín troops advance,
and Wèi dares not face east.
If Qín's horizontal alliance is formed,
then Chǔ's situation will be perilous.
Moreover, abandoning Nányáng,
cutting off the right territory,
and preserving Jìběi—
this is surely their plan.
Now Chǔ and Wèi have both withdrawn,
Yān's rescue does not come,
and Qí has no designs from the world.
Yet you hold Liáochéng against a year of exhaustion—
I foresee that you cannot succeed.
Qí will surely decide at Liáochéng.
Do not hesitate further.
That Yān is in great chaos,
with ruler and ministers miscalculating,
and high and low confused—
Lì Fù with a million troops
suffered five defeats abroad.
A state of ten thousand chariots
was besieged by Zhào,
its territory reduced, its lord distressed,
and mocked by the world—
have you heard of this?
Now the King of Yān is isolated and fearful,
his ministers unreliable,
the state weakened and plagued by disasters,
and the people's hearts without direction.
Now you, with the exhausted people of Liáochéng,
resist the full force of Qí's army,
holding out for a year without relief—
this is the defense of Mò Dí.
Eating human flesh and burning bones for fuel,
yet your soldiers have no thought of desertion—
this is the army of Sūn Bìn and Wú Qǐ.
Your abilities are visible to the world!
Thus, for your sake,
it would be better to cease hostilities and rest your troops,
preserve your chariots and armor,
and return to report to the King of Yān.
The King of Yān will surely be pleased.
The officers and people will see you
as they see their parents.
Friends will roll up their sleeves and discuss you in the world,
and your achievements will be clear.
Above, assist the isolated lord
to control the ministers;
below, nurture the common people
to provide material for persuaders.
Rectify the state and reform customs for the world,
and merit and fame can be established.
Perhaps,
you might also abandon Yān and leave the world,
traveling east to Qí?
I request land be granted and a fief established,
making you as wealthy as Táo and Wèi,
called 'the solitary one' for generations,
enduring long with Qí—
this is also a plan.
Both options bring clear fame and substantial gain.
I hope you will consider carefully and choose one.
Moreover, I have heard that
those who cling to minor principles cannot exercise great authority,
and those who hate small shames cannot establish glorious fame.
In the past, Guǎn Zhòng shot Duke Huán and hit his belt hook—
this was usurpation.
He abandoned Prince Jiǔ and did not die for him—
this was cowardice.
Bound in fetters,
he humiliated himself.
For these three actions,
he was not welcomed in his hometown,
and lords of the age would not have him as minister.
Had Guǎn Zhòng remained in dire straits,
imprisoned and unable to emerge,
ashamed and unseen,
living out his years to the end of his life,
he would have been nothing but a disgraced man of lowly conduct.
Yet Guǎnzi combined the faults of three actions,
seized control of Qí's government,
unified the world under one standard,
nine times assembled the feudal lords,
became the leader of the Five Hegemons,
his name renowned throughout the world,
his glory shining upon neighboring states.
Cáo Mò served as general for the lord of Lǔ,
three battles and three defeats,
losing a thousand lǐ of territory.
Had Cáo Mò's feet never left the battle formation,
his plans disregarding the future, charging forth to certain death without hope of survival,
he would have been nothing but a defeated general captured in battle.
For Cáo Mò to be a defeated and captured general would not have been bravery;
his achievements ruined, his name extinguished,
unpraised by later generations—that would not have been wisdom.
Therefore, he cast aside the shame of three defeats,
withdrew and plotted with the lord of Lǔ,
and Cáo Mò considered this an opportunity.
Duke Huán of Qí held sway over the world,
receiving homage from the feudal lords.
Cáo Mò, relying on the strength of a single sword,
seized Duke Huán upon the altar platform,
his countenance unchanged,
and his words unwavering.
All that was lost in three battles
was recovered in a single morning,
shaking and astonishing the world,
spreading his awe to Wú and Chǔ,
his name passed down to later ages.
These two gentlemen
were not incapable of upholding minor principles
or dying for petty shames,
but they believed that to sacrifice oneself and cut off one's line,
without establishing merit and fame,
was not wisdom.
Therefore, they cast aside feelings of resentment and anger,
and achieved the fame of Chóng'ěr;
they removed the shame of humiliation and indignation,
and established merit for generations.
Thus, their deeds rivaled those of the Three Sovereigns,
and their names endured as long as heaven and earth.
Consider this carefully!
The Yān general said:
"I respectfully heed your command!"
Thereupon, he withdrew his troops from Dúlí and departed.
Thus, the siege of Qí was lifted,
and the people were saved from death—
all due to Zhònglián's persuasion.
Yān attacked Qí,
and Qí was defeated.
King Mǐn fled to Jǔ,
where Zhuō Chǐ killed King Mǐn.
Tián Dān defended the city of Jímò,
defeated the Yān army,
and restored Qí's territory.
King Xiāng was then the crown prince.
After Qí had defeated Yān,
doubts arose about Tián Dān's intentions,
and among the people of Qí,
all believed Tián Dān intended to seize the throne for himself.
When King Xiāng ascended the throne,
Tián Dān served as his chancellor.
Crossing the Zī River,
they encountered an old man fording the river who was cold,
unable to walk after emerging,
and sat down in the sand.
Tián Dān, seeing he was cold,
wished to have the following carriage share clothing,
but there was none to share,
so Dān removed his own fur robe and clothed him.
King Xiāng was displeased by this,
saying:
"Tián Dān's act of charity—
does he intend to seize my state?
If we do not plan early,
I fear it will be too late."
Looking around and seeing no one nearby,
there was a pearl-gatherer beneath the cliff.
King Xiāng called him and asked:
"Did you hear my words?"
He replied:
"I heard them."
The king said:
"What do you think?"
He replied:
"Your Majesty should instead take this as your own good deed.
Praise Tián Dān's goodness,
and issue an order: 'I worry about the people's hunger,
and Tián Dān gathers and feeds them;
I worry about the people's cold,
and Tián Dān removes his robe to clothe them;
I worry and toil for the people,
and Tián Dān also worries for them,
fulfilling my intentions.'
Tián Dān has this goodness, and if Your Majesty praises him,
praising Tián Dān's goodness
becomes Your Majesty's own goodness."
The king said:
"Excellent!"
Thereupon, he bestowed upon Tián Dān oxen and wine,
praising his conduct.
Several days later,
the pearl-gatherer again saw the king and said:
"On the day of court assembly,
Your Majesty should summon Tián Dān and bow to him in the court,
personally commending him.
Then issue an order seeking out the hungry and cold among the people,
and gather grain to aid them."
Thereupon, he sent people to listen in the villages,
and heard men conversing with each other,
all saying:
"How Tián Dān loves the people!
Ah, but this is due to the king's benevolent influence!"
Diāo Bó often spoke ill of Tián Dān,
saying:
"Lord Ānpíng
is a petty man."
Lord Ānpíng heard of this,
and deliberately held a banquet to summon Diāo Bó,
saying:
"How have I offended you, sir,
that you often praise me at court?"
Diāo Bó said:
"A dog barks at Yáo for Zhí,
not because it honors Zhí and disdains Yáo,
but because a dog naturally barks at those who are not its master.
Moreover, suppose now that Gōngsūnzǐ is worthy,
and Xúzǐ is unworthy.
Yet if Gōngsūnzǐ and Xúzǐ were to fight,
Xúzǐ's dog
would still seize Gōngsūnzǐ's calf and bite it.
If it could leave the unworthy master
and become the dog of a worthy one,
would it merely seize the calf and bite it?"
Lord Ānpíng said: "I respectfully heed your words."
The next day, he recommended him to the king.
The king had nine favored ministers in his circle,
who wished to harm Lord Ānpíng.
They spoke together to the king, saying:
"When Yān attacked Qí,
the king of Chǔ sent a general with ten thousand men to aid Qí.
Now the state is settled,
and the altars of state are secure.
Why not send an envoy to thank the king of Chǔ?"
The king said: "Who among you is suitable?"
The nine ministers said:
"Diāo Bó is suitable."
Diāo Bó was sent to Chǔ.
The king of Chǔ received him and feasted him,
and he did not return for several days.
The nine ministers spoke together to the king, saying:
"For one man
to detain a ruler of ten thousand chariots—
is it not because he relies on powerful backing?
Moreover, Lord Ānpíng and Your Majesty—
there is no propriety between ruler and minister,
and no distinction between superior and inferior.
Furthermore, his intentions are to do evil.
Internally, he governs the people,
soothing their hearts,
relieving poverty and aiding the needy,
spreading virtue among the people;
externally, he wins over the Róng and Dí, and the worthy scholars of the world,
secretly allying with the heroic and outstanding among the feudal lords.
His intention is to achieve great things.
We hope Your Majesty will investigate this."
Another day, the king said:
"Summon Chancellor Dān here."
Tián Dān removed his cap, went barefoot, bared his shoulders, and advanced,
then withdrew and requested punishment by death.
After five days,
the king said:
"You have committed no offense against me.
You perform your minister's rites,
and I perform my kingly rites, that is all."
When Diāo Bó returned from Chǔ,
the king bestowed a feast before him.
When the wine was flowing freely,
the king said:
"Summon Chancellor Tián Dān here."
Diāo Bó left his mat, kowtowed, and said:
"How can Your Majesty utter such words that would destroy a state?
Who is superior, Your Majesty or King Wén of Zhōu?"
The king said:
"I am not his equal."
Diāo Bó said:
"Indeed,
I certainly know that Your Majesty is not his equal.
Who among those of lower status can compare with Duke Huán of Qí?"
The king said:
"I am not his equal."
Diāo Bó said:
"Indeed,
I certainly know that Your Majesty is not his equal.
Yet King Wén of Zhōu obtained Lǚ Shàng and honored him as 'Grand Duke',
Duke Huán of Qí obtained Guǎn Yíwú and honored him as 'Uncle Zhòng',
but now Your Majesty has obtained Ānpíng Jūn and merely calls him 'Dān'.
Moreover, since the opening of heaven and earth,
and the governance of the people,
among the achievements of ministers,
who has greater merit than Ānpíng Jūn?
Yet Your Majesty says 'Dān, Dān'.
How can such words that lead to the ruin of a state be uttered?
Furthermore, Your Majesty could not defend the altars of soil and grain of your ancestors,
the Yān people raised an army and attacked the ruins of Qí,
Your Majesty fled and went into the mountains of Chéngyáng.
Ānpíng Jūn, with the trembling city of Jímò,
a city wall of three lǐ,
an outer wall of five lǐ,
and a weary army of seven thousand,
captured their commander,
and restored the thousand-lǐ state of Qí—
this was the achievement of Ānpíng Jūn.
At that time,
had he closed off Chéngyáng and declared himself king,
no one in Chéngyáng or all under heaven could have stopped him.
However, considering the Way,
and returning to righteousness,
he deemed it improper,
so he built plank roads and wooden pavilions,
and welcomed Your Majesty and the queen from the mountains of Chéngyáng.
Only then did Your Majesty return,
to oversee the people.
Now the state is already settled,
and the people are already at peace,
yet Your Majesty says 'Dān'.
Even a child's plan would not be like this.
If Your Majesty does not swiftly execute these nine men to apologize to Ānpíng Jūn,
if not,
the state will be in peril!"
The king then executed the nine men and exiled their families,
and further enfeoffed Ānpíng Jūn with ten thousand households in Yèyì.
Tián Dān was about to attack Dí,
and went to see Lǔ Zhòngzǐ.
Zhòngzǐ said: "General, in attacking Dí,
you will not be able to take it."
Tián Dān said: "I, with a city wall of five lǐ,
an outer wall of seven lǐ,
and the remnant troops of a defeated and ruined army,
defeated the mighty state of Yān with ten thousand chariots,
and restored the ruins of Qí.
If I attack Dí and cannot take it,
why is that?"
He boarded his carriage without bidding farewell and left.
He then attacked Dí,
but after three months had not conquered it.
The children of Qí sang a rhyme:
"His great hat like a winnowing basket,
his long sword propping his chin,
attacking Dí he cannot succeed,
camped atop a barren hill."
Tián Dān then became fearful,
and asked Lǔ Zhòngzǐ:
"Sir, you said I could not take Dí,
I beg to hear your explanation."
Lǔ Zhòngzǐ said:
"When you, General, were at Jímò,
you sat weaving baskets,
stood holding a spade,
and exhorted the soldiers, saying:
'We can go forth!
The ancestral temple is lost!
Our days are numbered!
To which faction shall we return!'
At that time,
you, General, had the heart to die,
and the soldiers had no will to live.
Hearing such words,
none failed to wipe away tears, raise their arms, and desire to fight.
This is why you defeated Yān.
Now, General, you have the revenues of Yèyì in the east,
the pleasures of Zīshàng in the west,
a golden belt across your waist,
and gallop between the Zī and Miǎn rivers.
You have the joys of life,
but no heart for death.
This is why you cannot win."
Tián Dān said: "I have the heart,
sir, you have recognized it."
The next day,
he then roused his spirit and patrolled the city walls,
standing where arrows and stones fell,
then took up the drumsticks and beat the drum.
The Dí people then surrendered.
Regarding the affair at Púshàng,
Zhuìzǐ died,
Zhāngzǐ fled,
Pànzǐ said to the King of Qí:
"It would be better to exchange our surplus grain with Sòng.
The King of Sòng will certainly be pleased.
Liáng will not dare to cross Sòng to attack Qí.
Qí is inherently weak,
so we use surplus grain to win over Sòng.
Once Qí's state is strong again,
even if we demand repayment from Sòng, it is acceptable;
if they do not repay,
we can use that as a pretext to attack them,
which is also acceptable."
When King Mǐn of Qí was killed,
his son Fǎzhāng changed his name,
and became a laborer in the household of the Grand Scribe of Jǔ.
The daughter of Grand Scribe Jiǎo,
marveling at Fǎzhāng's appearance,
thought him an extraordinary man,
took pity on him and often secretly provided him with clothing and food,
and became intimate with him.
The people in Jǔ and the surviving ministers of Qí gathered,
seeking the son of King Mǐn,
wishing to establish him.
Fǎzhāng then revealed himself in Jǔ.
Together they established Fǎzhāng as King Xiāng.
When King Xiāng was established,
he made the daughter of the Grand Scribe clan his queen,
and she bore a son, Jiàn.
Grand Scribe Jiǎo said:
"A daughter who marries without a matchmaker,
is not of my kind,
she sullies my lineage."
He never saw her again for the rest of his life.
Queen Jūnwánghòu was virtuous,
and did not, because he refused to see her,
neglect the rites due to a father.
When King Xiāng died,
his son Jiàn was established as King of Qí.
Queen Jūnwánghòu served Qín cautiously,
and kept faith with the other feudal lords,
so for over forty years Jiàn did not suffer military attack.
Qín Shǐhuáng once sent an envoy to present Queen Jūnwánghòu with a jade interlocking chain,
saying:
"Qí has many wise people,
can they solve this chain?"
Queen Jūnwánghòu showed it to her ministers,
but none knew how to solve it.
Queen Jūnwánghòu took a hammer and smashed it,
apologizing to the Qín envoy, saying:
"Respectfully, it is solved."
When Queen Jūnwánghòu fell ill and was near death,
she admonished Jiàn, saying:
"Among the ministers, those who can be employed are so-and-so."
Jiàn said:
"Please write it down."
Queen Jūnwánghòu said:
"Good."
She took brush and tablet to receive her words.
Queen Jūnwánghòu said:
"This old woman has already forgotten!"
After Queen Jūnwánghòu died,
later Hòu Shèng became chancellor of Qí,
and received much gold and jade from Qín spies,
sending guests into Qín,
all of whom spoke deceitful words,
urging the king to pay court to Qín,
and not to prepare for attack or defense.
When King Jiàn of Qí went to pay court at Qín,
the Yongmén Commandant came forward and said:
"For what purpose is a king established?
Is it for the altars of soil and grain?
Or is it for the king that a king is established?"
The king said:
"For the altars of soil and grain."
The Commandant said:
"If a king is established for the altars of soil and grain,
why does Your Majesty leave the altars of soil and grain to go to Qín?"
The King of Qí turned his carriage around and returned.
The Grand Master of Jímò and the Yongmén Commandant, seeing that their remonstrance was heeded,
thought that plans could be made,
and went in to see the King of Qí, saying:
"The territory of Qí extends several thousand lǐ,
with armored troops numbering several million.
The ministers of the Three Jìn,
are all discontent with Qín,
and there are hundreds of them between Ā and Juàn.
If Your Majesty gathers them and gives them a million troops,
and has them recover the former territories of the Three Jìn,
then the pass of Línjìn can be entered;"
The ministers of Yān and Yǐng,
unwilling to serve Qín,
number in the hundreds beneath the city walls.
If Your Majesty gathers them and gives them an army of a million,
sending them to recover the old territories of Chǔ,
then they can enter through Wǔguān.
In this way,
the might of Qí can be established,
and the state of Qín can be destroyed.
To abandon the title of sovereign facing south,
and instead face west to serve Qín,
is something I do not consider advisable for Your Majesty."
The King of Qí did not listen.
Qín sent Chén Chí to entice the King of Qí to come within,
promising him five hundred lǐ of land.
The King of Qí did not heed the minister of Jímò but listened to Chén Chí,
and thus entered Qín.
He was placed among the pines and cypresses of Gòng,
where he starved to death.
Before this, the people of Qí sang a song about him:
"Pines, oh!
Cypresses, oh!
The one who dwells in Gòng,
is he a guest, oh!"
Qí, due to the turmoil caused by Nào Jūn, troubled Qín.
Afterward, Qín wanted to win over Qí,
so it sent Sū Juān to Chǔ,
and ordered Rèn Gù to go to Qí.
Qí Míng said to the King of Chǔ:
"The King of Qín desires Chǔ,
but not as much as he desires Qí.
He sends Juān here
to show Qí that Chǔ is involved,
thereby aiding Gù in Qí.
When Qí sees Chǔ's involvement,
it will surely accept Gù.
If Your Majesty listens to Juān,
it will precisely drive Gù to unite Qí and Qín.
If Qí and Qín unite,
it will not be to Chǔ's advantage.
Moreover, the words Juān brings
are certainly not the same words Gù will use in Qí.
Your Majesty should instead have someone use Juān's words to deceive Gù in Qí,
and Qí and Qín will surely not unite.
If Qí and Qín do not unite,
then Your Majesty's importance will increase.
If Your Majesty wishes to win over Qí to attack Qín,
Hànzhōng can be obtained.
If Your Majesty wishes to use Qín to attack Qí,
the region between Huái and Sì can also be obtained."
When Qí and Chǔ became embroiled in conflict, Sòng requested neutrality.
Qí pressured Sòng urgently,
and Sòng agreed.
Zǐ Xiàng, on behalf of Chǔ, said to the King of Sòng:
"Chǔ lost Sòng by being slow,
and will now emulate Qí's urgency.
Qí gained Sòng through urgency,
and will henceforth always use urgency.
To follow Qí and attack Chǔ
may not be advantageous.
If Qí defeats Chǔ in battle,
its power will inevitably endanger Sòng;
if it does not win,
then it is using weak Sòng to offend strong Chǔ.
To allow two states of ten thousand chariots
to constantly use urgency to seek what they desire,
will surely endanger the state."
Five states made a pact to attack Qí.
Zhāo Yáng said to the King of Chǔ:
"After the five states defeat Qí, Qín
will certainly plan against Chǔ in the south."
The King said:
"What then should be done?"
He replied:
"Hán is a supporting state;
it loves profit and hates difficulty.
Loving profit,
it can be tempted;
hating difficulty,
it can be intimidated.
If we bribe it heavily with profit,
its mind will certainly be tempted.
If we deploy all our troops to confront it,
its mind will certainly fear us.
If it fears our troops and is tempted by our profit,
the alliance of the five states can surely be broken.
After the pact is severed,
we need not even give it land."
The King of Chǔ said:
"Excellent."
He then ordered Dàgōng Shì to go to Hán,
where he met Gōng Zhòng and said:
"The affair of Niúlán,
the disaster of Mǎlíng—these were witnessed by Your Majesty.
If Your Majesty does not join the five states in using troops,
we offer five cities in a row,
and will deploy the entire army of Chǔ
to oppose Qí."
After Qí turned against Zhào and Wèi,
and Chǔ indeed did not give the land,
the alliance of the five states was thwarted.
King Xuān of Jīng asked his ministers:
"I hear that the northern states fear Zhāo Xīxù.
Is this truly so?"
None of the ministers replied.
Jiāng Yī responded:
"A tiger sought to eat all the beasts,
and caught a fox.
The fox said:
'You dare not eat me.
The Heavenly Emperor made me the leader of all beasts.
If you eat me now,
you defy the Heavenly Emperor's command.
If you think I am not truthful,
I will walk ahead of you,
and you follow behind me,
and see if any beast dares not flee at the sight of me.'
The tiger thought this reasonable,
so he went along with the fox.
All the beasts fled at the sight of them.
The tiger did not know the beasts fled from fear of himself,
but thought they feared the fox.
Now Your Majesty's territory spans five thousand lǐ,
with a million armored troops,
yet you delegate full authority to Zhāo Xīxù.
Thus, when the northern states fear Xīxù,
they are actually fearing Your Majesty's armored troops,
just as the beasts feared the tiger."
When Zhāo Xīxù and Péngchéng Jūn were debating before the King,
the King summoned Jiāng Yǐ and asked him about it.
Jiāng Yǐ said:
"Both men's words are good,
so I dare not comment on which is better.
This is called considering the worthy."
During the crisis of Hándān,
Zhāo Xīxù said to the King of Chǔ:
"Your Majesty should not rescue Zhào,
but rather strengthen Wèi.
If Wèi is strengthened,
it will certainly carve deeply into Zhào.
If Zhào does not comply,
it will surely hold firm in defense,
resulting in mutual exhaustion."
Jǐng Shě said:
"Not so.
Zhāo Xīxù does not understand.
When Wèi attacks Zhào,
it fears Chǔ will attack its rear.
If we do not rescue Zhào,
Zhào will face imminent destruction,
and Wèi will have no worry about Chǔ.
This means Chǔ and Wèi together press Zhào,
and the harm will surely be deep!
How can there be mutual exhaustion?
Moreover, if Wèi orders its troops to carve deeply into Zhào,
and Zhào, seeing its imminent destruction,
realizes Chǔ will not rescue it,
it will certainly ally with Wèi to plot against Chǔ.
Therefore, Your Majesty should send a small force
to aid Zhào.
Relying on Chǔ's strength,
Zhào will certainly fight Wèi.
Wèi, angered by Zhào's resistance,
and seeing Chǔ's rescue as insufficient to fear,
will not release Zhào.
When Zhào and Wèi exhaust each other,
and Qí and Qín respond to Chǔ,
then Wèi can be defeated."
Chǔ then sent Jǐng Shě to raise troops and rescue Zhào.
After Hándān was captured,
Chǔ took the region between Suī and Huì.
Jiāng Yǐn wanted to make Zhāo Xīxù odious to the King of Chǔ,
but lacked the power to do so,
so he requested a fief in Chǔ for Liáng Shānyáng Jūn.
The King of Chǔ said:
"Agreed."
Zhāo Xīxù said:
"Shānyáng Jūn has rendered no service to the state of Chǔ,
and should not be enfeoffed."
Jiāng Yǐn thus gained Shānyáng Jūn as an ally to jointly make Zhāo Xīxù odious.
The people of Wèi made Zhāo Xīxù odious to the King of Chǔ,
and the King informed Zhāo Zǐ.
Zhāo Zǐ said:
"I serve and obey orders morning and night,
yet the people of Wèi intrude between ruler and minister.
I am greatly afraid."
I am not afraid of Wèi!
But if he reveals the intimacy between our sovereign and his ministers,
and the world believes him,
then his character is indeed close to being bitter.
If he does not find it difficult to act against us externally,
how could he forget to act against us internally?
My offense will be upon me any day now."
The king said,
"I understand, why should you worry?"
Jiāng Yǐ hated Zhāo Xīxù,
and said to the king of Chǔ:
"There was a man who loved his dog for being vigilant.
The dog once urinated in a well.
His neighbor saw the dog urinating in the well
and wanted to go in and tell him.
The dog hated this,
and stood at the gate biting him.
The neighbor was afraid of it,
and thus could not go in to speak.
During the crisis at Hándān,
Chǔ advanced troops to Dàliáng,
and captured it.
Zhāo Xīxù took the precious vessels of Wèi,
and because I, residing in Wèi, knew of it,
therefore Zhāo Xīxù always hates my seeing the king."
Jiāng Yǐ wanted to make Zhāo Xīxù hated by Chǔ,
and said to the king of Chǔ:
"If those below form cliques,
then those above are endangered;
if those below are divided and contentious,
then those above are secure.
Does the king also know this?
I hope the king does not forget it.
Moreover, if there is someone who likes to praise others' good points,
what does the king think of him?"
The king said:
"This is a gentleman,
draw close to him."
Jiāng Yǐ said:
"If there is someone who likes to expose others' faults,
what does the king think of him?"
The king said:
"This is a petty man,
keep away from him."
Jiāng Yǐ said:
"If so, then there will be cases of sons killing their fathers,
and ministers assassinating their lords,
yet the king in the end remains unaware of them.
Why is that?
Because the king likes to hear of people's goodness and dislikes hearing of people's faults."
The king said:
"Well said.
I wish to hear both."
Jiāng Yǐ advised Ānlíng Jūn, saying:
"You have not a foot or inch of land,
nor kinship ties of flesh and blood,
yet you occupy a lofty position,
receive a generous salary,
and all the people of the state,
when they see you, none fail to straighten their garments and bow,
and bow their heads in submission.
How is this so?"
He replied:
"It is merely the king's excessive promotion.
Otherwise,
there would be no way to reach this point."
Jiāng Yǐ said:
"Those who form friendships through wealth,
when the wealth is exhausted, the friendship ends;
those who form friendships through looks,
when the beauty fades, the love changes.
Thus, a favored concubine does not outlast the mat,
and a favored minister does not outlast the carriage.
Now you wield the power of the state of Chǔ,
yet have no means to deeply bind yourself to the king.
I privately worry for your danger."
Ānlíng Jūn said:
"If so, then what should I do?"
"I hope you will certainly request to follow him in death,
offering your body as a sacrifice.
If you do this, you will surely long enjoy importance in Chǔ."
He said:
"I respectfully accept your instruction."
Three years passed and he did not speak of it.
Jiāng Yǐ saw him again and said:
"The advice I gave you,
has to this day shown no effect.
If you do not use my plan,
I beg leave not to see you again."
Ānlíng Jūn said: "I dare not forget the master's words,
I have just not found the right moment."
Thereupon,
the king of Chǔ was traveling in Yúnmèng,
with a thousand four-horse chariots in train,
banners and flags blotting out the sun,
the wild fires rising like clouds and rainbows,
the roars of rhinoceroses and tigers like peals of thunder.
A mad rhinoceros came charging straight at the wheels of the chariot.
The king personally drew his bow and shot,
with one arrow he killed it.
The king pulled out a banner and pressed down the rhinoceros's head,
looked up to heaven and laughed, saying:
"How joyful
is today's excursion!
After I, the solitary one, pass on ten thousand years from now,
who will share this joy with me?"
Ānlíng Jūn, tears streaming down, came forward and said:
"When I enter, I share your mat,
when I go out, I accompany your carriage.
After Your Majesty passes on ten thousand years from now,
I wish to test the Yellow Springs with my body,
to be a mat for the ants and insects.
How then could I obtain such joy and enjoy it?"
The king was greatly pleased,
and thereupon enfeoffed Tán as Ānlíng Jūn.
A gentleman heard of this and said:
"Jiāng Yǐ can be said to be skilled in planning,
and Ānlíng Jūn can be said to know the right moment."
Jiāng Yǐ, as an envoy from Wèi to Chǔ,
said to the king of Chǔ:
"Since entering your borders,
I have heard of a custom in Chǔ:
not to conceal others' good points,
and not to speak of others' faults.
Is this truly so?"
The king said: "It is truly so."
Jiāng Yǐ said:
"If so, then the rebellion of Bái Gōng,
could it have succeeded?
If it were truly as you say,
then the crimes of us ministers would be pardoned."
The king of Chǔ said: "Why is that?"
Jiāng Yǐ said:
"Zhōu Hóu served as minister of Chǔ,
extremely noble and decisive in judgment.
Those around him all said 'there is none',
as if speaking with one mouth."
A man of Yǐng had a lawsuit unresolved for three years,
so he deliberately had someone request his house,
to divine his guilt.
The visitor therefore spoke to Zhāo Xīxù on his behalf, saying:
"The house of a certain man of Yǐng, I wish to have it."
Zhāo Xīxù said:
"That certain man of Yǐng,
should not be found guilty,
therefore his house cannot be obtained."
The visitor took his leave and departed.
Zhāo Xīxù later regretted it,
and thus said to the visitor:
"Xīxù has served you,
why did you use a pretext with Xīxù?"
The visitor said:
"I did not use a pretext."
He said:
"When told you could not obtain it,
you showed a pleased expression.
If not a pretext, then what was it?"
Chéng Hún left Zhōu,
three men traveling together,
journeyed south to Chǔ,
and reached Xīnchéng.
Chéng Hún persuaded its magistrate, saying:
"Zhèng and Wèi
are weak states to Chǔ;
while Qín
is Chǔ's powerful enemy.
Against the weakness of Zhèng and Wèi,
Chǔ uses Shàngliáng to respond;
against the greatness of Yíyáng,
Chǔ uses weak Xīnchéng to encircle it.
Púfǎn and Píngyáng are a hundred lǐ apart,
yet when the men of Qín attacked them overnight,
Ānyì did not know;
Xīnchéng and Shàngliáng are five hundred lǐ apart,
if the men of Qín attacked them overnight,
Shàngliáng would also not know.
Now what the border towns rely on
is not the region south of the Jiāng and Sì rivers.
Therefore, why does the king of Chǔ not make Xīnchéng the chief commandery?
The border towns would greatly benefit from it."
The Lord of Xīnchéng was greatly pleased,
and thereupon prepared a four-horse carriage and five hundred gold for his journey to Chǔ.
Chéng Hún obtained them,
then went south and made connections in Chǔ.
The king of Chǔ indeed made Xīnchéng the chief commandery.
Hán Gōngshū has the support of Qí and Wèi,
while the crown prince has the support of Chǔ and Qín
in contending for the state.
Zhèng Shēn was sent by Chǔ as an envoy to Hán,
and he falsely granted Xīnchéng and Yángrén to the crown prince.
The King of Chǔ was enraged,
and intended to punish him.
He replied:
"I falsely granted them
for the sake of the state.
By securing Xīnchéng and Yángrén for the crown prince, I enabled him to contend with Gōngshū for the state and win.
Qí and Wèi are certain to attack Hán.
When Hán is in dire straits,
it will have to entrust its fate to Chǔ.
How then would it dare to demand Xīnchéng and Yángrén?
If the crown prince does not prevail,
yet does not perish,
he will come fleeing in disarray,
and how would he dare speak of land?"
The King of Chǔ said:
"Excellent."
He then did not punish him.
Chǔ's Dù Hè persuaded the King of Chǔ to win over Zhào.
The king was about to grant him the rank of Wǔ Dàfū,
and ordered him to undertake a private mission.
Chén Zhěn said to the King of Chǔ:
"If Hè fails to win over Zhào,
the rank of Wǔ Dàfū cannot be revoked,
resulting in reward without merit.
If he succeeds in winning over Zhào and the king adds nothing further,
that would be failing to reward good service.
It would be better for the king to send him with ten chariots.
If the mission succeeds,
then grant him the rank of Wǔ Dàfū."
The king said:
"Excellent."
He then sent him with ten chariots.
Dù Hè was angry and did not go.
Chén Zhěn said to the king: "This means he cannot win over Zhào."
The King of Chǔ asked Fàn Huán:
"I wish to appoint a chancellor in Qín.
Who would be suitable?"
He replied: "I am not qualified to know."
The king said: "Could my chancellor Gān Mào be suitable?"
Fàn Huán replied: "He is not suitable."
The king said:
"Why not?"
He said:
"That Shǐ Jǔ
was a gatekeeper in Shàngcài.
In major matters, he was not good at serving his lord;
in minor matters, he was not good at managing his household.
He was known throughout the world for being harsh and incorruptible,
yet Gān Mào served him obediently.
Thus, under the brilliance of King Huì [of Qín]
and the discernment of King Wǔ [of Qín],
and despite Zhāng Yí's fondness for slander,
Gān Mào served them,
attained ten offices without incurring blame,
so Mào is indeed a worthy man.
However, he should not be made chancellor of Qín.
For Qín to have a worthy chancellor
is not beneficial to the state of Chǔ.
Moreover, the king once used [Zhāo] Huá in Yuè and annexed Gōuzhāng.
During the troubles of Mò,
Yuè fell into chaos,
thus Chǔ inspected Làihú in the south and extended its territory east of the Jiāng.
Considering how the king's achievements could reach such a level,
it was because Yuè was in chaos while Chǔ was well-governed.
Now the king has applied this strategy to Yuè,
but forgets it regarding Qín.
I believe the king is forgetting far too quickly.
If the king wishes to appoint a chancellor in Qín,
someone like Gōngsūn Hè would be suitable.
For Gōngsūn Hè, regarding the King of Qín,
is a close relative.
In youth, he shared clothes with him;
in adulthood, he shared chariots with him.
He wears the king's robes when attending to affairs—
truly, he is already the king's chancellor.
If the king makes him chancellor,
it would be of great benefit to the state of Chǔ."
Sū Qín, forming a vertical alliance for Zhào,
persuaded King Wēi of Chǔ, saying:
"Chǔ
is a powerful state in the world.
Your Majesty
is a worthy king in the world.
The lands of Chǔ: to the west, there are Qiánzhōng and Wūjùn;
to the east, there are Xiàzhōu and Hǎiyáng;
to the south, there are Dòngtíng and Cāngwú;
to the north, there are the passes of Fénxíng
and Xúnyáng.
The territory spans five thousand lǐ,
with a million armored troops,
a thousand chariots,
ten thousand cavalry,
and grain supplies to last ten years.
These are the resources for a hegemon or king.
With the strength of Chǔ and the worthiness of Your Majesty,
no one in the world can withstand you.
Yet now you wish to face west and serve Qín.
Then the various lords will all face south and pay court beneath the Zhāngtái.
Of all the states in the world, none is as harmful to Qín as Chǔ.
When Chǔ is strong, Qín is weak;
when Chǔ is weak, Qín is strong.
Their circumstances are such that they cannot coexist.
Therefore, the best strategy for Your Majesty is to form a vertical alliance to isolate Qín.
If Your Majesty does not join the vertical alliance,
Qín is sure to raise two armies:
one army will exit Wǔguān;
one army will descend upon Qiánzhōng.
If this happens,
then Yān and Yǐng will be shaken.
I have heard that one should govern before disorder arises,
and act before events occur.
If one worries only after calamity arrives,
then it will be too late.
Thus, I hope Your Majesty will plan early.
"If Your Majesty truly can heed my words,
I will request that the states east of the mountains
offer seasonal tributes
to follow Your Majesty's enlightened rule,
entrust their altars of state and ancestral temples,
train soldiers and sharpen weapons,
all for Your Majesty to employ as you see fit.
If Your Majesty truly can heed my humble plan,
then the exquisite music and beautiful women of Hán, Wèi, Qí, Yān, Zhào, and Wèi
will surely fill your rear palace.
The fine horses and camels of Zhào and Dài
will surely fill your outer stables.
Thus, if the vertical alliance succeeds, Chǔ will become king;
if the horizontal alliance succeeds, Qín will become emperor.
Now to abandon the enterprise of hegemon or king
and accept the name of serving others—
I privately believe Your Majesty should not choose this.
