"That Qín
is a state of tigers and wolves,
with a mind to devour the world.
Qín
is the enemy of the world.
Those advocating the horizontal alliance all wish to cut off the lands of the various lords to serve Qín.
This is what is called nurturing an enemy and serving a foe.
For a minister to cut off his lord's land
to form external ties with the strong, tiger-and-wolf state of Qín, thereby encroaching upon the world—
when the calamity of Qín finally arrives,
he does not consider the disaster.
Using the external might of strong Qín
to internally coerce his own lord,
seeking to cut off land—
great treason and disloyalty
have no greater example than this.
Therefore, if the vertical alliance is formed,
the various lords will cut off land to serve Chǔ;
if the horizontal alliance is formed,
then Chǔ will cut off land to serve Qín.
These two strategies
are far apart,
differing by hundreds of millions.
Which of the two will Your Majesty choose?
Therefore, my humble sovereign, the King of Zhào,
has sent me to present this humble plan,
offering a clear covenant,
awaiting Your Majesty's command."
The King of Chǔ said: "My state
borders Qín to the west. Qín
has the intention of seizing Bā-Shǔ and annexing Hànzhōng.
Qín
is a state of tigers and wolves,
and cannot be befriended.
But Hán and Wèi are pressured by the threat of Qín,
and one cannot deeply conspire with them,
fearing that traitors might deliver our plans to Qín,
so before the plan is launched, the state would already be in danger.
I have considered myself:
with Chǔ confronting Qín,
I do not see victory.
Internally, consulting with my ministers,
they are not reliable.
I lie down without peaceful rest,
eat without savoring flavor,
my heart swaying like a hanging banner,
with nothing to finally settle upon.
Now you, sir, wish to unify the world,
pacify the various lords,
preserve states in peril.
I respectfully offer my altars of state to follow you."
Zhāng Yí, in service of Qín, destroyed the vertical alliance and promoted the horizontal alliance,
and addressed the King of Chǔ, saying:
"The territory of Qín comprises half of the world,
its military rivals that of the four states,
it is backed by mountains and girded by rivers,
with four strategic passes making it secure.
It has over a million fierce warriors,
a thousand chariots,
ten thousand cavalry horses,
and grain piled up like hills.
Its laws and decrees are clear,
and its soldiers face hardship with ease and are willing to die.
The ruler is strict and discerning,
the generals are wise and martial.
Even without mobilizing troops,
they could sweep across the perilous Chángshān,
break the spine of the world,
and those who submit later among the states will perish first.
Moreover, those who advocate the vertical alliance
are no different from driving a flock of sheep to attack a fierce tiger.
Between a tiger and sheep,
it is clear they are no match.
Now, Your Majesty sides not with the fierce tiger but with the flock of sheep—
I privately believe Your Majesty's strategy is mistaken.
Of all the powerful states in the world,
if not Qín then it is Chǔ,
if not Chǔ then it is Qín.
These two states are evenly matched and contend with each other,
their situation is such that they cannot coexist.
If Your Majesty does not ally with Qín,
Qín will dispatch troops,
seize Yíyáng,
and the upper lands of Hán will be cut off;
descend to Hédōng,
capture Chénggāo,
and Hán will inevitably submit to Qín.
Once Hán submits,
Wèi will follow like the wind.
With Qín attacking Chǔ from the west,
and Hán and Wèi attacking from the north,
how could your altars of state remain secure?
Moreover, those who form the vertical alliance
gather a crowd of weak states to attack the strongest.
For the weak to attack the strong,
without assessing the enemy and lightly engaging in war,
while the state is impoverished and hastily raises troops—
this is a path to peril and ruin.
I have heard it said,
if your troops are inferior,
do not provoke a challenge;
if your grain is insufficient,
do not engage in prolonged warfare.
Those who advocate alliances
adorn their arguments with empty words,
exalt the ruler's integrity and conduct,
speak of the benefits but not the harms,
and when disaster suddenly befalls Chǔ,
it will be too late to act.
Therefore, I hope Your Majesty will consider this carefully.
To the west, Qín possesses Bā and Shǔ,
where large ships stockpile grain,
setting out from Wènshān,
following the river downstream,
reaching Yǐng in over three thousand lǐ.
Barge ships carry soldiers,
each barge carrying fifty men
and three months' provisions.
Floating downstream,
they can travel over three hundred lǐ in a day;
though the distance is great,
it does not tire the horses,
and within ten days they will reach Hànguān.
Once Hànguān is alarmed,
then from Jìnglíng eastward,
all cities will be on guard,
and Qiánzhōng and Wūjùn will no longer belong to Your Majesty.
If Qín raises troops and marches out of Wǔguān,
attacking southward,
then the northern territories will be severed.
When Qín's troops attack Chǔ,
the crisis will occur within three months.
Yet Chǔ relies on rescue from the other states,
which will take over half a year—
this situation makes it impossible to match.
To rely on rescue from weak states
and forget the calamity from strong Qín—
this is what I worry about for Your Majesty.
Moreover, Your Majesty once fought five battles with the people of Wú, winning three but ultimately perishing,
with your ranks of soldiers exhausted;
you partially defended new cities, and the residents suffered.
I have heard it said,
attacking a great power easily leads to peril,
and when the people are exhausted, they resent their superiors.
To defend achievements easily imperiled,
and oppose the will of strong Qín—
I privately fear for Your Majesty.
Moreover, the reason Qín has not sent troops out of Hángǔguān for fifteen years to attack the other states
is because it secretly plots to swallow the world.
Chǔ once engaged in conflict with Qín,
fighting at Hànzhōng.
The people of Chǔ did not prevail,
with over seventy marquises and holders of the jade tablet dying,
and they lost Hànzhōng.
The King of Chǔ was greatly angered,
raised an army to attack Qín,
fought at Lántián,
and was again repelled.
This is what is called two tigers fighting each other.
When Qín and Chǔ exhaust each other,
Hán and Wèi can fully control the aftermath—
no strategy is more mistaken than this.
Therefore, I hope Your Majesty will consider this carefully.
If Qín sends troops to attack Wèi and Yángjìn,
it will surely open the chest of the world,
and Your Majesty can raise all your troops to attack Sòng.
Within a few months, Sòng can be taken.
With Sòng taken and pointing eastward,
then the twelve states of Sìshàng
will all belong to Your Majesty.
Of all those in the world who advocated the vertical alliance and close bonds, Sū Qín
was enfeoffed as the Lord of Wǔ'ān and became chancellor of Yān,
yet secretly plotted with the King of Yān to destroy Qí and divide its land.
Then he feigned guilt,
fled to Qí,
and the King of Qí accepted him and made him chancellor.
After two years, this was discovered,
and the King of Qí was greatly angered,
having Sū Qín torn apart by chariots in the market.
With a deceitful and fickle person like Sū Qín
attempting to manage the world
and unify the states,
it is clear that success was impossible.
"Now, between Qín and Chǔ,
borders connect,
so they are naturally close states.
If Your Majesty truly listens to me,
I will request that the crown prince of Qín be sent as a hostage to Chǔ,
and the crown prince of Chǔ be sent as a hostage to Qín.
I will ask for a daughter of Qín to serve as Your Majesty's humble consort,
present a city of ten thousand households
as a fief for bathing and grooming,
so that we may long be brotherly states,
never attacking each other for life.
I believe no strategy is more advantageous than this.
Therefore, the King of Qín of my humble state
has sent me, his envoy, to present this letter to Your Majesty's attendants,
awaiting your decision on the matter."
The King of Chǔ said:
"Chǔ is a remote and uncultured state,
perched on the eastern sea.
I am young in years,
and unfamiliar with the long-term strategies of the state.
Now, honored guest, you have kindly instructed me with clear guidance,
and having heard it,
I respectfully submit my state to follow."
Then he dispatched a hundred envoy carriages,
presenting rhinoceros horns of the jīhài type and luminous night pearls to the King of Qín.
Zhāng Yí, as chancellor of Qín,
said to Zhāo Jū:
"If Chǔ loses Yān, Yǐng, and Hànzhōng,
will it gain anything else?"
He replied:
"It will not."
Zhāng Yí said:
"If Chǔ loses Zhāo Jū and Chén Zhěn,
will it gain anything else?"
He replied:
"It will gain nothing else."
Zhāng Yí said:
"For my sake, tell the King of Chǔ to expel Zhāo Jū and Chén Zhěn,
and I will request the return of Yān, Yǐng, and Hànzhōng."
Zhāo Jū returned and reported to the King of Chǔ,
and the King of Chǔ was pleased.
Someone said to Zhāo Jū:
"How extreme it is
that the King of Chǔ does not understand the contest for reputation.
When Hán sought the artisan Chén Jí as chancellor, Zhōu did not agree;
when Wèi sought Qímǔ Huī as chancellor, Zhōu did not agree.
Why?
Because Zhōu treats us as a subordinate county.
Now Chǔ
is a powerful state of ten thousand chariots;
Your Majesty is a worthy ruler of the world.
Now Zhāng Yí says to expel you and Chén Zhěn, and Your Majesty listens—
this means Chǔ acts in a manner inferior to Zhōu,
and Zhāng Yí is more esteemed than the kings of Hán and Wèi."
Moreover, the path that Zhāng Yí treads,
the achievements and fame he seeks lie in Qín,
while the wealth and honor he desires are in Wèi.
If he wishes to launch an attack against Wèi,
he must first campaign south against Chǔ.
Therefore, in waging war there is a method:
externally, sever its alliances;
internally, expel its strategists.
Chén Zhěn
is a man of Xià,
well-versed in the affairs of the Three Jìn.
Thus, if he is expelled,
then Chǔ will be without a strategist.
Now, if you, my lord, can employ the masses of Chǔ,
then expel him as well,
and the masses of Chǔ will not be employed.
This is what is called attacking from within,
yet the king does not know to examine this.
Now, why does my lord not present me to the king,
and allow me to request, on the king's behalf, to ensure that diplomatic relations with Qí are not severed?
If relations with Qí are not severed,
when Zhāng Yí hears of it,
he will certainly slow his planned seizure of Yān, Yǐng, and Hànzhōng.
Thus, Zhāo Jū's words will prove untrustworthy,
and the king will surely hold him in low regard. 」
King Wēi asked Mò'áo Zǐhuá, saying:
"From the time of our former ruler King Wén down to my own person,
have there not been those who were not urged by rank,
nor encouraged by salary,
yet who worried for the altars of soil and grain?"
Mò'áo Zǐhuá replied:
"Someone like Huá is insufficient to know of such."
The king said:
"If not from the great officer,
from whom shall I hear of it?"
Mò'áo Zǐhuá replied:
"What manner of men does my lord king wish to ask about?
There are those who make their rank pure,
keep their person poor,
to worry for the altars of soil and grain;
there are those who elevate their rank,
enrich their salary,
to worry for the altars of soil and grain;
there are those who sever their necks, split their bellies,
close their eyes once and never see again for ten thousand generations,
not knowing what benefit it brings,
to worry for the altars of soil and grain;
there are those who toil their bodies,
distress their minds,
to worry for the altars of soil and grain;
and there are also those who are not urged by rank,
nor encouraged by salary,
to worry for the altars of soil and grain."
The king said:
"Great officer, in saying this,
whom do you refer to?"
Mò'áo Zǐhuá replied:
"In the past, Lìngyǐn Zǐwén
wore robes of black silk to court,
and deerskin at home;
he stood at court before dawn,
and returned to eat only after dusk;
he did not plan for the evening in the morning,
and had not a month's store of grain.
Thus, he who made his rank pure,
kept his person poor,
to worry for the altars of soil and grain—
that was Lìngyǐn Zǐwén.
In the past, Yègōng Zǐgāo,
his person was obtained from humble origins,
yet his wealth came from being Zhùguó;
he settled the disaster of Báigōng,
brought peace to the affairs of Chǔ;
he restored the former ruler and covered the lands beyond Fāngchéng,
the four borders saw no invasion,
and his name suffered no setback among the feudal lords.
At that time,
none under heaven dared to turn arms southward.
Yègōng Zǐgāo
had six hundred zhěn of fields for sustenance.
Thus, he who elevated his rank,
enriched his salary,
to worry for the altars of soil and grain—
that was Yègōng Zǐgāo.
In the past, when Wú and Chǔ fought at Bǎijǔ,
between the two chariots the foot soldiers clashed.
Mò'áo Dàxīn patted his charioteer's hand,
looked back and heaved a great sigh, saying:
'Alas, my men!
The month of Chǔ's destruction has arrived!
I shall plunge deep into the Wú army;
if I strike down one man,
if I seize one man,
to share with Dàxīn,
might the altars of soil and grain perhaps be preserved?'
Thus, he who severed his neck, split his belly,
closed his eyes once and never saw again for ten thousand generations,
not knowing what benefit it brought,
to worry for the altars of soil and grain—
that was Mò'áo Dàxīn.
In the past, when Wú and Chǔ fought at Bǎijǔ,
after three battles they entered Yǐng.
Our ruler fled in person,
the great officers were all scattered,
the common people were dispersed.
Fénmào Bósū said:
'If I don armor and grasp sharp weapons,
rush upon a strong enemy and die,
this is still but one soldier's death;
it is not like fleeing to the feudal lords.'
Thereupon, carrying dry rations, he traveled in secret,
climbed Zhēng Mountain,
crossed deep ravines,
until his soles were pierced and his knees exposed,
and on the seventh day he reached the court of the King of Qín.
He stood like a bird, unmoving,
moaning by day and weeping by night.
For seven days he could not deliver his message.
Not a drop of water entered his mouth;
he fell into a faint, exhausted and senseless,
unconscious and unaware of others.
The King of Qín, hearing of it, ran to him,
his cap and sash not yet properly donned;
with his left hand he supported his head,
with his right he moistened his mouth, and Bósū then revived.
The King of Qín personally asked him:
'Who are you, sir?'
Fénmào Bósū replied:
'Your servant is no stranger;
I am a newly arrived envoy from Chǔ,
Fénmào Bósū.
Wú and the men of Chǔ fought at Bǎijǔ;
after three battles they entered Yǐng.
Our ruler fled in person,
the great officers were all scattered,
the common people were dispersed.
Your humble servant has come to report our ruin and to beg for rescue.'
The King of Qín, looking at him, ordered him not to rise:
'I have heard that
if the ruler of a ten-thousand-chariot state offends one scholar,
the altars of soil and grain may be endangered—
now this is what is meant.'
Thereupon he sent out a thousand armored chariots
and ten thousand soldiers,
placing them under the command of Zǐ Mǎn and Zǐ Hǔ.
They descended east from the pass
and fought the men of Wú at Zhuóshuǐ,
greatly defeating them;
this was also heard of at Suìpǔ.
Thus, he who toiled his body,
distressed his mind,
to worry for the altars of soil and grain—
that was Fénmào Bósū.
"When Wú and Chǔ fought at Bǎijǔ,
after three battles they entered Yǐng.
My lord king fled in person,
the great officers were all scattered,
the common people were dispersed.
Méng Gǔ joined the fight at Gōngtáng,
then abandoned the fight and rushed to Yǐng, saying:
'If there is an orphaned heir,
might the altars of soil and grain of Chǔ perhaps be preserved?'
Thereupon he entered the great palace,
shouldered the Jīcì法典 and floated on the Jiāng,
fleeing into the midst of Yúnmèng.
When King Zhāo returned to Yǐng,
the five offices had lost their laws,
the common people were in chaos and disorder.
Méng Gǔ presented the法典,
the five offices regained their laws,
and the common people were greatly well-governed.
This achievement of Méng Gǔ
was as great as preserving the state.
He was enfeoffed with the Zhíguī rank
and six hundred zhěn of fields.
Méng Gǔ angrily said:
'Gǔ is no mere servant of a ruler;
he is a servant of the altars of soil and grain.
If the altars of soil and grain continue their blood sacrifices,
how could I, the remainder, be without a lord?'
Thereupon he cast himself away in the Móshān mountains,
and to this day has not sought glory.
Thus, he who was not urged by rank,
nor encouraged by salary,
to worry for the altars of soil and grain—
that was Méng Gǔ."
The king then heaved a great sigh and said:
"These were men of antiquity.
Men of today—
how could there be such?"
Mò'áo Zǐhuá replied:
The Wei chancellor Zhái Qiáng died.
Someone spoke to the King of Chǔ on behalf of Gān Mào:
"The one most likely to become chancellor of Wèi
is the prince Jìn.
If Jìn becomes chancellor of Wèi,
the relations between Wèi and Qín will certainly become good.
If the relations between Qín and Wèi are solid,
then Chǔ will be slighted.
Therefore, Your Majesty should rather make a pact with Qí
to have Gān Mào made chancellor in Wèi.
The King of Qí likes to elevate men of high reputation;
now if you, as his envoy, request the chancellorship of Wèi for him,
Qí will certainly be pleased.
If the Wèi house does not comply,
their relations with Qí will turn sour;
if the relations between Qí and Wèi turn sour,
they will certainly compete to serve Chǔ.
If the Wèi house complies,
Gān Mào and Chūlǐ Jí
are sworn enemies;
and the relations between Wèi and Qín will certainly turn sour,
which will also make them both value Chǔ more highly."
Qí and Qín made a pact to attack Chǔ.
Chǔ ordered Jǐng Cuì to bribe Qí with six cities,
with the crown prince as a hostage.
Zhāo Jū said to Jǐng Cuì:
"Qín, fearing, will likely follow Jǐng Lǐ and Sū Lì's lead and offer land to Chǔ.
You, sir, are ceding land to win over Qí,
while Lǐ and Lì will likely gain land to win over Qín.
Your undertaking will certainly fail.
You, sir, should rather have the king heavily bribe Jǐng Lǐ and Sū Lì,
and send them into Qín.
Qín, fearing,
will certainly not demand land but will ally with Chǔ.
If Qí then makes no demands,
it will be you, sir, who has kept the pact."
Shù Shì attacked Chǔ.
Chǔ ordered Zhāo Shǔ to station a hundred thousand troops in Hànzhōng.
Zhāo Jū defeated Qín at Chóngqiū.
Sū Lì said to the Lord of Wǎn, Zhāo Shǔ:
"If the king wishes Zhāo Jū to press Qín,
he will certainly divide your troops to reinforce him.
If Qín learns that your troops have been divided,
they will certainly march out of Hànzhōng.
Allow me, on your behalf, to have Xīn Róng tell the king:
'The Qín troops are about to march out of Hànzhōng.'
Then your troops will remain intact."
Four states attacked Chǔ.
Chǔ ordered Zhāo Jū to lead troops to resist Qín.
The King of Chǔ wanted to attack Qín,
but Zhāo Hóu did not wish to.
Huán Zāng spoke to the King of Chǔ on behalf of Zhāo Jū:
"If Jū wins the battle,
the three other states, resenting Chǔ's strength,
and fearing that Qín might change its mind and heed Chǔ,
will certainly attack Chǔ fiercely to strengthen Qín.
The King of Qín, angered by defeat in battle,
will certainly mobilize all his forces to attack Chǔ.
This would mean Your Majesty and Qín wearing each other out,
to the benefit of the three other states.
If we do not defeat Qín in battle,
Qín will advance its troops and attack.
It would be better to reinforce Zhāo Jū's troops,
ordering him to show Qín that we are determined to fight.
The King of Qín dislikes the prospect of mutual exhaustion with Chǔ being witnessed by all under heaven;
Qín can then be made to accept minor territorial concessions and cease its harmful actions.
If Qín and Chǔ ally,
then Yān, Zhào, and Wèi will not dare disobey,
and the three states can be pacified."
King Huáiwáng of Chǔ detained Zhāng Yí,
intending to kill him.
Jìn Shàng spoke to the King of Chǔ on behalf of Yí:
"If you detain Zhāng Yí,
the King of Qín will certainly be angry.
When all under heaven see that Chǔ has lost Qín's favor,
Chǔ will certainly be slighted."
He also said to the king's favored consort, Zhèng Xiù:
"Do you yourself know that you are about to be degraded by the king?"
Zhèng Xiù said: "Why?"
Shàng said: "Zhāng Yí
is a loyal, trustworthy, and meritorious minister of the King of Qín.
Now Chǔ has detained him;
the King of Qín wishes to secure his release.
The King of Qín has a beloved daughter who is beautiful.
He has also selected from his palace lovely and charming women skilled in music,
to accompany her for pleasure;
he has provided her with treasures of gold, jade, and precious vessels,
and presented the six counties of Shàngyōng as her bath and grooming estate,
intending to use Zhāng Yí to introduce her to the King of Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ will certainly love her.
The Qín woman, relying on powerful Qín for importance,
and possessing rich lands as her resources,
will, by her position as the king's wife, hold sway over Chǔ.
The king, infatuated with new pleasures,
will certainly deeply respect, honor, and love her, and forget you.
You will be increasingly degraded and daily estranged."
Zhèng Xiù said: "I entrust this matter to you, sir.
What should be done about it?"
He said: "Why don't you urgently speak to the king
to release Master Zhāng.
If Master Zhāng gains his release,
his gratitude to you will be endless.
The Qín woman will certainly not come,
and Qín will certainly value you.
Internally, you will monopolize the honors of Chǔ;
externally, you will forge ties with Qín.
Nurturing Master Zhāng for your own use,
your sons and grandsons will certainly become the crown princes of Chǔ.
This is no ordinary commoner's benefit."
Zhèng Xiù immediately persuaded the King of Chǔ to release Master Zhāng.
The King of Chǔ was about to release Master Zhāng,
but feared he would bring about his own ruin.
Jìn Shàng said to the King of Chǔ:
"I request to accompany him.
If Yí does not serve Your Majesty well,
I request permission to kill him."
A minor minister of Chǔ,
an enemy of Jìn Shàng,
said to Zhāng Máo:
"With Zhāng Yí's wisdom,
and the support of Qín and Chǔ,
you, sir, will certainly be cornered.
You, sir, should rather
send someone to secretly waylay Jìn Shàng and assassinate him.
The King of Chǔ will certainly be furious with Yí.
When that Yí is cornered,
then you, sir, will be important.
If Chǔ and Qín trouble each other,
then Wèi will have no worries."
Zhāng Máo indeed sent someone to waylay Jìn Shàng and assassinate him.
The King of Chǔ was greatly angered,
and Qín raised troops to fight.
Qín and Chǔ competed to serve Wèi,
and Zhāng Máo indeed became greatly important.
Qín defeated Chǔ at Hànzhōng.
The King of Chǔ entered Qín,
and the King of Qín detained him.
Yóu Téng spoke to the King of Qín on behalf of Chǔ:
"If Your Majesty holds the King of Chǔ captive,
and joins with all under heaven to attack Chǔ,
then you will damage your conduct.
If you do not join with all under heaven to attack him,
then you will lose the advantage.
Your Majesty should rather make a covenant with him and send him back.
The King of Chǔ, in fear,
will certainly not dare to break the covenant.
Your Majesty can then join with the three states to attack him,
which would be righteous."
When King Xiāngwáng of Chǔ was crown prince,
he was a hostage in Qí.
When King Huáiwáng died,
the crown prince took leave of the King of Qí to return.
The King of Qí obstructed him:
"Give me five hundred lǐ of your eastern lands,
then I will let you return.
If you do not give them to me,
you may not return."
The crown prince said: "I have a tutor;
allow me to go and consult my tutor."
His tutor, Shènzǐ, said: "Offering the land
is for the sake of your own person.
To begrudge the land and not send off your deceased father
is unrighteous.
Therefore I say,
offering it is expedient."
The crown prince entered,
and delivered his reply to the King of Qí: "I respectfully offer five hundred lǐ of land."
The King of Qí sent the crown prince of Chǔ back.
The crown prince returned,
and ascended the throne as king.
Qí sent fifty chariots
to come and collect the eastern lands from Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ told Shènzǐ: "Qí has sent envoys to demand the eastern lands.
What should be done about it?"
Shènzǐ said: "Your Majesty should hold court tomorrow with all your ministers,
and order each to present his plan."
The Senior Pillar of State, Zǐ Liáng, entered for an audience.
The king said:
"The reason I, the unworthy one, was able to seek to return, to visit the royal tombs,
to reunite with my ministers, and to restore the altars of state,
was that I promised Qí five hundred lǐ of the eastern lands.
Now Qí has sent envoys to demand the land.
What should be done about it?"
Zǐ Liáng said: "Your Majesty cannot but give it.
Your Majesty personally uttered a jade-like word,
promising the powerful ten-thousand-chariot state of Qí and then not giving,
would be untrustworthy.
Thereafter you could not make pacts with the various lords.
I request that you give it and then attack to recover it.
Giving it shows trustworthiness;
attacking it shows martial prowess.
Therefore I say give it."
Zǐ Liáng left,
and Zhāo Chǎng entered for an audience.
The King said:
"An envoy from Qí has come demanding five hundred lǐ of our eastern territory.
What should we do about it?"
Zhāo Chǎng said:
"It cannot be given.
A state of ten thousand chariots
is considered such because of its vast territory.
Now, to cede five hundred lǐ of the eastern land
is to lose half of what makes us a contender among the warring states.
We would have the title of a ten-thousand-chariot state but not the resources of even a thousand chariots.
It cannot be done.
Therefore, I say do not give it.
I, Chǎng, request to defend it."
Zhāo Chǎng left,
and Jǐng Lǐ entered for an audience.
The King said:
"An envoy from Qí has come demanding five hundred lǐ of our eastern territory.
What should we do about it?"
Jǐng Lǐ said:
"It cannot be given.
However,
Chǔ cannot defend it alone.
Your Majesty, with your jade-like words,
promised the powerful state of Qí, ten thousand chariots strong, and then renege—
that would bear the stigma of injustice throughout the world.
Chǔ also cannot defend it alone.
I request to go west and seek rescue from Qín."
Jǐng Lǐ left,
and Shènzǐ entered.
The King informed Shènzǐ of the plans proposed by the three senior officials, saying:
"Zǐ Liáng came to see me and said:
'We cannot but give it,
but after giving it, we can attack and take it back.'
Chǎng came to see me and said:
'It cannot be given.
I, Chǎng, request to defend it.'
Lǐ came to see me and said:
'It cannot be given.
However, Chǔ cannot defend it alone.
I request to seek rescue from Qín.'
Whose plan among these three should I adopt?"
Shènzǐ replied:
"Your Majesty should use them all."
The King, flushing with anger, said:
"What do you mean?"
Shènzǐ said:
"Allow me to explain my proposal,
and Your Majesty will see its feasibility.
Dispatch the Supreme Pillar of State Zǐ Liáng with fifty chariots
north to present the five hundred lǐ of land to Qí.
The day after dispatching Zǐ Liáng,
send Zhāo Chǎng as Grand Marshal,
ordering him to go and defend the eastern territory.
The day after dispatching Zhāo Chǎng,
send Jǐng Lǐ with fifty chariots
west to seek rescue from Qín."
The King said:
"Excellent."
He then dispatched Zǐ Liáng north to present the land to Qí.
The day after dispatching Zǐ Liáng,
he appointed Zhāo Chǎng as Grand Marshal,
ordering him to defend the eastern territory.
He also dispatched Jǐng Lǐ west to seek rescue from Qín.
Zǐ Liáng arrived in Qí,
and Qí sent men in armor to take possession of the eastern land.
Zhāo Chǎng responded to the Qí envoy, saying:
"I am in charge of the eastern territory,
and I am prepared to live and die with it.
From youths five feet tall to men of sixty,
we have over three hundred thousand in worn armor and blunt weapons,
and we are ready to meet your dust."
The King of Qí said to Zǐ Liáng:
"You, sir, came to present the land,
but now Chǎng is defending it. How do you explain this?"
Zǐ Liáng said:
"I personally received the command from the king of my humble state.
This Chǎng is acting without authority.
Your Majesty should attack him."
The King of Qí raised a great army,
attacked the eastern territory,
and campaigned against Zhāo Chǎng.
Before they crossed the border,
Qín approached the right border of Qí with five hundred thousand troops,
saying:
"To detain the crown prince of Chǔ and not let him leave is unrighteous;
moreover, to desire to seize five hundred lǐ of their eastern land is unjust.
If you withdraw your armor, all is well;
if not,
then we are prepared to await battle."
The King of Qí was alarmed.
He then requested Zǐ Liáng to go south to inform Chǔ,
and west to envoy to Qín,
to resolve the crisis for Qí.
Without using their soldiers,
the eastern territory was fully restored.
Nǚ'ē said to Sūzǐ:
"Qín detained the King of Chǔ,
and endangered the crown prince—
this was your doing.
Now that the King of Chǔ has returned,
and the crown prince is in the south,
you are certainly in danger.
You would do better to have someone tell the crown prince:
'Sūzǐ knows that the crown prince resents him,
and will surely strive to do what is不利 to the crown prince.
The crown prince would do better to treat Sūzǐ well,
and Sūzǐ will certainly work for the crown prince's interests.'"
Sūzǐ then had someone tell this to the crown prince.
The crown prince again requested to treat Sūzǐ well.
Sūzǐ said to the King of Chǔ:
"A benevolent person, in regard to the people,
loves them with his heart,
and serves them with good words.
A filial son, in regard to his parents,
loves them with his heart,
and serves them with material goods.
A loyal minister, in regard to his ruler,
must recommend worthy men to assist him.
Now, Your Majesty's senior ministers and paternal elders
take pleasure in harming the worthy to serve their own purposes,
heavily taxing the various officials and the common people,
causing Your Majesty to incur the hatred of the people—
they are not loyal ministers.
The senior ministers broadcast Your Majesty's faults among the people,
and bribe the various feudal lords with Your Majesty's lands.
Thus, they cause retreat to what Your Majesty loves;
they are also not loyal ministers,
and therefore the state is endangered.
I wish that you would not listen to the mutual slander among your ministers,
but be cautious with your senior ministers and paternal elders;
employ what the people consider good,
restrain your own desires and indulgences,
for the sake of the people.
For a minister, nothing is more difficult than being free of jealousy and recommending the worthy.
To die for one's ruler is easy—
in the affair at Chuíshā,
those who died numbered in the thousands.
To suffer disgrace for one's ruler is easy—
from the Prime Minister down,
those who serve the king number in the thousands.
But as for being free of jealousy and recommending the worthy,
I have yet to see a single one.
Therefore, when an enlightened ruler examines his ministers,
he must know whether they are free of jealousy and recommend the worthy.
When a worthy serves his ruler,
he too must be free of jealousy and recommend the worthy.
The difficulty in recommending the worthy lies in this:
when the worthy are employed, it may cause one's own dismissal;
when they are honored, it may cause one's own humiliation.
Therefore, people find it difficult."
Sū Qín went to Chǔ,
and only after three days did he get to see the King.
When the conversation ended,
he took his leave and prepared to depart.
The King of Chǔ said:
"I have heard of you, sir,
as if hearing of an ancient.
Now you have come not minding the thousand lǐ to visit me,
yet you refuse to stay.
I wish to hear your reason."
He replied:
"In the state of Chǔ, food is more expensive than jade,
firewood is more expensive than cassia,
the receptionists are as hard to see as ghosts,
and the King is as hard to see as the Heavenly Emperor.
Now you have me eat jade and cook with cassia,
and through ghosts seek an audience with the Emperor."
The King said:
"Sir, please retire to your lodgings.
I have received your instruction."
The King of Chǔ sought to expel Zhāng Yí from Wèi.
Chén Zhěn said:
"Why does Your Majesty wish to expel Master Zhāng?"
He said:
"For being a minister who is neither loyal nor trustworthy."
Chén Zhěn said:
"If he is not loyal, Your Majesty need not have him as a minister;
if he is not trustworthy, Your Majesty should not make covenants with him.
Moreover, if a minister of Wèi is neither loyal nor trustworthy,
what harm does it do to Your Majesty?
If he is loyal and trustworthy,
what benefit is it to Your Majesty?
To expel him and have it heeded is one thing,
but if it is not heeded,
then Your Majesty's order is thwarted.
Moreover, to have a state of ten thousand chariots dismiss its prime minister—
that is a matter of a city under siege."
When Zhāng Yí went to Chǔ,
he was poor.
His retainer grew angry and wanted to return home.
Zhāng Zǐ had an audience with the King of Chǔ,
but the King of Chǔ was displeased.
Zhāng Zǐ said:
"Since Your Majesty has no use for your servant,
I request permission to go north and see the ruler of Jìn."
The King of Chǔ said:
"Very well."
Zhāng Zǐ said:
"Does Your Majesty have no demands to make of the state of Jìn?"
The King said:
"Gold, pearls, rhinoceros horns, and ivory all come from Chǔ;
I have no demands to make of the state of Jìn."
Zhāng Zǐ said:
"Is it merely that Your Majesty does not appreciate feminine beauty?"
The King said: "What do you mean?"
Zhāng Zǐ said:
"The women of Zhèng and Zhōu,
with faces powdered white and hair black as ink,
stand at the crossroads and alley gates.
Those who do not know and see them
would take them for goddesses."
The King of Chǔ said: "Chǔ
is a remote and uncultured state;
we have never seen women of the Central States so beautiful.
How could I alone not appreciate feminine beauty?"
Thereupon, he supplied him with pearls and jade.
Queen Nánhòu and Zhèng Xiù heard of this and were greatly alarmed.
They sent someone to tell Zhāng Zǐ:
"We have heard the General is going to Jìn;
by chance, we have a thousand catties of gold,
which we present to you,
to provide for fodder."
Zhèng Xiù also gave five hundred catties of gold.
Zhāng Zǐ took leave of the King of Chǔ, saying:
"The passes of the world are closed and impassable;
it is unknown when I shall see you again.
I wish Your Majesty would grant me a farewell drink."
The King said: "Very well."
Thereupon, he offered him wine.
While Zhāng Zǐ was drinking,
he bowed twice and requested:
"There are no others here;
I wish Your Majesty would summon your favorites to drink with us."
The King said: "Very well."
Thereupon, he summoned Queen Nánhòu and Zhèng Xiù to drink with them.
Zhāng Zǐ bowed twice and requested:
"Yí has committed a capital offense against Your Majesty."
The King said:
"What is it?"
He said:
"Yí has traveled all over the world,
yet I have never seen anyone so beautiful.
And I said I could obtain beauties for you;
this was deceiving Your Majesty."
The King said:
"Let it go.
I have always believed that no one in the world could match these two."
The King of Chǔ ordered Zhāo Jū to go to Qín and promote Zhāng Yí.
Before he arrived,
King Huì died.
King Wǔ expelled Zhāng Yí.
The King of Chǔ then arrested Zhāo Jū to win over Qí.
Huán Zāng spoke to the King of Chǔ on behalf of Jū, saying:
"The failure of the horizontal alliance
was because Yí was honored by King Huì and was on good terms with Jū.
Now King Huì is dead,
King Wǔ is on the throne,
Yí has fled,
and Gōngsūn Hǎo
and Gān Mào are honored.
Gān Mào is friendly with Wèi,
and Gōngsūn Hǎo is friendly with Hán.
These two are certainly not on good terms with Jū;
they will surely use Qín to ally with Hán and Wèi.
Hán and Wèi valued Yí,
and Yí, having Qín's support, was further promoted by Jū from Chǔ.
Now Yí is in distress in Qín and Jū is arrested in Chǔ;
Hán and Wèi, wishing to win over Qín,
will surely befriend these two men.
They will then win over Hán and Wèi, slight Yí, and attack Chǔ;
Fāngchéng will certainly be in danger.
Your Majesty would do better to reinstate Jū
and promote Yí in Hán and Wèi.
Yí, relying on Chǔ's influence
and backed by Wèi's importance,
will contend with Qín.
If Wèi does not ally with Qín,
and Hán also does not follow,
then Fāngchéng will have no worries."
Zhāng Yí expelled Huì Shī from Wèi.
Huìzǐ went to Chǔ,
and the King of Chǔ received him.
Féng Hǎo said to the King of Chǔ:
"The one who expelled Huìzǐ
was Zhāng Yí.
Yet Your Majesty personally made an agreement with him;
this is deceiving Yí.
I consider this inadvisable for Your Majesty.
Huìzǐ came because of Yí's actions,
and he resents Your Majesty's friendship with Zhāng Yí;
Huìzǐ will certainly not stay.
Moreover, the worth of Huìzǐ to King Sòng
is known throughout the world.
Now his dislike for Zhāng Yí
is also known throughout the world.
For the sake of expediency,
to abandon one valued by an enemy—
I consider this a slight by Your Majesty.
And is it even expedient?
Your Majesty would do better to recommend Huìzǐ and send him to Sòng,
and then say to Zhāng Yí:
'I beg you, let me not receive him.'
Yí will certainly be grateful to Your Majesty.
As for Huìzǐ, a man in distress,
whom Your Majesty assists,
he will also certainly be grateful to Your Majesty.
This does not lose the substance of supporting Yí,
and can also earn Huìzǐ's gratitude."
The King of Chǔ said: "Good."
Thereupon, he assisted Huìzǐ and sent him to Sòng.
The five states attacked Qín.
Wèi wanted to make peace,
and sent Huì Shī to Chǔ.
Chǔ was about to send him to Qín to conduct peace negotiations.
Dù Hè said to Zhāo Yáng:
"It was Chǔ that led the attack on Qín.
Now Shī has come from Wèi,
and you, sir, are sending him to Qín;
this makes Chǔ's attack obvious and confirms Wèi's desire for peace.
You, sir, would do better not to heed Huì Shī,
but secretly send someone to request peace with Qín."
Zhāozǐ said: "Good."
Thereupon, he said to Huì Shī:
"It was Wèi that led the attack on Qín.
Now you follow Chǔ to make peace;
Chǔ gains the advantage,
while Wèi incurs the resentment.
You return, and I will send someone to make peace through Wèi."
Huìzǐ returned,
and the King of Wèi was displeased.
Dù Hè said to Zhāo Yáng:
"Wèi fought first for you,
losing half its troops;
it pleaded hardship but was not heeded,
requested peace but could not obtain it.
If Wèi, defeated, turns to Qí and Qín,
how will you save the situation?
To the east, there is the burden of Yuè;
to the north, there is no Jìn;
and relations with Qí
and Qín are not yet settled—this leaves Chǔ isolated.
It would be better to make peace quickly."
Zhāozǐ said:
"Good."
Thereupon, he sent someone to request peace with Wèi.
Chén Zhěn announced he was leaving Chǔ for Wèi.
Zhāng Yí slandered him to the King of Wèi, saying:
"Zhěn is still friendly with Chǔ
and is vigorously seeking territory for them."
Zuǒ Shuǎng said to Chén Zhěn:
"Yí is in favor with the King of Wèi,
and the King of Wèi trusts him greatly.
Even if you argue a hundred times,
he still will not listen.
You would do better to use Yí's words as leverage
to return to Chǔ."
Chén Zhěn said: "Good."
Thereupon, he sent someone to report Yí's words to Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ was pleased
and wanted to reinstate him.
Qín attacked Yíyáng.
The King of Chǔ said to Chén Zhěn:
"I have heard that Hán Chǐ is a clever man,
well-versed in the affairs of the feudal lords;
he will probably be able to extricate himself.
Since he is sure to escape,
I wish to secure his favor first by showing him kindness."
Chén Zhěn replied: "Let him be, Your Majesty; do not secure him.
With Hán Chǐ's wisdom,
he is in a predicament here.
Now, among the beasts of the mountains and marshes,
none is more cunning than the elk.
The elk knows that the hunter sets a net
and drives it forward,
so it turns and runs, charging at the man,
repeatedly.
The hunter, knowing its trick,
pretends to raise the net and advance toward it,
and thus the elk is caught."
Now the feudal lords clearly know that this is full of deceit,
and those who falsely raise the net and advance will certainly be numerous.
Abandon it,
Your Majesty should not rely on it.
Hán Chǐ's wisdom,
is trapped by this."
The King of Chǔ listened to him,
and Yíyáng was indeed captured.
Chén Zhěn had foreseen this.
Táng Jū visited Chūnshēn Jūn and said:
"The people of Qí adorn themselves and cultivate their conduct to gain benefits,
but I am ashamed and do not learn from them.
Not avoiding crossing rivers and lakes,
traveling over a thousand miles to come,
I secretly admire the righteousness of the great lord,
and praise your lordship's achievements.
I have heard that,
Bēn and Zhū, carrying awls and blades,
are considered brave by the world,
and Xī Shī, wearing coarse cloth, is praised as beautiful by the world.
Now you, as the chancellor of the ten-thousand-chariot state of Chǔ,
defend against the difficulties of the Central States,
yet what you desire is not achieved,
what you seek is not obtained,
is because we, your servants, are few.
The reason the xiāo piece in liubo can be effective,
is because it is assisted by the scattered pieces.
That one xiāo piece cannot overcome five scattered pieces,
is also clear.
Now why does your lordship not become the xiāo of the world,
and let us, your servants, be the scattered pieces?"
Someone said to the King of Chǔ:
"I have heard that
those advocating the vertical alliance wish to unite the world to pay homage to Your Majesty,
I hope Your Majesty will listen to them.
Turning humiliation into trust,
transforming old troubles into success,
is what the brave consider righteous.
Controlling misfortune to create fortune,
turning little into much,
is what the wise administer.
The reversal of retribution,
the transformation of darkness,
only the great lord can achieve.
Misfortune and fortune are interconnected,
life and death are neighbors,
not inclined solely toward death,
not inclined solely toward life,
is insufficient to bear a great name.
Without experiencing invasion and hardship,
one cannot dominate the world.
Qín has long abandoned virtue and severed the mandate,
yet the world does not know.
Now those advocating the horizontal alliance clamor with sharp tongues for profit,
above they interfere with the ruler's mind,
below they exploit the common people,
publicly advocating while privately seeking gain,
thus the state's authority becomes lighter than a goose feather,
and accumulated calamities become heavier than a mountain."
The King of Wèi sent a beautiful woman to the King of Chǔ,
and the King of Chǔ was pleased with her.
The consort Zhèng Xiù, knowing that the king was pleased with the new woman,
showed great affection for the new woman.
Clothing and playthings,
she chose what the new woman liked and provided them;
palace rooms and bedding,
she chose what the new woman preferred and arranged them.
She loved her more than the king did.
The king said: "What women use to serve their husbands,
is their beauty;
and jealousy,
is their nature.
Now Zhèng Xiù knows that I am pleased with the new woman,
and she loves her more than I do,
this is how a filial son serves his parents,
and a loyal minister serves his lord."
Zhèng Xiù, knowing that the king considered her not jealous,
then said to the new woman:
"The king loves your beauty.
However,
he dislikes your nose.
When you see the king,
you must cover your nose."
The new woman saw the king,
and covered her nose.
The king said to Zhèng Xiù:
"When the new woman sees me,
she covers her nose,
why is that?"
Zhèng Xiù said:
"I know."
The king said:
"Even if it is unpleasant, you must say it."
Zhèng Xiù said:
"It seems she dislikes smelling Your Majesty's odor."
The king said:
"How vicious!"
He ordered her nose cut off,
not allowing any disobedience.
The queen of Chǔ died,
and a new queen had not been established.
Someone said to Zhāo Yú:
"Why do you not request the establishment of a queen?"
Zhāo Yú said: "If the king does not listen,
then I would be in a difficult position and my relationship with the future queen would be severed."
"Then why not buy five pairs of earrings,
have one pair be particularly fine and present them to the king,
the next day see which pair of fine earrings is worn,
and then request that she be established as queen."
Zhuāng Xīn said to King Xiāng of Chǔ:
"Your Majesty has Zhōu Hóu on the left,
Xià Hóu on the right,
and is followed by chariots carrying Yānlíng Jūn and Shòulíng Jūn,
indulging exclusively in licentiousness and extravagance,
with no regard for state affairs,
Yǐngdū will certainly be endangered."
King Xiāng said: "Is the gentleman old and confused?
Or do you consider this an ominous sign for Chǔ?"
Zhuāng Xīn said: "I truly see that this is inevitable,
I dare not consider it an ominous sign for the state.
If Your Majesty continues to favor these four without decline,
Chǔ will certainly perish.
I request to withdraw to Zhào,
and remain there to observe."
Zhuāng Xīn left and went to Zhào,
stayed for five months,
and Qín indeed captured the lands of Yān, Yǐng, Wū, Shàngcài, and Chén,
and King Xiāng was forced into exile and took refuge in Chéngyáng.
Thereupon he sent someone to dispatch a mounted escort,
to summon Zhuāng Xīn from Zhào.
Zhuāng Xīn said:
"Yes."
When Zhuāng Xīn arrived,
King Xiāng said:
"I could not use the gentleman's advice,
now matters have come to this,
what should be done?"
Zhuāng Xīn replied: "I have heard a common saying:
'Seeing the rabbit and then looking for the hound,
is not too late;
losing the sheep and then mending the pen,
is not too delayed.'
I have heard that in the past, Tāng and Wǔ flourished with a hundred lǐ,
while Jié and Zhòu perished with the entire world.
Now although Chǔ is small,
cutting the long and supplementing the short,
it still measures several thousand lǐ,
how could it be only a hundred lǐ?
"Has Your Majesty not seen the dragonfly?
With six legs and four wings,
flying between heaven and earth,
looking down to peck mosquitoes and gadflies to eat,
looking up to receive sweet dew to drink,
thinking itself free from worry,
and having no conflict with others.
Not knowing that the five-foot-tall child,
is just preparing lead paste and silk thread,
to attach to itself from a height of four rèn,
and then fall down to be eaten by ants and insects.
The dragonfly is a small example,
the yellow sparrow is like this.
Looking down to peck white grains,
looking up to perch in lush trees,
flapping its wings and spreading its feathers,
thinking itself free from worry,
and having no conflict with others.
Not knowing that the young nobles,
with a slingshot in the left hand,
and pellets in the right hand,
are about to strike it from a height of ten rèn,
using its kind as a target.
By day it wanders among lush trees,
by evening it is seasoned with sour and salty flavors,
in a fleeting moment,
it falls into the hands of the young noble.
"The sparrow is a small example,
the yellow swan is like this.
Swimming in rivers and seas,
lingering in great marshes,
looking down to peck eels and carp,
looking up to nibble water chestnuts and lotus stems,
spreading its six pinions,
and riding the clear breeze,
soaring high and fluttering,
thinking itself free from worry,
and having no conflict with others.
Not knowing that the archer is just preparing his bow and adjusting his arrow with silk thread,
to shoot it from a height of a hundred rèn.
That sharp arrow, drawn by the fine silk thread,
breaks through the clear breeze and falls.
Thus by day it wanders the rivers and lakes,
by evening it is cooked in the cauldron.
"The yellow swan is but a minor example;
the affair of Cài Shèng Hóu is also like this.
He roamed south to the high slopes,
ascended north to Wū Shān,
drank from the flowing waters of Rú Xī,
feasted on fish from the waves of Xiāng,
held his young concubine on the left,
embraced his favored women on the right,
galloping with them through the lands of Gāo Cài,
paying no heed to affairs of state.
Unaware that Fūzǐ Fā had just received orders from King Xuān,
to bind him with crimson silk and present him.
"The affair of Cài Shèng Hóu is but a minor example;
Your Majesty's affairs are also like this.
With Zhōu Hóu on the left,
Xià Hóu on the right,
accompanied by Yānlíng Jūn and Shòulíng Jūn,
dining on grain from fiefs and salaries,
and carrying gold from the square treasury,
galloping with them through the midst of Yún Mèng,
paying no heed to the affairs of the realm and state.
Unaware that Ráng Hóu had just received orders from the King of Qín,
to fill the interior of Miǎn Sāi,
and cast you beyond Miǎn Sāi."
Upon hearing this, King Xiāng
changed countenance,
his body trembling.
Thereupon, he bestowed upon him the seal of Zhí Guī and appointed him as Yánglíng Jūn,
granting him the lands north of the Huái.
Qí Míng persuaded Zhuó Huá to attack Qín,
but Huá did not listen.
Qí Míng said to Zhuó Huá:
"In my coming here,
it was to divine friendship for Chūlǐ Jí.
I persuaded the great officers of Chǔ to attack Qín,
and all accepted my persuasion,
only you did not accept it.
I now have words to report back to Chūlǐzǐ."
Zhuó Huá thus esteemed him.
Someone said to Huáng Qí:
"Everyone says that you are not on good terms with Fù Zhì.
Have you not heard how Lǎo Láizǐ instructed Confucius on serving a ruler?
He showed him how firm his teeth were,
yet by sixty they had all worn each other down.
Now Fù Zhì is capable,
and you, sir, are greatly at odds with him,
this is mutual destruction.
The proverb says:
'When you see the ruler's carriage,
dismount;
when you see his staff,
rise.'
Now, the king favors Fù Zhì,
and you, sir, are not on good terms with him,
this is disloyalty."
During the Chángshā crisis,
the Chǔ crown prince Héng was a hostage in Qí.
When the King of Chǔ died,
Xuē Gōng returned Crown Prince Héng,
and then, with the troops of Hán and Wèi,
followed to attack the eastern territories.
The crown prince was afraid.
Zhāo Gài said: "It would be better to order Qū Shǔ to offer the new eastern territories to Qí to make peace, thereby stirring Qín.
Qín fears that Qí will defeat the eastern territories,
and its orders will prevail throughout the realm,
so it will surely come to our rescue."
The crown prince said: "Good."
He hastily ordered Qū Shǔ to offer the eastern territories to Qí to make peace.
The King of Qín heard of this and became alarmed,
ordering Xīn Róng to inform Chǔ:
"Do not give the eastern territories to Qí,
and I will send troops to aid you."
Someone presented an elixir of immortality to the King of Jīng.
The court usher carried it in.
A palace archer asked:
"May it be eaten?"
He replied: "It may."
Thereupon, he seized it and ate it.
The king was enraged,
and sent someone to kill the palace archer.
The palace archer sent someone to persuade the king, saying:
"I asked the usher,
and the usher said it could be eaten,
so I ate it.
Thus, I am without fault,
and the fault lies with the usher.
Moreover, the guest presented an elixir of immortality,
I ate it and the king kills me,
then it is a death elixir.
If the king kills an innocent subject,
it will prove that others have deceived the king."
The king then did not kill him.
A guest persuaded Chūnshēn Jūn, saying:
"Tāng with Bó,
King Wǔ with Hào,
both had no more than a hundred lǐ to possess the realm.
Now Sūnzǐ,
is a worthy man of the realm,
and you, sir, lend him the power of a hundred lǐ.
I privately believe this is not beneficial for you.
What do you think?"
Chūnshēn Jūn said: "Good."
Thereupon, he sent someone to dismiss Sūnzǐ.
Sūnzǐ left for Zhào,
and Zhào appointed him as senior minister.
The guest again persuaded Chūnshēn Jūn, saying:
"In the past, Yī Yǐn left Xià and entered Yīn,
and Yīn became king while Xià perished.
Guǎn Zhòng left Lǔ and entered Qí,
and Lǔ weakened while Qí strengthened.
Wherever a worthy man resides,
his ruler has never failed to be honored,
and the state has never failed to prosper.
Now Sūnzǐ,
is a worthy man of the realm.
Why did you dismiss him?"
Chūnshēn Jūn again said: "Good."
Thereupon, he sent someone to invite Sūnzǐ back from Zhào.
Sūnzǐ wrote a letter declining, saying:
"The leper pities the king—
this is an irreverent saying.
Nevertheless,
it cannot be left unexamined.
This refers to rulers who are seized, assassinated, or meet death.
When a ruler is young and proud of his talents,
lacking methods and arts to recognize treachery,
then great ministers will control state affairs for private gain and suppress criticism against themselves.
Thus, they assassinate the worthy and elder and establish the young and weak,
depose the rightful heir and set up the unrighteous.
The *Spring and Autumn Annals* warns, saying:
'The Chǔ prince Wéi was on a mission to Zhèng,
before he had left the borders,
he heard the king was ill,
returned to inquire after his health,
and then used his cap strings to strangle the king,
killing him,
and thereupon made himself king.
Cuī Zhù of Qí had a beautiful wife,
and Duke Zhuāng had an affair with her.
Cuī Zhù led his lord's partisans to attack.
Duke Zhuāng begged to share the state with him,
but Cuī Zhù refused;
he wished to stab himself in the temple,
but Cuī Zhù refused.
Duke Zhuāng fled,
climbed over the outer wall,
was shot in the thigh,
and was then killed,
and his younger brother Duke Jǐng was established.'
In recent times, we have seen:
Lǐ Duì controlling Zhào,
starving the Lord Father at Shāqiū,
and killing him after a hundred days;
Nào Chǐ controlling Qí,
pulling out the sinews of King Mǐn,
hanging him on the temple beam,
where he died overnight.
Though leprosy is a festering, ulcerous disease,
compared with antiquity,
it does not reach strangling with cap strings or shooting in the thigh;
compared with recent times,
it does not reach pulling out sinews or starving to death.
As for rulers who are seized, assassinated, or meet death,
the worries of their hearts,
the hardships of their bodies,
must be far greater than leprosy.
From this perspective,
even if the leper pities the king, it is permissible."
Thereupon, he composed a rhapsody, saying:
"Precious pearls and Suí's gem,
you know not to wear them.
Coarse cloth and fine silk,
you know not to distinguish them.
The beauties Lǘ Shū and Zǐ Shē,
you know not to matchmake them.
The ugly Mó Mǔ you seek,
and even delight in her.
Taking the blind for clear-sighted,
the deaf for keen-hearing,
wrong for right,
auspicious for ominous.
Alas, O Heaven above,
when will you ever be the same!"
The *Book of Songs* says:
"Heaven above is most divine,
do not bring calamity upon yourself."
The states of the world formed a vertical alliance.
The state of Zhào sent Wèi Jiā to see Chǔ’s Lord Chūnshēn and said:
"Do you have a general?"
He replied: "Yes,
I intend to make Línwǔ Jūn the general."
Wèi Jiā said: "When I was young, I enjoyed archery.
I wish to use archery as an analogy,
may I?"
Lord Chūnshēn said:
"You may."
Jiā said:
"On another day,
Gēng Léi and the King of Wèi were beneath the Jīng Terrace,
looking up, they saw a flying bird.
Gēng Léi said to the King of Wèi:
'I will draw the bow for Your Majesty and shoot without an arrow to bring down the bird.'
The King of Wèi said: 'Can archery reach such a level?'
Gēng Léi said:
'It can.'
After a while,
a wild goose came from the east,
Gēng Léi shot without an arrow and brought it down.
The King of Wèi said: 'Can archery reach such a level?'
Gēng Léi said:
'This one was wounded.'
The King said:
'How did you know, sir?'
He replied: 'Its flight was slow and its cry mournful.
Its flight was slow
because of old wound pain;
its cry was mournful
because it had long been separated from the flock.
Thus, its wound had not yet healed,
and its frightened heart had not yet settled.
Hearing the sound of the bowstring,
it strained to fly high,
and thus its old wound caused it to fall.'
Now, Línwǔ Jūn
was once wounded by Qín,
he cannot be the general to resist Qín."
Hàn Míng sought an audience with Lord Chūnshēn,
he waited for three months,
and only then did he get to see him.
After their conversation ended,
Lord Chūnshēn was greatly pleased with him.
Hàn Míng wished to speak further,
Lord Chūnshēn said:
"I already know you, sir,
you may rest now."
Hàn Míng, appearing uneasy, said:
"I wish to ask you something but fear it may be presumptuous.
I do not know how your sagacity
compares to Yáo?"
Lord Chūnshēn said: "You overpraise me, sir,
how could I possibly compare to Yáo?"
Hàn Míng said:
"Then, how do you estimate I compare to Shùn?"
Lord Chūnshēn said: "You, sir, are Shùn."
Hàn Míng said: "Not so,
allow me to finish speaking for you.
Your worthiness is truly not equal to Yáo,
my ability does not reach Shùn.
For the worthy Shùn to serve the sagely Yáo,
it took three years before they truly knew each other.
Now you know me in a single moment,
this means you are more sagely than Yáo and I am more worthy than Shùn."
Lord Chūnshēn said: "Well said."
He summoned the gate officer to register Mr. Hàn as a guest,
and to see him once every five days.
Hàn Míng said: "Have you also heard of the steed?
When the steed reached maturity,
it was harnessed to a salt cart and ascended Tàiháng Mountain.
Its hooves stretched, its knees bent,
its tail drooped, its skin broke out in sores,
sweat dripped and soaked the ground,
white sweat flowed in streams,
mid-slope it struggled and delayed,
bearing the yoke it could not ascend.
Bólè encountered it,
dismounted, held it and wept for it,
took off his hempen robe to cover it.
The steed then lowered its head and snorted,
raised its head and neighed,
its sound reached the heavens,
as if issuing a sound of metal or stone.
Why was this?
It saw that Bólè understood it.
Now, I am unworthy,
trapped in local districts,
in a humble dwelling in a poor alley,
sunk in base customs for a long time.
Do you alone have no intention to cleanse and raise me,
enabling me to cry out my grievances for you in Liáng?"
King Kǎoliè of Chǔ had no son,
Lord Chūnshēn was troubled by this,
he sought women suitable for bearing children to present to him,
very many,
but in the end, there was no son.
A man from Zhào, Lǐ Yuán,
held his younger sister,
wishing to present her to the King of Chǔ.
Hearing that the king was not suitable for having children,
he feared she would also gain no favor.
Lǐ Yuán sought to serve Lord Chūnshēn as a retainer.
After a while, he requested leave to return home,
and deliberately missed the return date.
Upon returning and paying his respects,
Lord Chūnshēn asked about the situation.
He replied: "The King of Qí sent an envoy to seek my younger sister,
I drank with his envoy,
so I missed the date."
Lord Chūnshēn said:
"Has the betrothal gift been presented?"
He replied:
"Not yet."
Lord Chūnshēn said:
"May I see her?"
He said: "You may."
Thereupon, Yuán presented his younger sister,
and she soon gained favor with Lord Chūnshēn.
Knowing she was pregnant,
Yuán then conspired with his younger sister.
Yuán's younger sister seized an opportunity to persuade Lord Chūnshēn, saying:
"The King of Chǔ honors and favors you,
even brothers are not as close.
Now you have been chancellor to the King of Chǔ for over twenty years,
yet the king has no son.
After his passing, they will establish one of his brothers.
If the King of Chǔ is replaced,
they will each honor their own former intimates,
how then can you long retain favor?
Is it not just so?
You have been in power long,
and have often been disrespectful to the king's brothers.
If a brother is truly established,
disaster will befall you.
How then to preserve your chancellor's seal and the fief of Jiāngdōng?
Now I know myself that I am pregnant,
but others do not know.
My favor with you has not been long,
if truly, using your importance, you present me to the King of Chǔ,
the king is sure to favor me.
If I rely on heaven and bear a son,
then your son will be king,
all the fiefs of Chǔ can be obtained.
How does this compare to facing immeasurable crime?"
Lord Chūnshēn greatly agreed with this.
He then sent Yuán's younger sister to a carefully guarded residence,
and spoke of her to the King of Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ summoned her in,
and favored her.
She then gave birth to a son,
who was established as crown prince,
and Lǐ Yuán's younger sister was established as queen.
The King of Chǔ honored Lǐ Yuán,
and Lǐ Yuán came to power.
After Lǐ Yuán had his younger sister enter as queen
and her son as crown prince,
he feared Lord Chūnshēn might leak the secret and become more arrogant,
so he secretly raised assassins,
wanting to kill Lord Chūnshēn to silence him,
and many in the state knew of this.
Lord Chūnshēn had been chancellor of Chǔ for twenty-five years
when King Kǎoliè fell ill.
Zhū Yīng said to Lord Chūnshēn:
"The world has unforeseen fortune,
and also unforeseen disaster.
Now you are in an unforeseen age,
serving an unforeseen lord,
how can there not be an unforeseen man?"
Lord Chūnshēn said: "What is unforeseen fortune?"
He said: "You have been chancellor of Chǔ for over twenty years,
though nominally chancellor,
in reality, you are the King of Chǔ.
Your five sons are all chancellors to various lords.
Now the king is gravely ill,
and may pass away morning or night.
The crown prince is weak,
ill and unable to rise.
If you serve as chancellor to the young lord,
and thus act as regent ruling the state,
like Yī Yǐn and the Duke of Zhōu.
When the king grows up, you return the government;
if not,
then you may face south and call yourself 'the solitary one,'
thus possessing the state of Chǔ.
This is what is called unforeseen fortune."
Lord Chūnshēn said, "What is meant by an unexpected calamity?"
The reply was, "Lǐ Yuán does not govern the state,
but he is the king's maternal uncle.
He does not serve as a military commander,
yet he has long been secretly nurturing assassins.
When the King of Chǔ passes away,
Lǐ Yuán will surely enter first,
seize control according to the original plan, issue orders in the king's name,
wield power, and kill you to silence you.
This is what is called an unexpected calamity."
Lord Chūnshēn said, "What is meant by an unexpected person?"
The reply was, "If you first appoint me as a court gentleman,
and when the king passes away,
Lǐ Yuán enters first,
I will request to stab him in the chest and kill him for you.
This is what is called an unexpected person."
Lord Chūnshēn said, "Sir, set this aside,
do not speak of it again.
Lǐ Yuán
is a weak man,
and I am on good terms with him.
How could it come to this?"
Zhū Yīng grew fearful,
and fled.
Seventeen days later,
King Kǎoliè of Chǔ passed away.
Lǐ Yuán indeed entered first,
stationed assassins, and halted them inside the Thorn Gate.
Lord Chūnshēn entered later,
and halted at the Thorn Gate.
Lǐ Yuán's assassins flanked and stabbed Lord Chūnshēn,
cut off his head,
and threw it outside the Thorn Gate.
Thereupon, he sent officials to exterminate Lord Chūnshēn's entire household.
And Lǐ Yuán's younger sister,
who had initially been favored by Lord Chūnshēn and became pregnant,
and then entered the king's palace, giving birth to a son,
was subsequently established as King Yōu of Chǔ.
That year,
Qín Shǐhuáng had been on the throne for nine years.
Lào Ǎi also caused turmoil in Qín.
When discovered, his three clans were exterminated,
and Lǚ Bùwéi was dismissed.
Yú Qīng said to Lord Chūnshēn:
"I have heard it said in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*,
'In safety, think of danger;
in danger, plan for safety.'
Now the King of Chǔ is advanced in years,
and your fiefdom
must be settled early.
For the lord considering a fief,
nothing is better than being far from Chǔ.
Duke Xiào of Qín enfeoffed Lord Shāng,
but after Duke Xiào died,
he could not avoid being killed.
King Huì of Qín enfeoffed Rǎnzǐ,
but after King Huì died,
the subsequent king seized it.
Gōngsūn Yǎng
was a meritorious minister;
Rǎnzǐ
was a relative by marriage.
Yet they could not avoid being deprived and killed—
it was because their fiefs were too close.
Tàigōng Wàng was enfeoffed in Qí,
Shào Gōng Shì was enfeoffed in Yān,
because they were far from the royal court.
Now Yān's crimes are great and Zhào's anger is deep,
so you would do better to march north to show virtue to Zhào,
subdue chaotic Yān,
and thereby secure your own fief. This is a once-in-a-hundred-generations
opportunity."
The lord said:
"The route to attack Yān
must pass through either Qí or Wèi.
Wèi and Qí have recently resented Chǔ.
Even if Chǔ wishes to attack Yān,
what route can be taken?"
The reply was:
"I request to make the King of Wèi agree."
The lord said:
"How?"
The reply was:
"I request to go to Wèi,
and arrange a way to gain their trust."
Thereupon, he said to the King of Wèi:
"Chǔ is indeed powerful,
matchless under heaven,
and now intends to attack Yān."
The King of Wèi said:
"Earlier,
you said Chǔ was matchless under heaven;
now,
you say it intends to attack Yān.
Why is that?"
The reply was:
"Now, to say a horse is strong is true,
but to say it can lift a thousand jūn is not—
why?
Because a thousand jūn is not within a horse's capacity.
Now, to say Chǔ is powerful is true,
but to cross Zhào and
Wèi to wage war on Yān—
is that within Chǔ's capacity?
If it is not within Chǔ's capacity yet Chǔ attempts it,
it will exhaust Chǔ.
An exhausted Chǔ facing a strong Wèi—
which is more advantageous for you, King?"
Zhì Bó led Hán and
Wèi troops to attack Zhào, besieging Jìnyáng and flooding it.
The city walls were only three planks above the water.
Xì Cī said to Zhì Bó:
"The lords of Hán and Wèi will surely rebel."
Zhì Bó said:
"How do you know?"
Xì Cī said:
"I know from their behavior.
Leading Hán and Wèi troops to attack Zhào—
if Zhào perishes,
disaster will surely reach Hán and Wèi.
Now they have agreed to defeat Zhào and divide its land three ways.
Now the city is only three planks from being submerged,
mortars and stoves have spawned frogs,
men and horses are eating each other,
the city will surrender any day,
yet the lords of Hán and Wèi show no joy but have worried expressions.
If this is not rebellion, what is it?"
The next day,
Zhì Bó told the lords of Hán and Wèi:
"Xì Cī says you are about to rebel."
The lords of Hán and Wèi said:
"Defeating Zhào and dividing its land three ways,
the city is about to fall.
Even if we three families are foolish,
we would not abandon such great profit before us,
break a sworn covenant,
and undertake a perilous, impossible task.
The situation is clear.
This is Xì Cī scheming for Zhào,
making you doubt our loyalty,
and slackening the attack on Zhào.
Now you listen to a slanderous minister's words
and estrange the friendship between us two lords.
We regret this for you."
They hurried out.
Xì Cī said to Zhì Bó:
"Why did you tell the lords of Hán and Wèi what I said?"
Zhì Bó said:
"How did you know?"
The reply was:
"The lords of Hán and Wèi looked at me intently and hurried away."
Xì Cī knew his advice would not be heeded,
requested a mission to Qí,
and Zhì Bó sent him.
The lords of Hán and Wèi indeed rebelled.
Zhì Bó led Zhào, Hán, and Wèi to attack the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans,
and exterminated them.
After resting several years,
he sent a man to demand land from Hán.
Lord Kāng of Hán wanted to refuse,
but Duàn Guī advised:
"Do not.
Zhì Bó's nature
is covetous and fiercely vengeful.
If we refuse his demand for land,
he will surely attack Hán.
You should give it to him.
If we give it, he will grow accustomed,
and will demand land from other states.
If other states refuse,
he will surely attack them with troops.
Then Hán can avoid calamity
and await a change in the situation."
Lord Kāng said, "Good."
He sent an envoy to present Zhì Bó with a city of ten thousand households.
Zhì Bó was pleased.
He then sent a man to demand land from Wèi.
Lord Xuān of Wèi wanted to refuse.
Zhào Jiā advised:
"He demanded land from Hán,
and Hán gave it.
He demands land from Wèi;
if Wèi refuses,
then Wèi internally strengthens itself,
but externally angers Zhì Bó.
Then he will surely turn his troops against Wèi!
Better to give it."
Xuānzǐ said, “Agreed.”
He then sent someone to deliver a city of ten thousand households to Zhì Bó.
Zhì Bó was pleased.
He then sent someone to Zhào,
requesting the lands of Cài and Gāoláng.
Zhào Xiāngzǐ refused to give them.
Zhì Bó then secretly allied with Hán and Wèi,
intending to attack Zhào.
Zhào Xiāngzǐ summoned Zhāng Mèngtán and told him:
“Now, as for Zhì Bó’s character,
he feigns friendship outwardly but is inwardly distant.
He has sent envoys to Hán and Wèi three times,
yet I have not been included.
He will certainly turn his troops against me.
Where should I settle now to be secure?”
Zhāng Mèngtán said, “Dǒng Yān’ānyú,
a talented minister of Lord Jiǎn,
governed Jìnyáng for generations,
and Yǐn Zé continued his methods.
The remnants of his administration and teachings still remain.
You should settle in Jìnyáng.”
The lord said, “Agreed.”
He then sent Yánlíng Wáng to lead the chariots and cavalry ahead to Jìnyáng,
and the lord followed afterward.
Upon arrival, he inspected the city walls,
checked the treasuries,
and examined the granaries.
He summoned Zhāng Mèngtán and said:
“Our city walls are complete,
the treasuries are sufficient for use,
and the granaries are full.
But what shall we do if we have no arrows?”
Zhāng Mèngtán said, “I have heard that when Master Dǒng governed Jìnyáng,
the walls of the ducal palace
were all made of reeds, wormwood, thorn bushes, and stalks,
piled up to over ten feet high.
You can break them apart and use them.”
Thereupon, they broke them apart and tested them;
their hardness could not be surpassed even by the strength of fine bamboo for arrows.
The lord said:
“That is sufficient.
But what shall we do if we are short of copper?”
Zhāng Mèngtán said:
“I have heard that when Master Dǒng governed Jìnyáng,
the pillars of the ducal palace halls all had bases made of refined copper.
I request that you break them apart and use them;
then you will have more than enough copper.”
The lord said, “Excellent.”
Orders were thus fixed,
and preparations for defense were completed.
The armies of the three states approached the walls of Jìnyáng,
and battle commenced.
For three months they could not capture it,
so they spread out their troops and besieged it,
diverting the Jìn River to flood it.
They besieged Jìnyáng for three years.
Within the city, people nested in trees to live,
hung their cauldrons to cook,
supplies and food were nearly exhausted,
and the soldiers were weak and ill.
Xiāngzǐ said to Zhāng Mèngtán: “Provisions are depleted,
the city’s strength is exhausted,
the officers are ill,
I cannot hold out any longer.
I intend to surrender the city. What do you think?”
Zhāng Mèngtán said: “I have heard that
if one cannot preserve what is perishing,
or secure what is in danger,
then there is no point in valuing wise men.
Abandon this plan,
and say no more about it.
I request to meet with the lords of Hán and Wèi.”
Xiāngzǐ said, “Agreed.”
Zhāng Mèngtán then secretly met with the lords of Hán and Wèi, saying:
“I have heard that when the lips are gone, the teeth feel cold.
Now Zhì Bó leads the two of you, lords, to attack Zhào.
Zhào is about to perish.
Once it perishes, you two lords will be next.”
The two lords said: “We know this is so.
Now, Zhì Bó’s character
is crude at heart and shows little affection.
If our plan is not yet realized and he finds out,
then disaster will certainly befall us.
What should we do?”
Zhāng Mèngtán said: “The plan comes from your mouths,
enters my ears,
and no one else will know of it.”
The two lords then secretly agreed with Zhāng Mèngtán on the three armies’ plans,
setting a date with him, saying:
“At night,
we will send men into Jìnyáng.”
Zhāng Mèngtán reported this to Xiāngzǐ,
and Xiāngzǐ bowed to him twice.
Zhāng Mèngtán then went to pay respects to Zhì Bó and left.
Outside the camp gate, he encountered Zhì Guò.
Zhì Guò entered to see Zhì Bó and said:
“The two lords are likely about to change sides.”
The lord said:
“How so?”
He replied:
“I encountered Zhāng Mèngtán outside the camp gate.
His demeanor was proud,
and his bearing lofty.”
Zhì Bó said: “Not so.
I have made a strict agreement with the two lords.
After destroying Zhào, we will divide its land in three. I personally oversaw this;
they certainly will not deceive me.
Let this go,
and do not speak of it again.”
Zhì Guò went out to see the two lords,
then returned to persuade Zhì Bó, saying:
“The two lords’ expressions changed and their intentions shifted;
they will certainly betray you.
It would be better to have them killed.”
Zhì Bó said:
“Our troops have been stationed at Jìnyáng for three years; morning or evening we should capture it and enjoy its benefits.
How could they have other intentions?
It cannot be.
Be careful not to speak of this again.”
Zhì Guò said:
“If you do not kill them, then at least draw closer to them.”
Zhì Bó said:
“How should I draw closer to them?”
Zhì Guò said: “Wèi Xuānzǐ’s strategist is named Zhào Jiā,
and Kāngzǐ’s strategist is named Duàn Guī.
Both are capable of changing their lords’ plans.
You should make an agreement with the two lords:
after destroying Zhào, enfeoff these two men each with a county of ten thousand households.
If you do this, the two lords’ minds will not change,
and you will achieve what you desire.”
Zhì Bó said:
“After destroying Zhào and dividing its land in three,
to also enfeoff these two men each with a county of ten thousand households—
then what I gain will be less.
It cannot be done.”
Zhì Guò, seeing that the lord would not heed him,
that his words were not listened to,
left,
changed his surname to Fǔ,
and departed, never to be seen again.
Zhāng Mèngtán heard of this,
entered to see Xiāngzǐ, and said:
“I encountered Zhì Guò outside the camp gate.
His gaze showed he suspected me.
He entered to see Zhì Bó,
then left and changed his surname.
If we do not attack tonight,
we will certainly be too late.”
Xiāngzǐ said: “Agreed.”
He sent Zhāng Mèngtán to see the lords of Hán and Wèi, saying:
“Tonight, as agreed,
kill the officials guarding the dikes,
and breach the waters to flood Zhì Bó’s army.”
Zhì Bó’s army was thrown into chaos trying to deal with the floodwaters.
Hán and Wèi attacked from the flanks,
while Xiāngzǐ led his troops to assault from the front.
They greatly defeated Zhì Bó’s army and captured Zhì Bó.
Zhì Bó died,
his state perished and his lands were divided,
becoming a laughingstock for all under heaven.
This was due to his insatiable greed and desire.
As for not listening to Zhì Guò,
that too was a reason for his downfall.
The Zhì clan was completely exterminated,
only the Fǔ clan survived.
After Zhāng Mèngtán had consolidated the Zhào lineage
and expanded its territories,
he presented a tally of five hundred households,
and then cited the way of Lord Jiǎn to inform Xiāngzǐ, saying:
“In the past,
a saying from the former ruler who governed the state’s lands stated:
‘The reason the five hundred households could bring order to all under heaven
was that they bound the two lords’ power so they could control their ministers,
and did not allow ministers to control their lords.
Therefore, those honored as marquises
were not placed in the position of chancellor;
from general and above,
they did not serve as close senior officials.’
Now my name is illustrious and my person is honored,
my authority is great and the multitude obeys me.
I wish to relinquish my achievements and fame, abandon authority and power, and distance myself from the multitude.”
Xiāngzǐ was displeased and said:
“Why is this?
I have heard that those who assist their lord gain illustrious names,
those with great achievements gain personal honor,
those who bear responsibility for the state gain great authority,
and faithfulness and loyalty within oneself cause the multitude to obey.
This is how the former sages brought order to the state
and secured the altars of soil and grain!
Why do you wish to do this?”
Zhāng Mèngtán replied:
"What you, my lord, have spoken of,
is the beauty of achieving success.
What I, your servant, speak of,
is the way to maintain the state.
I observe accomplished affairs,
and hear of ancient times;
the beauties of the world are the same,
but that the authority of minister and ruler being equal can be beautiful,
has never been.
Not forgetting past affairs
is the teacher for future affairs.
If you, my lord, do not consider this,
then my strength is insufficient."
With a sorrowful expression, he showed determination.
Xiāngzǐ dismissed him.
After lying down for three days,
he sent someone to say to him:
"Regarding the governance of Jìnyáng,
what if your subordinates are not compliant?"
He replied: "Death penalty."
Zhāng Mèngtán said: "The Left Minister of War, being employed by the state,
to secure the altars of soil and grain,
does not avoid death,
to fulfill his loyalty;
my lord, please implement this."
The lord said:
"You handle the matter."
Then he agreed.
Zhāng Mèngtán then used wealth to secure his reputation,
surrendered his lands, relinquished his duties to remove his authority and prestige,
and plowed at Fùqīn Hill.
Therefore it is said,
the conduct of a worthy man,
is the governance of an enlightened ruler.
After plowing for three years,
Hán, Wèi, Qí, and Yǎn, bearing grudges, plotted against Zhào.
Xiāngzǐ went to see Zhāng Mèngtán and told him:
"In the past, the lands of the Zhì clan,
when divided by the Zhào clan, yielded more than ten cities.
They have come again,
and now the various lords are conspiring against me;
what should be done about it?"
Zhāng Mèngtán said:
"My lord, please gird your sword and drive me to the state,
lodge me in the ancestral temple,
appoint me as an official among the ministers,
and I will attempt a plan."
The lord said: "Agreed."
Zhāng Mèngtán then set out,
sending his wife to Chǔ,
his eldest son to Hán,
his second son to Wèi,
and his youngest son to Qí.
The four states became suspicious and their plot failed.
Yù Ràng, grandson of Bì Yáng of Jìn,
initially served the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans but was not pleased,
left and went to serve Zhì Bó,
who favored him.
When the three Jìn families divided the Zhì clan,
Zhào Xiāngzǐ bore the greatest grudge against Zhì Bó,
and made his skull into a drinking vessel.
Yù Ràng fled into the mountains,
saying:
"Alas!
A man of worth dies for one who understands him,
a woman adorns herself for one who pleases her.
I shall avenge the Zhì clan."
He then changed his name,
became a convict,
entered the palace to plaster the latrine,
intending to assassinate Xiāngzǐ.
When Xiāngzǐ went to the latrine,
his heart stirred; he seized and questioned the plasterer,
and it was Yù Ràng.
Holding a dagger,
he said:
"I wish to avenge Zhì Bó!"
The attendants wanted to kill him.
Zhào Xiāngzǐ said: "He is a righteous man;
I will carefully avoid him.
Moreover, Zhì Bó is already dead,
without heirs,
yet his minister goes so far as to seek revenge;
this is a worthy man of the world."
He finally released him.
Yù Ràng then lacquered his body to appear leprous,
removed his beard and eyebrows,
mutilated himself to change his appearance,
became a beggar and went begging.
His wife did not recognize him,
saying:
"His appearance does not resemble my husband,
but his voice is very much like my husband's."
He then swallowed charcoal to become hoarse,
changing his voice.
His friend said to him:
"Your way is very difficult and without success;
to say you have determination is true,
but to say you are wise is not.
With your talent,
if you served Xiāngzǐ well, Xiāngzǐ
would certainly favor you;
once close, you could do as you wish;
this is very easy and success would be certain."
Yù Ràng laughed and replied:
"That would be avenging a former understanding for a later one,
harming a new lord for an old one;
