nothing is more disruptive to the righteousness between ruler and minister than this.
All that I do is for this purpose:
to clarify the righteousness between ruler and minister,
not to follow the easy path.
Moreover, to pledge oneself and serve a man,
and then seek to assassinate him,
is to serve one's lord with a divided heart.
What I do is difficult,
and also to shame those ministers of the world and later generations who harbor divided hearts."
After a short while,
when Xiāngzǐ was about to go out,
Yù Ràng hid under the bridge he was to pass.
When Xiāngzǐ reached the bridge, his horse startled.
Xiāngzǐ said: "This must be Yù Ràng."
He sent someone to inquire,
and it was indeed Yù Ràng.
Then Zhào Xiāngzǐ confronted Yù Ràng and enumerated:
"Did you not once serve the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans?
Zhì Bó destroyed the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans,
yet you did not avenge them,
but instead pledged yourself to serve Zhì Bó.
Now that Zhì Bó is dead,
why do you alone seek revenge so deeply?"
Yù Ràng said: "I served the Fàn and Zhōngháng clans;
they treated me as an ordinary man,
so I repaid them as an ordinary man.
Zhì Bó treated me as a man of the state,
so I repay him as a man of the state."
Xiāngzǐ then sighed tearfully and said:
"Alas, Master Yù!
Master Yù's actions for Zhì Bó
have already established your name.
I spared you before,
and that should suffice.
You make your own plans;
I will not spare you again."
He ordered soldiers to surround him.
Yù Ràng said:
"I have heard that an enlightened lord does not obscure a man's righteousness,
and a loyal minister does not cherish life to achieve fame.
You, my lord, previously generously spared me;
the world all praised your worthiness.
In today's matter,
I am ready to receive execution,
but I wish to strike your robe,
so that even in death I will have no regret.
This is not what I hoped for,
but I dare to lay bare my heart."
Then Xiāngzǐ, considering him righteous,
sent an attendant to bring his robe to Yù Ràng.
Yù Ràng drew his sword and leaped three times,
crying to heaven and striking it, saying:
"Now I can avenge Zhì Bó."
Then he fell on his sword and died.
On the day of his death,
the men of worth in Zhào heard of it,
and all wept for him.
Wèi Wénhóu requested passage through Zhào to attack Zhōngshān.
The lord of Zhào was about to refuse.
Zhào Lì said:
"That is a mistake.
If Wèi attacks Zhōngshān and cannot take it,
then Wèi will be exhausted,
and exhaustion will strengthen Zhào.
If Wèi captures Zhōngshān,
it certainly cannot cross Zhào to hold Zhōngshān.
Thus, the one using troops
is Wèi;
but the one gaining territory
is Zhào.
My lord, you should agree to it.
If you agree too eagerly,
they will realize it benefits us,
and will stop.
My lord, you should grant them passage,
but show it is done reluctantly."
Qín and Hán besieged Liáng,
while Yān and Zhào came to its rescue.
Someone said to Shānyáng Jūn:
"If Qín fights and defeats the three states,
Qín will certainly pass through Zhōu and Hán to possess Liáng.
If the three states defeat Qín,
the strength of the three states,
though insufficient to attack Qín,
is enough to capture Zhèng.
The strategist should ally the three states to attack Qín."
Fù Jī built a house of great size,
and Jīng Gǎn reported this to his lord.
The lord said to Fù Jī:
"Why have you built such a large house?"
Fù Jī replied:
"I am a traveler from afar.
My rank is high, but my stipend is meager;
my residence is small, and my family is not numerous.
Although you, my lord, trust me,
the common people all say:
'If the state faces a great crisis,
Jī will certainly not be of use.'
Now, by building this large palace,
I intend to gain the trust of the common people."
The lord said:
"Well said."
Sū Qín persuaded Lǐ Duì, saying:
"I, Sū Qín of Luòyáng, riding in a carriage,
come from a poor family with elderly parents.
I have no fine carriage or sturdy horses,
only a mulberry-wood wheeled cart with a thatched box and worn bags,
carrying books on my back and bundles on my shoulder,
braving dust and dirt,
enduring frost and dew,
crossing the Zhāng and Hé rivers,
my feet covered with calluses,
traveling a hundred lǐ a day before resting,
arriving at your outer gate,
hoping to have an audience with you,
to speak of the affairs of the world."
Lǐ Duì said:
"If you, sir, come to see me with ghostly talk, that is acceptable;
but if you come to speak of human affairs,
I already know all about them."
Sū Qín replied:
"I have indeed come to see you, my lord, with ghostly talk,
not with human words."
Lǐ Duì then granted him an audience.
Sū Qín said:
"Today, I arrived late,
after the city gates had closed.
Unable to find a mat to rest on,
I lodged in someone's field,
beside which stood a large thicket.
At midnight,
a clay figurine and a wooden figurine argued, saying:
'You are not as good as I,
for I am made of earth.
If I encounter a fierce wind or pouring rain,
I will crumble and collapse,
and return to the earth.
But you are not the root of a tree,
merely a branch.
If you encounter a fierce wind or pouring rain,
you will be swept into the Zhāng or Hé River,
flowing east to the sea,
drifting aimlessly with no place to stop.'
I secretly believe the clay figurine has the advantage.
Now, you have killed the lord's father and exterminated his clan;
your standing in the world
is as precarious as a pile of eggs.
If you heed my plan, you will live;
if you do not heed my plan, you will die."
Lǐ Duì said:
"Sir, please retire to your lodgings;
come again tomorrow to see me."
Sū Qín left.
A retainer of Lǐ Duì said to him:
"I have observed your conversation with Sū Qín.
His eloquence surpasses yours,
his breadth of knowledge surpasses yours.
Can you, my lord, accept Sū Qín's plan?"
Lǐ Duì said:
"I cannot."
The retainer said:
"Since you cannot,
I urge you to firmly block both ears,
and not listen to his talk."
The next day, Sū Qín came again,
and they talked all day before he left.
The retainer escorted Sū Qín out,
and Sū Qín said to the retainer:
"Yesterday, my talk was rough, yet your lord was moved;
today, it was refined, yet your lord remained unmoved.
Why is this?"
The retainer said:
"Your plan is grand and ambitious,
but my lord cannot employ it.
It was I who urged him to block both ears,
and not listen to your talk.
Nevertheless,
if you come again tomorrow,
I will request that he provide you with ample resources."
The next day, Sū Qín came,
and they talked with great enthusiasm.
Lǐ Duì presented Sū Qín with a bright moon pearl,
the Héshì jade,
a black sable fur coat,
and a hundred yì of gold.
With these resources, Sū Qín
traveled west to enter Qín.
Zhào gathered the forces of the world,
intending to attack Qí.
Sū Qín, on behalf of Qí, sent a letter to persuade the King of Zhào, saying:
"I have heard that the virtuous rulers of old
did not extend their moral conduct throughout the land,
nor did they spread teachings of kindness and love
to all the people.
Their sacrificial offerings and seasonal rituals
were not necessarily pleasing to the gods and spirits.
Yet sweet dew descended,
wind and rain came in due season,
farmers reaped abundant harvests,
the year's grain was plentiful,
and the people rejoiced,
while the wise ruler remained wary.
Now, Your Majesty's achievements and efforts
have not repeatedly inflicted severe pain on Qín,
nor have your accumulated grievances and hatreds
deeply afflicted Hán.
I have privately heard the discussions among your ministers and lower officials,
all saying that Your Majesty previously insisted
that Qín loves Zhào and hates Hán.
I observe the matter from the circumstances:
how could Qín possibly love Zhào and hate Hán?
It desires to destroy Hán and swallow the lands of the two Zhōu,
so it uses Hán as bait,
first making a declaration to the world,
hoping neighboring states will hear and observe.
Fearing its plan might not succeed,
it sends troops to feign action against Zhào and Wèi.
Fearing the world might awaken to its intentions,
it subtly alienates Hán to create division.
Fearing the world might doubt its sincerity,
it sends hostages to show good faith.
It proclaims virtue to allied states,
while in reality it attacks an emptied Hán.
I have observed its schemes:
in deliberating about Qín's strategies,
they are certain to arise from this.
"Moreover, the plans of persuaders
all say that if Hán loses Sānchuān,
and Wèi destroys the state of Jìn,
relying on Hán before it is exhausted,
disaster will reach Zhào.
Now, things in the world inherently have different circumstances but similar calamities,
and also similar circumstances but different calamities.
In the past,
while Chǔ was long under attack, Zhōngshān perished.
Now, if Yān seizes all of Hán's territory south of the river,
and advances to Shāqiū,
it will be only three hundred lǐ to the borders of Jùlù;
from Hánguān,
it will be fifteen hundred lǐ to Yúzhōng.
If Qín seizes all of Hán and Wèi's Shàngdǎng,
then its territory will be contiguous with your capital for seven hundred lǐ, with shared borders.
If Qín stations its three armies with strong crossbows at Yángtáng,
it will be only twenty lǐ from Hándān.
Moreover, if Qín attacks Your Majesty's Shàngdǎng with three armies and threatens the north,
then west of Gōuzhù,
will no longer belong to Your Majesty.
Now, if Lǔ Gōuzhù guards Chángshān and defends it,
the three hundred lǐ passage to Yān's Táng and Qūwú
will prevent the horses of Dài and the colts of Hú from coming east,
and the jade of Kūnlún from emerging.
These three treasures
will also no longer belong to Your Majesty.
Now, if you follow the powerful state of Qín in attacking Qí,
I fear disaster will arise from this.
In the past,
the kings of five states
once formed a horizontal alliance to plot an attack on Zhào,
dividing Zhào's territory into three parts,
inscribing it on plates and vessels,
and entrusting it to sworn allies.
The armies of the five states were set to move on a fixed day,
but Hán then sent troops west to restrain Qín,
forcing Qín to issue orders, dress in plain clothes, and submit,
returning Wēn, Zhǐ, and Gāopíng to Wèi,
and Sāngōng and Shíqīng to Zhào.
This is well known to Your Majesty.
Hán's service to Zhào should rightly be considered a superior alliance;
yet now it is being attacked for its crimes.
I fear that in the future, those who serve Your Majesty will not dare to be certain of their fate.
Now, if Your Majesty gathers the forces of the world,
all will surely consider it a gain for Your Majesty.
If Hán endangers its own altars of state to serve Your Majesty,
the world will surely respect Your Majesty.
Thus, if Hán, out of righteousness, brings the world to follow Your Majesty,
or if, at the least, Hán, out of admiration, brings the world to submit to Your Majesty,
then the destiny of this generation
will be controlled by Your Majesty.
I hope Your Majesty will deeply consult with your left and right ministers, deliberate thoroughly,
and plan carefully before taking action."
The state of Qí attacked Sòng,
but Fèngyáng Jūn was unwilling.
A guest addressed Fèngyáng Jūn, saying:
"Your Lordship's years are advanced,
yet your fief land is not settled.
You cannot but carefully consider this.
Qín is greedy; Hán and Wèi are in danger;
Wèi and Chǔ are upright;
the land of Zhōngshān is poor;
Sòng's crimes are grave;
Qí's anger is deep.
To destroy the chaotic state of Sòng,
secure your own fief,
and gain favor with powerful Qí—
this is an opportunity that comes once in a hundred generations."
The King of Qín said to Gōngzǐ Tuō: "In the events of last year at Xiáo,
Hán served as the central army,
joining the other feudal lords to attack Qín.
Hán borders Qín,
its territory not reaching a thousand lǐ,
and it vacillates, unreliable.
Recently, Qín and Chǔ fought at Lántián,
Hán sent crack troops to assist Qín,
but when Qín's battle went unfavorably,
it turned and allied with Chǔ,
not holding firm to its pledged alliance,
following only what was expedient.
Hán, to us,
is a disease in the heart and belly.
I intend to attack it;
what do you think?"
Gōngzǐ Tuō replied: "If Your Majesty sends troops against Hán,
Hán will surely fear,
and in its fear, we may deeply extract concessions without fighting."
The King said: "Excellent."
He then raised an army,
one force approaching Xíngyáng,
one force approaching Tàiháng.
Hán grew fearful,
sending Yángchéng Jūn to enter Qín and apologize,
offering to cede the land of Shàngdǎng to make peace.
He ordered Hán Yáng to inform the governor of Shàngdǎng, Jìn Tǒu, saying:
"Qín has raised two armies to press upon Hán,
and Hán cannot withstand it.
Now the King orders Hán to mobilize troops and offer Shàngdǎng to make peace with Qín.
I am sent to inform the Grand Administrator,
the Grand Administrator should cede it."
Jìn Tǒu said:
"There is a saying:
Even the knowledge of one who carries a bottle
does not fail to guard his vessel.
The King may have his order,
but I, as Grand Administrator,
even if it is the King and you, I must be wary.
I request to fully mobilize the garrison to resist Qín.
If we cannot hold out to the end,
then I will die for it."
Hán Yáng hurried to report to the King,
who said: "I have already promised Yìnghóu,
and now if I do not give it,
that would be deceiving him."
He then sent Féng Tíng to replace Jìn Tǒu.
Féng Tíng held out for thirty days,
then secretly sent someone to request of the King of Zhào, saying:
"Hán cannot hold Shàngdǎng,
and is about to give it to Qín,
but its people all do not wish to become subjects of Qín,
and instead desire to become subjects of Zhào.
Now there are seventy walled cities and towns,
I wish to respectfully present them to Your Majesty,
hoping Your Majesty will accept them."
The King of Zhào was pleased,
summoned Píngyuán Jūn and told him:
"Hán cannot hold Shàngdǎng,
and is about to give it to Qín,
its officials and people do not wish to become subjects of Qín,
and all desire to become subjects of Zhào.
Now Féng Tíng has sent an envoy to give it to me;
what do you think?"
Zhào Bào replied: "Your servant has heard that the sage considers profit without cause to be a great calamity."
The King said:
"The people cherish my righteousness;
how can you say it is without cause?"
He replied:
"Qín has been nibbling away at the territory of the Hán clan,
cutting it off in the middle so that orders cannot pass through,
therefore it naturally assumes it will sit and receive Shàngdǎng.
Moreover, the reason Hán is offering it to Zhào
is to shift its calamity onto us.
Qín bears the toil,
yet Zhào receives the benefit.
Even if a strong and large state cannot obtain it from a small and weak one,
how can a small and weak one obtain it from a strong and large one?
Now if Your Majesty takes it,
can it be said to have cause?
Furthermore, Qín uses oxen for farming,
transports grain by water,
its daring warriors are all ranked as superior troops,
its commands are strict and governance effective;
we cannot fight them.
Your Majesty, consider this yourself!"
The King grew greatly angry and said:
"To use a million troops,
attacking and fighting year after year,
not even seeing a single city.
Now without using troops, I obtain seventy cities;
why should I not do it?"
Zhào Bào withdrew.
The King summoned Zhào Shèng
and Zhào Yǔ and told them:
"Hán cannot hold Shàngdǎng,
now its governor is giving it to me,
there are seventy walled cities and towns."
The two men replied:
"Using troops for years,
not seeing a single city,
now sitting still and obtaining cities—
this is a great benefit."
He then sent Zhào Shèng to go and receive the land.
Zhào Shèng arrived and said:
"The king of our humble state
has sent his envoy, your servant Shèng.
The Grand Administrator has a decree,
ordering your servant Shèng to say:
'We request to enfeoff the Grand Administrator with a city of thirty thousand households,
enfeoff the county magistrate with one thousand households,
all officials shall be increased three ranks in nobility,
and for the people who can gather together,
each family shall be granted six jin of gold.'"
Féng Tíng shed tears and declined, saying:
"This places me in three acts of unrighteousness:
To hold land for my lord and yet not die for it,
but instead give it to others—
this is the first unrighteousness;
my lord intended to give it to Qín,
yet I disobeyed my lord's command—
this is the second unrighteousness;
to sell my lord's land and profit from it—
this is the third unrighteousness."
He declined the enfeoffment and entered Hán, telling the King of Hán:
"Zhào has heard that Hán cannot hold Shàngdǎng,
and now has sent troops to take it."
Hán informed Qín, saying:
"Zhào has raised troops and taken Shàngdǎng."
The King of Qín was enraged,
and ordered Gōngsūn Qǐ and Wáng Yǐ to lead troops to meet Zhào at Chángpíng.
Sū Qín was sent by the King of Zhào as an envoy to Qín.
Upon his return,
for three days he was not granted an audience.
He said to the King of Zhào:
"Qín recently passed by Zhùshān,
where there were two trees.
One seemed to be calling to its companions,
one seemed to be weeping.
I asked the reason,
and they replied:
'I am already large,
my years are already advanced,
I suffer from the craftsmen,
who will use ink lines, compasses, squares, and carving tools upon me.'
The other seemed to say:
'That is not what I suffer from,
for that is my destined duty.
What I suffer from is the iron drill,
which enters of itself and comes out through others.'
Now your servant was envoy to Qín,
and for three days was not received;
is there not someone who considers your servant an iron drill?"
Gān Mào, for Qín, made a pact with Wèi to attack Hán's Yíyáng.
He also went north to Zhào.
Lěng Xiàng said to Qiáng Guó:
"It would be better to have Zhào detain Gān Mào,
not let him leave,
and use him to bargain with Qí, Hán, and Qín.
The King of Qí, wishing to seek aid for Yíyáng,
will surely offer the county of Húshì.
Hán, wishing to possess Yíyáng,
will surely bribe Zhào with Lùshè and Duānshì.
The King of Qín, wishing to obtain Yíyáng,
will not begrudge famous treasures.
Moreover, detain Mào,
and use this to establish Gōngsūn Hè and Chūlǐ Jí."
He said to Chancellor Pí:
"With Zhào being weak, yet relying on Jiànxìn Jūn,
why is it that Shè Mèng harbors such resentment?
It is because he considers the vertical alliance to be meritorious.
If Qí does not join the alliance,
Jiànxìn Jūn will know that the vertical alliance brings no merit.
How then can Jiànxìn Jūn, with no merit, oppose Qín?
If he cannot oppose Qín without merit,
then he will send troops to aid Qín in attacking Wèi,
using Chǔ and Zhào to divide Qí,
and thus his strength will be fully exerted.
If Jiànxìn and Chūnshēn join the vertical alliance,
they will have no merit and oppose Qín.
If Qín divides Qí,
and Qí destroys Wèi,
then they will have merit and be friendly with Qín.
Therefore, between these two lords,
how can one choose between having merit and having no merit as a measure of wisdom?"
Someone said to Chancellor Pí:
"Wèi killed Lǚ Liáo and Wèi raised troops,
lost its northern territory of Yáng and Liáng was endangered,
the fief of Héjiān was not settled and Qí was endangered,
Wénxìn could not achieve his ambitions,
this is the worry of the Three Jìn turning against him.
Now Wèi's disgrace is not yet erased,
Zhào's troubles have arisen again,
Wénxìn Hóu's worries are great.
If Qí does not join,
the hearts of the Three Jìn will be suspicious.
Those with great worries will form alliances without careful consideration,
those with suspicious hearts will serve Qín urgently.
If Qín and Wèi form an alliance,
it will be accomplished without waiting for territorial cessions.
If Qín, along with Chǔ and
Wèi, attacks Qí, and alone devours Zhào,
then Qí and Zhào will surely both perish."
The King of Zhào enfeoffed Mèngcháng Jūn with Wǔchéng.
Mèngcháng Jūn selected a retainer to serve as an official of Wǔchéng,
and sent him off, saying:
"Does not the common saying go,
'He who borrows a carriage drives it hard,
he who borrows a robe wears it out'?"
They all replied:
"Indeed it does."
Mèngcháng Jūn said: "Wén finds this quite unacceptable.
Those from whom one borrows robes and carriages,
if not close friends,
then are brothers.
To drive hard the carriage of a close friend,
to wear out the robe of a brother,
Wén considers this improper.
Now the King of Zhào, unaware of Wén's lack of virtue,
has enfeoffed me with Wǔchéng.
I hope that when you go there, sir,
you will not cut down trees,
nor dismantle houses,
but act prudently so that the King of Zhào may come to understand and know Wén.
Take care to ensure it can be fully returned to him."
He said to the King of Zhào:
"When the Three Jìn unite, Qín is weakened;
when the Three Jìn are divided, Qín is strengthened;
this is clear to all under heaven.
When Qín has Yān, it attacks Zhào;
when it has Zhào, it attacks Yān;
when it has Liáng, it attacks Zhào;
when it has Zhào, it attacks Liáng;
when it has Chǔ, it attacks Hán;
when it has Hán, it attacks Chǔ;
this is clearly seen by all under heaven.
Yet the states east of the mountains cannot change this course,
because their military is weak.
Weak and unable to unite,
how is it that Chǔ understands this,
while the states east of the mountains are foolish?
This is what I worry about for the states east of the mountains.
When a tiger is about to pounce on its prey,
the prey does not know the tiger is about to seize it,
but instead fight among themselves until both are exhausted,
and then meet their death at the tiger's jaws.
Thus, if the prey knew the tiger was about to seize them,
they would certainly not fight among themselves.
Now the rulers east of the mountains do not know that Qín is about to seize them,
and still fight among themselves until both are weakened,
only to deliver their states to Qín.
Their understanding falls far short of that of animals.
I hope Your Majesty will consider this carefully.
"Now there are matters that require urgent attention.
Qín's desire to attack Hán and Liáng, and to spy on the royal house of Zhōu in the east, is extreme,
and I lose sleep over it.
Now its attack on Chǔ in the south
is because it hates the great union of the Three Jìn.
Now it attacks Chǔ, rests, and attacks again,
for already five years,
seizing over a thousand lǐ of territory.
Now it says to the King of Chǔ:
'If you will but deign to come and see me,
I will surely make Chǔ a brother state,
and will surely attack Hán and Liáng for Chǔ,
returning Chǔ's former territories.'
The King of Chǔ, pleased by Qín's words,
and angered that Hán and Liáng did not come to his aid,
will surely go to Qín.
Having a scheme, Qín deliberately sent an envoy to Zhào,
using Yān as bait for Zhào,
to divide the Three Jìn.
Now if Your Majesty, pleased by Qín's words, wishes to attack Yān,
attacking Yān,
before you are sated, disaster will already have arrived.
If the King of Chǔ goes to Qín,
Qín and Chǔ will become one,
and attack Hán from the east.
Hán will have no Chǔ to the south,
and no Zhào to the north,
Hán will not wait to be attacked,
but will cut territory, seize horses, and flee west.
Qín and Hán will form a close alliance,
and Qín's calamity will then shift to Liáng.
With Qín's strength,
and the use of Chǔ and Hán,
Liáng will not wait to be attacked.
It will cut territory, seize horses, and flee west.
Qín and Liáng will form a close alliance,
and Qín's calamity will then be directed at Zhào.
With a strong Qín having Hán, Liáng, and Chǔ,
and Yān's anger,
the territorial cuts will surely be deep.
If the state acts thus,
it is why I have come.
Therefore I say:
there are matters that require urgent action.
"Before the King of Chǔ enters Qín,
if the Three Jìn are close and firm with each other,
and dispatch elite troops to guard the western borders of Hán and Liáng,
the King of Chǔ, hearing of this,
will surely not enter Qín.
Qín will surely be angry and attack Chǔ again,
so Qín's calamity will not leave Chǔ,
which benefits the Three Jìn.
If the King of Chǔ enters Qín,
and Qín sees the great and firm union of the Three Jìn,
it will surely not release the King of Chǔ,
but will demand much territory.
Thus, Qín's calamity will not leave Chǔ,
which benefits the Three Jìn.
I hope Your Majesty will urgently consider this carefully!"
The King of Zhào then raised troops and went south to guard the western borders of Hán and Liáng.
When Qín saw the firmness of the Three Jìn,
it indeed did not release the King of Chǔ,
but demanded much territory.
Sū Qín went from Yān to Zhào,
beginning the vertical alliance,
and persuaded the King of Zhào, saying:
"All the ministers, officials,
and even commoners under heaven,
none do not highly esteem Your Majesty's righteous conduct,
and all have long wished to offer advice and present their loyalty before you.
However,
Fèngyáng Jūn was jealous,
and Your Majesty could not fully assume your duties,
so foreign guests and traveling persuaders
dared not exhaust their loyalty before you.
Now that Fèngyáng Jūn has passed away,
Your Majesty can only now become close to the scholars and people.
Therefore, I dare to offer my foolish thoughts,
and present my humble loyalty.
In planning for Your Majesty,
nothing is better than keeping the people at peace and without troubles,
I beg you not to engage in unnecessary actions.
The foundation of keeping the people at peace
lies in choosing alliances.
If alliances are chosen well, the people will be at peace;
if alliances are not chosen well, the people will never be at peace.
Let me speak of external threats:
If Qí and Qín are both enemies,
the people will not be at peace;
if you rely on Qín to attack Qí,
the people will not be at peace;
if you rely on Qí to attack Qín,
the people will not be at peace.
Therefore, those who scheme against other rulers,
and attack other states,
often bitterly use words to sever others' alliances.
I hope Your Majesty will be careful not to let such words leave your mouth.
"I beg you to dismiss your attendants,
and I will speak of what makes the difference,
which is simply the interplay of yīn and yáng.
If Your Majesty truly listens to me,
Yān will surely present lands of felt, furs, dogs, and horses,
Qí will surely present coastal lands of fish and salt,
Chǔ will surely present lands of oranges, pomelos, and Yúnmèng,
Hán and Wèi can both be made to present fiefs and bathhouse towns,
and your noble relatives and elder brothers can all receive marquisates."
To cede territory and offer tribute—
this is what the Five Hegemons sought through crushing armies and capturing generals;
to enfeoff marquises and honor relatives—this is why Tāng and Wǔ overthrew and slew rulers in their struggles.
Now Your Majesty, with folded hands, possesses both advantages,
which is why I consider this a blessing for Your Majesty.
If Your Majesty allies with Qín,
then Qín will inevitably weaken Hán and Wèi;
if you ally with Qí, then Qí will inevitably weaken Chǔ and Wèi.
If Wèi is weakened, it will cede the lands beyond the Yellow River;
if Hán is weakened, it will offer Yíyáng.
Once Yíyáng is offered, the connection to Shàngjùn will be severed;
once the lands beyond the river are ceded, the routes will be impassable.
If Chǔ is weakened, there will be no support.
These three strategies
must be carefully considered.
If Qín descends via Zhǐdào, then Nányáng will be shaken;
if it coerces Hán and encircles Zhōu, then Zhào will melt away on its own;
if it occupies Wèi and seizes Qí, then Qí will surely come to pay court.
Once Qín’s desires are fulfilled east of the mountains,
it will inevitably raise its armor and turn toward Zhào.
When Qín’s armored troops cross the Yellow River and traverse the Zhāng River,
occupying Pānwú,
then battle will surely be fought beneath Hándān.
This is what I consider a danger for Your Majesty.
"In the present time,
among the states established east of the mountains,
none is as strong as Zhào.
Zhào’s territory spans two thousand lǐ,
with armored troops numbering several hundred thousand,
a thousand chariots,
ten thousand cavalry,
and grain supplies lasting ten years;
to the west lies Chángshān,
to the south the Yellow River and Zhāng River,
to the east the Qīnghé River,
to the north the state of Yān.
Yān is inherently a weak state,
not worthy of fear.
Moreover, among all under heaven, whom Qín fears and regards as harmful,
none compares to Zhào.
Yet why does Qín not dare raise troops and armor to attack Zhào?
It fears that Hán and Wèi will scheme against its rear.
Thus, Hán and Wèi
are the southern shield of Zhào.
When Qín attacks Hán and Wèi,
it is not so.
There are no great mountains or rivers to limit it;
gradually it nibbles away at them,
advancing until it reaches their capitals and stops.
Hán and Wèi cannot withstand Qín;
they will inevitably submit as vassals.
Once Hán and Wèi become vassals of Qín,
with no barrier from Hán and Wèi,
disaster will strike Zhào.
This is what I consider a danger for Your Majesty.
"I have heard
that Yáo did not possess the division of three families,
Shùn did not have an inch of land,
yet they possessed all under heaven.
Yǔ did not have a gathering of a hundred men,
yet he became king over the feudal lords.
The troops of Tāng and Wǔ did not exceed three thousand men,
their chariots not more than three hundred,
yet they were established as Sons of Heaven.
Truly, they grasped the Way.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler externally assesses the strength and weakness of his enemy states,
internally measures the numbers of his soldiers, their worthiness or lack thereof,
and without waiting for the two armies to confront each other,
the mechanisms of victory or defeat, survival or destruction,
are already clearly seen in his mind.
How could he be obscured by the words of the multitude
and decide matters in darkness?
"I have privately examined the maps of the world.
The territories of the feudal lords are five times that of Qín;
estimating the troops of the feudal lords,
they are ten times those of Qín.
If the six states unite their strength as one,
facing west to attack Qín,
Qín will surely be defeated.
Now, to be defeated by Qín,
facing west to serve it,
to be subjugated by Qín—
to defeat others versus being defeated by others,
to subjugate others versus being subjugated by others—
how can these be spoken of in the same breath?
Those who advocate the horizontal alliance
all wish to cede the lands of the feudal lords to make peace with Qín.
Once peace is made with Qín,
they will have high towers and beautiful palaces,
listen to the sounds of yú and sè,
savor the harmony of the five flavors,
with carriages in front,
long courtyards behind,
beauties with clever smiles.
Yet when the disaster of Qín arrives,
they do not share in the worry.
Therefore, the horizontal alliance advocates day and night strive to use Qín’s power to intimidate the feudal lords,
in order to seek ceded territory.
I hope Your Majesty will carefully consider this.
"I have heard
that an enlightened king cuts off doubts and removes slander,
banishes the traces of rumors,
blocks the gate of factionalism,
so that plans to honor the ruler, expand territory, and strengthen the army
may be presented with loyalty before him.
Thus, I privately plan for Your Majesty:
nothing is better than to unite Hán, Wèi, Qí, Chǔ, Yān, and Zhào,
the six states in a vertical alliance of kinship,
to jointly oppose Qín.
Have the generals and ministers of the world
gather together on the banks of the Huán River,
exchange hostages, slit a white horse, and swear an oath.
The covenant shall say:
If Qín attacks Chǔ,
Qí and Wèi each shall send elite troops to assist,
Hán shall cut off its supply routes,
Zhào shall cross the Yellow River and Zhāng River,
Yān shall guard north of Chángshān.
If Qín attacks Hán and Wèi,
then Chǔ shall cut off its rear,
Qí shall send elite troops to assist,
Zhào shall cross the Yellow River and Zhāng River,
Yān shall guard Yúnzhōng.
If Qín attacks Qí,
then Chǔ shall cut off its rear,
Hán shall guard Chénggāo,
Wèi shall block the Wǔdào route,
Zhào shall cross the Yellow River, Zhāng River, and Bóguān,
Yān shall send elite troops to assist.
If Qín attacks Yān,
then Zhào shall guard Chángshān,
Chǔ shall station troops at Wǔguān,
Qí shall cross the Bóhǎi Sea,
Hán and Wèi shall send elite troops to assist.
If Qín attacks Zhào,
then Hán shall station troops at Yíyáng,
Chǔ shall station troops at Wǔguān,
Wèi shall station troops beyond the Yellow River,
Qí shall cross the Bóhǎi Sea,
Yān shall send elite troops to assist.
If any feudal lord first betrays the covenant,
the five states shall jointly attack it.
If the six states form a vertical alliance of kinship to oppose Qín,
Qín will certainly not dare send troops out of Hángǔ Pass to harm the lands east of the mountains!
Thus, the hegemon’s enterprise will be achieved!"
The King of Zhào said:
"I am young,
and my days ruling the state are few;
I have never heard long-term strategies for the altars of soil and grain.
Now, our distinguished guest intends to preserve the world,
and pacify the feudal lords.
I respectfully commit our state to follow."
Thereupon, he enfeoffed Sū Qín as the Lord of Wǔ'ān,
adorned a hundred chariots,
with a thousand yì of gold,
a hundred pairs of white jade discs,
a thousand bolts of brocade and embroidery,
to covenant with the feudal lords.
When Qín attacked Zhào,
Sūzǐ spoke on its behalf to the King of Qín, saying:
"I have heard that an enlightened king, regarding his people,
broadly discusses and employs their skills,
so that offices are not lacking in tasks and strength is not exhausted;
regarding their words,
he listens widely and uses them timely,
so that affairs are not ruined and evil is not manifest.
I hope Your Majesty will examine what I present,
and apply it for immediate use.
I have heard that one who carries heavy treasures
does not travel by night;
one who undertakes great achievements
does not treat the enemy lightly.
Thus, the worthy bear heavy responsibilities yet act with humility;
the wise achieve great merits yet speak with deference.
Therefore, the people do not resent their honor,
and the age does not envy their achievements.
I have heard:
A state a hundred times stronger
does not make its people delight in lagging behind;
one whose achievements surpass the age
does not repeat actions as a ruler;
people whose strength is exhausted
are not used by the benevolent;
to seek gain and then return to tranquility
is the system of a sage ruler;
to achieve great merit and then let the people rest
is the way of using troops."
Now, if you employ troops in endless campaigns without rest,
exhausting your strength without respite,
Zhào’s anger will certainly turn upon its own cities,
and Zhào will barely survive!
Yet it is a state with chariots on all four sides,
and even if you now capture Hándān,
it will not be a lasting benefit for the state.
I suspect that,
with lands vast but left uncultivated,
the people exhausted and given no rest,
and further oppressed by punishments and penalties,
then even if they follow you, they will not remain settled.
As the saying goes:
‘When a state is victorious in war yet endangered,
it is because resources are not managed properly.
When achievements are great but authority is light,
it is because territory is not integrated.’
Thus, for tasks that exceed one’s capacity,
a father cannot rely on his son;
for demands that are endless,
a ruler cannot rely on his ministers.
Therefore, he who discerns the subtle becoming manifest is strong;
he who understands that giving the people rest is the way to employ them becomes a hegemon;
he who comprehends that the light can become weighty becomes a true king.”
The King of Qín said:
“If I hold back my troops and give the people rest,
then the world will certainly form a vertical alliance,
intending to oppose Qín.”
Sūzǐ said: “I have reason to know that the world cannot form a vertical alliance to oppose Qín.
I consider Tián Dān and Rú Ěr to be greatly mistaken.
Is it only Tián Dān and Rú Ěr who are greatly mistaken?
The rulers of the world are all mistaken!
To contemplate rallying the defeated Qí, the exhausted Chǔ, the weakened Wèi, and the unpredictable Zhào,
hoping to exhaust Qín and break Hán,
I consider this the height of folly.
Now, King Wēi and King Xuān of Qí
were worthy rulers of their age,
virtuous and broad, with vast territories,
the state wealthy and able to employ its people,
their generals martial and soldiers strong.
King Xuān employed them,
later enriching Hán and intimidating Wèi,
leading campaigns south against Chǔ,
and west to attack Qín.
Yet the Qí army was trapped at the Xiáo Pass,
for ten years they seized land,
the Qín people kept their distance and did not submit,
and Qí was left empty and desolate.
The reason the Qí army was defeated,
and Hán and Wèi barely survived,
what was it?
It was because they attacked Chǔ and assaulted Qín,
and afterward suffered the calamity.
Now, the wealth is not what remains from Qí’s Wēi and Xuān,
the elite troops are not from the arsenals of a rich Hán and strong Wèi,
and the generals do not possess the strategic mind of Tián Dān or Simǎ.
To rally a broken Qí, an exhausted Chǔ, a weakened Wèi, and an unpredictable Zhào,
hoping to exhaust Qín and break Hán,
I consider this the gravest error.
I believe a vertical alliance cannot succeed.
There is a guest who raises objections,
and now I have a concern about the world.
Those of the School of Names,
all say
that
‘a white horse is not a horse.’ But if a white horse is indeed a horse,
then there is the reality of a white horse being a horse.
This is what concerns me.
“In the past,
the Qín people sent troops down to attack Huái,
subjugated its people,
and three states followed them.
Zhào Shē and Bào Náo led,
and four men from Chǔ rose to follow them.
They faced Huái but did not rescue it,
the Qín people left and they did not pursue.
I do not know whether the three states hated Qín and loved Huái?
Or forgot their hatred of Huái and loved Qín?
To attack but not rescue,
to leave and not pursue,
thus the troops of the three states were trapped,
and that was the ability of Zhào Shē and Bào Náo.
Therefore, they divided land and were defeated by Qí.
Tián Dān, leading Qí’s finest,
with his troops ran rampant within for fourteen years,
yet never dared to deploy troops to attack Qín or break Hán,
but raced only within his own borders.
I do not see how a vertical alliance could ever succeed.”
Thereupon, the King of Qín disbanded his troops and did not venture beyond his borders, the feudal lords rested,
the world was at peace,
and for twenty-nine years they did not attack each other.
Zhāng Yí, promoting the horizontal alliance for Qín,
persuaded the King of Zhào, saying:
“My humble state’s King of Qín has sent me to dare present this letter to Your Majesty’s minister.
Your Majesty has gathered and led the world to oppose Qín,
so that Qín’s troops have not dared to exit the Hángǔ Pass for fifteen years.
Your Majesty’s might
prevails throughout the world east of the mountains.
My humble state, fearful and trembling,
has repaired armor and sharpened weapons,
prepared chariots and cavalry,
practiced riding and archery,
labored in the fields and stored grain,
guarded within our four borders,
dwelling anxiously and apprehensively,
not daring to make a move,
solely because Your Majesty might intend to reprimand us.
Now, thanks to Your Majesty’s efforts, Qín
has raised troops west to take Bā and Shǔ,
annexed Hànzhōng,
taken the two Zhōu in the east and moved the Nine Tripods west,
and guards the ford at Báimǎ.
Although Qín is remote and distant,
our hearts have long been filled with resentment and pent-up anger.
Now we have some worn armor and blunt weapons,
stationed at Miǎnchí,
wishing to cross the Hé River and traverse the Zhāng,
occupy Pānwú,
and meet battle beneath Hándān.
We wish to join battle on the jiǎzǐ day,
to rectify the affairs of King Zhòu of Shāng.
I respectfully send this messenger first to inform Your Majesty’s attendants.
“All that Your Majesty believes in forming the vertical alliance
relies on Sū Qín’s schemes.
He deluded the feudal lords,
turning right into wrong,
and wrong into right,
wishing to overturn Qí but unable to do so,
ending with his own body torn apart by chariots in Qí’s marketplace.
That the world cannot be united is also clear.
Now Chǔ and Qín are brotherly states,
and Hán and Wèi are called eastern vassals,
Qí has offered its lands of fish and salt,
this severs Zhào’s right arm.
To sever the right arm and seek to fight others,
losing allies and dwelling in isolation,
hoping to be without danger—how can it be achieved?
Now Qín dispatches three generals:
one army blocks the Wǔ road,
informs Qí to raise troops and cross the Qīnghé River,
stationing east of Hándān;
one army stations at Chénggāo,
driving Hán and Wèi to station north of the Hé River;
one army stations at Miǎnchí.
The covenant states:
four states unite as one
to attack Zhào,
break Zhào and divide its land four ways.
Therefore, I dare not conceal my intentions,
but first inform Your Majesty’s attendants.
I earnestly advise Your Majesty
that nothing is better than meeting Qín at Miǎnchí,
facing each other and personally forming a bond.
I beg to hold back troops and not attack,
hoping Your Majesty will decide on a plan.”
The King of Zhào said:
“In the time of my late father,
Fèngyáng Jūn was chancellor,
monopolizing power and controlling authority,
obscuring my late father,
solely managing official affairs.
I resided in the palace,
attended by tutors,
unable to participate in state planning.
When my late father left his ministers,
I was young,
the time since I assumed sacrificial duties was brief,
and in my heart I secretly harbored doubts.
I believed that exclusively following the vertical alliance and not serving Qín
was not a lasting benefit for the state.
I was thus willing to change my mind and alter my plans,
ceding territory to apologize for past faults and serve Qín.
I was just about to arrange carriages and hasten on my way,
when I happened to hear the envoy’s clear decree.”
Thereupon, he took three hundred chariots and went to court at Miǎnchí,
ceding Héjiān to serve Qín.
King Wǔlíng was at leisure during the day,
Féi Yì attended by his side,
and said:
“Is Your Majesty pondering the changes in worldly affairs,
weighing the use of armor and weapons,
reflecting on the deeds of Jiǎn and Xiāng,
and considering the benefits of the Hú and Dí?”
The king said:
"To succeed to the throne and not forget the virtue of one's ancestors
is the way of a ruler;
to devote oneself to making clear the ruler's merits
is the principle of a minister.
Therefore, a worthy ruler in times of peace has teachings that guide the people and facilitate affairs,
and in times of action achieves accomplishments that illuminate antiquity and surpass previous generations.
As for a minister,
in adversity he maintains the integrity of fraternal deference and humility,
and in success he undertakes enterprises that benefit the people and assist the ruler.
These two aspects
define the roles of ruler and minister.
Now I wish to continue the enterprise of Lord Xiāng,
opening up the lands of the Hú and Dí,
yet throughout my lifetime I have not seen it accomplished.
When the enemy is weak,
little effort yields great achievement;
one can avoid exhausting the toil of the common people
and yet enjoy the merit of ancient times.
Those who achieve accomplishments surpassing their age
inevitably bear the burden of defying convention;
those who possess unique insights
are inevitably feared by the multitude.
Now I intend to adopt Hú clothing and mounted archery to instruct the people,
and the world will surely criticize me."Féi Yì said:
"I have heard that
doubtful undertakings bring no achievement,
and hesitant actions gain no fame.
Now that Your Majesty has resolved to bear the burden of defying convention,
you should disregard the criticism of the world.
Those who discuss supreme virtue
do not conform to custom;
those who accomplish great deeds
do not consult the multitude.
In ancient times, Shùn performed the dance of the Yǒumiáo,
and Yǔ bared his body to enter the naked country,
not to indulge desires and please their minds,
but to discuss virtue and seek achievement.
The foolish are blind to accomplished affairs,
while the wise perceive what has not yet sprouted.
May Your Majesty proceed with this."The king said:
"It is not that I doubt adopting Hú clothing;
I fear the world will laugh at me.
What delights the madman,
the wise mourn;
what amuses the fool,
the worthy grieve.
If there are those in the world who follow me,
then the achievement of adopting Hú clothing cannot be known.
Even if the whole world mocks me,
I will surely possess the lands of the Hú and Zhōngshān."The king then adopted Hú clothing.He sent Wángsūn Xiè to inform Lord Chéng, saying:
"I have adopted Hú clothing
and will soon appear at court in it.
I also wish for you, uncle, to wear it.
At home, one obeys one's parents;
in the state, one obeys the ruler.
This is the universal practice of past and present.
A son does not oppose his parents;
a minister does not defy his ruler.
This is the established principle of the former kings.
Now that I have initiated this teaching and changed clothing,
if you, uncle, do not adopt it,
I fear the world will criticize it.
Governing a state has constant principles,
with benefiting the people as the foundation;
administering governance has its norms,
with the enforcement of orders as paramount.
Therefore, making virtue clear lies in considering the lowly,
and implementing governance lies in trusting the noble.
The intention behind adopting Hú clothing now
is not to indulge desires and please the mind.
Affairs have their origins,
and achievements have their limits.
When affairs are accomplished and achievements established, then virtue will be manifest.
Now I fear that you, uncle, would oppose the norms of governance
and thereby support the criticism of you, lord uncle.
Moreover, I have heard that
affairs that benefit the state involve no wrongdoing,
and relying on noble relatives brings no burden to one's name.
Therefore, I wish to enlist your righteousness, lord uncle,
to accomplish the achievement of adopting Hú clothing.
I have sent Xiè to visit you, uncle,
to request that you adopt it."Lord Chéng bowed twice and said:
"I had indeed heard of the king's adoption of Hú clothing,
but due to my incompetence and illness,
I was unable to hasten to court,
and thus did not come forward earlier.
Now that the king commands it,
I dare to exhaust my foolish loyalty.
I have heard that
the Central States
are where the intelligent and wise reside,
where the wealth and resources of all things gather,
where the teachings of sages and worthies are imparted,
where benevolence and righteousness are practiced,
where the Shī, Shū, rites, and music are employed,
where extraordinary skills and arts are tested,
where distant regions come to observe and attend,
and where the barbarians take as their model for righteous conduct.
Now if the king abandons this
and adopts the clothing of distant regions,
alters the teachings of antiquity,
changes the ways of old,
opposes people's hearts,
defies scholars,
and distances yourself from the Central States,
I beg Your Majesty to consider this."The messenger reported to the king.The king said:
"I had indeed heard of my uncle's illness."He then went to Lord Chéng's homeand personally requested, saying:
"Clothing
is for the sake of convenience;
rites
are for the sake of facilitating affairs.
Therefore, the sage observes local conditions and adapts appropriately,
establishes rites according to affairs,
so as to benefit the people and enrich the state.
Those with loose hair and tattooed bodies,
crossed arms and left-lapped garments,
are the people of Ōuyuè.
Those with blackened teeth and tattooed foreheads,
wearing fish-skin caps and hempen seams,
are the state of Dàwú.
Their ceremonial clothing differs,
but their convenience is the same.
Therefore, as regions differ, practices change;
as affairs differ, rites alter.
Thus, if it can benefit their people,
the sage does not unify practices;
if it can truly facilitate their affairs,
he does not make rites uniform.
Even Confucian scholars share one teacher yet their rites differ;
the Central States share customs yet their teachings diverge,
how much more so for the convenience of mountain valleys?
Therefore, in changes of adoption or rejection,
even the wise cannot unify;
in clothing of distant or near regions,
even sages and worthies cannot make them the same.
Remote regions have many differences;
narrow learning breeds much dispute.
Not to doubt what one does not know,
and not to condemn what differs from oneself,
is to be impartial in seeking goodness.
Now what you, sir, speak of
is custom.
What I speak of
is the means to shape custom.
Now our state to the east has the Hé and Bóluò rivers,
shared with Qí and Zhōngshān,
yet we lack the use of boats and oars.
From Chángshān to Dài and Shàngdǎng,
to the east are the borders of Yān and the Eastern Hú,
to the west are the frontiers of Lóufán, Qín, and Hán,
yet we lack preparedness in mounted archery.
Therefore, I will gather boats and oars,
seek river-dwelling people, to guard the Hé and Bóluò rivers;
change clothing for mounted archery,
to prepare the borders against the Cānhú, Lóufán, Qín, and Hán.
Moreover, in the past, Lord Jiǎn did not block Jìnyáng
but extended to Shàngdǎng,
and Lord Xiāng annexed the Róng and took Dài,
driving away the various Hú tribes.
This is clear to both foolish and wise.
Previously, Zhōngshān relied on Qí's strong army,
invaded and plundered our lands,
bound and captured our people,
diverted water to besiege Hào.
Were it not for the divine spirits of the state,
Hào would have nearly been lost.
The former king was enraged by this,
and his grievance remains unavenged.
Now, adopting mounted archery and clothing
can in the near term prepare the situation in Shàngdǎng,
and in the long term avenge the grievance against Zhōngshān.
Yet you, uncle, conform to the customs of the Central States and oppose the intentions of Jiǎn and Xiāng,
detest the name of changing clothing,
and forget the shame of state affairs.
This is not what I expect of you!"Lord Chéng bowed twice and touched his head to the ground, saying:
"I am foolish and did not comprehend the king's proposal,
daring only to speak of common worldly opinions.
Now, wishing to continue the intentions of Jiǎn and Xiāng,
and to follow the will of the former kings,
how dare I not obey the command?"He bowed twice.The king then bestowed Hú clothing upon him.
Zhào Wén remonstrated, saying:
"Farmers toil while gentlemen are nourished—this is the constant principle of governance.
The foolish present their views while the wise deliberate on them—this is the way of instruction.
When ministers do not conceal their loyalty,
and rulers do not suppress speech,
that is the fortune of the state.
Though I am foolish,
I wish to exhaust my loyalty."
The king said:
"Plans are not harmed by discussion,
loyalty is not faulted for excess.
Speak your mind."
Zhào Wén said:
"Conforming to the times and assisting customs—this is the ancient way.
Clothing having fixed standards—this is the regulation of ritual.
Cultivating laws without error—this is the duty of the people.
These three
are what the former sages used for instruction.
Now you, my lord, abandon these
and adopt the clothing of distant regions,
alter the ancient teachings,
and change the ancient way.
Therefore, I wish Your Majesty to consider this."
The king said:
"You speak of the common world.
Ordinary people are immersed in customs;
scholars are sunk in what they have heard.
These two
are what enable one to fulfill office and comply with governance,
but are not what allow one to observe afar and discuss origins.
Moreover, the Three Dynasties did not wear the same clothing yet achieved kingship;
the Five Hegemons did not share the same teachings yet governed effectively.
The wise create teachings,
and the foolish are constrained by them.
The worthy deliberate on customs,
while the unworthy are bound by them.
Those constrained by clothing
are not worth discussing intentions with;
those bound by customs
are not worth conveying ideas to.
Thus, circumstances change with customs,
and ritual evolves with transformation—
this is the way of the sage.
To act in accordance with instruction,
and follow the law without selfishness—
this is the duty of the people.
Those who understand learning
can change with what they hear;
those who comprehend the changes of ritual
can transform with the times.
Therefore, those who act for themselves do not wait for others;
those who govern the present do not imitate the ancients.
You should set this aside."
Zhào Zào remonstrated, saying:
"To conceal loyalty and not exhaust it
is a kind of treachery.
To use private interests to deceive the state
is a type of baseness.
Those who commit treachery are put to death;
those who debase the state have their clans exterminated.
Regarding these two,
the former sages established clear punishments,
which are grave crimes for ministers.
Though I am foolish,
I wish to exhaust my loyalty,
and not avoid death."
The king said:
"To exhaust one's thoughts without concealment—that is loyalty.
For superiors not to suppress speech—that is enlightenment.
Loyalty does not shun danger;
enlightenment does not reject others.
Speak your mind."
Zhào Zào said:
"I have heard that
sages do not change the people to instruct them;
the wise do not alter customs to act.
Those who instruct according to the people
succeed without toil; those who act based on customs
find their plans straightforward and easily seen.
Now, Your Majesty changes the foundations and does not follow customs,
adopts Hú clothing without regard for the world—
this is not the way to instruct the people and perfect ritual.
Moreover, strange clothing leads to licentious intent;
perverse customs confuse the people.
Therefore, those who govern a state do not adopt strange and perverse clothing;
the Central States do not approach the practices of barbarians—
this is not the way to instruct the people and perfect ritual.
Moreover, following the law ensures no error;
cultivating ritual ensures no deviation.
I wish Your Majesty to consider this."
The king said:
"Ancient and modern customs differ—
which antiquity should be followed?
Emperors and kings did not imitate one another—
which ritual should be adhered to?
Fúxī and Shénnóng instructed without punishment;
Huángdì, Yáo, and Shùn punished without wrath.
When it came to the Three Kings,
they observed the times to establish laws,
and according to affairs, they instituted ritual.
Laws, measures, regulations, and orders
each suited what was appropriate;
clothing and tools
each facilitated their use.
Thus, ritual for an age need not unify its way;
benefiting the state need not imitate antiquity.
When sages arose,
they did not imitate one another yet achieved kingship.
When Xià and Yīn declined,
they did not change ritual yet perished.
Thus, opposing antiquity cannot be faulted,
and adhering to ritual is not necessarily praiseworthy.
Moreover, if strange clothing leads to licentious intent,
then Zōu and Lǔ would have no extraordinary conduct;
if perverse customs make the people fickle,
then Wú and Yuè would have no outstanding people.
Therefore, the sage calls that which benefits the body 'clothing,'
and that which facilitates affairs 'instruction.'
Advance and retreat are called 'propriety.'
The regulations of clothing
are to standardize ordinary people—
they are not for discussing the worthy.
Thus, the sage flows with customs,
and the worthy change with transformation.
A proverb says:
'Those who use books to drive chariots
do not fully understand the nature of horses.
Those who use antiquity to govern the present
do not comprehend the changes of affairs.'
Thus, the merit of following the law
is insufficient to rise above the age;
the learning of imitating antiquity
is insufficient to govern the present.
Do not oppose this."
The king appointed Zhōu Shào as tutor, saying:
"When I first toured the counties,
passing by Pānwú,
at the time when you were a son,
all who stepped upon stone steps spoke of your filial piety.
Therefore, I inquired about you with a jade disc,
sent you wine and food,
and sought to see you.
You pleaded illness and declined.
There were those who spoke of you, saying:
'A filial son to his father,
a loyal minister to his lord.'
Therefore, I consider your wisdom and planning
sufficient to guide others with discernment,
your steadfastness sufficient to uphold difficulties,
your loyalty capable of expressing intent,
your trustworthiness reliable for distant expectations.
The Odes say:
'To overcome difficulty with courage,
to bring order to chaos with wisdom—
this is the plan of affairs.
To establish a tutor based on conduct,
to instruct the young with learning—
this is the constant principle of righteousness.
Following planned affairs,
even if lost, brings no burden;
pursuing deliberated conduct,
even if destitute, brings no worry.'
Therefore, I wish you to adopt Hú clothing to tutor the prince."
Zhōu Shào said:
"Your Majesty's judgment is mistaken—
this is not something a humble minister dares undertake."
The king said:
"None knows a son like his father;
none knows a minister like his lord.
I am your lord."
Zhōu Shào said:
"There are six ways to establish a tutor."
The king said:
"What are the six?"
Zhōu Shào said:
"Wisdom and planning, not rash, comprehending transformation;
personal conduct, broad and kind, comprehending ritual;
majesty and dignity not used to alter position;
great profit not enough to change his heart;
reverent in instruction and not lax;
harmonious with subordinates and not perilous.
These six
are the talents of a tutor,
and I possess none of them.
To conceal within and not exhaust
is my crime.
To appoint a tutor from among lowly officials,
troubling the responsible officers,
is the shame of the officials.
I ask Your Majesty to reconsider."
The king said: "Understanding these six principles,
is the means by which I employ you."
Zhōu Shào said: "However, the state has not yet been informed of Your Majesty's adoption of Hu attire.
Nevertheless, I am Your Majesty's subject,
and since Your Majesty commands me with such gravity,
how dare I not obey the order?"
He bowed twice,
and was bestowed with Hu attire.
The king said:
"I consider the prince as your responsibility,
desiring that you deeply care for him,
leaving no room for disgrace.
Guide him along the path with righteous conduct,
do not let him drown in the hardship of study.
One who serves his lord,
follows his lord's intentions,
and does not oppose his will.
One who serves his predecessor,
honors his predecessor's eminence,
and does not betray his orphaned heir.
Therefore, having a minister who can be entrusted with such a command,
is the fortune of the state.
If you can act according to this,
then your service to me is complete.
The *Shū* says:
'Remove the wicked without hesitation,
employ the worthy without doubt.'
Between you and me,
there will be no use for others."
Thereupon, he bestowed upon Zhōu Shào Hu attire, cap and gown,
a complete belt with a golden shìbǐ buckle,
to serve as tutor to the prince.
Zhào Yān was later in adopting Hu attire.
The king sent an order reprimanding him, saying:
"The conduct of one who serves his lord
involves exhausting his mind and exerting his strength,
offering subtle remonstrance without clamor,
responding to inquiries without resentment,
not opposing superiors to boast of oneself,
not establishing private interests to gain fame.
The way of a son is obedience without opposition,
the conduct of a minister is yielding without contention.
If a son employs private ways, the family will surely fall into disorder;
if a minister employs private righteousness, the state will surely face peril.
To act contrary to one's parents,
even a kind father will not acknowledge such a son;
to achieve success by opposing one's lord,
even a benevolent lord will not acknowledge such a minister.
I have adopted Hu attire,
yet you alone refuse to wear it.
Opposing one's lord
— no crime is greater than this.
To consider compliance with governance a burden,
and to regard opposition to one's lord as lofty,
— no act of private interest is greater than this.
Therefore, I fear you will personally incur the crime of punishment and execution,
to clarify the laws of the officials."
Zhào Yān bowed twice and touched his head to the ground, saying:
"Previously, the officials ordered the adoption of Hu attire,
extending the command to your humble servant.
I failed to obey the order and exceeded the deadline.
Yet, instead of subjecting me to further humiliation and reprimand,
Your Majesty shows grace.
I respectfully comply with the attire,
awaiting Your Majesty's command today."
The king conquered Yuányáng,
and made it a cavalry district.
Niú Zàn offered remonstrance, saying:
"The state has established records,
the military has constant regulations.
To alter the records brings disorder,
to lose the regulations brings weakness.
Now Your Majesty conquers Yuányáng,
and makes it a cavalry district.
This is to alter the records and abandon the regulations.
Moreover, those familiar with their weapons underestimate the enemy;
those accustomed to their tools find difficulties easy.
Now the people are accustomed to their tools, yet Your Majesty changes them.
This harms the ruler and weakens the state.
Therefore, if the benefit is not a hundredfold, do not change customs;
if the achievement is not tenfold, do not alter tools.
Now Your Majesty breaks up infantry units and disperses soldiers,
to devote them to cavalry and archery.
I fear the gains from attack and capture
will not match the cost of what is lost."
The king said:
"Ancient and modern times differ in advantages,
distant and near places vary in their tools.
Yīn and yáng follow different paths,
the four seasons are not uniformly suitable.
Therefore, the worthy observe the times,
but are not confined by the times;
they control weapons,
but are not controlled by weapons.
You know the records of the government offices,
but do not know the advantages of weaponry;
you know the use of soldiers and armor,
but do not know the suitability of yīn and yáng.
Therefore, if weapons are not suitable for use,
what weapons cannot be changed?
If training is not convenient for affairs,
what customs cannot be altered?
In the past, our former lord, Lord Xiāng, bordered the territory of Dài,
built a wall to seal the border,
and named it the Gate of Infinity,
to illuminate the future and anticipate the distant.
Now, heavy armor and following infantry
cannot traverse perilous terrain;
benevolence, righteousness, the Way, and virtue
cannot make others come to court.
I have heard that faithfulness does not abandon achievement,
wisdom does not miss the opportune moment.
Now you use the records of the government offices
to confuse my affairs.
This is beyond your understanding."
Niú Zàn bowed twice and touched his head to the ground, saying:
"How dare I not obey the command?"
Thereupon, he adopted Hu attire,
led cavalry into Hú territory,
exited through the Gate of Yíyí,
traversed the nine fortified limits,
crossed the perilous five passes,
reached Yúzhōng,
and expanded the territory by a thousand *lǐ*.
In the thirtieth year of King Huìwén of Zhào,
the chancellor, Lord Dūpíng,
Tián Dān asked Zhào Shē:
"It is not that I do not appreciate
the general's art of war,
but what I do not accept
is solely the general's use of large numbers.
Using large numbers
prevents the people from farming,
and the transportation and supply of provisions cannot be sustained.
This is the path to sitting still and defeating oneself,
not what I
would do.
I have heard that
the armies of emperors and kings
used no more than thirty thousand,
and the world submitted.
Now the general insists on relying on a host of one hundred thousand or two hundred thousand to be effective.
This is what I cannot accept."
Mǎfú said:
"Not only do you not understand warfare,
you also do not comprehend the circumstances of the time.
Take the swords of Wú and Gān:
tested on flesh, they cut through oxen and horses;
tested on metal, they slice through basins and ewers;
but if placed thinly against a pillar and struck,
they break into three pieces;
if placed against a stone and struck,
they shatter into a hundred fragments.
Now, to use a host of thirty thousand to respond to the armies of a powerful state
is like placing a sword thinly against a pillar or striking it against a stone.
Moreover, the material of Wú and Gān swords:
if the spine lacks thickness,
the tip will not penetrate;
if the edge lacks thinness, the blade will not cut.
Even possessing both qualities,
without the convenience of a hilt, guard, and cord,
grasping the blade to stab,
the hand would be severed before it penetrates.
If you do not have a host of over one hundred or two hundred thousand
to serve as the convenience of hilt, guard, and cord,
and merely march thirty thousand across the world,
how could you succeed?
Furthermore, in ancient times,
within the Four Seas,
it was divided into ten thousand states.
Even the largest city walls did not exceed three hundred *zhàng*;
even the most populous
did not exceed three thousand households.
To gather an army of thirty thousand
and withstand such a force — what difficulty was there!
Now, take the ancient ten thousand states
and divide them into the seven Warring States,
each able to raise armies of several hundred thousand,
engaging in prolonged warfare,
lasting for years —
take your own state of Qí as an example.
Qí attacked Jīng with a host of two hundred thousand,
and only ceased after five years.
Zhào attacked Zhōngshān with a host of two hundred thousand,
and only returned after five years.
Now,
Qí and Hán confront each other,
and your state is besieged.
Would anyone dare say,
'I will rescue this with thirty thousand'?"
Now, cities with walls a thousand zhang high,
and settlements of ten thousand households are seen everywhere,
yet you seek to besiege a city with walls a thousand zhang high
with a force of only thirty thousand men,
which cannot even hold one corner of it,
and is insufficient for open-field battles.
What do you intend to achieve with this?"
Dū Píngjūn sighed deeply and said:
"Dān has not considered this!"
Zhào sent Jī Hǎo to Qín,
requesting that Wèi Rǎn be appointed as chancellor.
Sòng Tū said to Jī Hǎo:
"If Qín does not agree,
Lóu Huǎn will surely resent you.
You might as well secretly decline Lóu Zǐ, saying:
'Please do not press the King of Qín urgently.'
When the King of Qín sees that Zhào's appointment of Wèi Rǎn as chancellor is not urgent,
he will not heed your words.
If this matter is not accomplished,
Wèi Rǎn will certainly be grateful to you."
Qí defeated Yān,
and Zhào wished to preserve it.
Yuè Yì said to the King of Zhào:
"If we attack Qí without an alliance,
Qí will surely harbor enmity toward Zhào.
It would be better to request exchanging the land east of the Yellow River for Yān's territory with Qí.
Zhào will have the land north of the Yellow River,
and Qí will have the land east of the Yellow River.
Yān and Zhào will certainly not contend over it.
This will bring the two states closer.
Using the land east of the Yellow River to strengthen Qí,
and having Yān and Zhào assist it,
the world will resent it,
and all will surely serve Your Majesty to attack Qí.
This is using the world to defeat Qí."
The King said:
"Excellent."
He then exchanged the land east of the Yellow River with Qí.
Chǔ and Wèi resented this,
and sent Nào Huá and Huì Shī to Zhào,
requesting to attack Qí and preserve Yān.
Qín attacked Zhào,
capturing Lìn, Líshí, and Qí.
Zhào sent Prince Wú as a hostage to Qín,
and requested to cede the cities of Jiāo, Lí, and Niúhú,
in exchange for returning Lìn,
Líshí, and Qí to Zhào.
Zhào betrayed Qín,
and did not give up Jiāo, Lí, and Niúhú.
The King of Qín was enraged,
and ordered Prince Zēng to request the land.
The King of Zhào then ordered Zhèng Zhū to reply:
"The lands of Lìn,
Líshí, and Qí
are remote and distant from Zhào,
but close to your great state.
Only due to the wisdom of our former kings and the efforts of our former ministers
were we able to possess them.
Now, I am incapable,
and cannot even care for my own altars of state.
How could I recover and care for Lìn,
Líshí, and Qí?
I have disobedient ministers
who are truly responsible for this matter.
It is not something I dare to acknowledge."
In the end, they betrayed Qín.
The King of Qín was greatly angered,
and ordered Wèi Húyì to attack Zhào,
assaulting Yānyǔ.
Zhào Shē led troops to rescue it.
Wèi ordered Prince Jiù to station elite troops at Ānyì,
to threaten Qín.
Qín was defeated at Yānyǔ,
and turned to attack Wèi's Jǐ.
Lián Pō rescued Jǐ,
and severely defeated the Qín army.
Fù Dīng wished to ally Zhào with Qí and Wèi,
while Lóu Huǎn wished to ally Zhào with Qín and Chǔ.
Fù Dīng feared that Lord Fǎther would listen to Lóu Huǎn and ally with Qín and Chǔ.
Sīmǎ Qiǎn spoke to Lord Fǎther on behalf of Fù Dīng, saying:
"It would be better to comply with Qí.
If we do not comply with Qí to attack Qín now,
Qín and Chǔ will surely ally and attack Hán and Wèi.
When Hán and Wèi urgently seek help from Qí,
if Qí does not wish to attack Qín,
it will surely use Zhào as an excuse,
and then Zhào will be the one attacking Qín.
Hán and Wèi will surely resent Zhào.
If Qí's troops do not march west,
Hán will surely heed Qín and defy Qí.
Defying Qí and drawing closer,
the troops will surely turn against Zhào.
If we comply and Qí does not march west,
Hán and Wèi will surely break with Qí.
Breaking with Qí, they will all serve us.
Moreover, if we comply with Qí,
Qí will have no reason to march west.
Previously,
Lóu Huǎn stayed in Wèi for three months,
but could not dissolve the alliance between Qí and Wèi.
Now, if we comply and Qí and Wèi indeed march west,
this will exhaust Qí and weary Qín,
and Zhào will surely become a powerful state in the world."
Lord Fǎther said:
"If we join the three states to attack Qín,
we will all be exhausted."
He replied:
"Not so.
We can make a pact with the three states and inform Qín,
on the grounds that we have not yet dealt with Zhōngshān.
If the three states truly wish to attack Qín,
they will surely listen to us,
and seek to make peace with us.
If Zhōngshān agrees,
then we, with the king's authority, can enrich Zhōngshān and seize its land.
If Zhōngshān does not agree,
the three states will surely break with it,
and Zhōngshān will be isolated.
If the three states cannot make peace with us, we can still send a small force.
We divide our troops and isolate Zhōngshān,
and Zhōngshān will surely perish.
Once we have destroyed Zhōngshān,
we can use the remaining troops to join the three states in attacking Qín.
This way, we gain land from both Qín and Zhōngshān in one move."
Wèi, through Fù Dīng, was about to ally with Qín.
Zhào grew fearful,
and offered to cede land to Wèi and heed Lord Xuē.
Jiào Zǐ Kǎi said to Lǐ Duì:
"Zhào fears the horizontal alliance,
so it wishes to cede land to Wèi and heed Lord Xuē.
You should have Lord Fǎther use land to support Zhōu Zuì,
and request that he be appointed chancellor of Wèi.
Zhōu Zuì is someone who has humiliated Qín in the eyes of the world.
If he becomes chancellor of Wèi now,
Wèi and Qín will surely become estranged.
Even if Qí and Wèi are strong,
without Qín, they cannot harm Zhào.
If the King of Wèi agrees, he will be slighting Qí. Even if Qín and Wèi are strong, without Qí, they cannot win over Zhào. This benefits Zhào and is convenient for Zhōu Zuì."
Wèi sent someone to request an alliance with Zhào through Lord of the Plain.
He spoke three times,
but the King of Zhào did not agree.
Upon leaving, he encountered Yú Qīng and said:
"When you go in, you must speak of the alliance."
Yú Qīng entered,
and the King said:
"Just now, Lord of the Plain requested an alliance on behalf of Wèi,
and I did not agree.
What do you think?"
Yú Qīng said: "Wèi is mistaken."
The King said: "Indeed,
so I did not agree."
Yú Qīng said: "Your Majesty is also mistaken."
The King said: "Why?"
He said:
"In all matters between the strong and the weak,
the strong receive the benefits,
and the weak suffer the harm.
Now, Wèi seeks an alliance,
and Your Majesty does not agree.
This means Wèi seeks harm,
and Your Majesty declines benefits.
Therefore, I say, Wèi is mistaken,
and Your Majesty is also mistaken."
Lord of the Plain asked Féng Jì:
"I wish to march north to attack Shàngdǎng,
and send troops to attack Yān.
What do you think?"
Féng Jì replied: "It cannot be done.
When the Qín general Wǔ'ānjūn Gōngsūn Qǐ, riding on the prestige of seven victories,
fought against Mǎfú's son at Chángpíng,
he severely defeated the Zhào army,
and with his remaining troops,
besieged the city of Hándān.
Zhào, with its remnants of defeated troops,
gathered its broken army to defend weakly,
yet Qín grew weary under Hándān's walls.
The reason Zhào held and could not be taken
is that attack is difficult, while defense is easy.
Now, Zhào does not possess the prestige of seven victories,
and Yān does not suffer the disaster of Chángpíng.
The calamity of seven defeats has not yet been recovered from,
and you wish to use a weary Zhào to attack a strong Yān.
This is making weak Zhào the target of strong Qín's attacks,
and making strong Yān adopt the defensive stance of weak Zhào.
And strong Qín, with rested troops, will take advantage of Zhào's weakness.
This is precisely why strong Wú perished,
and weak Yuè became hegemonic.
Therefore, I do not see that Yān can be attacked."
Lord of the Plain said:
"Well said!"
Lord Píngyuán said to Lord Píngyáng:
"Lord Móu traveled to Qín,
and when he was about to return east,
he took leave of Marquis Yìng.
Marquis Yìng said: 'You are about to depart,
have you no advice to give me?'
He replied:
'Even without your command to instruct me,
I would certainly have something to offer you.
Nobility does not seek wealth,
yet wealth arrives;
wealth does not seek fine grain and meat,
yet fine grain and meat arrive;
fine grain and meat do not seek arrogance and extravagance,
yet arrogance and extravagance arrive;
arrogance and extravagance do not seek death and ruin,
yet death and ruin arrive.
For generations past,
many have been brought down by this.'
Marquis Yìng said:
'The advice you have given me is profound.'
I heard this,
and have not forgotten it in my heart.
I hope you, my lord, will not forget it either."
Lord Píngyáng said: "I respectfully heed your words."
Qín attacked Zhào at Chángpíng,
inflicted a great defeat,
and led its troops back.
It then sent someone to demand six cities from Zhào in exchange for peace.
Zhào had not yet decided on a plan.
Lóu Huǎn had newly arrived from Qín,
and the King of Zhào consulted with Lóu Huǎn, saying:
"What about giving the cities to Qín?
What about not giving them?"
Lóu Huǎn declined, saying:
"This is not something a subject can know."
The king said: "Nevertheless,
try to speak your private opinion."
Lóu Huǎn said:
"Has Your Majesty heard of the mother of Gōngfǔ Wénbó?
Gōngfǔ Wénbó served as an official in Lǔ and died of illness.
Sixteen women in his household committed suicide for him.
When his mother heard of it,
she refused to weep.
The steward said:
'How can there be a mother who does not weep when her son dies?'
His mother said: 'Confucius,
a worthy man,
was driven out of Lǔ,
yet this man did not follow him.
Now that he is dead,
sixteen women have died for him.
In such a case,
was he indifferent to the worthy
but generous to women?'
Thus, from the mother's perspective,
she is a worthy mother;
from the women's perspective,
she would inevitably be considered a jealous woman.
So the words are the same,
but if the speaker is different,
then people's minds change.
Now I have newly arrived from Qín,
and if I say not to give them,
it would not be a good plan;
if I say to give them,
then I fear Your Majesty will think I am acting for Qín.
Therefore, I dare not respond.
But if I were to plan for Your Majesty,
it would be better to give them."
The king said: "Very well."
Yú Qīng heard of this,
entered to see the king,
and the king told him what Lóu Huǎn had said.
Yú Qīng said:
"This is deceptive talk."
After Qín had lifted the siege of Hándān,
and the King of Zhào went to court [in Qín],
he sent Zhào Hào to negotiate matters with Qín,
ceding six counties to make peace.
The king said: "What do you mean?"
Yú Qīng said: "When Qín attacked Zhào,
did it withdraw because it was weary?
Or does Your Majesty think its strength could still advance,
but it spared you and did not attack?"
The king said: "When Qín attacked us,
it spared no effort,
so it must have withdrawn because it was weary."
Yú Qīng said:
"Qín used its strength to attack what it could not take,
and withdrew wearily.
If Your Majesty now gives it what its strength could not take,
this is helping Qín attack yourself.
Next year when Qín attacks Your Majesty again,
you will have no means to save yourself."
The king also told Lóu Huǎn what Yú Qīng had said.
Lóu Huǎn said:
"Can Yú Qīng fully know the extent of Qín's strength?
If he truly knows that Qín's strength is insufficient,
then this tiny land
should still not be given,
but if Qín attacks again next year,
will you not have to cede inner territories to make peace?"
The king said: "If I truly listen to you and cede them,
can you guarantee that Qín will not attack me again next year?"
Lóu Huǎn replied:
"This is not something I dare to take responsibility for.
In the past, the Three Jìn states had relations with Qín,
and they were on good terms.
Now Qín spares Hán and Wèi and attacks only Your Majesty,
so Your Majesty's service to Qín must be inferior to that of Hán and Wèi.
Now I am helping you resolve the attack due to your betrayal of closeness,
open your borders and communicate your weaknesses,
and align your relations with Hán and Wèi.
If by next year Your Majesty alone is not favored by Qín,
then Your Majesty's service to Qín
must be behind that of Hán and Wèi.
This is not something I dare to take responsibility for."
The king told Yú Qīng what Lóu Huǎn had said.
Yú Qīng said:
"Lóu Huǎn says that if we do not make peace, next year Qín will attack again,
and we will have to cede more inner territories to make peace.
If we make peace now,
Lóu Huǎn still cannot guarantee that Qín will not attack again,
so what good is ceding territory?
If it attacks again next year,
we will again cede what its strength cannot take to make peace,
this is a path to self-destruction.
It is better not to make peace.
Even if Qín is skilled at attacking,
it cannot take six cities;
even if Zhào cannot defend,
it will not lose six cities.
Qín withdrew wearily,
its troops must be exhausted.
If we use five cities to rally the world to attack the exhausted Qín,
then we lose to the world,
but take compensation from Qín.
Our state would still benefit.
How does this compare to sitting and ceding territory,
weakening ourselves to strengthen Qín?
Now Lóu Huǎn says:
'If Qín is good to Hán and Wèi but attacks Zhào,
it must be because Your Majesty's service to Qín is inferior to that of Hán and Wèi.'
This would have Your Majesty serve Qín with six cities yearly,
and you would sit until your land is exhausted.
Next year when Qín demands more territory,
will Your Majesty give it?
If not,
then you abandon previous efforts and provoke Qín's wrath;
if you give it, then you have no land to give.
As the saying goes:
'The strong are skilled at attacking,
and the weak cannot defend themselves.'
Now if we sit and obey Qín,
Qín's troops will not be worn out yet gain much land,
this strengthens Qín and weakens Zhào.
To increase the strength of an already strong Qín,
and cut apart an already weak Zhào,
such plans certainly will not stop.
Moreover, Qín
is a state of tigers and wolves,
with no sense of ritual or righteousness.
