Its demands are endless,
while Your Majesty's land is finite.
To use finite land
to satisfy endless demands,
the situation will inevitably lead to Zhào's demise.
Therefore I say:
this is deceptive talk.
Your Majesty must not give them."
The king said: "Very well."
Lóu Huǎn heard of this,
entered to see the king,
and the king again told him what Yú Qīng had said.
Lóu Huǎn said: "Not so.
Yú Qīng knows one aspect,
but not the other.
When Qín and Zhào are locked in conflict,
why is the whole world pleased?
They say
'We will take advantage of the strong to overpower the weak.'
Now Zhào's troops are hard-pressed by Qín,
and those in the world who congratulate the victors
will certainly all side with Qín.
Therefore, it is better to quickly cede territory to seek peace,
to sow doubt in the world,
and to appease Qín's heart.
Otherwise,
the world will take advantage of Qín's anger
and the exhaustion of Qín and Zhào to carve them up.
Zhào will face destruction, so what can be planned against Qín?
Your Majesty should decide based on this,
Yú Qīng heard of this,
and again entered to see the king, saying:
"Dangerous indeed,
is Lóu Zǐ's actions on behalf of Qín!
Now Zhào's troops are besieged by Qín,
and you further cede territory to sue for peace—
this only increases the suspicions of the world,
and how can it appease Qín's heart?
Is this not greatly displaying Zhào's weakness to the world?
Moreover, when I said not to give,
it was not simply a matter of not giving.
Qín demands six cities from Your Majesty,
Your Majesty should use five cities to bribe Qí.
Qí is Qín's deep-seated enemy;
upon obtaining Your Majesty's five cities,
they will join forces and strike westward against Qín.
Qí's compliance with Your Majesty
will not wait for the words to be finished.
Thus, Your Majesty loses to Qí but seeks compensation from Qín,
in one move forming close ties with three states,
and exchanging positions with Qín."
King Zhào said:
"Excellent."
Thereupon, he sent Yú Qīng east to see the King of Qí,
to plan against Qín with him.
Before Yú Qīng returned,
Qín's envoy was already in Zhào.
Lóu Huǎn heard of this,
and fled.
Qín attacked Zhào,
and Píngyuán Jūn sent someone to seek aid from Wèi.
Xìnlíng Jūn dispatched troops to the walls of Hándān,
and Qín's forces withdrew.
Yú Qīng requested additional territory for Píngyuán Jūn,
saying to King Zhào:
"Without fighting a single soldier,
without breaking a single halberd,
yet resolving the troubles of two states—
this is the merit of Píngyuán Jūn.
To use someone's efforts
and forget their achievements
is not permissible."
King Zhào said:
"Excellent."
He was about to grant him additional land.
Gōngsūn Lóng heard of this,
and went to see Píngyuán Jūn, saying:
"You have no merit of crushing armies or killing generals,
yet you were enfeoffed with Dōngwǔchéng.
Among the heroes and outstanding men of Zhào,
many are superior to you,
yet you became chancellor due to kinship.
You accepted the enfeoffment of Dōngwǔchéng without declining despite having no merit,
you wore the seal of Zhào's chancellor without refusing despite lacking ability;
now, having resolved a single state crisis,
you seek additional land—
this is relatives receiving fiefs,
while the state's people calculate merit.
For your consideration,
it would be better not to accept."
Píngyuán Jūn said:
"I respectfully accept your instruction."
Thereupon, he did not accept the enfeoffment.
Qín and Zhào fought at Chángpíng;
Zhào was not victorious,
and lost a commandant.
King Zhào summoned Lóu Chāng and Yú Qīng, saying:
"The army is not victorious in battle,
the commandant is again dead;
I intend to have them roll up their armor and advance—what do you think?"
Lóu Chāng said:
"It is of no benefit;
it would be better to send an important envoy to sue for peace."
Yú Qīng said:
"Those who speak of peace
believe that without peace, the army will surely be destroyed,
and the power to decide peace lies with Qín.
Moreover, in Your Majesty's assessment of Qín,
do they wish to destroy Your Majesty's army,
or do they not?"
The king said:
"Qín spares no effort;
they will surely destroy Zhào's army."
Yú Qīng said:
"Your Majesty, please listen to me:
send envoys with valuable treasures to attach to Chǔ and Wèi.
Chǔ and Wèi, desiring Your Majesty's valuable treasures,
will surely admit our envoys.
When Zhào's envoys enter Chǔ and Wèi,
Qín will surely suspect a vertical alliance among the world,
and will certainly fear.
In this way,
peace can then be sought."
King Zhào did not listen,
but made peace with Píngyáng Jūn,
sending Zhèng Zhū into Qín,
and Qín admitted him.
King Zhào summoned Yú Qīng, saying:
"I sent Píngyáng Jūn to sue for peace with Qín;
Qín has already admitted Zhèng Zhū—
what do you think of this?"
Yú Qīng said:
"Your Majesty will surely not obtain peace,
and the army will surely be destroyed,
for all in the world who congratulate the victor are in Qín.
Zhèng Zhū
is an eminent man of Zhào,
and upon entering Qín,
the King of Qín and Yìnghóu will surely display and honor him to show the world.
Chǔ and Wèi, believing Zhào has made peace,
will surely not rescue Your Majesty.
When Qín knows the world will not rescue Your Majesty,
then peace cannot be achieved."
In the end, Zhào did not obtain peace,
and the army was indeed greatly defeated.
The king entered Qín,
and Qín detained King Zhào before agreeing to peace.
Qín besieged Zhào's Hándān.
King Ānxī of Wèi sent General Jìn Bǐ to rescue Zhào.
Fearing Qín, he halted at Dàngyīn,
and did not advance.
The King of Wèi sent the guest general Xīnyuán Yǎn to secretly enter Hándān,
and through Píngyuán Jūn, he said to King Zhào:
"The reason Qín urgently besieges Zhào
is that previously, they contended with King Mǐn of Qí for supremacy as emperor,
but later returned the imperial title because of Qí.
Now King Mǐn of Qí has grown weaker.
At present, only Qín dominates the world;
this does not necessarily mean they covet Hándān—
their intention is to seek to become emperor.
If Zhào sincerely sends an envoy to honor King Zhāo of Qín as emperor,
Qín will surely be pleased,
and withdraw its troops."
Píngyuán Jūn hesitated and had not yet decided.
At this time, Lǔ Zhònglián happened to be traveling in Zhào,
and encountered Qín's siege of Zhào.
Hearing that the Wèi general wished to have Zhào honor Qín as emperor,
he went to see Píngyuán Jūn, saying:
"What will be done about the matter?"
Píngyuán Jūn said:
"How dare I speak of matters?
A million troops have been broken abroad,
and now we are besieged within Hándān and cannot escape.
The King of Wèi sent General Xīnyuán Yǎn to have Zhào acknowledge Qín as emperor.
Now this man is here—
how dare I speak of matters?"
Lǔ Lián said:
"At first, I thought you were a worthy lord of the world,
but only now do I realize you are not a worthy lord of the world.
Where is the Liáng guest Xīnyuán Yǎn?
I ask to reproach him on your behalf and send him back."
Píngyuán Jūn said:
"I ask to summon him and have him meet with you, sir."
Píngyuán Jūn then went to see Xīnyuán Yǎn, saying:
"In the eastern state, there is Master Lǔ Lián;
this man is here,
and I ask to introduce him
and have him meet with you, General."
Xīnyuán Yǎn said:
"I have heard of Master Lǔ Lián—
he is a lofty scholar of Qí.
I, Yǎn, am a subject, and my mission has its duties.
I do not wish to see Master Lǔ Lián."
Píngyuán Jūn said:
"I have already revealed it."
Xīnyuán Yǎn agreed.
Lǔ Lián saw Xīnyuán Yǎn but said nothing.
Xīnyuán Yǎn said:
"I observe that those dwelling in this besieged northern city
all have requests of Píngyuán Jūn.
Now, looking at your jade-like countenance, sir,
you do not seem to have requests of Píngyuán Jūn—
why do you long dwell in this besieged city and not leave?"
Lǔ Lián said:
"The world thinks Bào Jiāo died from lack of composure—
all are wrong.
Now, if the multitude does not understand,
then it is for one's own person.
That Qín
is a state that discards ritual and righteousness and exalts head-count merit.
It manipulates its scholars with power,
and enslaves its people like captives.
If they were to recklessly become emperor,
and by transgression then rule the world,
then I, Lián, would go and throw myself into the Eastern Sea to die.
I cannot bear to be their subject!
The reason I see you, General,
is to wish to aid Zhào."
Xīnyuán Yǎn said:
"How will you aid them, sir?"
Lǔ Lián said:
"It is because Liáng has not yet witnessed the harm of Qín proclaiming itself emperor.
If Liáng were to witness the harm of Qín proclaiming itself emperor,
then it would certainly aid Zhào."
Xīn Yuán Yǎn said:
"What would the harm of Qín proclaiming itself emperor be like?"
Lǔ Zhòng Lián said:
"In the past, King Wēi of Qí once practiced benevolence and righteousness,
leading the feudal lords of the realm to pay court to Zhōu.
Zhōu was poor and weak,
and none of the feudal lords paid court,
yet Qí alone paid court to it.
After a little over a year,
King Liè of Zhōu died.
All the feudal lords came to offer condolences,
but Qí arrived late.
Zhōu was angered
and sent a message to Qí, saying:
'Heaven has collapsed and earth has split;
the Son of Heaven has descended from his mat.
The minister of the eastern vassal, Tián Yīng Qí, arrived late;
he shall be beheaded.'
King Wēi flew into a rage and said:
'Bah!
Your mother was a slave girl.'
In the end, he became a laughingstock of the realm.
Thus, while alive, he paid court to Zhōu;
when dead, he reviled it.
This was truly because he could not endure its demands.
That is the nature of the Son of Heaven;
there is nothing strange about it."
Xīn Yuán Yǎn said:
"Sir, have you not seen servants?
When ten men follow one man,
is it because their strength is insufficient,
or their wisdom inferior?
It is because they fear him."
Lǔ Zhòng Lián said:
"Then, is Liáng compared to Qín like a servant?"
Xīn Yuán Yǎn said:
"Yes."
Lǔ Zhòng Lián said:
"Then I will have the King of Qín boil and mince the King of Liáng."
Xīn Yuán Yǎn, displeased and resentful, said:
"Alas!
This is too extreme,
your words, sir!
And how, sir, could you make the King of Qín boil and mince the King of Liáng?"
Lǔ Zhòng Lián said:
"Certainly;
wait until I explain.
In the past,
Guǐ Hóu, È Hóu, and King Wén
were the three dukes of Zhòu.
Guǐ Hóu had a daughter who was beautiful,
so he presented her to Zhòu.
Zhòu considered her ugly,
and minced Guǐ Hóu.
È Hóu argued urgently on his behalf,
pleading vehemently,
so Zhòu dried È Hóu into jerky.
King Wén heard of this,
sighed deeply,
and so was imprisoned in the Yǒulǐ jail,
for a hundred days, intending to put him to death.
Why, when both are called emperors and kings,
do they end up in the place of being made into jerky and mince?
When King Mǐn of Qí was going to Lǔ,
Yí Wéi Zǐ held the whip and followed,
and said to the people of Lǔ:
'How will you receive my lord?'
The people of Lǔ said:
'We will receive your lord with ten sets of sacrificial animals.'
Wéi Zǐ said:
'From where do you take this ritual to receive my lord?
That lord of mine
is the Son of Heaven.
When the Son of Heaven tours the realm,
the feudal lords vacate their palaces,
hand over the keys,
tuck in their robes and hold the tables,
serve meals below the hall,
and after the Son of Heaven has eaten,
withdraw to attend court.'
The people of Lǔ locked their gates
and did not admit him.
Unable to enter Lǔ,
he was going to Xuē,
passing through Zōu.
At that time, the lord of Zōu had died,
and King Mǐn wished to enter to offer condolences.
Yí Wéi Zǐ said to the orphaned heir of Zōu:
'When the Son of Heaven offers condolences,
the host must turn the coffin around,
setting it facing north in the southern position,
and then the Son of Heaven faces south to offer condolences.'
The ministers of Zōu said:
'If it must be like this,
we will fall upon our swords and die.'
Thus, he did not dare enter Zōu.
The ministers of Zōu and Lǔ,
while alive, could not serve and support their lords adequately,
and when dead, could not place rice and jade in their mouths.
Yet he wished to perform the rituals of the Son of Heaven upon the ministers of Zōu and Lǔ,
and they did not admit him.
Now Qín is a state of ten thousand chariots,
and Liáng is also a state of ten thousand chariots.
Both occupy states of ten thousand chariots,
both bear the name of king,
yet upon seeing it win a single battle,
you wish to follow and make it emperor.
This would make the great ministers of the Three Jìn inferior to the servants and concubines of Zōu and Lǔ.
Moreover, if Qín, insatiable, becomes emperor,
it will then replace the great ministers of the feudal lords.
It will remove those it deems unworthy
and give to those it deems worthy;
remove those it hates
and give to those it loves.
It will also make its daughters and slandering concubines the consorts and concubines of the feudal lords,
residing in the palaces of Liáng.
How could the King of Liáng then rest peacefully?
And how could you, General, retain your former favor?"
Thereupon, Xīn Yuán Yǎn rose,
bowed twice, and apologized, saying:
"At first, I considered you, sir, an ordinary man,
but only today have I realized that you, sir, are a scholar of the realm.
I beg to take my leave,
and dare not speak again of making Qín emperor."
The Qín general heard of this
and withdrew his army fifty lǐ.
It happened that Lord Wújì of Wèi seized Jìn Bǐ's army
to rescue Zhào and attack Qín,
and the Qín army withdrew and left.
Thereupon, Lord Píngyuán wished to enfeoff Lǔ Zhòng Lián.
Lǔ Zhòng Lián declined three times,
and in the end refused to accept.
Lord Píngyuán then set out wine,
and when the drinking was at its height,
rose and came forward, offering a thousand pieces of gold as a longevity gift to Lǔ Lián.
Lǔ Lián laughed and said:
"What is valued in a scholar of the realm
is that he resolves troubles for others,
dispels difficulties, untangles chaos, and takes nothing.
If he takes something,
he is a merchant.
Zhòng Lián cannot bear to be such."
Thereupon, he declined Lord Píngyuán and left,
never to be seen again for the rest of his life.
He persuaded Chancellor Zhāng, saying:
"How can you, sir, belittle the people of Zhào
and yet make the people of Zhào esteem you?
How can you, sir, hate the people of Zhào
and yet make the people of Zhào love you?
Glue and lacquer
are extremely adhesive,
yet they cannot join distant things;
the feather of a swan
is extremely light,
yet it cannot lift itself.
But if carried by a clear breeze,
it can travel freely across the four seas.
Thus, there are affairs that are simple yet achieve merit,
because they rely on circumstances.
Now Zhào is a strong state of ten thousand chariots,
with the Zhāng and Fǔ rivers in front,
Chángshān on the right,
Héjiān on the left,
and Dài to the north.
It has a million armored soldiers
and once subdued powerful Qí.
For over forty years, Qín has been unable to obtain what it desires.
From this perspective,
Zhào's position in the realm is not insignificant.
Now you, sir, exchange the strong Zhào of ten thousand chariots
for the admiration of the small, unattainable Liáng.
I privately consider this unworthy for you, sir."
The lord said: "Well said."
From then on,
in the midst of crowds and large gatherings,
he never failed to speak of the strengths of the people of Zhào,
and never failed to speak of the goodness of Zhào's customs.
Zhèng Tóng went north to see the King of Zhào.
The King of Zhào said:
"You, sir, are a learned scholar from the south;
what do you have to instruct me?"
Zhèng Tóng said:
"I am but a rustic from the southern wilds;
what am I worth asking?
Nevertheless,
since Your Majesty has summoned me before you,
how dare I not respond?
In my youth,
I was personally taught military affairs."
The King of Zhào said:
"I do not favor military affairs."
Zhèng Tóng thereupon clapped his hands, looked up to the sky, and laughed, saying:
"Military affairs are indeed what the cunning of the world delight in;
that is precisely why I assumed Your Majesty would not favor them.
I once also spoke of military affairs to King Wèi Zhāo,
and King Zhāo likewise said:
'I do not like them.'
I said:
'Can Your Majesty's conduct compare to that of Xǔ Yóu?
Xǔ Yóu had no burdens of the world upon him,
therefore he did not accept them.
Now that Your Majesty has received the legacy of your predecessors,
do you desire the security of your ancestral temples,
that your lands not be diminished,
and that the altars of soil and grain continue to receive blood sacrifices?'
The king said: 'Indeed.'
Suppose there is a man holding the pearl of Suíhóu,
the jade ring of Qiū,
and wealth worth ten thousand in gold,
who spends the night in the wilderness.
If he lacks the might of Mèng Bēn within,
the decisiveness of Jīng Qìng,
and has no bows or crossbows for defense without,
before a single night passes,
others will surely endanger him.
Now suppose there is a strong and greedy state
approaching Your Majesty's borders,
demanding Your Majesty's territory.
If you appeal to reason, it will not agree;
if you argue with righteousness, it will not listen.
If Your Majesty lacks the tools of a warring state for defense,
with what will you withstand it?
If Your Majesty has no military,
your neighboring state will achieve its ambition."
The King of Zhào said: "I beg to receive your instruction."
Jiànxìn Jūn was honored in Zhào.
The nobleman Wèi Móu passed through Zhào,
and the King of Zhào welcomed him.
Upon returning and taking his seat,
before him was a foot of silk,
and he was about to order a craftsman to make a cap from it.
The craftsman, seeing a guest arrive,
withdrew.
The King of Zhào said:
"You, noble sir, have driven your carriage from afar,
gracing me with your presence.
I wish to hear how to govern the world."
Wèi Móu said:
"If Your Majesty could value your state as much as this foot of silk,
then your state would be greatly well-governed."
The King of Zhào was displeased;
it showed on his face.
He said:
"Does the gentleman not know that I, though unworthy,
have been entrusted with the altars of state?
How would I dare to treat the state so lightly?"
Wèi Móu said: "Your Majesty, do not be angry;
allow me to explain it to you."
He said:
"Your Majesty has this foot of silk;
why not order the gentleman in front of you to make a cap from it?"
The king said: "The gentleman does not know how to make a cap."
Wèi Móu said: "If making the cap ruins it,
what loss is that to Your Majesty's state?
Yet Your Majesty insists on waiting for a craftsman before having it made.
Now, as for the craftsmen of the world,
some are unsuitable.
If the altars of state become desolate ruins,
and the former kings receive no blood sacrifices,
yet Your Majesty does not entrust them to a craftsman,
but instead gives them to a youthful favorite.
Moreover, Your Majesty's late father, the former emperor,
harnessed Xī Shǒu and had Mǎ Fú as outriders,
to contend with Qín.
Qín at that time
met their vanguard head-on.
Now Your Majesty, in your uncertainty,
takes Jiànxìn in your carriage to contend with powerful Qín.
I fear Qín will break the linchpin of Your Majesty's chariot."
Duke Líng of Wèi favored Yōng Jū and Mí Zǐxiá.
These two men
monopolized the ruler's authority and obscured those around him.
Fùtú Zhēn said to the ruler:
"The other day, I dreamed of you, my lord."
The ruler said:
"What did you dream?"
He said:
"I dreamed of the Kitchen God."
The ruler angrily changed countenance and said:
"I have heard that one who dreams of a ruler
dreams of the sun.
Now you say you dreamed of the Kitchen God and yet speak of me.
If you have an explanation, well and good;
if not, you die."
He replied:
"The sun
illuminates the entire world together;
no single thing can obscure it.
As for the kitchen stove, it is not so.
If someone in front is warming himself by it,
then those behind cannot see.
Now I suspect there is someone warming himself before you, my lord;
therefore I dreamed of the Kitchen God."
The ruler said: "Well said."
Thereupon,
he dismissed Yōng Jū and Mí Zǐxiá,
and appointed Sīkōng Gǒu.
Someone said to Jiànxìn:
"The means by which you serve the king
is your looks.
The means by which 𦱫 serves the king
is wisdom.
Looks age and fade,
but wisdom grows with age.
With wisdom increasing daily
driving out fading, deteriorating looks,
you will surely be in trouble."
Jiànxìn Jūn said: "What should I do?"
He said:
"If you run alongside a fine horse,
you will be exhausted after five lǐ;
but if you mount the horse and drive it,
you will not tire and cover much more road.
You should order him to mount a chariot of sole authority,
wield the power of sole authority,
and reside in Hándān;
order him to govern internal state affairs internally,
and probe the feudal lords externally.
Then his affairs will have unspoken aspects.
You should then speak to the king and have him impose heavy responsibilities on him;
his axle will now break."
Jiànxìn Jūn
bowed twice and accepted the advice.
He went in and spoke to the king,
entrusting him with weighty tasks according to his ability, imposing heavy responsibilities on him.
Before a year had passed, Qí fled and ran away.
Kǔchéng Cháng said to Jiànxìn Jūn:
"All under heaven are forming a vertical alliance,
yet Zhào alone is hated by Qín.
Why is that?
Wèi killed Lǚ Yí,
and all under heaven turned against it.
Now if you seize Héjiān,
how is that different from killing Lǚ Yí?
If you merely abandon empty deceit and haste,
Wénxìn will still know of it.
If the alliance succeeds and achieves merit,
why worry about not being able to seize Héjiān?
If the alliance fails and achieves no merit,
what good is seizing Héjiān?"
Xī Xiě visited Jiànxìn Jūn.
Jiànxìn Jūn said:
"Wénxìn Hóu, in his treatment of me,
is extremely discourteous.
Qín sent a man to seek office,
I gave him a position as chancellor,
with the rank of Fifth Rank Grandee.
Wénxìn Hóu, in his treatment of me,
his discourtesy is extreme."
Xī Xiě said:
"I believe those in power in the present age
are inferior to merchants."
Jiànxìn Jūn angrily said:
"Do you, sir, look down on those in power and esteem merchants?"
He said:
"Not so.
A good merchant does not argue with others over the price of buying and selling,
but carefully observes the timing.
When prices are low, he buys;
though they were once high, they are now low.
When prices are high, he sells;
though they were once low, they are now high.
In ancient times,
King Wén was imprisoned in Yǒulǐ,
and King Wǔ was detained at the Jade Gate,
yet they finally cut off Zhòu's head and hung it on the Tàibái banner—
this was King Wǔ's achievement.
Now you cannot match Wénxìn Hóu in contending with authority,
yet you blame Wénxìn Hóu for being slightly discourteous.
I privately consider this inadvisable for you."
Wèi Gà said to Jiànxìn Jūn:
"There was a man who set a snare and caught a tiger.
The tiger, enraged,
bit off its own paw and escaped.
The tiger's nature was not that it did not love its paw.
Yet it did not let a paw of mere inches
endanger its seven-foot body—
this was a matter of weighing priorities.
Now you possess a state,
which is not merely a seven-foot body.
And your person, to the king,
is not a paw of mere inches.
I hope you will consider this carefully."
Qín attacked Zhào,
and the sound of drums and bells was heard in the northern hall.
Xībēi said:
"When Qín attacks Zhào,
it should not be so urgent.
This is a call to arms.
There must be a high minister who wishes to form an alliance.
If the king wishes to know who it is,
tomorrow assemble all the ministers and question them.
The first to speak of an alliance
will be that man."
Jiànxìn Jūn indeed was the first to speak of an alliance.
A man of Qí named Lǐ Bó had an audience with King Xiàochéng.
King Xiàochéng was pleased with him
and appointed him as governor of Dài Commandery.
Not long after he took office,
someone reported that he was rebelling.
King Xiàochéng was just then eating,
and did not drop his food.
Not long after,
the informant came again,
and King Xiàochéng did not respond.
Later,
he sent a messenger to say:
"Qí raised troops to attack Yān,
and I feared they might use attacking Yān as a pretext
to instead send troops to surprise Zhào.
Therefore I mobilized troops for self-defense.
Now Yān and Qí have already made peace,
and I request to take advantage of their exhaustion,
so that much territory may be seized."
From this time onward,
those who served King Xiàochéng in external affairs
had no doubts in their hearts.
A memorial was presented to the King of Zhào on behalf of Qí,
sent by the envoy Yǔ Fùchǒu, which said:
"With one audience,
I could make the king sit and have the world send him famous treasures.
Yet I privately wonder why the king does not try to see me,
but instead keeps me in obscurity.
The many ministers must mostly consider me incapable,
hence the king hesitates to see me.
Those who consider me incapable
do so for no other reason
than that they wish to use the king's troops
to achieve their private ends.
If not that,
then they are biased in their associations;
if not that,
then their knowledge is insufficient;
if not that,
then they wish to use the weight of the world to intimidate the king,
and thereby gain influence over the king.
I use Qí to serve the king in due order.
The king can destroy Yān,
can destroy Hán and Wèi,
can attack Qín,
can isolate Qín.
I believe that if Qí presents honorable fame to the king,
who in the world would dare not present honorable fame to the king?
If I use Qí to present territory to the king,
who in the world would dare not present territory to the king?
If I use Qí to seek fame for the king from Yān, Hán, and Wèi,
who would dare refuse?
My abilities can be seen beforehand.
If Qí first esteems the king,
then the whole world will esteem the king;
without Qí,
the world will certainly all despise the king.
Qín's strength
causes it to esteem the king because Qí is absent;
Yān and Wèi themselves esteem the king because Qí is absent.
Now if the king lacks Qí, how can he alone avoid being esteemed by the world?
Therefore, those who urge the king to do without Qí
are either lacking in knowledge,
or are disloyal.
If not that,
then they wish to use the king's troops to achieve their private ends;
if not that,
then they wish to belittle the king with the weight of the world,
to gain influence over the king;
if not that,
then they are of high rank but low ability.
I hope the king will carefully consider the advantages and disadvantages of being without Qí."
Qí wished to attack Sòng,
but Qín ordered Qǐ Jiǎ to prevent it.
Qí then sought aid from Zhào to attack Sòng.
The King of Qín was angry,
and directed his resentment toward Zhào.
Lǐ Duì formed an alliance of five states to attack Qín,
but achieved no success. He kept the troops of the world at Chénggāo,
while secretly negotiating with Qín.
He further wished to join Qín in attacking Wèi,
to resolve his resentment and gain a fief.
The King of Wèi was displeased.
He went to Qí
and said to the King of Qí:
"I said to the King of Wèi on your behalf:
'The three Jìn all suffer from Qín's menace.
Now this attack on Qín
is for Zhào's sake.
If five states attack Zhào,
Zhào will surely perish.
Qín will expel Lǐ Duì,
and Lǐ Duì will surely die.
Now this attack on Qín
is to save Lǐ Zǐ from death.
Now Zhào keeps the world's armor at Chénggāo,
while secretly selling it to Qín.
Once an agreement is reached,
it will order Qín to attack Wèi to achieve its private fief.
What will Your Majesty gain from serving Zhào?
Moreover, Your Majesty once crossed the Zhāng River
and personally attended court at Hándān,
embracing Yīn and Chéng,
bearing Hāo, Gé, and Bì,
to serve as Zhào's shield,
yet Zhào has done nothing for Your Majesty.
Now it further uses Héyáng and Gūmi to enfeoff its son,
and then orders Qín to attack Your Majesty,
to conveniently seize Yīn.
Men must be compared before one knows whether they are worthy or not.
If Your Majesty were to use half the effort spent serving Zhào to win over Qí,
who in the world would dare plot against Your Majesty?
If Your Majesty serves Qí,
there will be no humiliation of attending court,
no expense of ceding territory.
For Your Majesty's sake, Qí would empty
its state before Yān and Zhào, and employ troops two thousand lǐ away,
so in attacking cities and fighting in the wilds,
it would always be the first to face arrows and stones for Your Majesty.
It would gain two capitals,
seize Hédōng,
and fully present them to Your Majesty.
From then on,
whenever Qín attacks Wèi,
Qí's troops will surely come to Your Majesty's borders every year.
May I ask what Your Majesty would use to repay Qí?
Hán Mǐn resides in Zhào,
three thousand lǐ from Qí.
Your Majesty therefore suspects Qí,
saying it has secret ties with Qín.
Now Your Majesty further relies on the former Xuē Gōng to serve as chancellor,
befriends Hán Xú as a close associate,
and honors Yú Shāng as a great guest.
Can Your Majesty still conversely suspect Qí?'
When the King of Wèi heard these words, he was greatly persuaded,
and his desire to serve Your Majesty became very sincere.
He resents Zhào.
I hope Your Majesty will hear about Wèi and not need to show dislike.
I request to shift its resentment onto Zhào for Your Majesty.
I hope Your Majesty will secretly esteem Zhào,
but not let Qín see that Your Majesty esteems Zhào.
If Qín sees it, it too will esteem Zhào.
If Qí and Qín both esteem Zhào,
I will surely see Yān, Hán, and Wèi also esteem Zhào,
and none will dare to contend with Zhào.
If five states serve Zhào,
and Zhào forms a close alliance to unite with Qín,
it will surely elevate Your Majesty.
Therefore, I wish Your Majesty to coerce all under heaven,
and privately sweeten relations with each.
Your Majesty sends me to use Hán, Wèi, and Yān to coerce Zhào,
and have Dān sweeten it;
use Zhào to coerce Hán and Wèi,
and have me sweeten it;
use the three Jìn to coerce Qín,
and have Shùn sweeten it;
use all under heaven to coerce Chǔ,
and have Mǐn sweeten it.
Then all under heaven will pressure Qín to serve Your Majesty,
and none will dare act privately.
Once relations are settled,
then Your Majesty may choose."
Qí was about to attack Sòng,
but Qín and Chǔ prevented it.
Qí then wished to ally with Zhào,
but Zhào would not agree.
Qí then ordered Gōngsūn Yǎn to persuade Lǐ Duì to attack Sòng and thereby secure a fief.
Lǐ Duì then said to the King of Qí:
"The reason I urged the three states of Jìn to attack Qín
was not because I thought Qí would benefit from Qín's destruction,
but because I wanted to use this to attack Sòng.
However, Sòng installed its crown prince as king,
the people below became close to their ruler above, and their defense became firm.
That is why I wanted Your Majesty to quickly return and let your soldiers and people rest.
Now the crown prince has fled,
and all those who supported the crown prince
are resolved to die.
If we attack again,
their state will certainly fall into chaos.
With the crown prince abroad,
this is also the time to conquer Sòng.
"I, on Your Majesty's behalf, sent Gōngsūn Yǎn to persuade Fèngyáng Jūn, saying: 'You, my lord, are growing old,
and your fief must be settled early.
Considering a fief for you, my lord,
none is better than in Sòng;
no other state will do.
The people of Qín are greedy,
Hán and Wèi are perilous,
Yān and Chǔ are remote,
the land of Zhōngshān is poor—
none compares to Yīn.
If we miss this opportunity now,
it will be impossible to obtain again.
Sòng's crimes are grave,
Qí's anger is deep.
Destroying the chaotic Sòng,
gaining the great favor of Qí,
and securing your personal fief—
this is a chance that comes once in a hundred generations.'
Fèngyáng Jūn was very tempted by this;
as long as he obtains a great fief,
Qí has no major objection.
I hope Your Majesty will greatly launch the campaign against Sòng,
without needing to send troops yourself.
Just wait until the farming is done,
and observe how Fèngyáng Jūn responds to Your Majesty.
Dangle Yīn as a sweetener,
follow up by having Yān press upon him,
while I await the fief of Zhōng,
and the affair is sure to achieve great success.
I also hope Your Majesty will have land granted to Xiāng'ān Jūn to assist me.
If Your Majesty indeed destroys Sòng,
this is the time for both these lands.
What would Your Majesty begrudge?
If Your Majesty fails to achieve ambition in Sòng,
what hope dare our allied states have?
If Your Majesty uses this to assist me,
I will follow Yān and observe Zhào,
then Your Majesty can strike decisively and settle All Under Heaven.'"
The five states' campaign against Qín achieved no success
and disbanded at Chénggāo.
Zhào sought to ally with Qín,
and Chǔ, along with Wèi and Hán, were about to respond to this,
but Qín was unwilling.
Sū Dài said to the King of Qí:
"I thought Your Majesty had already met with Fèngyáng Jūn.
I said to Fèngyáng Jūn:
'If All Under Heaven splits and serves Qín,
Qín will certainly seize Sòng.
Wèi Rǎn will certainly envy your possession of Yīn.
The King of Qín is greedy,
Wèi Rǎn is envious—
then Yīn will be impossible to obtain.
If you, my lord, do not form an alliance,
Qí will certainly attack Sòng.
If Qí attacks Sòng,
then Chǔ will certainly attack Sòng,
Wèi will certainly attack Sòng,
and Yān and Zhào will assist them.
With the five states seizing Sòng,
in no more than a month or two,
Yīn will certainly be obtained.
Once Yīn is obtained and an alliance is formed,
even if Qín changes its stance,
you, my lord, will have no worries.
If it becomes unavoidable and an alliance must be formed,
then I hope the five states will renew their firm covenant.
I hope to win over Zhào,
so that Your Majesty may soar like a hero,
and along with the high officials of Hán, move east to avoid conflict.
The King of Qí will certainly not summon Mǐn.
Have me uphold the covenant:
if any state violates the covenant,
the four states will attack it.
If none violate the covenant,
but Qín infringes upon it,
the five states will renew their firm stance and resist it.
Now Hán and Wèi are suspicious of Qí.
If they do not renew the firm covenant and instead negotiate,
I fear great chaos among the allied states.
If Qí and Qín do not reunite,
there will certainly be one side gaining dominance.
Whether they reunite or one side gains dominance,
neither is beneficial to Zhào.
Moreover, if All Under Heaven splits and serves Qín,
then Qín will control All Under Heaven.
If Qín controls All Under Heaven,
what will become of All Under Heaven?
I hope you, my lord, will plan early.'
'There are six scenarios if All Under Heaven contends for Qín's favor,
all unfavorable to Zhào.
If All Under Heaven contends for Qín's favor,
the King of Qín will accept the states from across the sea,
unite those who have betrayed their allies,
to occupy the Central States,
and seek advantage from the three Jìn states—
this is Qín's first move.
If Qín carries out this plan,
it is unfavorable to Zhào,
and you, my lord, will never obtain Yīn—
the first.
If All Under Heaven contends for Qín's favor,
the King of Qín will place Hán Mín in Qí,
place Chéngyáng Jūn in Hán,
make Wèi Huái chancellor in Wèi,
restore Yǎn
to liaise with the two kings,
and have Wáng Bēn, Hán Tuō, and their associates
all rise to handle affairs—
this is Qín's second move.
If Qín carries out this plan,
it is unfavorable to Zhào,
and you, my lord, will again not obtain Yīn—the second.
If All Under Heaven contends for Qín's favor,
the King of Qín will accept Qí and accept Zhào,
forming a triple alliance and triple intimacy,
to occupy Wèi and demand Ānyì—
this is Qín's third move.
If Qín carries out this plan,
Qí and Zhào will respond,
Wèi will not wait to be attacked
but will embrace Ānyì and trust Qín.
Qín will gain the riches of Ānyì,
Wèi will become its closest ally,
Hán will certainly pay court
to Qín, and passing Zhào, Qín will already have Ānyì—
this is Qín's fourth move.
If Qín carries out this plan, it is unfavorable to Zhào,
and you, my lord, will certainly not obtain Yīn—the third.
If All Under Heaven contends for Qín's favor,
Qín will strengthen its ties with Yān and Zhào
to attack Qí,
win over Chǔ, ally with Hán Mǐn, and attack Wèi—
this is Qín's fifth move.
If Qín carries out this plan,
Yān and Zhào will respond.
Yān and Zhào attacking Qí,
once the troops are engaged,
Qín will then win over Chǔ and attack Wèi.
In no more than a month or two,
Wèi will certainly be crushed.
Qín will seize Ānyì and block Nǚjǐ,
cutting off Hán's Tàiyuán,
descending Zhǐdào
and Gāo,
taking Nányáng, attacking Wèi,
severing Hán,
encircling the two Zhōu,
and then Zhào will itself melt away.
The state will be scorched by Qín,
its troops divided against Qí—
this is not beneficial to Zhào.
And you, my lord, will never obtain Yīn in your lifetime—
the fourth.
If All Under Heaven contends for Qín's favor,
Qín will strengthen the three Jìn states' alliance to attack Qí.
The state will be broken, its strength exhausted,
and its troops divided east against Qí.
Qín will then mobilize troops to attack Wèi,
taking Ānyì—
this is Qín's sixth move.
If Qín carries out this plan,
and you, my lord, mobilize to rescue Wèi,
you will be attacking Qí when it is already weakened,
rescuing and contending with Qín in battle.
If you, my lord, do not rescue,
how can Hán and Wèi avoid uniting with the west?
The state will be caught in the midst of schemes,
and you, my lord, will never obtain Yīn in your lifetime—the fifth.
If All Under Heaven contends for Qín's favor,
Qín will act righteously,
preserving the perishing and continuing the extinct,
stabilizing the endangered and supporting the weak,
installing guiltless rulers,
and will certainly revive Zhōngshān and Shèng.
If Qín revives Zhōngshān and Shèng,
then Zhào and Sòng will share the same fate.
What leisure will there be to speak of Yīn?—the sixth.
Therefore, I say if you, my lord, certainly do not negotiate,
then Yīn will certainly be obtained.'
"Fèngyáng Jūn said:
'Excellent.'
He then broke off peace with Qín
and won over Qí and Wèi to succeed in taking Yīn."
Lóu Huǎn was about to depart on a diplomatic mission.
He prostrated himself to attend to affairs,
and upon taking his leave,
said to the King of Zhào:
"Although I will exert all my strength and exhaust my wisdom,
I fear I shall not see Your Majesty again, even in death."
The King said: "What kind of talk is this?
I will certainly write a letter and entrust you with an important task."
Lóu Zǐ said:
"Has Your Majesty not heard of Gōngzǐ Móuyí in Sòng?
He would eat nothing but meat.
Wén Zhāng was favored in Sòng,
but he hated Gōngzǐ Móuyí,
and it was a matter of course.
Now, my relationship with Your Majesty is not like that of Sòng with Gōngzǐ Móuyí,
yet those who hate me surpass Wén Zhāng.
Therefore, I fear I shall not see Your Majesty again, even in death."
The King said:
"You must go forth with effort,
for I have made a solemn oath with you."
Lóu Zǐ then departed.
Later, he rebelled with Zhōngmóu
and fled to Liáng.
When scouts came to report this,
the King would not listen,
saying:
"I have already made a promise with Lóu Zǐ."
Yú Qīng requested an audience with the King of Zhào, saying:
"In human nature,
does one prefer to have others come to pay court,
or to go and pay court to others?"
The King of Zhào said:
"People naturally prefer to have others come to pay court to them;
why would they prefer to go and pay court to others?"
Yú Qīng said:
"Now, Wèi is the leader of the vertical alliance,
and the one opposing it is Fàn Zuò.
If Your Majesty can offer a territory of a hundred *lǐ*,
or a city of ten thousand households,
to request that Wèi kill Fàn Zuò.
Once Fàn Zuò is dead,
then the leadership of the alliance can be transferred to Zhào."
The King of Zhào said:
"Excellent."
He then sent an envoy with an offer of a hundred *lǐ* of territory,
to request that Wèi kill Fàn Zuò.
The King of Wèi agreed,
and ordered the Minister of Justice to arrest Fàn Zuò,
but had not yet killed him.
Fàn Zuò presented a letter to the King of Wèi, saying:
"I have heard that the King of Zhào is offering a hundred *lǐ* of territory
in exchange for my life.
To kill the innocent Fàn Zuò
is a trivial matter for me;
but to gain a hundred *lǐ* of territory
is a great benefit.
I privately consider this advantageous for Your Majesty.
However,
there is one consideration:
if the hundred *lǐ* of territory cannot be obtained,
and the dead cannot be brought back to life,
then Your Majesty will surely be laughed at by all under heaven!
I humbly believe that rather than trading with a dead man,
it would be better to trade with a living one."
He also sent a letter to the subsequent minister, Lord Xìnlíng, saying:
"Zhào and Wèi
are rival states at war.
The King of Zhào sends a letter of a few words,
and the King of Wèi lightly agrees to kill the innocent Zuò.
Although I, Zuò, am unworthy,
I was once the dismissed chancellor of Wèi.
I once, for the sake of Wèi,
offended Zhào.
If within the state there are no capable ministers,
even if territory is gained abroad,
it will be impossible to hold it.
No one is as capable as you, my lord.
And now, no one can defend Wèi
better than you, my lord. After the King listens to Zhào and kills me,
if the powerful Qín, following Zhào's desire,
offers double what Zhào has offered,
how will you, my lord, stop it?
This will be a burden for you, my lord."
Lord Xìnlíng said:
"Well said."
He immediately spoke to the King and secured Fàn Zuò's release.
Yān enfeoffed the Sòng man Róng Fén as Lord Gāoyáng,
and sent him to lead an attack against Zhào.
The King of Zhào then ceded three cities east of the Jì River—Lìnglú, Gāotáng, and Píngyuán—along with fifty-seven towns and marketplaces in the hilly regions,
ordering that they be given to Qí,
in order to request Lord Ānpíng to command the army.
Lord Mǎfú said to Lord Píngyuán:
"Is our state so lacking in men!
You request Lord Ānpíng to command the army,
and cede three cities east of the Jì River along with fifty-seven towns and marketplaces to give to Qí.
This is what one gains after battling an enemy state,
destroying armies and killing generals, and then ceding territory to the enemy state.
Now you give this to Qí,
and request Lord Ānpíng to command the army.
Is our state so lacking in men!
Moreover, why do you not appoint Shē to command?
Shē once resided in Yān to atone for a crime,
and Yān appointed Shē as the governor of Shànggǔ.
I am thoroughly familiar with Yān's passes, valleys, and strategic strongholds.
Within a hundred days,
before the armies of all under heaven can gather,
I will have already conquered Yān.
So then, why do you seek Lord Ānpíng to command?"
Lord Píngyuán said:
"General, let it go.
I have already spoken of this to my lord.
My lord has fortunately listened to me.
General, say no more."
Lord Mǎfú said:
"You are mistaken!
The reason you seek Lord Ānpíng
is because of Qí's relationship with Yān—
it is a hatred of devouring livers and wading through blood.
But with Shē, it is not so.
If Lord Ānpíng is foolish,
he certainly cannot withstand Róng Fén; if
Lord Ānpíng is wise,
he will also be unwilling to fight against the men of Yān.
Between these two statements,
Lord Ānpíng must fall into one of them.
However,
one of the two is true.
If Lord Ānpíng is wise,
then why would he use the strength of Zhào?
If Zhào becomes strong, then Qí will no longer be hegemon.
Now, with the strong army of Zhào,
to block the Yān general,
prolonging the war for several years,
exhausting the strength of the officers and the common people
in building trenches and fortifications, with chariots,
armor, feathers, and banners torn and worn out,
treasuries and granaries emptied,
and both states becoming accustomed to the conflict,
he will then lead his troops and return home.
To exhaust the armies of both states—
nothing could be clearer than this."
In summer,
the army hung their cauldrons to cook.
They obtained three cities,
but none of the cities were larger than a hundred *zhì*.
It indeed turned out as Lord Mǎfú had said.
Three states attacked Qín,
while Zhào attacked Zhōngshān,
capturing Fúliǔ,
and within five years gaining control over Hūtuó.
The Qí men Róng Guō and Sòng Tū said to Qiú Hǎo:
"It would be better to return all the newly acquired territory of Zhōngshān.
If Zhōngshān reports this to Qí, saying
that the four states will borrow a route through Wèi
to bypass Zhāng Zǐ's road.
When Qí hears this,
they will surely offer Gǔ."
Zhào sent Zhào Zhuāng to form a vertical alliance,
intending to attack Qí.
Qí offered territory,
and Zhào consequently disparaged Zhào Zhuāng.
Qí Míng spoke on his behalf to the King of Zhào, saying:
"Qí fears the formation of the vertical alliance,
hence they offered territory.
Now, hearing that Zhào Zhuāng is disparaged
and Zhāng Qín is esteemed,
Qí will certainly not offer territory."
The King of Zhào said:
"Well said."
He then summoned Zhào Zhuāng and honored him.
Zhái Zhāng came from Liáng,
and was on very good terms with the King of Zhào.
The King of Zhào three times invited him to become chancellor,
but Zhái Zhāng declined and did not accept.
Tián Sì said to the Pillar of State Hán Xiàng:
"I request to assassinate him for you, my lord.
If the guest dies,
then the King will surely be angry and execute Jiànxìn Jūn.
If Jiànxìn Jūn dies,
then you, my lord, will surely become chancellor.
If Jiànxìn Jūn does not die,
you will have established a connection with him, which will never deteriorate for life,
and you will thereby be indebted to Jiànxìn Jūn."
Féng Jì spoke to the King of Zhào on behalf of Lúlíng Jūn, saying:
"Your Majesty is exiling Lúlíng Jūn
for the sake of Yān."
The King said: "What I value
has nothing to do with Yān or Qín."
He replied: "Qín has repeatedly spoken of Yú Qīng,
yet Your Majesty did not expel him.
Now Yān has only once spoken of the Lord of Lúlíng,
yet Your Majesty expels him.
This shows that Your Majesty regards powerful Qín lightly and values weak Yān heavily."
The king said: "I am not doing this for Yān's sake;
I was determined to expel him anyway."
"If so, then Your Majesty expels the Lord of Lúlíng, and it is not for Yān's sake either.
To act by expelling a beloved younger brother,
while also gaining neither Yān nor Qín,
I privately believe this is not something Your Majesty should adopt."
Féng Jì requested an audience with the King of Zhào,
and the usher introduced him.
Féng Jì clasped his hands and bowed his head,
wishing to speak but not daring to.
The king asked the reason,
and he replied:
"A guest once recommended someone to Fú Zǐ,
and later asked about his faults.
Fú Zǐ said:
'Your guest alone has three faults:
He looks at me and smiles—this is familiarity;
he speaks without mentioning his teacher—this is betrayal;
our acquaintance is shallow, yet he speaks deeply—this is disorder.'
The guest said: 'Not so.
To look at someone and smile—this is harmony;
to speak without mentioning one's teacher—this is ordinary speech;
with shallow acquaintance to speak deeply—this is loyalty.
In ancient times, Yáo saw Shùn among the thatched huts,
shared a mat on the ridge of the field and sheltered under mulberry trees,
and as the shade shifted, he handed over the world to him.
Yī Yǐn carried tripods and cutting boards to seek out Tāng,
and before his name was known, he received the rank of Sāngōng.
If those with shallow acquaintance could not speak deeply,
then the world would not have been transmitted,
and the position of Sāngōng would not have been obtained.'"
The King of Zhào said: "Very good."
Féng Jì said:
"Now, as an outsider with shallow acquaintance, I wish to speak deeply—
may I?"
The king said: "I ask to receive your instruction."
Thereupon, Féng Jì spoke.
A guest visited the King of Zhào and said:
"I have heard that Your Majesty sends people to buy horses—
is this true?"
The king said:
"It is true."
"Why has no one been sent yet?"
The king said:
"I have not yet found a skilled horse appraiser."
He replied: "Why does Your Majesty not send Jiàn Xìn Jūn?"
The king said: "Jiàn Xìn Jūn has state affairs to attend to,
and moreover, he does not know how to appraise horses."
He said:
"Why does Your Majesty not send Jì Jī?"
The king said: "Jì Jī is a woman;
she does not know how to appraise horses."
He replied: "If the horse bought is good,
what benefit does it bring to the state?"
The king said: "It brings no benefit to the state."
"If the horse bought is bad,
what danger does it pose to the state?"
The king said: "It poses no danger to the state."
He replied: "Then whether the horse bought is good or bad,
it neither endangers nor benefits the state.
Yet when Your Majesty buys horses,
you must wait for a skilled appraiser.
Now in governing the world,
if actions and measures are wrong,
the state will become empty and desolate,
and the altars of soil and grain will receive no blood sacrifices.
Yet Your Majesty does not wait for skilled men,
but instead relies on Jiàn Xìn Jūn—
why is this?"
The King of Zhào had no response.
The guest said:
"In the laws of Yānguō,
there is something called 'sāng yōng'—does Your Majesty know of it?"
The king said: "I have not heard of it."
"The so-called 'sāng yōng'
refers to the favored attendants close by your side,
as well as your consorts, entertainers, and beloved young ones.
These are all able to take advantage of Your Majesty's drunken stupor
to seek what they desire from you.
If they can obtain it within,
then the great ministers will bend the law for them without.
Thus, though the sun and moon shine brightly without,
the harm lies within.
Guard carefully against those you hate,
yet disaster comes from those you love."
Qín attacked Wèi,
captured Níngyì,
and all the feudal lords offered congratulations.
The King of Zhào sent an envoy to offer congratulations,
but after three attempts, he was not received.
The King of Zhào grew worried
and said to his attendants:
"With Qín's strength,
having obtained Níngyì,
they can control Qí and Zhào.
All the feudal lords have offered congratulations,
yet when I send congratulations, I alone am not received.
This surely means they will attack us with troops.
What should we do?"
The attendants said: "That the envoy was not received after three attempts
must mean the envoy sent was not the right person.
There is one named Liàng Yì—
he is a skilled debater.
Your Majesty might try sending him."
Liàng Yì personally received the order and went.
Arriving in Qín,
he presented a letter to the King of Qín, saying:
"Your Majesty has expanded your territory with Níngyì,
and all the feudal lords have offered congratulations.
Our humble ruler also privately praises this,
and not daring to remain idle,
he has sent his humble servant with gifts three times to Your Majesty's court,
yet I have not been received.
If our envoy is without fault,
I hope Your Majesty will not cut off the cordial relations;
if the envoy is at fault,
I beg to be informed of it."
The King of Qín sent an envoy to reply:
"If those I send to Zhào,
whether great or small, all heed my words,
then I will accept the letter and gifts.
If they do not heed my words,
then the envoy may return."
Liàng Yì replied:
"This humble servant has come
precisely wishing to comply with the great state's intentions—
how dare I cause difficulty?
If Your Majesty has orders to give,
I beg to receive them and carry them west to execute,
without any doubt."
Thereupon, the King of Qín received the envoy
and said:
"Zhào Bào and Píngyuán Jūn
have repeatedly deceived and made a fool of me.
If Zhào can kill these two men,
then it is acceptable.
If they cannot be killed,
I ask to now lead the feudal lords to receive your submission beneath the walls of Hándān."
Liàng Yì said:
"Zhào Bào and Píngyuán Jūn
are the beloved younger brothers of our ruler's mother,
just as Your Majesty has Yèyáng Jūn and Jīngyáng Jūn.
Your Majesty is renowned throughout the world for governing with filial piety.
Clothing is made to fit the body comfortably,
food and drink are made to please the palate,
and nothing is not shared with Yèyáng Jūn and Jīngyáng Jūn.
The carriages, horses, and clothing of Yèyáng Jūn and Jīngyáng Jūn
are all provided by Your Majesty.
I have heard it said:
'If nests are overturned and eggs destroyed,
the phoenix will not soar;
if wombs are cut open and young burned,
the qílín will not come.'
Now if I receive Your Majesty's order and return to report it,
our humble ruler,
in fear, will not dare not to comply,
but would this not wound the hearts of Yèyáng Jūn
and Jīngyáng Jūn?"
The King of Qín said:
"Very well.
Do not let them participate in government."
Liàng Yì said:
"Our humble ruler,
having younger brothers he could not instruct properly,
thus offending the great state,
asks to dismiss them,
not allowing them to participate in government affairs,
to satisfy the great state."
The King of Qín was pleased,
accepted the gifts, and treated him generously.
Zhào sent Yáo Jiǎ to ally with Hán and Wèi,
and Hán and Wèi became friendly with him.
Jǔ Máo spoke to the King of Zhào on behalf of Yáo Jiǎ, saying:
"Jiǎ is
a loyal minister of Your Majesty.
Hán and Wèi wish to obtain him,
so they befriended him,
intending to have Your Majesty banish him,
so that they themselves could then take him in.
Now if Your Majesty banishes him,
it would fulfill Hán and Wèi's desire to obtain him,
and Your Majesty's loyal minister would be found guilty.
Therefore, Your Majesty should not banish him,
to demonstrate Your Majesty's wisdom,
and thwart Hán and Wèi's attempt to recruit him."
Wèi defeated Chǔ at Xíngshān,
capturing Táng Míng.
The King of Chǔ was afraid,
and ordered Zhāo Yìng to escort the crown prince to entrust peace negotiations to Xuē Gōng.
Zhǔfù wished to thwart this,
so he forged alliances with Qín and established connections with Chǔ and Sòng,
appointing Chóu Hǎo as chancellor of Sòng,
and Lóu Huǎn as chancellor of Qín.
The King of Chǔ captured Zhào and Sòng,
and Wèi's peace negotiations ultimately failed.
Qín summoned Chūn Píng Hóu,
and detained him.
Shì Jūn spoke on his behalf to Wén Xìn Hóu, saying:
"Chūn Píng Hóu
is someone the King of Zhào deeply loves,
but the court officials are very jealous of him,
so they conspired together, saying:
'If Chūn Píng Hóu goes to Qín,
Qín will certainly detain him.'
Therefore, they plotted to send him into Qín.
Now if you detain him,
it would sever ties with Zhào for nothing,
and fall right into the court officials' scheme.
Therefore, you should send Chūn Píng Hóu back and detain Píng Dū Hóu instead.
Chūn Píng Hóu, through his words and actions with the King of Zhào,
will certainly cede substantial territory from Zhào to serve you,
and ransom Píng Dū Hóu."
Wén Xìn Hóu said:
"Good."
He then treated him with courtesy and sent him back.
The Queen Dowager of Zhào had newly taken power,
and Qín urgently attacked them.
The Zhào state sought help from Qí.
Qí said:
"You must send Cháng'ān Jūn as a hostage,
then we will send troops."
The Queen Dowager refused,
and the ministers strongly remonstrated.
The Queen Dowager clearly told her attendants:
"If anyone again suggests making Cháng'ān Jūn a hostage,
this old woman will certainly spit in their face."
The Left Tutor Chù Zhé requested an audience with the Queen Dowager.
The Queen Dowager received him with great anger.
He entered and slowly hurried forward,
and upon arrival apologized of his own accord,
saying:
"Your servant's legs are ailing,
and I truly cannot walk quickly,
so I have not been able to see you for a long time.
I privately excused myself,
but feared that Your Majesty's precious health might have some ailment,
so I wished to see you."
The Queen Dowager said: "This old woman relies on a carriage to get around."
He said:
"Your daily eating and drinking haven't diminished, I hope?"
She said:
"I rely on porridge."
He said:
"Your servant lately has had little desire to eat,
so I force myself to walk,
three or four lǐ a day,
which slightly increases my appetite,
and benefits my health."
The Queen Dowager said: "This old woman cannot."
The Queen Dowager's expression softened slightly.
The Left Tutor said: "Your servant's humble son Shū Qí,
is the youngest and most unworthy.
But as I am declining in years, I privately dote on him.
I wish for him to be able to fill a position among the black-clad guards,
to guard the royal palace.
I risk death to bring this to your attention."
The Queen Dowager said: "Very well.
How old is he?"
He replied: "Fifteen years old.
Although young,
I wish to entrust him before I fill the ditches and gullies."
The Queen Dowager said:
"Do men also dote on their young sons?"
He replied: "More than women."
The Queen Dowager laughed and said:
"Women are exceptionally so."
He replied:
"Your servant privately believes that your love for Yān Hòu surpasses that for Cháng'ān Jūn."
She said:
"You are mistaken,
it is not as deep as for Cháng'ān Jūn."
The Left Tutor said:
"When parents love their children,
they plan deeply and far ahead for them.
When you sent off Yān Hòu,
you held her heel and wept for her,
thinking sadly of her going far away,
and grieving for her.
After she left,
it's not that you didn't miss her,
but during sacrifices you always prayed for her,
praying: 'May she never be sent back.'
Was this not planning for the long term,
so that her descendants would succeed each other as kings?"
The Queen Dowager said: "Indeed."
The Left Tutor said:
"Now, from three generations ago,
back to when Zhào became Zhào,
among the descendants of Zhào's rulers who were enfeoffed as marquises,
are their successors still present?"
She said: "There are none."
He said:
"Not only Zhào,
among the other feudal lords, are any still present?"
She said:
"This old woman has not heard of any."
"This shows that for the nearer ones, disaster befell themselves,
and for the farther ones, it reached their descendants.
Is it necessarily that the descendants of rulers are unworthy?
It is because their positions were noble yet they achieved no merit,
their emoluments were generous yet they performed no service,
and they possessed many precious vessels.
Now you have elevated Cháng'ān Jūn's position,
and enfeoffed him with fertile lands,
bestowed many precious vessels upon him,
yet you do not now order him to achieve merit for the state.
Once the mountains and hills crumble,
how will Cháng'ān Jūn establish himself in Zhào?
Your servant believes that your planning for Cháng'ān Jūn is short-sighted,
therefore I consider your love for him inferior to that for Yān Hòu."
The Queen Dowager said: "Very well.
I leave it to you to send him as you see fit."
Thereupon, they prepared one hundred chariots for Cháng'ān Jūn to go as a hostage to Qí,
and Qí's troops then marched out.
Zǐ Yì heard of this and said:
"The son of a ruler,
of flesh and blood kinship,
still cannot rely on a noble position without merit,
or generous emoluments without service,
to preserve the weight of gold and jade,
how much less can a minister?"
Qín sent Wáng Jiǎn to attack Zhào,
and Zhào sent Lǐ Mù and Sīmǎ Shàng to defend against him.
Lǐ Mù repeatedly defeated and drove back the Qín army,
killing the Qín general Huán Yǐ.
Wáng Jiǎn was troubled by this,
so he gave much gold to the King of Zhào's favored minister Guō Kāi and others,
to have them carry out counter-espionage,
saying:
"Lǐ Mù and Sīmǎ Shàng wish to ally with Qín to betray Zhào,
in order to gain more fiefs from Qín."
The King of Zhào became suspicious of them,
and sent Zhào Cōng and Yán Zuì to replace them as generals.
They beheaded Lǐ Mù,
and dismissed Sīmǎ Shàng.
Three months later,
Wáng Jiǎn launched a fierce attack,
greatly defeated Zhào,
killed the Zhào army,
captured the King of Zhào Qiān and his general Yán Zuì,
and thus destroyed Zhào.
Zhì Bó demanded land from Wèi Huánzǐ,
and Wèi Huánzǐ refused to give it.
Rén Zhāng said: "Why refuse to give it?"
Huánzǐ said: "He demands land without reason,
therefore I refuse to give it."
Rén Zhāng said:
"Demanding land without reason,
neighboring states will certainly fear;
heavy desires without satiety,
all under heaven will certainly dread.
If you give him land,
Zhì Bó will certainly become arrogant.
Arrogant and underestimating the enemy,
neighboring states, fearful, will draw closer together.
With troops that are mutually affectionate,
awaiting a state that underestimates its enemy,
the fate of the Zhì clan will not be long!
The "Zhōu Shū" says:
"If you wish to defeat them,
you must first assist them;
if you wish to take from them,
you must first give to them."
You, my lord, should give to them,
to make Zhì Bó arrogant.
Why would you abandon the opportunity to have the world conspire against the Zhì clan,
and instead make our state the target of the Zhì clan alone?"
The lord said:
"Good."
Then he gave them a city of ten thousand households.
Zhì Bó was greatly pleased.
He then demanded Cài and Gāoliáng from Zhào,
but Zhào refused to give them,
so he besieged Jìnyáng.
Hán and Wèi rebelled from the outside,
and the Zhào clan responded from within,
and thus the Zhì clan perished.
Hán and Zhào were in conflict.
Hán requested troops from Wèi, saying:
"I wish to borrow an army to attack Zhào."
Marquis Wén of Wèi said:
"I am like a brother to Zhào,
and dare not comply."
Zhào also requested troops to attack Hán,
and Marquis Wén said:
"I am like a brother to Hán,
and dare not comply."
Both states failed to obtain troops,
and in anger, they turned away.
Later, they realized that Marquis Wén had mediated between them,
and both came to pay homage to Wèi.
Yuè Yáng served as a general of Wèi and attacked Zhōngshān.
His son was in Zhōngshān,
and the lord of Zhōngshān boiled his son and sent the broth to him.
Yuè Yáng sat under the tent and drank it,
finishing the entire cup.
Marquis Wén said to Dǔshī Zàn:
"For my sake, Yuè Yáng ate
the flesh of his own son."
Zàn replied:
"If he can eat the flesh of his own son,
who would he not eat?"
After Yuè Yáng had pacified Zhōngshān,
Marquis Wén rewarded his achievements but doubted his heart.
Xīmén Bào was appointed magistrate of Yè and took leave of Marquis Wén of Wèi.
Marquis Wén said:
"Go now,
and you will surely accomplish great deeds
and establish your reputation."
Xīmén Bào said:
"May I ask,
is there a method to accomplish great deeds and establish a reputation?"
Marquis Wén said:
"There is.
In the villages and towns, the elders and those who are first to receive seats,
you should enter and inquire about the virtuous and worthy among them and serve them as teachers.
Seek out those who are fond of concealing others' merits and exposing their faults,
and use them for cross-examination.
Many things appear similar but are not the same.
The young shoots of wild millet resemble grain,
the yellow of a black ox resembles a tiger,
white bones may be mistaken for ivory,
and wǔfū stones resemble jade.
These all appear similar but are not the real thing."
Marquis Wén had arranged a hunting date with the gamekeeper.
On that day,
he was drinking and enjoying himself, and it rained.
Marquis Wén was about to go out,
when his attendants said:
"Today you are drinking and enjoying yourself,
and it is raining again.
Where are you going, my lord?"
Marquis Wén said:
"I arranged a hunting date with the gamekeeper.
Even though I am enjoying myself,
how can I fail to keep the appointment?"
So he went,
and personally canceled the hunt.
It was from this that Wèi began to grow strong.
Marquis Wén of Wèi was drinking with Tián Zǐfāng and discussing music.
Marquis Wén said:
"The bell tones are not harmonious,
the left side is too high."
Tián Zǐfāng laughed.
Marquis Wén said:
"Why are you laughing?"
Zǐfāng said:
"I have heard that
when a ruler is wise, he delights in governance; when he is unwise, he delights in music.
Now, my lord, you are so discerning about sounds,
I fear you may be deaf to governance."
Marquis Wén said:
"Well said,
I respectfully heed your words."
Marquis Wǔ of Wèi was floating on the Western River with his ministers and exclaimed:
"The perilousness of these mountains and rivers,
is it not indeed a solid defense!"
Wáng Zhōng, attending the king, said:
"This is why the state of Jìn was strong.
If we maintain them well,
the foundation for hegemony is complete."
Wú Qǐ replied:
"My lord's words are the path to endangering the state;
and you, sir,附和 him,
this is dangerous."
Marquis Wǔ angrily said:
"Do your words have an explanation?"
Wú Qǐ replied:
"The perilousness of mountains and rivers
is truly insufficient to rely on for protection.
The achievement of hegemony
does not come from this.
In ancient times,
the Sānmiáo people dwelled
with the waves of Pénglí on the left,
and the waters of Dòngtíng on the right,
with Wénshān to the south
and Héngshān to the north.
Relying on these perils,
they governed poorly,
and Yǔ exiled them.
As for the state of Xià Jié,
it had Tiānmén's shade on the left
and Tiānxī's sunlight on the right,
with Lú and Gāo to the north
and the Yī and Luò rivers flowing from the south.
Though it had these perils,
it governed poorly,
and Tāng attacked it.
The state of Yīn Zhòu
had Mèngmén on the left and the Zhāng and Fǔ rivers on the right,
with the river in front
and mountains behind.
Though it had these perils,
it governed poorly,
and King Wǔ attacked it.
Moreover, my lord, you personally led your ministers to capture surrendered cities.
The walls were not low,
and the people were not few,
yet they could be annexed
because their governance was corrupt.
From this perspective,
how can perilous terrain alone suffice for hegemony!"
Marquis Wǔ said:
"Well said.
Only today have I heard the words of a sage!
The governance of the Western River
I entrust entirely to you."
Gōngshū Cuó of Wèi served as a general of Wèi
and fought against Hán and Zhào north of Huì,
capturing Yuè Zuò.
The king of Wèi was pleased and welcomed him outside the city,
rewarding him with a million acres of land.
Gōngshū Cuó retreated, bowed twice, and declined, saying:
"That the soldiers did not collapse,
stood straight without wavering,
and did not retreat even when pressed—
this was due to the remaining teachings of Wú Qǐ,
which I could not achieve.
Surveying the perilous terrain beforehand,
deciding on preparations for advantages and disadvantages,
and ensuring the three armies were not confused—
this was the effort of Bā Níng and Cuàn Xiāng.
Establishing rewards and punishments beforehand
and making the people clearly trust them afterward—
this was due to your majesty's enlightened laws.
Seeing the enemy's vulnerability and drumming the advance,
not daring to slacken—
this was my doing.
If your majesty rewards me solely for my right hand not tiring,
why is that?
If you consider me有功, what merit do I truly have?"
The king said:
"Well said."
Then he sought out the descendants of Wú Qǐ
and granted them two hundred thousand acres of land.
Bā Níng and Cuàn Xiāng were each granted one hundred thousand acres.
The king said:
"Is Gōngshū not indeed a noble man!
Not only did he defeat a powerful enemy for me,
but he also did not forget the descendants of the worthy
Therefore, the Lǎo Zǐ says:
"The sage does not accumulate,
but gives everything to others,
and thereby he himself has more;
having given everything to others,
he himself possesses even more."
Gōngshū Cuó understood this.
When Gōngshū Cuó of Wèi fell ill,
King Huì went to inquire about him. He said:
"If you, Gōngshū, are ill,
and should the inevitable occur,
what will become of the altars of soil and grain?"
Gōngshū Cuó replied: "Cuó has a retainer, Gōngsūn Yāng.
I hope Your Majesty will entrust state affairs to him.
If you cannot heed this,
do not let him leave the state."
The King did not respond.
Upon leaving, he said to his attendants:
"Is it not lamentable!
With Gōngshū's wisdom,
he tells me I must entrust state affairs to Yāng—
is this not perverse!"
After Gōngshū Cuó died,
Gōngsūn Yāng heard of this.
Once the burial was over,
he went west to Qín,
and Duke Xiào received and employed him.
Qín indeed grew stronger day by day,
while Wèi weakened daily.
This was not Gōngshū's perversity,
but King Huì's perversity.
The trouble with the perverse
is that they invariably regard the non-perverse as perverse.
Sū Zǐ, forming an alliance for Zhào,
persuaded the King of Wèi, saying:
"Your Majesty's territory
has the Hóng Gōu, Chén, and Rǔnán to the south;
it has Xǔ, Yān, Kūnyáng, Shàolíng, Wǔyáng, and Xīnqī;
to the east, it has the Huái, Yǐng, Yí, Huáng, Zhǔzǎo, and Wúhǎiyán, <shū>
shū; to the west, it has the boundary of the Long Wall;
to the north, it has Héwài, Juǎn, Yǎn, Yān, and Suānzǎo.
The land extends a thousand lǐ.
Though the place names may seem small,
yet the fields, cottages, and farmhouses
leave no land for pasturing oxen and horses.
The multitude of people,
the abundance of chariots and horses,
moving day and night without cease,
are no different from the masses of three armies.
I privately estimate
that Your Majesty's state
is not inferior to Chǔ.
Yet those advocating horizontal alliances advise Your Majesty
to ally externally with the strong, tiger-like Qín,
to invade the world.
When calamity befalls the state,
they do not suffer its disaster.
To rely on the power of strong Qín
to coerce one's lord internally—
no crime surpasses this.
Moreover, Wèi
is a powerful state in the world;
Your Majesty is a worthy ruler in the world.
Now you intend to face west and serve Qín,
calling yourself an eastern vassal,
building an imperial palace,
accepting caps and sashes,
offering sacrifices in spring and autumn—
I privately feel shame for Your Majesty.
"I have heard that King Gōujiàn of Yuè, with three thousand scattered troops,
captured Fūchāi at Gānsuì;
King Wǔ with three thousand men,
three hundred armored chariots,
beheaded Zhòu at Mùzhīyě.
Was it because their soldiers were numerous?
It was truly because they could rouse their might.
Now I privately hear that Your Majesty's troops
include two hundred thousand warriors,
twenty million 'blue-turbaned' troops,
two hundred thousand shock troops,
one hundred thousand laborers,
six hundred chariots,
and five thousand cavalry horses.
This far surpasses King Gōujiàn of Yuè and King Wǔ!
Yet now you are coerced by the words of petty ministers
and wish to serve Qín as a subject.
To serve Qín inevitably means ceding territory and offering hostages,
so before the army is even used, the state is already diminished.
All ministers who speak of serving Qín
are treacherous ministers,
not loyal ones.
As ministers,
they cut their lord's land to seek external alliances,
stealing momentary merit without regard for the consequences,
ruining the public good to enrich private interests,
relying externally on strong Qín's power to coerce their lord internally for land cession—
I hope Your Majesty will examine this carefully.
"The Zhōu Shū says:
'If threads are unbroken,
they become tangled—what then?
If a hair is not plucked,
it will grow into an ax handle.'
If earlier plans are not settled,
great troubles will follow.
What can be done then?
If Your Majesty truly heeds me,
the six states form a vertical alliance,
uniting hearts and combining strength,
then surely there will be no trouble from strong Qín.
Thus, my humble ruler, the King of Zhào, has sent me to offer this foolish plan,
present a clear covenant,
awaiting Your Majesty's command."
The King of Wèi said: "I am unworthy,
and have never heard such enlightened teaching.
Now you, sir, bring the King of Zhào's command to instruct me.
I respectfully follow with my state."
Zhāng Yí, forming horizontal alliances for Qín,
persuaded the King of Wèi, saying:
"Wèi's territory does not reach a thousand lǐ,
and its troops do not exceed three hundred thousand.
The land is flat on all sides,
with access to the feudal lords in all directions,
like spokes meeting at a hub,
with no barriers of famous mountains or great rivers.
From Zhèng to Liáng is no more than a hundred lǐ;
from Chén to Liáng is over two hundred lǐ.
Horses gallop and men hasten, reaching Liáng before growing weary.
To the south, it borders Chǔ;
to the west, it borders Hán;
to the north, it borders Zhào;
to the east, it borders Qí.
Troops garrison the four directions,
with watchtowers and barriers arrayed in threes.
Grain transported by water and stored in granaries
is no less than a hundred thousand.
Wèi's geographical position
makes it a battlefield of old.
If Wèi allies with Chǔ to the south and not with Qí,
then Qí will attack from the east;
if it allies with Qí to the east and not with Zhào,
then Zhào will attack from the north;
if it does not ally with Hán,
then Hán will attack from the west;
if it is not close to Chǔ,
then Chǔ will attack from the south.
This is the so-called path of being torn apart four or five ways.
"Moreover, the feudal lords who form vertical alliances
do so to secure the altars of soil and grain, honor their lords, strengthen their armies, and make their names illustrious.
Those forming vertical alliances unite the world,
swear brotherhood, slaughter a white horse to swear an oath on the Huán Shuǐ to strengthen each other.
Yet even blood brothers,
born of the same parents,
still quarrel over money and property.
And you wish to rely on the deceitful, fickle remnants of Sū Qín's schemes—
it is clear they cannot succeed.
"If Your Majesty does not serve Qín,
Qín will send troops to attack Héwài,
capture Juǎn, Yǎn, Yān, and Suānzǎo,
coerce Wèi and take Jìnyáng.
Then Zhào will not move south;
if Zhào does not move south,
then Wèi will not move north;
if Wèi does not move north,
then the vertical alliance path is cut;
if the vertical alliance path is cut,
then Your Majesty's state, wishing to avoid danger, will find it impossible.
If Qín, with Hán in tow, attacks Wèi,
and Hán is coerced by Qín,
it will not dare disobey.
With Qín and Hán as one state,
Wèi's destruction can be awaited standing—
this is what I worry about for Your Majesty.
For Your Majesty's plan,
nothing is better than serving Qín.
If you serve Qín, then Chǔ and Hán will surely not dare act;
without the troubles of Chǔ and Hán,
Your Majesty can rest easy on a high pillow,
and the state will surely have no worries.
"Moreover, what Qín desires to weaken is none other than Chǔ,
and none can weaken Chǔ like Wèi.
Though Chǔ has a name for wealth and size,
in reality it is hollow;
though its troops are many,
they are talkative and flee easily,
easily defeated,
daring not to fight steadfastly.
If Wèi's army attacks southward,
it will surely defeat Chǔ."
To weaken Chǔ and strengthen Wèi,
to attack Chǔ and please Qín,
internally diverting disaster and securing the state—
this is an excellent course of action.
If Your Majesty does not heed your servant,
once Qín’s armored troops march eastward,
even should you wish to serve Qín, it will be impossible.
“Moreover, those advocating the vertical alliance often boast with grand words but offer little that can be trusted.
Persuading the king of a single feudal lord,
they go forth riding in his carriage;
forming an alliance with one state and returning,
they lay the foundation for being enfeoffed as a marquis.
Therefore, among the itinerant strategists of the world,
there is not one who does not day and night clench their wrists, glare with wide eyes, and gnash their teeth to speak of the advantages of the vertical alliance,
in order to persuade the rulers.
When rulers consider their words
and are swayed by their arguments,
how can they avoid being dazzled?
Your servant has heard that accumulated feathers can sink a boat,
a multitude of light things can break an axle,
and many mouths can melt metal.
Thus, I hope Your Majesty will carefully consider this.”
The King of Wèi said:
“I am foolish and ignorant;
my previous plan was mistaken.
I request to declare myself an eastern vassal,
build an imperial palace,
accept the cap and sash,
perform seasonal sacrifices,
and cede Héwài.”
Qí and Wèi made a pact to attack Chǔ,
and Wèi sent Dǒng Qìng as a hostage to Qí.
Chǔ attacked Qí,
inflicting a great defeat,
but Wèi did not come to the rescue.
Tián Yīng was enraged
and was about to kill Dǒng Qìng.
Gànyí spoke to Tián Yīng on behalf of Dǒng Qìng, saying:
“Chǔ attacked Qí
and inflicted a great defeat,
yet did not dare to advance deeply
because they believed Wèi was about to join forces with Qí
and strike their rear.
Now if you kill Dǒng Qìng,
you will show Chǔ that Wèi is not with you.
If Wèi becomes angry and allies with Chǔ,
Qí will surely be in peril.
It would be better to honor Dǒng Qìng to maintain good relations with Wèi,
thereby causing Chǔ to be suspicious.”
Sū Qín was detained in Wèi
and wanted to flee to Hán,
but the people of Wèi closed the passes and blocked his way.
Qí sent Sū Lì to speak to the King of Wèi on his behalf, saying:
“Qí offered to enfeoff Lord Jīngyáng with land in Sòng,
but Qín did not accept.
It was not that Qín did not benefit from having Qí’s friendship and obtaining land in Sòng,
but the reason it did not accept
was distrust of the King of Qí and Sū Qín.
Now if Qín sees that the discord between Qí and Wèi is so severe,
then Qí will certainly not deceive Qín,
and Qín will trust Qí.
If Qí and Qín ally and Lord Jīngyáng obtains land in Sòng,
that would not be to Wèi’s advantage.
Therefore, Your Majesty should rather allow Sū Qín to return east.
Qín will then suspect Qí and not heed them.
If Qí and Qín do not ally,
the world will have no worries,
and if an attack on Qí succeeds,
then your territory will be expanded.”
Chén Zhěn was on a mission for Qín to Qí,
passed through Wèi,
and sought an audience with Xīshǒu.
Xīshǒu declined to see Chén Zhěn.
Chén Zhěn said:
“The reason I have come
is on business.
If you, sir, do not see me,
I will be on my way,
and cannot wait for another day.”
Xīshǒu then received him.
Chén Zhěn said: “Do you, sir, dislike having business?
Why do you eat and drink with nothing to do?
If you have no business, I will come.”
Xīshǒu said: “I, Yǎn, am unworthy
and cannot obtain any business;
how dare I dislike it?”
Chén Zhěn said:
“Allow me to shift the world’s business onto you, sir.”
Xīshǒu said:
“How?”
Chén Zhěn said:
“The King of Wèi is sending Lǐ Cóng with a hundred chariots on a mission to Chǔ.
You, sir, can position yourself in the middle and create suspicion.
Tell the King of Wèi:
‘Your servant has old connections with Yān and Zhào,
and they have repeatedly sent people to summon me,
saying that if I have no business, I must come.
Now I have no business;
I request permission to visit them.
It will not be long—
a period of ten or five days.’
The king will certainly have no excuse to stop you.
Once you gain permission to go,
then announce in court:
‘Your servant has an urgent mission to Yān and Zhào;
quickly prepare carriages and travel gear.’”
Xīshǒu said: “Agreed.”
He requested an audience with the King of Wèi,
and the king consented.
He then openly declared his mission to Yān and Zhào.
When the guest strategists from the various states heard of this,
they all sent people to inform their kings, saying:
“Lǐ Cóng is going to Chǔ with a hundred chariots,
and Xīshǒu is also going to Yān and Zhào with thirty chariots.”
When the King of Qí heard this,
fearing to fall behind the others in gaining Wèi’s favor,
entrusted his affairs to Xīshǒu.
Xīshǒu accepted Qí’s business.
The King of Wèi halted Lǐ Cóng’s mission.
When Yān and Zhào heard of it,
they also entrusted their affairs to Xīshǒu.
When the King of Chǔ heard of it,
he said:
“Lǐ Cóng made a pact with me,
but now Yān, Qí, and Zhào have all entrusted their affairs to Xīshǒu.
Xīshǒu will certainly want me,
and I want him.”
He then broke with Lǐ Cóng
and entrusted his affairs to Xīshǒu.
The King of Wèi said:
“The reason I did not employ Xīshǒu before
was that I considered him unsuitable.
Now that four states have entrusted their affairs to him,
I too will entrust my affairs to him.”
Xīshǒu thus took charge of the world’s affairs
and once again became chancellor of Wèi.
Zhāng Yí spoke ill of Chén Zhěn to the King of Wèi, saying:
“Zhěn is adept at serving Chǔ
and seeks territory for them, exerting great effort on their behalf.”
Zuǒ Huá said to Chén Zhěn:
“Yí is skilled in dealing with the King of Wèi,
and the King of Wèi is very fond of him.
