accepts caps and girdles from Qín,
and offers seasonal sacrifices,
believing that Qín's strength is sufficient to be an ally.
Now the troops of Qí and Chǔ are already at the outskirts of Wèi.
If Your Majesty's rescue does not arrive,
then in its urgency, Wèi will cede territory and make a pact with Qí and Chǔ.
Even if Your Majesty then wishes to rescue it,
how could it be in time?
This would mean losing a Wèi of ten thousand chariots,
and strengthening two enemy states, Qí and Chǔ.
I humbly believe that Your Majesty's ministers in charge of planning are incompetent."
The King of Qín sighed with sudden realization and concern,
immediately dispatched troops, and day and night they rushed to Wèi.
Qí and Chǔ, hearing of this, then withdrew their troops and left.
The house of Wèi was restored to safety, thanks to Táng Jū's persuasion.
Lord Xìnlíng killed Jìn Bǐ,
rescued Hándān,
defeated the Qín army,
and preserved the state of Zhào.
The King of Zhào personally welcomed him at the outskirts.
Táng Jū said to Lord Xìnlíng:
"I have heard it said that
among affairs, there are those one need not know,
and those one must not fail to know;
there are those one must not forget,
and those one must not fail to forget."
Lord Xìnlíng said:
"What does that mean?"
He replied:
"If others hate me,
I must not fail to know it;
if I hate others,
I must not let it be known.
If others have shown me kindness,
I must not forget it;
if I have shown kindness to others,
I must not fail to forget it.
Now you, my lord, killed Jìn Bǐ,
rescued Hándān,
defeated the Qín army,
and preserved the state of Zhào—
this is a great kindness.
Now the King of Zhào personally welcomes you at the outskirts.
When you suddenly meet the King of Zhào,
I hope you, my lord, will forget this kindness."
Lord Xìnlíng said:
"Wújì respectfully accepts your instruction."
Wèi attacked Guǎn but could not capture it.
There was a man from Ānlíng named Suō Gāo,
whose son was the commander of Guǎn.
Lord Xìnlíng sent a man to tell the Lord of Ānlíng:
"You should send Suō Gāo,
and I will appoint him as a Grandee of the Fifth Rank,
making him a Commandant with the tally."
The Lord of Ānlíng said: "Ānlíng
is a small state,
and I cannot compel my people.
Let the envoy go himself.
I request to have a guide escort the envoy
to Suō Gāo's place,
to relay Lord Xìnlíng's command."
Suō Gāo said:
"For my lord to favor me
is to have me attack Guǎn.
For a father to attack a city defended by his son
would make people laugh greatly.
If my son were to submit because of me,
that would be betraying his lord.
For a father to teach his son to betray
is also not something my lord would be pleased with.
I dare to decline with repeated bows."
The envoy reported this to Lord Xìnlíng.
Lord Xìnlíng was greatly angered
and sent a senior envoy to Ānlíng, saying:
"The land of Ānlíng
is still part of Wèi.
Now if I attack Guǎn and cannot capture it,
then Qín troops will reach us,
and our altars of state will surely be endangered.
I hope you will capture Suō Gāo alive and deliver him to me.
If you do not deliver him,
Wújì will dispatch an army of a hundred thousand
to arrive at the walls of Ānlíng."
Lord Ānlíng said:
"My late lord, Marquis Chéng,
received the decree from King Xiāng
to guard this land,
and personally received the statutes from the Grand Repository.
The first section of the statutes says:
'If a son assassinates his father,
or a minister assassinates his ruler,
there is a fixed punishment without pardon.
Even if the state grants a great amnesty,
those who surrender cities or lose sons shall not be included.'
Now Suō Gāo respectfully declines the high position,
to preserve the righteousness between father and son,
yet you, my lord, say, 'You must capture him alive and deliver him,'
this would make me betray King Xiāng's decree and violate the statutes of the Grand Repository.
Even if I die, I dare not carry it out."
Suō Gāo heard this and said:
"Lord Xìnlíng's character
is fierce and self-willed.
This reply will be turned against him,
and will surely bring disaster to the state.
I have already preserved my own integrity,
and have fulfilled my duty as a subject.
How can I let my lord incur the enmity of Wèi?"
Then he went to the envoy's lodging,
and cut his own throat and died.
When Lord Xìnlíng heard of Suō Gāo's death,
he donned plain white mourning garments and vacated his residence,
sending an envoy to apologize to Lord Ānlíng, saying:
"Wújì
is a petty man,
confused in his thoughts,
and spoke wrongly to you, my lord.
I dare to bow twice to beg forgiveness for my offense."
The King of Wèi and Lord Lóngyáng were fishing together in a boat,
and Lord Lóngyáng caught more than ten fish and began to weep.
The king said:
"Is something troubling you?
If so,
why not tell me?"
He replied:
"I dare not say I am troubled."
The king said: "Then why are you weeping?"
He said:
"I weep for the fish I have caught for Your Majesty."
The king said: "What do you mean?"
He replied: "When I first caught a fish,
I was very happy.
Later, I caught even bigger ones,
and now I simply want to discard the fish I caught earlier. Now,
despite my humble and unworthy self,
I have been favored to attend to Your Majesty's pillow and mat.
Now my rank has reached that of a lord,
people make way for me in the court,
and avoid me on the roads.
Within the four seas,
there are many beautiful people.
When they hear that I have gained Your Majesty's favor,
they will surely lift their skirts and rush to Your Majesty.
I am just like the fish I caught earlier.
I too will be discarded.
How can I not weep?"
The King of Wèi said: "Wrong!
If you have such thoughts,
why not tell me?"
Thereupon, he issued an order throughout the four borders of the state, saying:
"Anyone who dares to speak of beauties will have his clan exterminated."
From this we can see that
those who are close and familiar,
their flattery and sycophancy are indeed deep-rooted,
and their self-preservation is complete.
Now, from a thousand miles away,
if one wishes to present a beauty,
is it certain that she will gain favor?
Even if she does gain favor,
is it certain that she will be of use to us?
And those who are close and familiar will resent it together.
I see disaster in this,
and no benefit;
I see resentment, and no virtue.
This is not the way to employ wisdom.
Qín attacked Wèi fiercely.
Someone said to the King of Wèi:
"Abandoning territory is not as easy as using it,
and dying for it is not as easy as abandoning it.
To be able to abandon it but not use it,
to be able to die for it but not abandon it,
this is a great fault of men.
Now, Your Majesty has lost several hundred miles of territory,
and dozens of cities,
yet the state's troubles remain unresolved.
This is because Your Majesty abandoned them,
not because you used them.
Now Qín is strong,
unmatched in the world,
and Wèi is extremely weak.
Yet Your Majesty uses this as a pledge to Qín.
Your Majesty is willing to die for it but not to abandon it.
This is a double fault.
If Your Majesty can adopt my plan,
the loss of territory will not be enough to harm the state,
and humbling yourself will not be enough to distress your person.
You will resolve the trouble and repay the grudge."
"Within the four borders of Qín,
from the law-enforcing officials down to the long-distance cart-pullers,
all say:
'Are you with the Lào clan?
Or with the Lǚ clan?'
Even at the gates and alleys below,
or in the corridors and temples above,
it is still like this.
Now, if Your Majesty cedes territory to bribe Qín,
it will be credited as Lào Ǎi's achievement;
if you humble yourself to honor Qín,
it will be because of Lào Ǎi.
If Your Majesty uses the state to support Lào Ǎi,
then Lào Ǎi will prevail.
If Your Majesty uses the state to support the Lào clan,
the Queen Dowager's gratitude toward Your Majesty
will penetrate to the marrow of your bones,
and Your Majesty's relations will be the highest in the world.
Qín and Wèi have interacted a hundred times,
and deceived each other a hundred times.
Now, through the Lào clan's good relations with Qín, your ties will become the highest in the world.
Who in the world would not abandon the Lǚ clan and follow the Lào clan?
If the world must unite with the Lǚ clan and follow the Lào clan,
then Your Majesty's grudge will be repaid."
The King of Qín sent a messenger to say to Lord Ānlíng:
"I wish to exchange five hundred li of land for Ānlíng.
Will Lord Ānlíng consent to this?"
Lord Ānlíng said: "Your Majesty bestows kindness,
exchanging large for small.
This is very good.
However, I received this land from my ancestors,
and wish to guard it to the end,
not daring to exchange it."
The King of Qín was displeased.
Lord Ānlíng then sent Táng Jū as an envoy to Qín.
The King of Qín said to Táng Jū:
"I offered to exchange five hundred li of land for Ānlíng,
but Lord Ānlíng did not heed me.
Why is this?
Moreover, Qín has destroyed Hán and annihilated Wèi,
yet your lord survives with only fifty li of land.
It is because I consider him an elder,
that I have not turned my attention to him.
Now I offer ten times the land,
to expand his territory,
yet he opposes me.
Does he slight me?"
Táng Jū replied: "No,
it is not like that.
Lord Ānlíng received this land from his ancestors and guards it.
Even a thousand li he would not dare exchange,
let alone merely five hundred li?"
The King of Qín flushed with anger and said to Táng Jū:
"Have you ever heard of the anger of a Son of Heaven?"
Táng Jū replied:
"I have never heard of it."
The King of Qín said:
"The anger of a Son of Heaven
leaves a million corpses lying on the ground,
with blood flowing for a thousand li."
Táng Jū said:
"Has Your Majesty ever heard of the anger of a commoner?"
The King of Qín said:
"The anger of a commoner
is merely to take off his cap and go barefoot,
dashing his head against the ground."
Táng Jū said:
"This is the anger of a mediocre man,
not the anger of a true knight. When Zhuān Zhū assassinated King Liáo,
a comet swept across the moon;
when Niè Zhèng assassinated Hán Kuī,
a white rainbow pierced the sun;
when Yāo Lí assassinated Qìng Jì,
a gray eagle struck the palace hall.
These three men
were all commoner knights.
Their anger had not yet erupted,
but ominous signs descended from heaven.
Adding me, there will be four."
If a true scholar is provoked to anger,
two corpses will fall,
blood will flow within five paces,
and the whole world will don mourning garments—
this very day shall be that day."
He drew his sword and rose.
The King of Qín turned pale,
straightened his posture, and apologized, saying:
"Sir, please be seated. Why must it come to this?
I understand now.
Though Hán and Wèi have perished,
Ānlíng survives with its mere fifty lǐ of land
solely because it has you, sir."
After the three states of Jìn had defeated the Zhì clan,
they were about to divide its territory.
Duàn Guī said to the King of Hán:
"In the division of land, you must obtain Chénggāo."
The King of Hán said: "Chénggāo
is a rocky, barren place;
I have no use for it."
Duàn Guī said:
"Not so.
I have heard that a strategic position of one lǐ in depth
can sway the power over a thousand lǐ—
this is the advantage of terrain.
A force of ten thousand men
can defeat three armies—
this is the element of surprise.
If Your Majesty follows my advice,
then Hán will surely seize Zhèng."
The king said: "Excellent."
They indeed took Chénggāo.
When Hán later captured Zhèng,
it indeed began from Chénggāo.
Dàchéng Wǔ came from Zhào
and said to Shēn Bùhài in Hán:
"You use Hán to give me weight in Zhào;
I ask to use Zhào to give you weight in Hán.
Thus you will have two Háns,
and I will have two Zhàos."
When Wèi besieged Hándān,
Shēn Bùhài had just begun to align with the King of Hán,
but he did not yet know what the king desired,
and feared that if he spoke, his words might not accord with the king's wishes.
The king asked Shēnzǐ:
"With whom should I ally?"
He replied:
"This is a crucial matter of safety and danger,
a great affair of the state.
I beg to ponder it deeply and think hard."
Then he privately said to Zhào Zhuō and Hán Cháo:
"You are both eloquent scholars of the state.
As ministers serving their lord,
if your words are certain to be heeded,
then simply exhaust your loyalty."
The two men each presented their proposals to the king on the matter.
Shēnzǐ subtly observed what pleased the king and then spoke to him accordingly,
and the king was greatly pleased.
Shēnzǐ requested an official post for his cousin,
but Marquis Zhāo refused.
Shēnzǐ showed a resentful expression.
Marquis Zhāo said:
"This is not what I learned from you.
Should I grant your petition
and abandon your principles?
Or should I implement your methods
and reject your petition?
You once taught me to follow merit and achievement,
and to observe proper order.
Now you make this request—
which course should I follow?"
Shēnzǐ then withdrew to his quarters and begged for punishment,
saying:
"You, my lord, are truly the right ruler!"
Sū Qín, advocating the vertical alliance for Chǔ, persuaded the King of Hán, saying:
"Hán has the strongholds of Gǒng, Luò, and Chénggāo to the north,
the passes of Yíyáng and Chángbǎn to the west,
the territories of Wǎn, Ráng, and the Wěi River to the east,
and the Xíng Mountains to the south.
Its land extends a thousand lǐ,
with armored troops numbering several hundred thousand.
The world's strongest bows and crossbows
all come from Hán.
The Xīzǐ, Shǎofǔ Shílì, and Jùlái bows
can all shoot beyond six hundred paces.
Hán soldiers, drawing with their feet,
can shoot a hundred arrows without pause,
piercing the chest at long range
and striking the heart at close range.
The swords and halberds of Hán soldiers
all come from Míngshān, Tángxī, Mòyáng, and Hébó.
Dèngshī, Wǎnféng, Lóngyuān, and Dà'ē swords
can cut through horses and oxen on land,
strike swans and geese in water,
and when facing the enemy, slice through solid armor.
Armor, shields, helmets, iron masks,
leather archer's thumb rings, and armguards—
all are fully equipped.
With the bravery of Hán soldiers,
clad in sturdy armor,
treading strong crossbows,
girded with sharp swords,
one man can stand against a hundred—
this is no exaggeration.
Given Hán's strength
and Your Majesty's wisdom,
to instead face west and serve Qín,
declare yourself an eastern vassal,
build an imperial palace for them,
accept their caps and sashes,
offer seasonal sacrifices to them,
and submit with folded arms—
to bring shame upon the altars of soil and grain and become the laughingstock of the world—
nothing surpasses this folly.
Therefore, I hope Your Majesty will consider this carefully.
If Your Majesty serves Qín,
Qín will surely demand Yíyáng and Chénggāo.
If you yield them this year,
next year they will demand more territory.
If you give it,
soon there will be no land left to offer;
if you refuse,
you will abandon past efforts and later suffer even greater calamity.
Moreover, Your Majesty's land is finite,
while Qín's demands are endless.
To oppose endless demands
with finite land—
this is what is called purchasing resentment and buying disaster;
without fighting, your land will already be whittled away.
I have heard a common saying:
'Better to be a rooster's beak
than an ox's rump.'
Now if Your Majesty faces west, folds your arms, and serves Qín as a subject,
how is that different from being an ox's rump?
With Your Majesty's wisdom
and the support of Hán's powerful troops,
to bear the name of an ox's rump—
I privately feel shame for Your Majesty."
The King of Hán flushed with anger,
rolled up his sleeves and grasped his sword,
looked up to heaven and sighed deeply, saying:
"Even if I die,
I will never serve Qín.
Now, sir, you have conveyed the teachings of the King of Chǔ—
I respectfully commit my state to follow."
Zhāng Yí, advocating the horizontal alliance for Qín, persuaded the King of Hán, saying:
"Hán's terrain is rugged and harsh,
nestled among mountains.
Of the five grains that grow there,
it is not wheat but beans;
what the people eat
is mostly bean meals and leaf soup.
If there is one poor harvest,
the people cannot even fill themselves with chaff and husks.
The land area does not reach nine hundred lǐ,
and there is not enough food for two years.
Estimating Your Majesty's troops,
even if fully mobilized, they do not exceed three hundred thousand,
and among them are laborers and porters.
Deducting those guarding outposts, barriers, and fortifications,
the actual combat troops are no more than two hundred thousand.
Qín has over a million armored soldiers,
a thousand chariots,
ten thousand cavalry,
tiger-like warriors,
barefoot and bareheaded,
who charge with halberds held high—
their numbers are beyond calculation.
Qín's horses are superb,
its soldiers numerous;
leaping forward and kicking back,
their strides span three xún—
they are beyond measure.
The soldiers from east of the mountains
wear armor and helmets when joining battle,
but the men of Qín cast off their armor and charge the enemy naked,
carrying heads in their left hands
and live captives under their right arms.
Comparing Qín's soldiers to those east of the mountains
is like comparing Mèng Bēn to a coward;
pitting heavy force against them
is like pitting Wū Huò against an infant.
To deploy warriors like Mèng Bēn and Wū Huò
to attack a weak state that refuses to submit—
it is no different from dropping a weight of a thousand jūn
upon a bird's egg—
there will certainly be no chance of survival.
The other feudal lords do not consider their military weakness
or their scarcity of food,
but instead heed the sweet words and fine rhetoric of persuaders,
who collude and embellish for each other,
all saying:
'Follow my plan and you can become strong and dominate the world.'"
To disregard the long-term interests of the state
and heed momentary advice,
thereby misleading one's ruler—
nothing surpasses this in error.
If Your Majesty does not serve Qín,
Qín will dispatch troops to seize Yíyáng,
cutting off Hán's upper territories;
eastward, taking Chénggāo and Yíyáng,
then the Hóngtái Palace
and Sānglín Garden
will no longer belong to Your Majesty.
If Chénggāo is blocked
and the upper territories severed,
Your Majesty's state will be divided.
Serving Qín first ensures safety;
not serving Qín invites danger.
To create calamity yet seek fortune,
employ shallow plans while incurring deep resentment,
oppose Qín and align with Chǔ—
even if one wishes to avoid ruin,
it will be impossible.
Thus, for Your Majesty's strategy,
nothing is better than serving Qín.
What Qín desires most
is to weaken Chǔ,
and none can weaken Chǔ like Hán.
Not because Hán is stronger than Chǔ,
but due to its geographical advantage.
If now Your Majesty turns westward to serve Qín and attack Chǔ,
acting for our humble state,
the King of Qín will surely be pleased.
Attacking Chǔ to privately gain its land,
transforming calamity into pleasing Qín—
no strategy is more advantageous than this.
Therefore, the King of Qín sent his envoy to present this letter to Your Majesty's Yùshǐ,
awaiting a decision on the matter."
The King of Hán said:
"You honor me with your instruction.
I request to be treated as a commandery and county,
build an imperial palace,
offer seasonal sacrifices,
proclaim myself an eastern vassal,
and cede Yíyáng."
King Xuān said to Jiū Liú:
"I wish to employ both Gōng Zhòng and Gōng Shū.
Is this feasible?"
He replied:
"It is not.
Jìn employed six ministers and the state was divided;
Duke Jiǎn employed Tián Chéng and Jiàn Zhǐ, and Duke Jiǎn was assassinated;
Wèi employed both Xīshǒu and Zhāng Yí, and the lands west of the Yellow River were lost.
If Your Majesty employs both now,
the more powerful will internally build their factions,
while the less powerful will rely on external authority.
Ministers may either internally build factions to dominate their ruler,
or externally form alliances to split the territory.
Then Your Majesty's state will surely be endangered."
Zhāng Yí said to the King of Qí:
"Your Majesty should rather support Hán Péng,
and with him expel Zhāng Yí from Wèi.
Wèi will then appoint Xīshǒu as chancellor,
and subsequently, with Qí and Wèi, depose Hán Péng,
appointing Gōng Shū to attack Qín.
When Gōng Zhòng hears of this,
he will certainly not go to Qí.
Secure your position in Wèi,
and you will have no worries."
Chǔ Zhāo Xiàn served as chancellor of Hán.
Qín was about to attack Hán,
so Hán dismissed Zhāo Xiàn.
Zhāo Xiàn sent someone to tell Gōng Shū:
"It would be better to honor Zhāo Xiàn to solidify relations with Chǔ.
Qín will surely say that Chǔ and Hán have allied."
Qín attacked Xíng.
Hán sent someone to cede the territory of Nányáng.
After Qín had accepted the cession,
it attacked Xíng again.
Hán then ceded the territory of Nányáng.
Qín accepted the land,
and attacked Xíng again.
Chén Zhěn said to the King of Qín:
"The state's situation was unfavorable, hence the cession;
relations were not amicable, hence the territorial concession.
Now concessions have been made, yet relations remain unfriendly;
cession has occurred, yet military action does not cease.
I fear the states east of the mountains will have no means to cede territory or serve Your Majesty.
Moreover, when Your Majesty sought a hundred gold from Sānchuān, it was unobtainable,
yet seeking a thousand gold from Hán,
it was furnished in a single day.
Now if Your Majesty attacks Hán,
this would sever superior relations and merely solidify your private treasury.
I privately consider this inadvisable for Your Majesty."
Five states allied to attack Qín, with the King of Chǔ as the alliance leader.
They could not harm Qín,
and the troops halted and remained at Chénggāo.
Wèi Shùn said to the Lord of Shìqiū:
"When the five states cease,
they will surely attack Shìqiū
to compensate for military expenses.
If you provide me resources,
I request to stop the world from attacking Shìqiū for you."
The Lord of Shìqiū said:
"Good."
He then sent him.
Wèi Shùn went south to see the King of Chǔ, saying:
"Your Majesty allied five states to attack Qín westward,
but could not harm Qín.
The world will thereby belittle Your Majesty and esteem Qín.
Why does Your Majesty not test your alliances?"
The King of Chǔ said:
"How?"
Wèi Shùn said:
"When the world ceases,
they will surely attack Shìqiū to compensate for military expenses.
Your Majesty should order them not to attack Shìqiū.
If the five states respect Your Majesty,
they will heed your words and not attack Shìqiū;
if they do not respect Your Majesty,
they will defy your words and attack Shìqiū.
Thus, Your Majesty's standing will surely be clarified."
Therefore, the King of Chǔ tested his alliances, and Shìqiū was preserved.
Zhèng Qiáng transported eight hundred gold into Qín,
requesting to attack Hán.
Líng Xiàng said to Zhèng Qiáng:
"You use eight hundred gold to request an attack on an allied state of others;
Qín will certainly not heed you.
You should instead make the King of Qín suspect Gōng Shū."
Zhèng Qiáng said:
"How?"
He said:
"When Gōng Shū attacked Chǔ,
it was because Jǐsè was still there,
hence he spoke of prioritizing Chǔ.
Now he has already made the King of Chǔ send Jǐsè with a hundred chariots to reside in Yángzhái,
ordering Zhāo Xiàn to turn and stay with him.
After more than ten days,
they will have realized.
Now Jǐsè
is Gōng Shū's enemy;
and Zhāo Xiàn
is Gōng Shū's man.
When the King of Qín hears of this,
he will surely suspect Gōng Shū is acting for Chǔ."
Zhèng Qiáng drove Zhāng Yí away from Qín,
saying that Zhāng Yí's envoy
would certainly go to Chǔ.
Thus, he said to the Grand Steward:
"If you detain Zhāng Yí's envoy,
I will request to go west and scheme against Zhāng Yí in Qín."
Therefore, he took the opportunity to request of the King of Qín:
"Zhāng Yí sent someone to deliver the territory of Shàngyōng,
hence he sent your servant to bow twice and pay respects to the King of Qín."
The King of Qín was angered,
and Zhāng Yí fled.
During the Yíyáng campaign,
Yáng Dá said to Gōngsūn Xiǎn:
"I request to attack Western Zhōu with fifty thousand troops for you.
If we capture it,
it would be using the Nine Tripods to seal Gān Mào's fate.
Otherwise,
if Qín attacks Western Zhōu,
the world will detest it,
and they will swiftly rescue Hán.
Then Gān Mào's affairs will fail."
Qín besieged Yíyáng.
Yóu Téng said to Gōng Zhòng:
"Why not give Zhào's Lín, Líshí, and Qí to Qín,
using hostages to pledge territory?
Then Lóu Huǎn will surely be defeated.
Gather the troops of Hán and Zhào to confront Wèi,
and Lóu Bí will surely be defeated.
If Hán unifies,
Wèi will certainly betray Qín,
and Gān Mào will surely be defeated.
Use Chéngyáng to support Dí Qiáng in Qí,
and Chǔ will surely defeat him.
Wait until Qín is certainly defeated;
Qín will lose Wèi,
and Yíyáng will surely not be captured."
Gōng Zhòng, because of the Yíyáng affair, bore a grudge against Gān Mào.
Afterward,
Qín returned Wǔsuì to Hán.
Later,
the King of Qín firmly suspected that Gān Mào had used Wǔsuì to reconcile with Gōng Zhòng.
Dù Hè spoke for Gōng Zhòng to the King of Qín, saying:
"Míng also wishes to serve Your Majesty through Gān Mào."
The King of Qín was greatly angered at Gān Mào,
so Chūlǐ Jí was very pleased with Dù Liáo.
The states of Qín and Hán fought at Zhuózé,
and Hán was in dire straits.
Gōng Zhòng Míng said to the King of Hán:
"We cannot rely on our allied states.
Now Qín's intention is to attack Chǔ.
Your Majesty should rather, through Zhāng Yí, make peace with Qín,
bribing them with one major city,
and join them in attacking Chǔ.
This is a plan of exchanging one for two."
The King of Hán said:
"Good."
He then prepared Gōng Zhòng for the journey,
intending to go west and negotiate with Qín.
The King of Chǔ heard this and was greatly alarmed.
He summoned Chén Zhěn and told him.
Chén Zhěn said:
"Qín has long desired to attack us.
Now they have obtained a major city from Hán and are fully armed.
Qín and Hán will combine their forces and head south.
This is what Qín has been praying for in their ancestral temples.
Now that they have obtained it,
Chǔ will certainly be attacked. If Your Majesty
listens to your servant,
prepare by selecting troops from within the four borders,
declare that you are rescuing Hán,
and fill the roads with war chariots;
dispatch trusted envoys,
increase their carriages,
and make their gifts lavish,
so that Hán will believe Your Majesty is truly rescuing them.
Even if Hán does not ultimately heed us,
Hán will surely be grateful to Your Majesty,
and will certainly not march in formation with Qín.
Thus Qín and Hán will be at odds.
Even if their troops arrive,
Chǔ will not suffer greatly.
If Hán is able to heed us and break off peace with Qín,
Qín will surely be enraged,
and harbor deep resentment toward Hán. ,
Hán, having obtained Chǔ's rescue,
will certainly look down on Qín.
Looking down on Qín,
their response to Qín will surely be disrespectful.
In this way, we will entangle the troops of Qín and Hán,
and spare Chǔ from calamity."
The King of Chǔ was greatly pleased.
He then prepared by selecting troops from within the four borders,
declared that he was rescuing Hán,
dispatched trusted envoys,
increased their carriages,
and made their gifts lavish.
He said to the King of Hán:
"Although my humble state is small,
I have already mobilized all my forces.
I hope your great state will act as you wish toward Qín.
My humble state will stand with Hán to the death."
The King of Hán was greatly pleased,
and stopped Gōng Zhòng.
Gōng Zhòng said:
"This will not do.
The one who has told us the truth is
Qín;
the one who rescues us with empty promises is
Chǔ.
To rely on Chǔ's empty promises
and lightly break off with the powerful enemy Qín
will surely make us the laughingstock of the world.
Moreover, Chǔ and Hán are not brotherly states,
nor have they previously agreed to jointly attack Qín.
Qín desires to attack Chǔ,
so Chǔ has raised troops under the pretext of rescuing Hán.
This must be Chén Zhěn's scheme.
Moreover, Your Majesty has already sent someone to report to Qín.
If you do not proceed now,
you will be deceiving Qín.
To lightly invite the disaster of a powerful Qín
and trust the schemes of Chǔ's minister—
Your Majesty will surely regret it."
The King of Hán did not listen,
and broke off peace with Qín.
Qín indeed became greatly enraged,
raised an army, and fought with Hán at Ànmén.
Chǔ's rescue did not arrive,
and Hán suffered a great defeat.
Hán's troops were not weakened,
nor were its people ignorant.
Yet its troops were captured by Qín,
and its wisdom was mocked by Chǔ,
all because it mistakenly listened to Chén Zhěn
and failed to heed the plans of Hán Míng.
Yán Shuài went to see Gōng Zhòng,
but Gōng Zhòng would not see him.
Yán Shuài said to Gōng Zhòng's attendant:
"Gōng Zhòng must think that I am insincere,
and therefore will not see me.
Gōng Zhòng is fond of women,
yet I say he is fond of scholars;
Gōng Zhòng is stingy with wealth,
yet I say he is generous;
Gōng Zhòng lacks virtue,
yet I say he is righteous.
From now on,
I will simply speak the truth."
Gōng Zhòng's attendant reported this to Gōng Zhòng,
and Gōng Zhòng immediately rose to see him.
Hán Gōng Zhòng said to Xiàng Shòu:
"A cornered beast will overturn the chariot.
You have defeated Hán,
humiliated me, Gōng Zhòng.
I, Gōng Zhòng, have gathered the state and again served Qín,
believing that I would surely be enfeoffed.
Now you have made peace with Chǔ,
and within Chǔ enfeoffed a minor official with Guìyáng.
If Qín and Chǔ unite,
and again attack Hán,
Hán will surely perish.
I, Gōng Zhòng, will personally lead my private followers to fight against Qín.
I hope you will consider this carefully."
Xiàng Shòu said:
"I united Qín and Chǔ
not to oppose Hán.
You should arrange a meeting for me."
Gōng Zhòng said:
"The alliance between Qín and Hán can be restored."
The reply was:
"I wish to report something to you.
There is a proverb:
'To value what makes one valuable is true value.'
Now the king's affection and familiarity with you
is not equal to that with Gōngsūn Hǎo;
his recognition of your abilities
is not equal to that with Gān Mào.
Now these two men
are both no longer trusted with affairs,
yet you alone share with the king the authority to decide state matters.
This is because they have lost their positions.
Gōngsūn Hǎo sides with Hán,
and Gān Wù sides with Wèi,
so the king does not trust them.
Now Qín and Chǔ contend for supremacy,
and you side with Chǔ.
This puts you in the same category as Gōngsūn Hǎo and Gān Mào.
How are you different from them?
Everyone says Chǔ is fickle,
yet you insist on it,
which is self-importance.
You should rather discuss with the king how to handle Chǔ's changes,
and befriend Hán to prepare for it.
If you do this,
then there will be no calamity.
Hán first followed Gōngsūn Hǎo with its state,
and later entrusted the state to Gān Mào.
Thus Hán
is your enemy.
Now if you speak of befriending Hán to prepare against Chǔ,
that is recommending externally without avoiding enemies."
Xiàng Shòu said:
"I very much wish to ally with Hán."
The reply was:
"Gān Mào promised Gōng Zhòng Wǔsuì,
and to return the people of Yíyáng.
Now if you merely order its recovery,
it will be very difficult."
Xiàng Zǐ said:
"Then what should be done?
Wǔsuì ultimately cannot be obtained."
The reply was:
"Why don't you, on behalf of Hán, ask Chǔ for Yǐngchuān through Qín?
This is land originally belonging to Hán.
If you ask and obtain it,
that will demonstrate your influence in Chǔ and earn Hán's gratitude with the land.
If you ask and do not obtain it,
then the enmity between Hán and Chǔ will remain unresolved,
and both will turn to Qín.
Qín and Chǔ contend for supremacy,
and if you blame Chǔ and attack Hán,
that benefits Qín."
Xiàng Zǐ said:
"What should be done?"
The reply was:
"This is a good plan.
Gān Mào wishes to use Wèi to take Qí,
Gōngsūn Hǎo wishes to use Hán to take Qí.
Now you have taken Yíyáng as an achievement,
and have won over Chǔ and Hán to secure it.
If you then condemn the crimes of Qí and Wèi,
that will render Gōngsūn Hǎo and Gān Mào useless."
Someone said to Gōng Zhòng:
"Listening means listening to the state,
not necessarily to facts.
Thus the former kings listened to proverbs in the market,
and I hope you will listen to my words."
You sought neutrality from Qin,
but were unable to obtain it.
You befriended Gōngsūn Hé to make things difficult for Gān Mào,
urged Qí troops to encourage stopping Wèi,
while Chǔ and Zhào are both your enemies.
I fear the state will suffer because of this,
and I hope you will again seek neutrality from Qin."
Gōng Zhòng said:
"What should I do?"
The reply was:
"The King of Qin believes Gōngsūn Hé sides with you and does not listen to him,
while Gān Mào is not on good terms with you and does not speak for you.
Why don't you take advantage of Xíng Yuàn to speak with the King of Qin?
Xíng Yuàn, as a minister of the King of Qin, is impartial.
I ask to speak to the King of Qin on your behalf:
'Is it more beneficial for Qin if Qí and Wèi unite or separate?
Is Qin stronger if Qí and Wèi are divided or united?'
The King of Qin will certainly say:
'If Qí and Wèi separate,
then Qin is weighty;
if they unite,
then Qin is light.
If Qí and Wèi are divided,
then Qin is strong;
if they unite,
then Qin is weak.'
I will then say:
'Now if Your Majesty listens to Gōngsūn Hé and uses Hán and Qín troops to respond to Qí and attack Wèi,
Wèi will not dare to fight,
will cede territory and unite with Qí—
this makes Qin light,
and I consider Gōngsūn Hé disloyal.
Now if Your Majesty listens to Gān Mào,
and uses Hán and Qín troops to hold Wèi and attack Qí,
Qí will not dare to fight,
will not seek to cede territory and unite with Wèi—
this also makes Qin light,
and I consider Gān Mào disloyal.
Therefore, it would be better for Your Majesty to order Hán to remain neutral and attack Qí.
The King of Qí will claim to rescue Wèi to strengthen it,
but Qí and Wèi will not be able to agree with each other,
and will remain separated by military affairs for a long time.
If Your Majesty wishes,
trust Gōngsūn Hé with Qí,
and for Hán take Nányáng,
exchange Gǔchuān and return—
this is King Huì's desire.
If Your Majesty wishes,
trust Gān Mào with Wèi,
and use Hán and Qín troops to hold Wèi and repel Qí—
this is King Wǔ's desire.
I believe ordering Hán to remain neutral and strengthen Qí
is Qin's most urgent matter.
Gōngsūn Hé sides with Qí and is unwilling to speak,
Gān Mào is weak and dares not petition—
these two men
are Your Majesty's great troubles.
I hope Your Majesty will consider this carefully.'"
Gōng Zhòng of Hán served as prime minister.
Qí and Chǔ maintained good relations with Qín.
Qín and Wèi met,
intending to befriend Qí and sever Qí's ties with Chǔ.
The King sent Jǐng Lǐ to Qín,
and Lǐ participated in the meeting between Qín and Wèi.
The King of Chǔ was angry with Jǐng Lǐ,
fearing that Qí would suspect Chǔ of having secret dealings with Qín and Wèi because of the meeting,
and intended to punish Jǐng Lǐ.
Someone spoke to the King of Chǔ:
"I congratulate Lǐ for participating in the meeting.
The meeting between Qín and Wèi
was intended to unite Qí and Qín and sever Qí's ties with Chǔ.
Now that Lǐ participated in the meeting,
Qí has no way to trust that Wèi has united with itself and Qín to attack Chǔ,
and Qí also fears that Chǔ has secret dealings with Qín and Wèi,
so it will certainly value Chǔ.
Therefore, Lǐ's participation in the meeting
is a great asset to Your Majesty.
If Lǐ had not participated in the meeting,
Wèi's severance of ties between Qí and Chǔ would have been clear.
Qí and Chǔ would have believed it,
and would certainly have looked down on Your Majesty.
Therefore, it would be better for Your Majesty not to punish Jǐng Lǐ,
so that Wèi,
by showing Qí that it has Qín, will certainly value Chǔ,
and moreover will suspect Qín and Wèi regarding Qí."
The King said:
"Agreed."
Thus, he did not punish him and instead increased his rank.
The King said:
"Earlier you said, 'The world lacks the Way,'
but now you say,
'They are about to attack Yān'—why is that?"
The reply was: "Now, to say a horse is very strong is true,
but to say it can lift a thousand jūn is not—why?
Because a thousand jūn
is not within a horse's capacity.
Now, to say Chǔ is powerful and large is true,
but to cross Zhào and Wèi to wage war against Yān—
is that within Chǔ's capacity?
Moreover, if it is not within Chǔ's capacity
and Chǔ attempts it,
it will exhaust Chǔ.
Which is more convenient for Your Majesty:
a strong Chǔ or an exhausted Chǔ?"
Someone said to the King of Wèi:
"Your Majesty should alert the four borders within your state:
those who follow Your Majesty
must within ten days
prepare fully or face death.
Your Majesty should then take your pleasure boats and strike upon them.
I will go to Chǔ for Your Majesty,
and when Your Majesty awaits my return,
then proceed."
Lord Chūnshēn heard of this,
and said to the envoy:
"You may return for me,
and do not see the King.
Within ten days,
tens of thousands of troops
will now cross into Wèi's territory."
The Qín envoy heard of this
and reported it to the King of Qín.
The King of Qín said to the King of Wèi:
"If the great state has intentions,
it is enough to come with this."
Guān Yǎng said to Lord Chūnshēn:
"Everyone considers Chǔ strong,
but you use it weakly—
in my view, it is not so.
Our former rulers
were not attacked for over twenty years.
Now Qín wants to send troops across the Miǎn'ài Pass,
but cannot;
to borrow the road through the two Zhōu states, bypass Hán, and attack Chǔ—
is impossible.
Now it is not so:
Wèi is about to perish soon,
and cannot cherish its Xǔ, Yānlíng, and Wú,
but will cede them to Qín, a distance of one hundred and sixty lǐ.
What I foresee
is that the day of battle between Qín and Chǔ has arrived."
Gōng Zhòng was repeatedly untrustworthy with the various states,
and the states shunned him.
He offered the state to Chǔ in the south,
but the King of Chǔ would not listen.
Sū Dài said to the King of Chǔ:
"It would be better to listen and guard against his betrayal.
When Gōng Zhòng betrays,
he often relies on Zhào and rebels against Chǔ,
or relies on Qí and rebels against Qín.
Now the four states shun him,
and he has nowhere to turn—
he is also deeply troubled.
This is when he acts like Wěi Shēng."
Chǔ besieged Yōngshì for five months.
Hán ordered envoys to seek aid from Qín,
with carriages and caps in constant view,
but the Qín army did not descend from Xiáo.
Hán again ordered Shàng Jìn to go to Qín as envoy,
who said to the King of Qín:
"Hán, in relation to Qín,
serves as a hidden shield when at rest,
and as geese in flight when on the move.
Now Hán is already in distress,
yet the Qín army does not descend from Xiáo.
I have heard it said:
'When the lips are gone, the teeth feel cold.'
I hope Your Majesty will consider this carefully."
Queen Dowager Xuān said:
"Many envoys have come,
but only Shàng Zǐ's words are correct."
She summoned Shàng Zǐ to enter.
Queen Dowager Xuān said to Shàng Zǐ:
"When I served the late king,
if the late king placed his thigh on my body,
I felt strained and weary;
but if he placed his whole body upon me,
I did not feel heavy—
why?
Because there was some benefit in it for me.
Now, to aid Hán,
if the troops are not numerous,
and the provisions not ample,
then it will not be enough to rescue Hán.
To rescue Hán in its crisis
costs a thousand gold daily—
is it not possible to let me have some benefit in it?"
Shàng Jìn returned and reported to the King of Hán in writing.
The King of Hán dispatched Zhāng Cuì.
Zhāng Cuì claimed to be ill,
traveling only one county per day.
When Zhāng Cuì arrived,
Gān Mào said:
"Hán is in urgent straits,
yet you, sir, have come despite your illness."
Zhāng Cuì said:
"Hán is not yet in urgent straits,
but it is about to be."
Gān Mào said:
"Qín is a powerful state and knows the King well.
Whether Hán is in urgency or not, none are unaware. Now you, sir, say it is not urgent—
is that acceptable?"
Zhāng Cuì said:
"If Hán were truly urgent, it would break and submit to Chǔ.
How would I dare to come?"
Gān Mào said:
"Sir, say no more."
Gān Mào entered and spoke to the King of Qín, saying:
"Gōng Zhòng, holding power, has obtained Qín's troops,
hence he dares to resist Chǔ.
Now Yōngshì is besieged,
yet Qín's troops do not descend from Xiáo,
this means abandoning Hán.
Gōng Zhòng will then bow his head and cease attending court,
and Gōng Shū will ally the state south with Chǔ.
If Chǔ and Hán become one,
Wèi will not dare to disobey,
thus Chǔ will use three states to plot against Qín.
In this way, the conditions for attacking Qín will be formed.
I do not know whether it is better to sit and await attack,
or to gain the advantage of attacking others?"
The King of Qín said:
"Well said."
He indeed dispatched troops to Xiáo to rescue Hán.
Chǔ besieged Yōngshì,
Hán ordered Lěng Xiàng to borrow aid from Qín,
Qín therefore sent the envoy Gōngsūn Mèi into Hán.
Gōng Zhòng said:
"Do you believe Qín will rescue Hán?
Or not?"
He replied:
"The King of Qín's words were:
'I request passage through Nánzhèng and Lántián to attack Chǔ,
and will dispatch troops to Sānchuān to await you.'
It seems they will not join,
but will encamp at Nánzhèng."
Gōng Zhòng said:
"What is to be done?"
He replied:
"The King of Qín will certainly follow Zhāng Yí's old scheme.
When King Wēi of Chǔ attacked Liáng,
Zhāng Yí said to the King of Qín:
'If we join Chǔ to attack Liáng,
Wèi will break and submit to Chǔ.
Hán is firmly its ally,
thus Qín will be isolated.
Therefore, it is better to send troops to strengthen Wèi.'
Thereupon they attacked Píshì.
Wèi was strengthened,
King Wēi was enraged,
Chǔ and Wèi fought a great battle,
and Qín took the lands west of the river and returned.
Now they will openly declare they will rescue Hán,
but secretly befriend Chǔ.
You, relying on Qín and feeling strengthened,
will certainly lightly engage Chǔ in battle.
Chǔ, secretly knowing Qín will not be used,
will certainly easily contend with you.
If you defeat Chǔ,
they will then join you in riding over Chǔ,
exchanging Sānchuān and returning.
If you do not defeat Chǔ,
they will block Sānchuān and defend it,
and you will be unable to rescue it.
I deeply fear this matter.
Sīmǎ Kāng has returned to Yǐng three times,
Gān Mào met Zhāo Xiàn at the border,
their words speak of receiving seals,
but in reality, there is still an agreement."
Gōng Zhòng said in fear:
"Then what is to be done?"
He replied:
"You must put Hán first and Qín second,
put yourself first and Zhāng Yí second.
It would be better for you to urgently ally the state with Qí and Chǔ.
Qín will certainly entrust the state to you to resolve the attack.
Thus, what you outwardly reject is merely Yí,
but in reality, you will not lose Qín."
Gōng Zhòng was exchanging territory between Hán and Wèi.
Gōng Shū opposed it but was not heeded,
and was about to flee.
Shǐ Tì said to Gōng Shū:
"If you flee,
then the exchange will certainly succeed.
You will have no excuse to return later,
and moreover, you will show the world that you are slighted.
You would do better to comply.
If Hán's territory is exchanged in the north,
it will harm Zhào;
if Wèi's territory is exchanged in the south,
it will harm Chǔ.
You should inform Chǔ and Zhào.
Chǔ and Zhào will detest it.
When Zhào hears of it,
they will raise troops and approach Yángcháng.
When Chǔ hears of it,
they will dispatch troops and approach Fāngchéng,
and the exchange will certainly fail."
Qí Xuān advised the King of Hán to win over Qín,
saying:
"Prepare one hundred chariots for Gōng Shū,
send word to Chǔ,
and exchange Sānchuān.
Then have Gōng Zhòng say to the King of Qín:
'Sānchuān says,
the King of Qín will certainly seize us.
The King of Hán's mind cannot be eased.
Why does Your Majesty not try sending Xiāngzǐ as a hostage to Hán,
to let the King of Hán know that Your Majesty will not seize Sānchuān?'
Thereby, you can send out Xiāngzǐ and show favor to the crown prince."
During the battle of Xiānglíng,
Bì Cháng said to Gōng Shū:
"I request that you do not use troops,
and both Chǔ and Wèi will be grateful to your state.
Chǔ wishes to install Prince Gāo,
and will certainly send troops against Wèi.
Why do you not have someone persuade Zhāozǐ, saying:
'The battle may not be won,
I request to raise troops for you to go to Wèi.'
You will have an excuse not to fight,
and thereupon Crown Prince Biǎn,
Zhāo Yáng, and the King of Liáng will all be grateful to you."
Gōng Shū sent Féng Jūn to Qín,
fearing he would be detained,
and instructed Yáng Xiàng to persuade the King of Qín, saying:
"Detaining Féng Jūn to please Hán's ministers
is not the wisest course.
My lord would do better to treat Féng Jūn well,
and provide him with resources from Qín.
If Féng Jūn broadens the King's favor and does not heed Gōng Shū,
contending with the crown prince,
then the King's grace will spread,
and it will harm Hán."
Someone said to Gōng Shū:
"You wish to obtain Wǔsuì from Qín, but do not worry that Chǔ can raise troops beyond the river.
You should have someone intimidate the King of Chǔ,
and have someone seek Wǔsuì from Qín for you.
Say to the King of Chǔ:
'Dispatch a heavy envoy to seek Wǔsuì from Qín for Hán.
If the King of Qín agrees,
this will show that your orders are heeded by a lord of ten thousand chariots.
Hán, obtaining Wǔsuì, will resent Qín,
and, free from Qín's troubles, will obtain Chǔ.
Hán will become merely a county of Chǔ.
If Qín does not agree,
then the enmity between Qín and Hán will deepen,
and they will turn to Chǔ.'"
Someone said to Gōng Shū:
"Riding in a boat,
if the boat leaks and is not plugged,
the boat will sink.
Plugging the leaky boat,
yet lightly regarding the waves of Yánghóu,
the boat will capsize.
Now you, relying on your persuasiveness with Xuē Gōng, slight Qín.
This is like plugging a leaky boat yet lightly regarding the waves of Yánghóu.
I hope you will consider this."
Qí ordered Zhōu Zuì to go to Zhèng,
to establish Hán Rǎo and depose Gōng Shū.
Zhōu Zuì was troubled by this,
saying:
"Gōng Shū has ties with the Lord of Zhōu.
Now I am sent to Zhèng,
to establish Hán Rǎo and depose Gōng Shū.
As the saying goes: 'Anger in the chamber shows on the face in the market.'
Now Gōng Shū will resent Qí,
and having no recourse,
will certainly turn to the Lord of Zhōu and deeply resent me."
Shǐ Shě said: "Go ahead,
I will ensure that Gōng Shū certainly values you."
Zhōu Zuì traveled to Zhèng,
and Gōng Shū was greatly angered.
Shǐ Shě entered and said:
"Zhōu Zuì originally did not wish to come as envoy,
I privately forced him.
Zhōu Zuì did not wish to come,
for your sake;
my forcing him,
was also for your sake."
Gōng Shū said: “I beg to hear your reasoning.”
The reply was:
“Among the ministers of Qí, one of the gentlemen had a dog,
a fierce dog that could not be shouted at,
for if shouted at, it would certainly bite people.
A guest requested to shout at it;
he glared at it fiercely and then shouted slowly,
and the dog did not move.
He shouted again,
and the dog then lost its intention to bite people.
Now, Zhōu Zuì is certainly willing to serve Your Excellency,
but due to unavoidable circumstances, he has come as an envoy.
He will courteously present his words and speak slowly,
so the King of Zhèng will certainly think the King of Qí is not urgent,
and will certainly not grant it.
If Zhōu Zuì does not come,
someone else will certainly come.
The envoy who comes will have no ties with you,
and will wish to gain favor with Hán Rǎo.
He will certainly act hastily,
and speak urgently,
so the King of Zhèng will certainly grant it.”
Gōng Shū said: “Excellent.”
He then treated Zhōu Zuì with great respect.
The king indeed did not grant Hán Rǎo’s request.
Hán Gōng Shū and Jǐsè contended for the state.
Zhèng Qiáng was sent by the King of Chǔ to Hán,
and falsely used Xīnchéng and Yángrén to support the heir,
enabling him to contend with Gōng Shū for the state.
Chǔ was angered
and intended to punish him.
Zhèng Qiáng said:
“Your servant falsely gave them to him
for the sake of the state.
Your servant said,
if the heir obtains Xīnchéng and Yángrén
to contend with Gōng Shū for the state,
and succeeds in preserving himself,
Wèi will certainly put pressure on the Hán clan;
when the Hán clan is under pressure,
they will certainly entrust their fate to Chǔ.
Then, how would they dare to demand Xīnchéng and Yángrén?
If they fight and do not win,
flee and do not die,
they will soon arrive here,
and how would they dare to speak of land?”
The King of Chǔ said: “Excellent.”
He then did not punish him.
Hán Gōng Shū and Jǐsè contended for the state.
The palace attendant Qiáng said to the heir:
“It would be better to strike Gōng Shū quickly
before the Qí army enters.”
The heir said: “That cannot be done.
Fighting within the state will certainly cause division.”
The reply was: “If the matter is not accomplished,
your person will certainly be in danger.
How can you still plan for the preservation of the state?”
The heir did not listen.
The Qí army indeed entered,
and the heir fled.
Qí Míng said to Gōng Shū:
“Qí expelled Jǐsè,
and Chǔ treated him well.
Now Chǔ greatly desires good relations with Qí.
Why do you not have the King of Qí say to the King of Chǔ:
‘Your Majesty, expel Jǐsè for me and drive him to desperation.’
If Chǔ listens,
then Qí and Chǔ will unite,
and Jǐsè will flee.
If the King of Chǔ does not listen,
then he will have secret dealings with Hán.”
Gōng Shū was about to kill Jǐsè.
Someone said to Gōng Shū:
“The heir values you
because he fears Jǐsè.
Now if Jǐsè dies,
the heir will have no worries,
and will certainly slight you.
The ministers of Hán see that the king is old,
and hope that the heir will take power,
so they are certainly eager to serve him.
If the heir has no external worries from Jǐsè,
and internally gathers the various ministers to assist him,
you will certainly be slighted.
It would be better not to kill Jǐsè,
but to use him to intimidate the heir.
Then the heir will certainly value you for life.”
Gōng Shū was about to kill Jǐsè.
Sòng Hè spoke on his behalf to Gōng Shū, saying:
“Jǐsè is able to cause turmoil
because internally he has the support of his father and brothers,
and externally he has the support of Qín and Chǔ.
Now if you kill him,
the heir will have no worries,
and will certainly slight you.
The ministers of Hán know that the king is old and the heir is settled,
so they will certainly secretly serve him.
If Qín and Chǔ lose Hán,
they will certainly secretly support Bó Yīng.
Bó Yīng is another Jǐsè.
It would be better for you not to kill him.
Bó Yīng, in fear,
will certainly seek protection from you.
The ministers of Hán cannot be certain that Jǐsè will not return,
so they will certainly not dare to assist Bó Yīng in causing turmoil.
Qín and Chǔ, supporting Jǐsè, will block Bó Yīng.
Bó Yīng will have no external authority from Qín and Chǔ,
and no internal support from his father and brothers,
so he will certainly be unable to cause turmoil.
This is advantageous for you.”
Someone said to Xīnchéng Jūn:
“Gōng Shū and Bó Yīng fear that Qín and Chǔ will support Jǐsè internally.
Why do you not seek a hostage from Chǔ for Hán?
If the King of Chǔ listens and sends a hostage to Hán,
then Gōng Shū and Bó Yīng will certainly know that Qín and Chǔ do not take Jǐsè seriously,
and will certainly ally Hán with Qín and Chǔ.
Qín and Chǔ, with Hán in hand, will pressure Wèi,
and the Wèi clan will not dare to move eastward,
leaving Qí isolated.
You can also have Qín seek a hostage from Chǔ.
If Chǔ does not listen,
then resentment will form with Hán.
Hán, with Qí and Wèi in hand, will look askance at Chǔ,
and the King of Chǔ will certainly value you.
You, with the weight of Qín and Chǔ,
and having accumulated virtue with Hán,
then Gōng Shū and Bó Yīng will certainly serve you with the affairs of the state.”
When Hú Yǎn sent Jǐsè out of Chǔ,
he instructed Gōng Zhòng to say to the King of Wèi:
“The heir is in Chǔ,
so Hán does not dare to break with Chǔ.
Why do you not try to support Gōngzǐ Jiù
and request the heir for him? Then have someone say to the King of Chǔ:
‘If Hán establishes Gōngzǐ Jiù and abandons Jǐsè,
then Your Majesty holds an empty hostage.
It would be better for Your Majesty to quickly return Jǐsè.
When Jǐsè enters,
he will certainly use the power of Hán to take revenge on Wèi,
and will be grateful to Your Majesty.’”
Jǐsè fled to Chǔ,
and Chǔ was about to win over Qín and restore him.
Someone said to Mǐ Róng:
“It was Chǔ that deposed Gōng Shū and made Jǐsè chancellor.
Now Jǐsè has fled to Chǔ,
and Chǔ is again winning over Qín to restore him.
On the day Jǐsè enters Zhèng,
Hán
will become a county of Chǔ.
It would be better for you to have the King of Qín congratulate Bó Yīng on his establishment.
If Hán breaks with Chǔ,
they will certainly eagerly serve Qín.
Qín, with Hán in hand, will befriend Wèi,
and Qí and Chǔ, arriving later, will be the first to perish.
This is the kingly enterprise.”
Lěng Xiàng said to Hán Jiù:
“Jǐsè has fled to Chǔ,
and the King of Chǔ greatly desires to restore him.
He has over a hundred thousand Chǔ troops outside Fāngchéng.
I request to have Chǔ build a city of ten thousand households next to Yōngshì.
Hán will certainly raise troops to stop it,
and you will certainly be appointed as commander.
You can then use the troops of Chǔ and Hán to support Jǐsè and bring him into Zhèng.
When Jǐsè enters, he will be grateful to you,
and will certainly use Hán and Chǔ to serve you.”
Chǔ ordered Jǐng Lǐ to enter Hán,
and Hán was about to send Bó Yīng to Qín.
Jǐng Lǐ was troubled by this.
Lěng Xiàng said to Bó Yīng:
“If the heir enters Qín,
Qín will certainly detain the heir and ally with Chǔ
to restore Jǐsè.
Then the heir will instead be abandoned.”
Hán Jiù was established as ruler but his position was not yet secure.
His younger brother was in Zhōu,
and Zhōu wished to send him with a hundred chariots and great ceremony,
but feared that if Hán Jiù entered Hán, he might not be established.
Qíwú Huī said:
“It would be better to give him a hundred gold pieces to follow him.
If Hán Jiù is established,
it can be considered a congratulatory gift;
if he is not established,
then say it was to deliver a criminal.”
Shǐ Jí was an envoy from Hán to Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ asked him:
"What doctrine does the guest follow?"
He replied:
"I study the teachings of Lièzǐ Yǔkòu."
The king asked:
"What does he value?"
He replied:
"He values correctness."
The king said:
"Can correctness also be used to govern a state?"
He replied:
"It can."
The king said:
"In the state of Chǔ, there are many robbers.
Can correctness be used to guard against robbers?"
He replied:
"It can."
The king said:
"How can one use correctness to guard against robbers?"
Shortly after, a magpie alighted on the roof.
Shǐ Jí said:
"May I ask what the people of Chǔ call this bird?"
The king said:
"They call it a magpie."
Shǐ Jí said:
"Can they call it a crow?"
The king said:
"They cannot."
Shǐ Jí said:
"Now, in Your Majesty's state, there are the Zhùguó, Lìngyǐn, Sīmǎ, and Diǎnlìng.
When appointing officials and setting up clerks,
they must be said to be honest and competent.
Yet now robbers and thieves act openly,
and they cannot be stopped.
This is a case where the crow is not a crow,
and the magpie is not a magpie."
Hán Guī was the chancellor of Hán.
Yán Suì was highly regarded by the ruler.
The two men harmed each other.
Yán Suì spoke frankly in political discussions,
pointing out Hán Guī's faults.
Hán Guī therefore berated him in court.
Yán Suì drew his sword and rushed at him,
but was separated and rescued.
Thereupon, Yán Suì, fearing execution,
fled and went into exile,
traveling to seek someone who could take revenge on Hán Guī for him.
He reached Qí.
Someone from Qí said:
"In Zhǐ, in Shēnjǐnglǐ, there is Niè Zhèng,
a brave and fierce warrior.
He is avoiding enemies and hiding among butchers."
Yán Suì secretly befriended Niè Zhèng,
treating him with deep affection.
Niè Zhèng asked:
"What do you wish to use me for?"
Yán Suì said:
"The time I have had to serve you is short,
and matters are now pressing.
How dare I make a request?"
Thereupon, Yán Suì prepared wine
and toasted before Niè Zhèng's mother.
Zhòngzǐ presented a hundred yì of gold,
stepping forward to offer longevity wishes to Niè Zhèng's mother.
Niè Zhèng was startled
and increasingly puzzled by his generosity,
firmly declining Yán Zhòngzǐ's offer.
Zhòngzǐ insisted on presenting it,
but Niè Zhèng declined, saying:
"I have an aged mother.
My family is poor.
I have traveled here and work as a dog butcher,
so I can obtain delicacies morning and evening to support my parent.
My parent's provisions are sufficient.
In righteousness, I dare not accept Zhòngzǐ's gift."
Yán Zhòngzǐ dismissed the others
and then said to Niè Zhèng:
"I have an enemy,
and I have traveled among many feudal lords.
Yet when I came to Qí,
I heard that your sense of righteousness is very high.
Therefore, I directly offered a hundred pieces of gold
specifically to cover the expenses for your mother's coarse food,
to befriend you and share joy.
How dare I have any request?"
Niè Zhèng said:
"The reason I lower my aspirations and humble myself,
living in the marketplace,
is solely to luckily support my aged mother.
While my aged mother is alive,
I, Zhèng, dare not pledge my life to anyone."
Yán Zhòngzǐ firmly insisted,
but Niè Zhèng ultimately refused to accept.
However, Zhòngzǐ finally performed the礼节 of host and guest and departed.
A long time later,
Niè Zhèng's mother died.
After she was buried
and the mourning period ended,
Niè Zhèng said:
"Alas!
I, Zhèng, am but a man of the marketplace,
wielding a knife to butcher.
Yet Yán Zhòngzǐ is a minister and chancellor of the feudal lords.
He did not consider a thousand lǐ too far,
but humbly came with his carriage and retinue to befriend me.
What I offered him in return was extremely meager and insignificant.
I have not accomplished any great deed worthy of mention,
yet Yán Zhòngzǐ offered a hundred pieces of gold for my parent's longevity.
Although I did not accept it,
this shows he deeply understood me, Zhèng.
A worthy man, moved by indignation over a slight grievance,
drew close and trusted a person in poverty and obscurity.
How could I, Zhèng, alone remain silent and do nothing?
Moreover, he previously sought me, Zhèng,
but I, Zhèng, only declined because of my aged mother.
Now my aged mother has ended her natural lifespan.
I, Zhèng, will be used by one who knows me."
Thereupon, he went west to Púyáng
and saw Yán Zhòngzǐ, saying:
"The reason I previously did not agree to Zhòngzǐ's request
was solely because my parent was alive.
Now, unfortunately, my parent is gone.
Whom does Zhòngzǐ wish to take revenge upon?"
Yán Zhòngzǐ fully informed him:
"My enemy is Hán's chancellor Guī. Guī
is also the younger uncle of the ruler of Hán.
His clan is powerful,
and guards are stationed around him.
I sent men to assassinate him,
but in the end, none could succeed.
Now, fortunately, you do not reject me.
I ask to prepare more carriages, riders, and strong men
to serve as your wings."
Zhèng said:
"Between Hán and Wèi,
the distance is not great.
Now, to kill the chancellor of another state,
who is also a relative of that state's ruler—
in such a situation, one cannot involve many people.
With many people, it is inevitable that something will go wrong.
If something goes wrong, then the plan will leak.
If the plan leaks,
then the entire state of Hán will become Zhòngzǐ's enemy.
Would that not be perilous!"
Thereupon, he declined the carriages, riders, and followers.
He took his leave
and went alone, carrying his sword, to Hán.
It happened that Hán was holding a meeting at Dōngmèng.
The King of Hán and the chancellor were both there,
with many guards holding weapons and halberds.
Niè Zhèng went straight in,
ascended the steps, and stabbed Hán Guī. Hán Guī ran and embraced Āihóu.
Niè Zhèng stabbed him,
also hitting Āihóu.
Those on the left and right fell into great chaos.
Niè Zhèng shouted loudly,
killing several tens of people.
Then he skinned his own face, gouged out his eyes,
cut open his own belly and pulled out his intestines,
and thus died.
Hán took Niè Zhèng's corpse to the marketplace
and offered a thousand pieces of gold for his identification.
For a long time, no one knew who he was.
Niè Zhèng's elder sister heard of this
and said:
"My brother was of utmost worthiness. I cannot cherish my own body
and extinguish my brother's name.
That would not be my brother's intent."
Thereupon, she went to Hán.
Looking at it, she said:
"How brave!
The loftiness of his heroic spirit!
This surpasses Bēn and Yù and elevates Chéng Jīng.
Now he has died without a name.
Our parents are already deceased.
There are no other brothers.
This he did for my sake.
To cherish my own life and not proclaim my brother's name—
I cannot bear it."
Thereupon, she embraced the corpse and wept over it, saying:
"This is my brother,
Niè Zhèng of Shēnjǐnglǐ in Zhǐ."
She then also killed herself beside the corpse.
Jìn, Chǔ, Qí, and Wèi heard of this and said:
"Not only was Zhèng capable,
but also his elder sister
was a woman of exceptional virtue."
The reason Niè Zhèng's name spread to later generations
was that his elder sister did not avoid the punishment of being minced into paste,
in order to make his name known.
Someone said to Hán Gōngzhòng:
"For twins who look alike,
only their mother can tell them apart;
for benefits and harms that appear similar,
only the wise can distinguish them.
Now your state,
its benefits and harms being similar,
is just like twins who look alike.
If you handle it with the right method,
then the ruler will be honored and you will be secure;
if you do not use the right method,
then the ruler will be demeaned and you will be endangered.
Now if peace between Qín and Wèi is achieved,
and it is not you who brokers it,
then Hán will certainly be plotted against.
If Hán follows Wèi in befriending Qín,
this would mean Hán is following Wèi's lead,
and then Hán will be slighted, the ruler
demeaned.
Once Qín has befriended Hán,
it will surely want to install someone it loves and trusts,
to wield power in Hán to consolidate this,
and then you will be endangered.
Now if you and Ānchéng Jūn broker peace between Qín and Wèi,
if successful, it will be a blessing,
if unsuccessful, it will also be a blessing.
If peace between Qín and Wèi is achieved,
and you broker it,
then Hán will be the gateway for Qín and Wèi,
and Hán will be weighty and the ruler honored.
Ānchéng Jūn will be esteemed in the east by Wèi,
and honored in the west by Qín,
holding the right tally and demanding gratitude for you from the rulers of Qín and Wèi,
carving out land to become a feudal lord—this is your task.
As for securing Hán and Wèi and becoming chancellor for life,
that is a lesser achievement for you,
but still means the ruler is honored and you are secure.
Qín and Wèi will not listen to each other forever.
Qí will be angry at failing to win over Wèi,
and will certainly want to befriend Hán to block Wèi;
Wèi, not obeying Qín,
will surely strive to befriend Hán to guard against Qín—this is you choosing cloth to cut.
If Qín and Wèi make peace,
both states will be grateful to you;
if they do not make peace,
both states will compete to serve you.
This is what is called: success is a blessing,
failure is also a blessing.
I hope you have no doubts about this."
Someone said to Gōngzhòng:
"Now there is one move that can show loyalty to the ruler,
benefit the state,
and profit yourself.
I hope you will carry it out.
If all under heaven scatter and serve Qín,
then Hán will be the most slighted;
if all under heaven unite and turn against Qín,
then Hán will be the weakest;
if alliance and opposition alternate,
then Hán will be the first to be endangered.
This is a great calamity for ruling the state and nurturing the people.
Now if you have Hán be the first to ally with Qín,
and all under heaven follow,
then Hán will have led all under heaven to serve Qín,
and Qín's gratitude toward Hán will be profound.
When Hán and all under heaven pay court to Qín,
and Hán alone receives deep gratitude,
this plan of yours,
is the utmost loyalty to the ruler.
If all under heaven do not ally with Qín,
and disobey Qín's orders,
Qín will certainly raise troops to punish the disobedient.
If Qín long remains at odds and entangled in conflict with all under heaven,
and the war is not resolved,
Hán can rest its soldiers and people, waiting for a flaw,
this plan of yours,
is for the state,
a great benefit.
In the past,
Zhōu Jiǎo, because Western Zhōu was friendly with Qín,
was enfeoffed at Gěngyáng;
Zhōu Qǐ, because Eastern Zhōu was friendly with Qín,
was enfeoffed at Píngyuán.
Now if you have Hán befriend Qín,
Hán's importance compared to the two Zhōu states is beyond measure,
and Qín's competition for opportunities,
is ten thousand times greater than in Zhōu's time.
Now if you have Hán be the first under heaven to ally with Qín,
Qín will certainly make you a feudal lord,
to clearly show all under heaven,
this plan of yours,
is a great profit for yourself.
I hope you will devote more effort to this."
The people of Hán attacked Sòng.
The King of Qín was greatly angered and said:
"I love Sòng,
as much as Xīnchéng and Yángjìn.
Hán Mín is friendly with me,
yet attacks what I love dearly;
why is this?"
Sū Qín spoke for Hán to the King of Qín, saying:
"Hán Mín's attack on Sòng,
is for Your Majesty's sake.
With Hán's strength,
augmented by Sòng,
Chǔ and Wèi will certainly fear.
Fearing,
they will certainly serve Qín in the west.
Your Majesty will not break a single soldier,
not kill a single person,
and without effort cut off Ānyì,
this is what Hán Mín prays for from Qín."
The King of Qín said:
"I have always worried that Hán is hard to understand,
now aligning, now opposing;
what does this argument mean?"
He replied: "All under heaven have certainly made Hán understandable.
Hán has already attacked Sòng,
if it serves Qín in the west,
it will use a ten-thousand-chariot state to support itself;
if it does not serve Qín in the west,
then the land of Sòng will not be secure.
The white-haired wandering persuaders of the central states,
all accumulate wisdom wanting to separate the alliance of Qín and Hán.
Those leaning on carriage rails and tightening reins galloping west,
not one speaks of befriending Hán;
those leaning on carriage rails and tightening reins galloping east,
not one speaks of befriending Qín.
Why do none want Hán
and Qín to unite?
Because Jìn
and Chǔ are wise, and Hán and Qín are foolish.
If Jìn and Chǔ unite,
they will certainly watch for an opportunity against Hán and Qín;
if Hán and Qín unite,
they will certainly scheme against Jìn and Chǔ.
I ask you to decide based on this."
The King of Qín said: "Good."
Someone said to the King of Hán:
"The King of Qín wants to take action against Liáng,
and wants to attack Jiàng and Ānyì.
What plan will Hán adopt?
Qín's desire to attack Hán,
is to spy on the Zhōu royal house from the east,
and it thinks of this even in sleep, never forgetting.
Now if Hán does not examine this,
and instead wants to ally with Qín,
it will certainly become a great disaster for the states east of the mountains.
Qín's desire to attack Liáng,
is to obtain Liáng to threaten Hán,
fearing that Liáng will not obey,
so it wants to weaken it to solidify the alliance.
If Your Majesty does not examine this,
and instead wants to remain neutral,
Liáng will certainly be angry that Hán does not side with itself,
and will certainly break and be used by Qín,
and Hán will certainly be overrun.
I hope Your Majesty will consider this carefully.
It would be better to urgently send important envoys to Zhào and Liáng,
to renew the covenant of brotherhood,
and have the states east of the mountains all send crack troops to garrison the western borders of Hán and Liáng.
If not for this,
the states east of the mountains will have no way to save themselves from destruction,
this is a plan for ten thousand generations.
Qín's desire to unite all under heaven and become king over them,
is not the same as in ancient times.
Even if you serve it like a son serves his father,
you will still be destroyed.
Even if your conduct is like Bóyí's,
you will still be destroyed.
Even if your conduct is like Jié and Zhòu's,
you will still be destroyed.
Even if you serve it well, it is of no benefit.
It cannot ensure survival,
but is precisely enough to make yourself quickly perish.
Thus, if the states east of the mountains cannot form a close alliance,
uniting and strengthening each other as one,
they will certainly all perish."
Someone said to the King of Zhèng:
"Zhāolí Hóu,
was a wise ruler of his generation;
Shēn Bùhài,
was a worthy scholar of his generation.
Hán and Wèi were rival states of equal strength.
Shēn Bùhài and Zhāolí Hóu held jade tablets and went to see the Lord of Liáng,
not because they liked lowliness and hated honor,
nor because their considerations were mistaken and their deliberations flawed.
Shēn Bùhài's planning of affairs,
He said:
'If I hold the jade tablet of office in Wèi,
the ruler of Wèi will surely achieve his ambitions in Hán,
and will inevitably exhaust himself externally against the world;
this will weaken Wèi.
The feudal lords, resenting Wèi, will surely serve Hán;
thus I will be freed from subordination to one man,
and will be trusted above ten thousand men.
To weaken Wèi's military
and increase Hán's power,
nothing is better than paying court to Wèi.'
Zhāo Lí Hóu listened and acted accordingly—
he was an enlightened ruler.
Shēn Bù Hài considered the matter and spoke of it—
he was a loyal minister.
The Hán of today is weaker than the Hán of the past,
and the Qín of today is stronger than the Qín of the past.
Now Qín has the same intentions as the ruler of Liáng had,
yet Your Majesty and your ministers do not act to honor Qín in order to secure Hán.
I privately believe that Your Majesty's wisdom is not equal to that of Zhāo Lí Hóu,
and the loyalty of Your Majesty's ministers is not equal to that of Shēn Bù Hài.
"In the past,
Duke Mú achieved a single victory at Hányuán and became hegemon of the western regions;
Duke Wén of Jìn achieved a single victory at Chéngpú and stabilized the world.
These examples show that a single victory can establish prestige and commands,
and achieve success and fame throughout the world.
Now Qín has been strong for several generations;
its great victories number in the thousands,
its minor victories in the hundreds.
Yet despite great victories, it does not become king;
despite minor victories, it does not become hegemon.
No prestige is established,
no commands are implemented.
However, the use of arms recorded in the *Spring and Autumn Annals*
was not for the purpose of seeking the ruler's prestige and establishing fame in the world.
In the past, when the former kings attacked,
some acted for reputation,
some acted for substance.
Those acting for reputation attacked the mind;
those acting for substance attacked the form.
In the past,
when Wú and Yuè fought,
the Yuè people were greatly defeated
and retreated to hold out on Kuàijī Mountain.
The Wú people entered Yuè and pacified the households.
The King of Yuè sent his minister Zhòng to seek peace with Wú,
offering that the men would become servants,
the women concubines,
and he himself would hold game as tribute and follow the charioteers.
The Wú people indeed listened to his words,
made peace but did not conclude a covenant—
this was attacking the mind.
Later, when Yuè fought Wú,
the Wú people were greatly defeated,
and also offered that the men would become servants,
the women concubines,
treating Yuè with the same courtesy that Yuè had formerly treated Wú.
The Yuè people did not listen,
but instead destroyed the state of Wú and captured Fū Chāi—
this was attacking the form.
Now, if you wish to attack the mind,
you should act like Wú;
if you wish to attack the form,
you should act like Yuè.
If your attack on form is not like Yuè,
and your attack on mind is not like Wú,
yet ruler and ministers,
high and low,
young and old, noble and base,
all shout about hegemony and kingship,
I privately believe this is like being in a well and saying:
'I will fetch fire for you.'
"At the meeting in Dōng Mèng,
Niè Zhèng and Yáng Jiān assassinated the minister and also the ruler.
Xǔ Yì kicked Āi Hóu and killed him,
establishing him as the ruler of Zhèng.
All the people of the Hán clan obeyed his commands—
this was because Xǔ Yì took the lead.
Therefore, when Āi Hóu became ruler,
Xǔ Yì served as his minister for life.
And the Hán clan's respect for Xǔ Yì
was equal to their respect for Āi Hóu.
Today, one cannot become the ruler of Zhèng;
even if one served as minister for life,
yet if I say I will not do it,
is this not a mistaken plan?
In the past, Duke Huán of Qí assembled the feudal lords nine times,
and never failed to invoke the command of King Xiāng of Zhōu.
Thus, although he honored King Xiāng,
Duke Huán also established his hegemony.
The nine assemblies' respect for Duke Huán
was equal to their respect for King Xiāng.
Today, one cannot become the Son of Heaven;
even if one became like Duke Huán, if I say I will not do it,
is this not a mistaken plan and a failure to understand honor?
The scholars of the Hán clan numbered in the hundreds of thousands,
all supporting Āi Hóu as ruler,
yet Xǔ Yì alone took the minister's position—
there was no other reason.
The rulers of the feudal lords
all served the Zhōu court in some capacity,
yet Duke Huán alone achieved hegemony—
there was also no other reason.
Now a strong state is about to have the opportunity for imperial kingship,
and those who put their state first in this
are of the same category as Duke Huán and Xǔ Yì.
Can this not be called good planning?
The advantage of allying first with a strong state is that
if the strong state can become king,
then I will surely become hegemon;
if the strong state cannot become king,
then I can avoid its armies,
causing it not to attack me.
Thus, if the strong state's affairs succeed,
then I establish an emperor and become hegemon;
if the strong state's affairs do not succeed,
it still treats me with great virtue.
Now, in allying with a strong state,
if the strong state's affairs succeed, there is fortune;
if they do not succeed, there is no calamity.
Thus, allying first with a strong state
is the plan of a sage."
Hán Yáng was stationed in Sān Chuān and wished to return;
Zú Qiáng persuaded the King of Hán, saying:
"Sān Chuān is pacified;
does Your Majesty know this?
The garrison will soon honor the young master."
The king then summoned the young masters stationed in Sān Chuān and had them return.
Qín
is a large state.
Hán
is a small state.
Hán is very distant from Qín.
Yet to appear close to Qín,
in planning it,
there is no way without gold;
therefore, they sold a beautiful woman.
The price of the beautiful woman was high;
the feudal lords could not buy her,
so Qín bought her for three thousand pieces of gold.
Hán then used that gold to serve Qín,
but Qín in turn obtained both the gold and Hán's beautiful woman.
Hán's beautiful woman then said to Qín: "Hán is very distant from Qín."
From this, it can be seen that
Hán lost both the beautiful woman and the gold,
and its distance from Qín only became more apparent.
Therefore, a persuader said to Hán:
"It would be better to stop wasteful expenditures,
and use that as gold to serve Qín.
This gold would surely be effective,
and Hán's distance from Qín would not be apparent.
Beautiful women know internal affairs;
therefore, those skilled in planning
do not reveal internal affairs."
When Zhāng Chǒu allied Qí
and Chǔ to negotiate with Wèi,
he said to Hán's Gōng Zhòng:
"If you now urgently attack Wèi's Yùn,
Wèi, in desperation,
will surely cede territory to make peace with Qí
and Chǔ; therefore, you should not attack.
If Wèi is not pressed, it will surely fight.
If it is victorious,
attacking Yùn and taking it will be easy.
If it is not victorious,
then Wèi will likely cede it internally."
Gōng Zhòng said:
"Agreed."
Zhāng Chǒu then said to Qí
and Chǔ:
"Hán has already allied with Wèi.
If you doubt this,
then observe Gōng Zhòng's attack."
Gōng Zhòng did not attack;
Qí and Chǔ grew fearful,
and thus negotiated with Wèi,
without informing Hán.
Someone said to the Prime Minister of Hán:
"The reason people value Biǎn Què
is because they have abscesses;
if they valued Biǎn Què but had no abscesses,
then no one would do so.
Now, the reason you serve and value Lord Píng Yuán
is because you are at odds with Qín;
but valuing Lord Píng Yuán is precisely what puts you at odds with Qín.
I hope you will consider this carefully."
Gōng Zhòng sent Hán Mín to Qín to request Wǔsuì,
but feared that Chǔ would be angered.
Táng Kè said to Gōng Zhòng:
"Hán's serving Qín,
is precisely to seek Wǔsuì,
which is not something our state detests.
Once Hán obtains Wǔsuì,
its situation will then allow it to treat Chǔ well.
I wish to speak,
but dare not scheme for Chǔ.
Now, among Hán's elders and nobles who have gained popular support, none are chancellor;
Hán cannot stand independently,
and its circumstances will inevitably not treat Chǔ well.
The King said:
'I wish to use the state to assist Hán Mín and make him chancellor—is this acceptable?
The elders and nobles dislike Mín,
so Mín will certainly rely on the state to protect Chǔ.'"
Gōng Zhòng was pleased,
recommended Táng Kè among the nobles,
and had him take charge of affairs between Hán and Chǔ.
Hán's chancellor Gōng Zhòng Mín sent Hán Chǐ to Qín,
to request an attack on Wèi,
and the King of Qín was pleased with this.
Hán Chǐ was in Táng,
when Gōng Zhòng Mín died.
Hán Chǐ said to the King of Qín:
"Wèi's envoy said to the subsequent chancellor Hán Chén:
'You must condemn Hán Chǐ for Wèi.'
Hán Chén said:
'That cannot be done.
The King of Qín appointed him to office,
and also made agreements with him.'
The envoy said:
'Qín's appointing Hán Chǐ to office,
was out of respect for Gōng Zhòng.
Now Gōng Zhòng is dead,
if Hán Chǐ goes to Qín,
Qín will certainly not admit him.
Even if admitted,
why would they support him to spite the King of Wèi?'
Hán Chén is troubled by this,
and is about to comply. If Your Majesty does not summon Hán Chǐ now,
Hán Chǐ will go into hiding in the mountains."
The King of Qín said: "What makes you think I am so fickle!
Where should he hide?"
He summoned Hán Chǐ and appointed him to office.
A visiting minister, speaking for Hán, said to the King of Qín:
"Hán Mín's deliberations
show he knows his own lord but not other lords,
knows his own state but not other states.
That Gōng Zhòng,
Qín's power can bend him.
As for Qín's strength,
being the first to submit,
Mín acted hastily.
He advanced the troops of Qí and Sòng to Shǒutǎn,
pressing close to Liáng's outer walls from afar,
the reason they did not reach Wèi,
was because they considered the matter settled and passed the road to Nányáng,
intending to lead the four states westward as the vanguard.
The reason they did not,
was that all said because Yān perished due to Qí,
Wèi perished due to Qín,
Chén and Cài perished due to Chǔ,
these all involved severing geographical advantages,
with ministers forming cliques to deceive their superiors,
and high ministers acting for the feudal lords to undermine their own state.
Now Your Majesty's position is correct:
Zhāng Yí's high status
does not allow him to criticize Gōngsūn Hè,
this means subordinate ministers do not serve the high ministers;
Gōngsūn Hè's high status
does not allow him to criticize Gān Wù,
then high ministers do not serve the close attendants.
High and low do not serve each other,
each keeps to their proper place,
converging like spokes to serve their superior,
then the worthiness or unworthiness of the ministers,
can be known.
This is the first point of Your Majesty's clarity.
Gōngsūn Hè once hated Qí and Hán but was not further honored,
then high ministers dare not act for feudal lords to undermine the state.
