Qí and Hán once tried to use Gōngsūn Hè but were not accepted,
then feudal lords dare not rely on ministers to gain influence.
External and internal do not act for each other,
then the true intentions of the feudal lords can be known.
This is the second point of Your Majesty's clarity.
Gōngsūn Hè and Chūlǐ Jí requested not to attack Hán,
presented four arguments to withdraw,
yet Your Majesty still attacked it.
Gān Mào made a pact with Chǔ and Zhào but instead respected Wèi,
this was him negotiating with us,
yet Mào was about to attack Yíyáng,
and Your Majesty still checked him.
The wisdom of the ministers
hardly matches Your Majesty's clarity,
therefore I wish Gōng Zhòng's state to serve Your Majesty,
and not act on its own from the left and right."
Hán Mín became chancellor of Qí,
ordered officials to expel Gōngchóu Shù,
and was greatly angered that Zhōu detained Chéngyáng Jūn.
Someone said to Hán Mín:
"You consider these two men to be worthy,
and wherever they go,
they will be employed, correct?
Then it would be better for them to remain in a small state.
Why?
Chéngyáng Jūn left Hán for Qín,
and Gōngchóu Shù
is well-regarded by the King of Chǔ.
Now if you expel them,
these two will certainly go to Qín and Chǔ,
and will surely cause you trouble.
Moreover, they will make clear your poor relations with all under heaven.
Those under heaven who are not on good terms with you,
and those who wish to seek something from Qí,
will gather them,
to pressure Qí and bargain over you."
Someone said to Shānyáng Jūn:
"Qín enfeoffed you with Shānyáng,
Qí enfeoffed you with Jǔ.
Qí and Qín did so not because they value Hán, but because they esteem your conduct.
Now Chǔ attacks Qí and takes Jǔ,
at best not allying with Qí,
at worst not admitting you,
this provokes the might of Qí and Qín and slights Hán."
Shānyáng Jūn then sent him to Chǔ.
Zhào and Wèi attacked Huáyáng,
Hán urgently appealed to Qín for help.
Carriages and envoys were in constant sight,
but Qín did not send aid.
Hán's chancellor said to Tián Líng:
"The situation is urgent,
I hope you, though ill,
will make a one-night journey."
Tián Líng went to see Ránghóu,
Ránghóu said:
"Is Hán in urgent straits?
What brings you here?"
Tián Líng replied: "It is not urgent."
Ránghóu angrily said: "Then how can you be an envoy for your king?
Carriages and envoys are in constant sight,
reporting to our state that it is very urgent,
yet you say it is not urgent,
why?"
Tián Líng said:
"If Hán were truly urgent, then it would change its stance."
Ránghóu said:
"You need not see the King,
I will request to dispatch troops to rescue Hán."
Within eight days,
they greatly defeated Zhào and Wèi below Huáyáng.
Qín summoned Chǔ to attack Qí,
Lěng Xiàng said to Chén Zhěn:
"The King of Qín will certainly turn outward.
Those of Chǔ who favor Qí, knowing they cannot ally with Qín in the west,
will surely strive to make Chǔ ally with Qí.
If Qí and Chǔ ally,
Yān and Zhào will not dare not comply.
Qí leading four states against Qín,
means Qí will not be cornered."
Xiàng said:
"Does the King of Qín truly desire to attack Qí?
Then it would be better to first win over those in Chǔ who favor Qí.
If those in Chǔ who favor Qí first strive to make Chǔ ally with Qí,
then Chǔ will certainly turn to Qín.
With a strong Qín having Jìn and Chǔ,
then Yān and Zhào will not dare not comply,
and Qí will be isolated.
I request to persuade the King of Qín on your behalf."
The Hán clan expelled Xiàng Jìn from Zhōu,
Zhōu's Chéng Huī spoke to the King of Wèi on his behalf:
"Zhōu will certainly be lenient and return him,
why does Your Majesty not speak first on his behalf,
thus Your Majesty will have Xiàng Jìn in Zhōu."
The King of Wèi said: "Agreed."
Chéng Huī then went to speak to the King of Hán:
"It was Hán who expelled Xiàng Jìn,
and it will be Wèi who restores him,
how can this compare to Hán itself restoring him!
This way, Wèi will have Xiàng Jìn in Zhōu,
and the King of Hán will lose him."
The King of Hán said: "Good."
He then also requested his restoration.
Zhāng Dēng requested of Fěi Xiè:
"Please have Gōngzǐ Nián say to the King of Hán:
'Fěi Xiè,
Western Zhōu considers him an enemy,
Eastern Zhōu treasures him.
His family has ten thousand in gold,
Why does Your Majesty not summon him,
and appoint him as the governor of Sānchuān?
This would bind Sānchuān to Xīzhōu in vigilance,
and he will certainly exhaust his family’s resources to serve Your Majesty.
Xīzhōu, resenting this,
will surely offer the vessels of the former kings to halt Your Majesty’s actions.”
The King of Hán will certainly do this.
When Xīzhōu hears of it,
it will absolve you of your crime,
and put an end to your affairs.”
The Yìshǐ of Ānyì died,
and his deputy feared he would not obtain the position.
A transport officer spoke on his behalf to the Magistrate of Ān, saying:
“Gōngsūn Qí made a request to the king on someone’s behalf for the position of Yìshǐ,
and the king said:
‘Does he already have a deputy?
I find it difficult to violate the established rule.’”
Thereupon, he hastily installed him.
The King of Wèi formed an alliance at Jiǔlǐ,
and intended to restore the Son of Heaven.
Fáng Xǐ said to the King of Hán:
“Do not listen to him.
The great states detest having a Son of Heaven,
while the small states benefit from it.
If Your Majesty and the great states do not listen,
how can Wèi establish it with the small states?”
Jiànxìn Jūn looked down upon Hán Xī,
and Zhào Áo spoke on his behalf to Jiànxìn Hóu, saying:
“Among states, there is one whose possession ensures survival,
and whose absence leads to ruin—that is Wèi.
There is one that cannot be without and yet must follow—that is Hán.
Now, your belittling of Hán Xī
is due to your friendly relations with Chǔ and Wèi.
When Qín sees that your relations have instead turned favorable toward Chǔ and Wèi,
it will certainly attach greater importance to winning over Hán.
If you follow the vertical alliance, Hán will be slighted;
if you follow the horizontal alliance, Hán will be valued.
Thus, there is no reason to slight Hán.
If Qín sends troops to Sānchuān,
it will then besiege Yān in the south,
and the routes to Cài and Shào will be cut off.
When Wèi is hard-pressed,
its rescue of Zhào will certainly be delayed.
If Qín raises troops and captures Hándān,
Zhào will surely perish.
Therefore, if you win over Hán,
you can avoid conflict.”
Duàn Chǎn said to Xīnchéng Jūn:
“One who walks at night can avoid committing crimes,
but cannot prevent dogs from barking at him.
Now, I serve as a Lángzhōng,
and while I can avoid criticizing you before the king,
I cannot prevent others from criticizing me before you.
I hope you will consider this.”
Duàngàn Yuèrén said to Xīnchéng Jūn:
“A disciple of Wáng Liáng was driving a carriage,
claiming it was a thousand-lǐ horse,
when he encountered a disciple of Zàofǔ.
The disciple of Zàofǔ said:
‘This horse cannot run a thousand lǐ.’
The disciple of Wáng Liáng said:
‘The horse is a thousand-lǐ horse;
the harness,
a thousand-lǐ harness.
Yet it cannot achieve a thousand lǐ—why is that?’
He replied:
‘Your reins are too long.
Thus, the reins in this matter,
though only one ten-thousandth of the whole,
hinder a thousand-lǐ journey.’
Now, although I am unworthy,
to Qín I am also one ten-thousandth,
yet the Chancellor regards me
without releasing the blockage—
this is because the reins are too long.”
Sū Qín was about to form a vertical alliance,
and went north to persuade Marquis Wén of Yān, saying:
“Yān has Cháoxiǎn and Liáodōng to the east,
Línhú and Lóufán to the north,
Yúnzhōng and Jiǔyuán to the west,
and Hūtuó and Yìshuǐ to the south.
Its territory spans over two thousand lǐ,
with armored troops numbering several hundred thousand,
seven hundred chariots,
six thousand cavalry horses,
and grain stores sufficient for ten years.
To the south, it enjoys the abundance of Jiéshí and Yànmén;
to the north, the benefits of dates and chestnuts.
Although the people do not engage in farming,
the fruits of dates and chestnuts
are enough to feed the people.
This is what is called a ‘heavenly storehouse.’
As for peace, joy, and freedom from troubles,
without the worry of armies being destroyed or generals killed,
none surpasses Yān.
Does Your Majesty know why this is so?
The reason Yān is not invaded by bandits or attacked by troops
is because Zhào serves as a shield to the south.
Qín and Zhào fought five battles,
with Qín winning twice and Zhào three times.
Qín and Zhào weakened each other,
while Your Majesty, with a whole Yān, controlled the aftermath.
This is why Yān does not face calamities.
Moreover, when Qín attacks Yān,
it must cross Yúnzhōng and Jiǔyuán,
pass through Dài and Shànggǔ,
traversing thousands of lǐ of winding roads,
and even if it captures Yān’s cities,
Qín’s plans certainly cannot hold them.
Thus, it is clear that Qín cannot harm Yān.
Now, when Zhào attacks Yān,
issuing orders and mobilizing troops,
in less than ten days,
its several hundred thousand troops
will be stationed at Dōngyuán.
Crossing the Hūtuó River,
and fording the Yìshuǐ,
in less than four or five days,
they will reach the capital.
Therefore, it is said:
When Qín attacks Yān,
the battle is fought a thousand lǐ away;
when Zhào attacks Yān,
the battle is fought within a hundred lǐ.
To not worry about a threat within a hundred lǐ,
yet to fear a threat a thousand lǐ away—
no strategy is more misguided than this.
Therefore, I hope Your Majesty will ally closely with Zhào in the vertical alliance,
uniting all under heaven as one,
so that your state will surely be free from troubles.”
The King of Yān said: “My state is small,
pressed by powerful Qín to the west,
and close to Qí and Zhào to the south.
Qí and Zhào
are powerful states.
Now, you have kindly instructed me,
to join the vertical alliance to secure Yān,
and I respectfully commit my state to follow.”
Thereupon, he provided Sū Qín with carriages, horses, gold, and silk to go to Zhào.
Fèngyáng Jūn Lǐ Duì was very unfavorable toward Sū Qín.
While Sū Qín was in Yān,
Lǐ Duì spoke on behalf of Sū Qín to Fèngyáng Jūn, saying:
“If Qí and Yān are estranged, Zhào’s importance increases;
if Qí and Yān unite, Zhào’s importance diminishes.
Now, your going to Qí
is not beneficial to Zhào.
I privately believe this is not advisable for you.”
Fèngyáng Jūn said:
“Why would I unite Yān with Qí?”
He replied: “The one who controls Yān is Master Sū.
And Yān is a weak state,
inferior to Qí in the east,
and inferior to Zhào in the west.
How can it be without Qí in the east and Zhào in the west?
Yet you are very unfavorable toward Sū Qín.
Can Sū Qín embrace weak Yān and stand alone in the world?
This is driving Yān to unite with Qí.
Moreover, Yān is the remnant of a perished state,
relying on expediency to establish itself,
valuing external relations,
and serving the powerful.
Therefore, for your sake,
whether you treat Sū Qín well or not, you should win him over,
to sow doubt between Yān and Qí.
If Yān and Qí are suspicious of each other,
then Zhào’s importance will increase.
If the King of Qí doubts Sū Qín,
then you will have many resources.”
Fèngyáng Jūn said: “Good.”
Thereupon, he sent an envoy to establish relations with Sū Qín.
During the conflict at Quán,
Yān fought twice without victory,
and Zhào did not come to its rescue.
Kuài Zǐ said to Duke Wén:
“It would be better to offer territory to seek peace with Qí.
Zhào will certainly rescue us.
If it does not rescue us,
we will have no choice but to submit.”
Duke Wén said: “Good.”
He ordered Guō Rèn to offer territory to seek peace with Qí.
When Zhào heard of this,
it immediately sent troops to rescue Yān.
During the time of Duke Wén of Yān,
King Huì of Qín gave his daughter in marriage to the Crown Prince of Yān.
When Duke Wén died,
King Yì ascended the throne.
King Xuān of Qí took advantage of Yān’s mourning to attack it,
and captured ten cities.
The Martial Peace Lord, Sū Qín, spoke to the King of Qí on behalf of Yān.
He bowed twice in congratulation,
then looked up and offered condolences.
The King of Qí pressed his halberd to the ground and retreated,
saying:
"Why do congratulations and condolences follow each other so quickly?"
Sū Qín replied:
"The reason a starving man will not eat aconite
is that he considers it merely a temporary filling of the belly,
yet it brings the same calamity as death.
Now, although Yān is weak and small,
it is the young son-in-law of mighty Qín.
Your Majesty covets its ten cities,
and thereby deeply makes an enemy of mighty Qín.
If now you make weak Yān lead the vanguard like wild geese in flight,
with mighty Qín controlling them from behind,
to summon the elite troops of the world against you,
this is the same as eating aconite."
The King of Qí said:
"Then what should be done?"
He replied: "When a sage handles affairs,
he turns disaster into blessing,
and transforms failure into achievement.
Thus, Duke Huán bore the burden of a woman, yet his name grew more revered;
Hán Xiàn incurred offense, yet his friendship became more solid.
These are examples of turning disaster into blessing,
and transforming failure into achievement.
If Your Majesty can heed your servant,
nothing is better than returning Yān's ten cities,
and using humble words to apologize to Qín.
When Qín knows Your Majesty returned Yān's cities for its sake,
Qín will surely feel grateful to Your Majesty.
Yān, obtaining ten cities without cause,
will also feel grateful to Your Majesty.
This is to cast off a powerful enemy and establish a firm friendship.
Moreover, if both Yān and Qín serve Qí,
then when Your Great Majesty issues commands to the world, all will follow.
Thus, Your Majesty uses empty words to attach Qín,
and uses ten cities to win over the world.
This is the enterprise of a hegemon-king.
It is what is called turning disaster into blessing,
and transforming failure into achievement."
The King of Qí was greatly pleased,
and so returned Yān's cities.
He sent a thousand catties of gold afterward to apologize,
knocked his head on the ground in the mud,
and wished to become a sworn brother, asking for forgiveness from Qín.
Someone spoke ill of Sū Qín to the King of Yān,
saying:
"The Martial Peace Lord
is an untrustworthy man in the world.
Your Majesty, with ten thousand chariots, lowers yourself before him,
honors him at court,
showing the world you associate with petty men."
When the Martial Peace Lord returned from Qí,
the King of Yān did not provide him lodging.
He said to the King of Yān:
"Your servant is a rustic from Eastern Zhōu.
When I first saw you, I had not an inch of merit,
yet you welcomed me in the suburbs,
and honored me at court.
Now I have served as your envoy,
gaining the benefit of ten cities,
achieving merit that preserves endangered Yān.
If you do not trust me now,
people will surely say I am untrustworthy,
injuring me in Your Majesty's eyes.
My being untrustworthy
is actually your blessing.
Suppose your servant were as trustworthy as Wěi Shēng,
as incorruptible as Bó Yí,
as filial as Zēng Shēn—
these three are the highest conduct in the world.
If I served you with these,
would it not be acceptable?"
The King of Yān said: "It would."
He said:
"If I had these,
I would not serve you either."
Sū Qín said:
"Moreover, one as filial as Zēng Shēn
would not, in duty, leave his parents to spend a single night away from home.
How could you have sent him to Qí?
One as incorruptible as Bó Yí
would not accept unearned meals,
disdained King Wǔ's righteousness and would not serve as his minister,
declined the lordship of Gūzhú,
and starved to death on Shǒuyáng Mountain.
One so incorruptible—
how would he be willing to walk several thousand miles
to serve the endangered ruler of weak Yān?
One as trustworthy as Wěi Shēng,
who, when his appointed one did not come,
clung to the bridge pillar and died.
Such extreme trustworthiness—
how would he be willing to promote Yān and Qín's might in Qí to achieve great merit?
Moreover, trustworthy conduct
is for self-cultivation,
not for serving others.
It is all a method of self-preservation,
not a way of striving for advancement.
Moreover, when the Three Sovereigns arose in succession,
and the Five Hegemons flourished one after another,
none relied on self-preservation.
Do you, my lord, consider self-preservation acceptable?
If so, then Qí would not have expanded beyond Yíngqiū,
and you would not have crossed the Chǔ border,
nor looked beyond the frontier cities.
Moreover, I have an aged mother in Zhōu.
I left my aged mother to serve you,
abandoning the method of self-preservation
to plan the way of striving for advancement.
My aims fundamentally do not align with yours.
You are entirely a ruler of self-preservation,
while I am a minister of striving for advancement.
This is what is called incurring offense against the ruler through loyalty and trustworthiness."
The King of Yān said: "Loyalty and trustworthiness—
what offense could they possibly incur?"
He replied: "You do not understand.
My neighbor had a man who went far away to serve as an official.
His wife took a lover.
When her husband was about to return,
her lover worried.
His wife said: 'Do not worry, sir.
I have already prepared poisoned wine to serve him.'
Two days later,
the husband arrived.
The wife had a concubine present a cup of wine to him.
The concubine knew it was poisoned wine.
If she presented it, she would kill her master;
if she spoke of it, she would get her mistress driven out.
So she pretended to stumble and spilled the wine.
Her master was furious and flogged her.
Thus, the concubine, by one stumble and spilling the wine,
saved her master above,
and preserved her mistress below.
Her loyalty was so extreme,
yet she could not avoid a flogging.
This is how one incurs offense through loyalty and trustworthiness.
My service to you
unfortunately resembles that concubine's spilling of the wine.
Moreover, in serving you,
I have upheld righteousness and benefited the state.
Now I have incurred offense.
I fear that in the future, no one in the world who serves you
will dare to be certain of themselves.
Furthermore, when I persuaded Qí,
I never deceived them.
Those who sent me to persuade Qí—
none spoke as I did.
Even with the wisdom of Yáo and Shùn,
they would not have dared to take such action."
Zhāng Yí, on behalf of Qín, destroyed the vertical alliance and promoted the horizontal alliance.
He said to the King of Yān:
"The one Your Majesty is closest to
is none other than Zhào.
Formerly, the King of Zhào gave his elder sister as wife to the King of Dài,
desiring to annex Dài.
He made an appointment to meet the King of Dài at the Jiùzhù Pass.
He then ordered craftsmen to make a metal ladle,
lengthening its handle,
so it could be used to strike a man.
While drinking with the King of Dài,
he secretly told the cook:
'When the wine brings merriment,
serve hot broth,
then use the ladle to strike him.'
So when the wine brought merriment, they called for hot broth.
The cook came forward to ladle the soup,
then turned the ladle and struck with it.
The King of Dài's brains were spilled on the ground.
His elder sister heard of it,
rubbed her hairpin and stabbed herself with it.
Thus, to this day there is Mójī Mountain,
known throughout the world.
"The King of Zhào's wolf-like cruelty and lack of kinship—
this is clearly seen and known by Your Majesty.
And do you consider the King of Zhào someone to be close to?
Zhào raised troops and attacked Yān,
twice besieging Yān's capital and coercing Your Majesty.
Your Majesty ceded ten cities and only then retreated with apologies.
Now the King of Zhào has already gone to court at Miǎnchí,
presenting Héjiān to serve Qín.
If Your Majesty does not serve Qín,
Qín will send troops down from Yúnzhōng and Jiǔyuán,
drive Zhào to attack Yān,
then the Yì River and the Great Wall will not belong to Your Majesty."
Moreover, at present, Zhào is to Qín
like a commandery or county,
and dares not recklessly raise armies to wage war.
If Your Majesty now serves Qín,
the King of Qín will surely be pleased,
and Zhào will not dare to act recklessly.
Thus, to the west you will have the support of a strong Qín,
and to the south you will have no trouble from Qí and Zhào.
Therefore, I hope Your Majesty will carefully consider this."
The King of Yān said: "I am a barbarian dwelling in a remote place;
though a grown man,
I am only like an infant.
My words are insufficient to seek correctness,
and my plans are insufficient to decide affairs.
Now that you, honored guest, have fortunately instructed me,
I ask to present my altars of soil and grain and face west to serve Qín,
offering the five cities at the foot of Chángshān."
Gōng Tuō was an envoy of Yān to Wèi.
Wèi did not grant him an audience,
detaining him for several months.
A guest said to the King of Wèi:
"Why do you not grant an audience to the Yān envoy?"
He replied:
"Because his state is in turmoil."
The guest responded: "When Tāng attacked Jié,
he desired his turmoil.
Thus, one who is in great turmoil can have his land taken;
one who is in minor turmoil can have his treasures taken.
Now the Yān guest has said:
'If the affair can be heard,
even if it means exhausting treasures and land,
I am still willing to do it.'
Why does Your Majesty not see him?"
The King of Wèi was pleased,
and thus granted an audience to the Yān guest and sent him off.
Sū Qín died,
and his younger brother Sū Dài wished to succeed him.
He then went north to see King Kuài of Yān and said:
"I am a humble man from Eastern Zhōu.
I have privately heard that Your Majesty's righteousness is very lofty and very proper.
I am not clever,
but I have privately laid aside my hoe and plow to seek an audience with Your Majesty.
When I reached Hándān,
what I heard in Hándān
was even loftier than what I had heard in Eastern Zhōu.
I privately cherished this ambition,
and thus came to the court of Yān.
Observing Your Majesty's various ministers and subordinate officials,
I see that Your Majesty is an enlightened ruler of the world."
The King said: "What kind of person do you call an enlightened ruler of the world?"
He replied: "I have heard that
an enlightened ruler strives to hear about his faults,
and does not wish to hear about his good deeds.
I ask to declare Your Majesty's faults.
Now Qí and Zhào
are Your Majesty's enemies;
Chǔ and Wèi
are Your Majesty's supporting states.
Now Your Majesty supports your enemies to attack your supporting states—
this is not the way to benefit Yān.
If Your Majesty considers this yourself, then your plan is mistaken.
Those who do not remonstrate about this
are not loyal ministers."
The King said:
"As for my relation to Qí and Zhào,
I dare not desire to attack them."
He said:
"To have no intention of plotting against others,
yet to cause others to suspect you—
that is perilous;
to have the intention of plotting against others,
yet to let others know it—
that is clumsy;
if a plot has not yet been launched but is heard abroad,
then it is dangerous.
Now I have heard that Your Majesty lives uneasily,
eats and drinks without relish,
broods on taking revenge against Qí.
You personally cut and tied armor plates,
saying there is a great number;
your wife personally wove armor cords,
saying there is a great number.
Is this true?"
The King said: "Since you have heard of it,
I dare not conceal it from you.
I have deep grievances and accumulated anger against Qí,
and have wished to take revenge for two years.
Qí
is my enemy state,
and thus what I desire to attack.
Only I worry that the state is exhausted,
and its strength is insufficient.
If you can use Yān to oppose Qí,
then I will present the state and entrust it to you."
He replied: "In all, there are seven warring states in the world,
and Yān is among the weak.
Fighting alone, it cannot prevail;
but if it attaches itself to someone, it invariably becomes weighty.
If it attaches itself to Chǔ in the south, then Chǔ becomes weighty;
if it attaches itself to Qín in the west, then Qín becomes weighty;
if it attaches itself to Hán and Wèi in the center, then Hán and Wèi become weighty.
Moreover, if the state to which it attaches becomes weighty,
this will surely make Your Majesty weighty as well.
Now the King of Qí
is a ruler of long standing,
and self-willed.
He attacked Chǔ in the south for five years,
and his stores were dispersed.
He distressed Qín in the west for three years,
the people were haggard and worn,
the officers exhausted and depleted.
In the north he fought with Yān,
destroying three armies
and capturing two generals.
And then with his remaining troops he turned south and raised an army against the strong Sòng of five thousand chariots,
enveloping twelve feudal lords.
This shows that his ruler's desires are fulfilled,
and his people's strength is exhausted.
How can he still take more?
Moreover, I have heard that frequent warfare wearies the people,
and prolonged campaigns exhaust the troops."
The King said:
"I have heard that Qí has the clear Jì River and the muddy Hé River,
which can serve as strong defenses;
it has the Long Wall and the great dikes, sufficient to serve as barriers.
Is this truly so?"
He replied: "If the timeliness of Heaven is not with you,
even if you have the clear Jì and the muddy Hé,
how can they suffice as strong defenses?
If the people's strength is impoverished and exhausted,
even if you have the Long Wall and the great dikes,
how can they suffice as barriers?
Moreover, in former times,
the area west of the Jì did not provide corvée labor,
in order to guard against Zhào;
the area north of the Hé did not provide troops,
in order to guard against Yān.
Now the areas west of the Jì and north of the Hé
have all been conscripted for service,
and the interior is exhausted.
Now an arrogant ruler certainly does not like planning,
and ministers of a perishing state are greedy for wealth.
If Your Majesty can truly not begrudge sending your favored sons and maternal brothers as hostages,
and precious pearls, jade, silk, and cloth to serve those around him,
he will then feel grateful to Yān and lightly destroy Sòng.
Then Qí can be destroyed."
The King said: "I will ultimately follow you, as if receiving a mandate from Heaven!"
He said:
"If internal troubles are not dealt with,
external enemies cannot be resisted.
Your Majesty should govern the external affairs yourself,
and I will take revenge internally.
This is the situation for destroying it."
After King Kuài of Yān had ascended the throne,
Sū Qín died in Qí.
When Sū Qín was in Yān,
he became related by marriage to the chancellor Zǐzhī, and
Sū Dài was friends with Zǐzhī.
When Sū Qín died,
King Xuān of Qí again employed Sū Dài.
In the third year of Yān Kuài,
he joined with Chǔ and the Three Jìn to attack Qín,
but was unsuccessful and returned.
Zǐzhī served as chancellor of Yān,
honored, weighty, and decisive in judgment.
Sū Dài was an envoy of Qí to Yān.
The King of Yān asked him:
"What is King Xuān of Qí like?"
He replied: "He certainly will not achieve hegemony."
The King of Yān said: "Why?"
He replied: "He does not trust his ministers."
Sū Dài wished to stimulate the King of Yān to give heavy responsibility to Zǐzhī.
Thereupon, the King of Yān greatly trusted Zǐzhī.
Zǐzhī then gave Sū Dài a hundred catties of gold,
allowing him to use it as he wished.
Lù Máo Shòu said to the King of Yān:
"It would be better to yield the state to Zǐzhī.
People say Yáo was a worthy,
because he yielded the world to Xǔ Yóu.
Yóu certainly would not accept it,
so he had the reputation of yielding the world,
yet in reality did not lose the world.
Now if Your Majesty yields the state to Chancellor Zǐzhī,
Zǐzhī certainly will not dare to accept it.
Thus, Your Majesty would act the same as Yáo."
The King of Yān thereupon entrusted the entire state to Zǐzhī,
and Zǐzhī became greatly weighty.
Someone said: "Yǔ appointed Yì to office but made Qǐ an official.
When he grew old,
he considered Qǐ unfit to rule the world,
so he passed it on to Yì.
Qǐ, along with his supporters, attacked Yì and seized the world from him.
Thus, while Yǔ ostensibly passed the world to Yì,
he actually allowed Qǐ to take it for himself.
Now, Your Majesty says you will entrust the state to Zǐzhī,
yet all the officials are men of the Crown Prince.
This is nominally entrusting it to Zǐzhī,
while the Crown Prince holds the real power."
The king then collected the seals of officials with salaries of three hundred shí or more and handed them over to Zǐzhī.
Zǐzhī assumed the throne and acted as king,
while Kuài, being old, no longer attended to governance,
but instead became a subject,
with all state affairs decided by Zǐzhī.
In the third year of Zǐzhī's rule, Yān fell into great turmoil,
and the common people were filled with grief and resentment.
General Shì Bèi and Crown Prince Píng plotted
to attack Zǐzhī.
Chǔ Zǐ said to King Xuān of Qí:
"If we take advantage of this to topple him,
we will surely defeat Yān."
The king then sent someone to tell Crown Prince Píng:
"I have heard of Your Highness's righteousness,
that you intend to abolish private interests and establish public good,
rectify the principles between ruler and subject,
and correct the positions of father and son.
My state is small,
and insufficient to lead or follow.
Nevertheless,
I will act solely according to Your Highness's commands."
The Crown Prince then gathered his followers and assembled a crowd.
General Shì Bèi surrounded the ducal palace,
attacking Zǐzhī,
but did not succeed.
General Shì Bèi and the common people then turned to attack Crown Prince Píng.
General Shì Bèi died in the conflict, and the state
was embroiled in strife for several months,
with tens of thousands dead.
The people of Yān were filled with grief and resentment,
and the common people became disaffected.
Mèng Kē said to King Xuān of Qí:
"Now is the time to attack Yān.
This is an opportunity like those of King Wén and King Wǔ,
and must not be missed."
The king then ordered Zhāng Zǐ to lead the troops of the five capitals,
and, with the support of the northern populace, to attack Yān.
The soldiers did not fight,
the city gates were not closed,
and King Kuài of Yān died.
Qí achieved a great victory over Yān,
and Zǐzhī fled.
Two years later,
the people of Yān established Gōngzǐ Píng as king,
who became King Zhāo of Yān.
Earlier,
Sū Qín's younger brother, Sū Lì, through the Yān hostage, sought an audience with the King of Qí.
The King of Qí harbored resentment toward Sū Qín,
and wanted to imprison Lì.
The Yān hostage interceded on his behalf, and the matter was dropped. Lì then offered his services and became a subject.
The Yān chancellor Zǐzhī was related by marriage to Sū Dài,
and, desiring to gain power in Yān,
he sent Sū Dài to accompany the hostage to Qí.
Qí sent Dài back to report to Yān.
King Kuài of Yān asked:
"Is the King of Qí likely to become a hegemon?"
He replied:
"He cannot."
The king asked:
"Why not?"
He said:
"He does not trust his ministers."
Thereupon, King Kuài entrusted all authority to Zǐzhī,
and later abdicated the throne, plunging Yān into great turmoil.
Qí attacked Yān,
killing King Kuài and Zǐzhī.
Yān established King Zhāo.
Sū Dài and Lì then did not dare enter Yān,
and both eventually returned to Qí,
where Qí treated them well.
Sū Dài passed through Wèi,
and Wèi arrested Dài on behalf of Yān.
Qí sent someone to tell the King of Wèi:
"Qí offered to grant Sòng territory to Lord Jīngyáng,
but Qín did not accept.
It is not that Qín does not benefit from having Qí's friendship and obtaining Sòng's land,
but rather that it does not trust the King of Qí and Master Sū.
Now, if Qí and Wèi are at odds,
and to such an extent,
then Qí will not deceive Qín.
If Qín trusts Qí,
and Qí and Qín unite,
and Lord Jīngyáng obtains Sòng's land,
this will not be to Wèi's advantage.
Therefore, Your Majesty should rather send Master Sū eastward.
Qín will surely become suspicious and no longer trust Master Sū.
If Qí and Qín do not unite,
and the world remains unchanged,
the conditions for attacking Qí will take shape."
Thereupon, they released Sū Dài and sent him to Sòng,
where Sòng treated him well.
After King Zhāo of Yān ascended the throne following the devastation of Yān,
he humbled himself and offered generous rewards
to recruit worthy men, intending to seek revenge.
Thus, he went to see Master Guō Wěi and said:
"Qí took advantage of the turmoil in our state
to launch a surprise attack and devastate Yān.
I am well aware that Yān is small and weak,
and insufficient to seek revenge.
However, if I can obtain worthy scholars to share in governing the state,
and thus wipe away the shame of my late father,
this is my wish.
May I ask how to take revenge for the state?"
Master Guō Wěi replied:
"A sovereign who would be an emperor treats others as his teachers;
a king who would be a true king treats others as his friends;
a hegemon treats others as his ministers;
a ruler of a doomed state treats others as his servants.
If you bend your will and serve them,
facing north to receive instruction,
then those a hundred times more capable than yourself will come.
If you are the first to act and the last to rest,
the first to inquire and the last to fall silent,
then those ten times more capable than yourself will come.
If you act only when others act,
then those equal to yourself will come.
If you lean on your desk and rely on your staff,
glancing around and pointing with your finger,
then only servants will come.
If you are reckless and violent,
shouting and berating,
then only slaves and convicts will come.
This is the ancient way of practicing the Dao and attracting scholars.
If Your Majesty truly widely selects the worthy men within the state,
and pays respects at their gates,
when the world hears that Your Majesty pays respects to his worthy ministers,
the scholars of the world will surely flock to Yān."
King Zhāo said:
"Whom should I pay respects to?"
Master Guō Wěi said:
"I have heard that in ancient times, there was a ruler
who sought a thousand-lǐ horse with a thousand pieces of gold,
but for three years could not obtain one.
A palace attendant said to the ruler:
'Allow me to seek it.'
The ruler sent him.
After three months, he found a thousand-lǐ horse,
but the horse was already dead.
He bought its head for five hundred pieces of gold,
and returned to report to the ruler.
The ruler was furious and said:
'What I sought was a live horse.
What use is a dead horse, and why waste five hundred pieces of gold?'
The attendant replied:
'If even a dead horse is bought for five hundred pieces of gold,
how much more a live one?
The world will surely consider Your Majesty able to buy horses,
and horses will now arrive.'
Thereupon, before a year had passed,
three thousand-lǐ horses arrived.
Now, if Your Majesty truly desires to attract scholars,
start with Wěi.
If even Wěi is treated with respect,
how much more those worthier than Wěi?
Would they consider a thousand lǐ too far?"
Thereupon, King Zhāo built a palace for Wěi and treated him as a teacher.
Yuè Yì came from Wèi,
Zōu Yǎn came from Qí,
Jù Xīn came from Zhào,
and scholars competed to gather in Yān.
The King of Yān mourned the dead and inquired after the living,
sharing both sweetness and bitterness with the common people.
In the twenty-eighth year,
Yān became prosperous and wealthy,
and the soldiers were content and eager for battle.
Thereupon, he appointed Yuè Yì as supreme general,
and, in alliance with Qín, Chǔ, and the Three Jìn, plotted to attack Qí.
The Qí army was defeated,
and King Mǐn fled abroad.
The Yān army alone pursued the fleeing forces and entered Línzī,
seizing all of Qí's treasures,
and burning its palaces and ancestral temples.
Of the Qí cities that did not fall,
Qí attacked Sòng,
and Sòng was in dire straits.
Sū Dài then sent a letter to King Zhāo of Yān, saying:
"To be ranked among the ten-thousand-chariot states,
yet to send a hostage to Qí,
is to have a lowly name and slight authority.
If Qí assists in attacking Sòng,
the people will be wearied and resources expended.
Destroying Sòng,
devastating Chǔ's territory north of the Huái River,
will fatten great Qí,
strengthen your enemy and
weaken your own state.
These three things
are all great failures for a state,
yet Your Majesty proceeds with them,
intending thereby to eliminate harm and gain trust from Qí.
But Qí has not increased its trust in Your Majesty,
and its suspicion of Yān grows ever stronger.
Thus, Your Majesty's service to Qí
has lost its purpose.
The people are wearied and resources expended,
yet not an inch of merit is gained;
destroying Sòng to fatten the enemy,
and the world will bear the calamity.
If Your Majesty adds Sòng to the territory north of the Huái,
it would be a strong ten-thousand-chariot state,
yet Qí annexes it,
which is to add another Qí.
The northern barbarian lands of seven hundred lǐ square,
plus Lǔ and Wèi,
this is what is called a strong ten-thousand-chariot state,
and Qí annexes it,
which is to add a second Qí.
With the strength of one Qí,
Yān still cannot withstand it;
now with three Qís facing Yān,
the calamity will surely be great.
Nevertheless,
I have heard that when the wise undertake affairs,
they turn calamity into blessing,
and from failure achieve success.
The people of Qí dye worn white silk purple,
and its price increases tenfold.
King Gōujiàn of Yuè dwelt on Kuàijī Mountain,
yet later destroyed Wú and dominated the world.
These are examples of turning calamity into blessing,
and from failure achieving success.
If now Your Majesty wishes to turn calamity into blessing,
and from failure achieve success,
then nothing is better than to ostensibly honor Qí and deeply respect it,
sending envoys to form an alliance in the Zhōu court,
burning all the tallies of covenant with Qín under heaven,
and agreeing:
'The best plan is to destroy Qín,
the next is to permanently keep it at a distance.'
Qín, held at a distance while awaiting destruction,
will surely trouble the King of Qín.
Qín for five generations has allied with the various lords,
now it is beneath Qí;
the King of Qín's ambition,
if it can exhaust Qí,
would not hesitate to use a whole capital city as an achievement.
Why then does Your Majesty not send an ordinary man
to persuade Qín with this argument of exhausting Qí,
saying to the King of Qín:
'Yān and Zhào destroying Sòng to fatten Qí and honor Qí, placing themselves beneath it—
Yān and Zhào do not benefit from this.
If they do not benefit yet are compelled to do it,
why?
Because they do not trust the King of Qín.
Now why does Your Majesty not send someone trustworthy to win over Yān and Zhào?
Let Jīngyáng Jūn or Gāolíng Jūn go first to Yān and Zhào;
if Qí changes,
they can serve as hostages,
then Yān and Zhào will trust Qín.
Let Qín be the Western Emperor,
Zhào the Central Emperor,
Yān the Northern Emperor,
establish three emperors to command the various lords.
If Hán and Wèi do not obey,
then Qín attacks them.
If Qí does not obey,
then Yān and Zhào attack it.
Who under heaven would dare not obey?
When all under heaven submit and obey,
then drive Hán and Wèi to attack Qí,
saying: you must return the land of Sòng,
and restore Chǔ's territory north of the Huái.
Returning the land of Sòng,
restoring Chǔ's territory north of the Huái,
is of shared benefit to Yān and Zhào.
Establishing three emperors together,
is the shared wish of Yān and Zhào.
Substantially gaining benefit,
nominally fulfilling wishes,
then Yān and Zhào abandoning Qí
would be like discarding worn-out sandals.
If now Your Majesty does not win over Yān and Zhào,
then Qí's hegemony will surely be achieved.
The various lords will support Qí,
and if Your Majesty alone does not follow,
your state will be attacked.
If the various lords support Qí,
and Your Majesty follows them,
your name will be lowly.
If Your Majesty does not win over Yān and Zhào,
your name will be lowly and your state endangered;
if Your Majesty wins over Yān and Zhào,
your name will be honored and your state secure.
To abandon honor and security for lowliness and danger—
the wise do not do such things.'
If the King of Qín hears such persuasion,
he will surely feel as if stabbed in the heart.
Then why does Your Majesty not diligently send a knowledgeable scholar to persuade Qín with these words?
Qín will certainly attack Qí.
To win over Qín is the highest alliance;
to attack Qí
is the correct benefit.
Honoring the highest alliance,
pursuing the correct benefit,
is the task of a sage king."
King Zhāo of Yān thought well of this letter,
and said:
"My ancestors once showed kindness to the Sū family;
during the rebellion of Zǐ Zhī,
the Sū family left Yān.
Yān wishes to take revenge on Qí,
and none but the Sū family can achieve it."
He then summoned the Sū family,
and treated them well again.
He plotted with them to attack Qí,
and eventually destroyed Qí,
causing King Mǐn to flee.
Sū Dài said to King Zhāo of Yān:
"Suppose there is a person here,
as filial as Zēng Shēn or Xiào Jǐ,
as trustworthy as Wěi Shēnggāo,
as incorruptible as Bào Jiāo or Shǐ Qiū,
and possessing all three of these virtues to serve Your Majesty—
what would you think?"
The King said:
"If so, it would be sufficient."
He replied:
"If Your Majesty considers this sufficient,
then I will not serve Your Majesty.
I would rather engage in non-action,
return to till the highlands of Zhōu,
plowing to eat,
weaving to clothe myself."
The King said: "Why so?"
He replied:
"To be as filial as Zēng Shēn or Xiào Jǐ
is merely to support one's parents.
To be as trustworthy as Wěi Shēnggāo
is merely not to deceive others.
To be as incorruptible as Bào Jiāo or Shǐ Qiū
is merely not to steal others' wealth.
Now I am one who strives for advancement.
I believe that incorruptibility does not lead to personal success,
nor righteousness to establishment in life.
Benevolence and righteousness
are ways of self-preservation,
not methods for advancement."
The King said: "Is self-cultivation not enough?"
He replied: "If self-cultivation were enough,
then Qín would not have emerged from the Xiáo Pass,
Qí would not have left Yíngqiū,
Chǔ would not have left Shūzhāng.
The Three Sovereigns succeeded each other,
the Five Hegemons reformed governance,
all because they did not rest content with self-cultivation.
If self-cultivation were enough,
then I too would go to Zhōu carrying a basket,
why trouble Your Majesty's court?
In the past, when Chǔ took Zhāngwǔ,
the various lords faced north and paid homage.
When Qín took the Western Mountains,
the various lords faced west and paid homage.
If formerly Yān had not abandoned its position above the Zhōu court,
then the various lords would not have paid homage to others' horses.
I have heard that
those skilled in handling affairs
first measure the size of their state,
and assess the strength of its military;
thus achievements can be made,
and fame established.
Those unable to handle affairs
do not first measure the size of their state,
nor assess the strength of its military;
thus achievements cannot be made and fame cannot be established.
Now Your Majesty has the intention to campaign east against Qí,
and this humble servant knows it."
The King said: "How do you know?"
He replied: "You polish halberds and sharpen swords,
ascend a hill, gaze east, and sigh—
thus this humble servant knows."
Now, Wū Huò could lift a weight of a thousand jūn,
but when he reached eighty years of age,
he sought support to walk.
Thus, although Qí is a powerful state,
if it wearies itself in the west with Sòng,
and exhausts itself in the south with Chǔ,
then the Qí army can be defeated,
and Héjiān can be taken."
The King of Yān said: "Excellent.
I ask to appoint you as a high minister,
and present you with a hundred chariots.
With these, you shall travel east for me to Qí. How is that?"
He replied: "If Your Majesty gives them to me out of affection,
then why not give them to your beloved sons, maternal uncles,
uncles, or grandsons leaning against the bed? Since you do not,
but instead give them to an incapable minister, why is that?
How does the King evaluate me,
as what kind of person?
What I now use to serve Your Majesty is
loyalty and trustworthiness.
I fear that because of this loyalty and trustworthiness,
I will incur offense from those around you."
The King said: "How can a minister who exhausts his strength
and uses all his abilities
incur offense?"
He replied: "I ask to use an analogy for the King.
In the past, there was such a case in the land of Zhōu.
A husband served in office for three years without returning.
His wife took a lover.
The one she loved said:
'When your husband comes back,
what shall we do then?'
His wife said: 'Do not worry.
I have already prepared poisoned wine and await his return.'
Later, her husband indeed returned.
Thereupon, she ordered her concubine to pour the poisoned wine and present it to him.
The concubine knew about it,
and stood halfway.
She pondered, saying:
'If I use this to give my master to drink,
then I will kill my master;
if I report this matter to my master,
then my mistress will be driven out.
Rather than killing my master or causing my mistress to be driven out,
I would rather pretend to stumble and overturn it.'
Thereupon, she pretended to stumble and spilled it.
The wife said: 'For your long journey and return,
I specially prepared fine wine,
and now this concubine presents it only to spill it.'
The husband did not know the truth,
so he bound the concubine and whipped her.
Thus, the reason the concubine was whipped was
due to her loyalty and trustworthiness.
Now, I am about to be sent by Your Majesty to Qí,
and I fear that my loyalty and trustworthiness will not be understood by those around you.
I have heard it said:
The ruler of a state with ten thousand chariots
should not be controlled by his ministers.
The head of a household with ten chariots
should not be controlled by the multitude.
An ordinary man on foot
should not be controlled by his wife and concubines.
How much more so should a worthy ruler of the present age?
I ask to take my leave now,
and I hope that Your Majesty will not be controlled by your many ministers."
The King of Yān said to Sū Dài:
"I greatly dislike the words of flatterers."
Sū Dài replied: "In Zhōu, matchmakers are looked down upon,
because they praise both sides.
To the man's family they say 'the woman is beautiful,'
to the woman's family they say 'the man is wealthy.'
Yet according to the customs of Zhōu,
one does not arrange a marriage for oneself.
Moreover, if a maiden has no matchmaker,
she will grow old and not marry;
if she abandons the matchmaker and promotes herself,
she will be worn out and not find a match.
To proceed smoothly without failure,
to find a match without being worn out—
this is only possible through a matchmaker.
Moreover, affairs cannot be established without expediency,
nor can they be accomplished without leverage.
Those who enable people to sit and receive accomplished results
are precisely the flatterers."
The King said: "Well said."
Qín summoned the King of Yān,
and the King of Yān wished to go.
Sū Dài restrained the King of Yān, saying:
"Chǔ obtained Zhǐ, yet its state perished;
Qí obtained Sòng, yet its state perished.
Why is it that Qí and Chǔ, despite having Zhǐ and Sòng, served Qín?
What is the reason?
It is because those who achieve merit
become Qín's deep-seated enemies.
When Qín seizes the world,
it does not act with righteousness,
but with violence.
Qín's acts of violence in the world
were plainly declared to Chǔ, saying:
'The armor from Shǔ territory,
on light boats floating on the Wèn River,
riding the summer floods down the Jiāng,
can reach Yǐng in five days.
The armor from Hànzhōng,
embarking from Bā,
riding the summer floods down the Hàn River,
can reach Wǔzhǔ in four days.
I have accumulated armor in Wǎn,
and will descend east to Suí.
The wise will have no time to plan,
the brave will have no time to rage.
I will be like shooting a falcon.
If you, King, wait for the forces of the world to attack Hángǔ,
is that not too far off?'
For this reason, the King of Chǔ
served Qín for seventeen years.
Qín plainly declared to Hán, saying:
'If I arise from Shǎoqū,
in one day I can cut off Tàiháng.
If I arise from Yíyáng and strike Píngyáng,
in two days nothing will not be thrown into turmoil.
If I leave the two Zhōu and strike Zhèng,
in five days your state will be taken.'
Hán considered this true,
and thus served Qín.
Qín plainly declared to Wèi, saying:
'If I raise Ānyì,
block Nǚjǐ,
and Hán's Tàiyuán is rolled up,
if I take Zhǐ, pass through Nányáng, Fēng, and Jì,
encircle the two Zhōu,
ride the summer floods,
float on light boats,
with strong crossbows in front
and sharp spears behind,
breach the Róngkǒu,
and Wèi will have no Dàliáng;
breach the Báimǎkǒu,
and Wèi will have no Jìyáng;
breach the Sùxūkǒu,
and Wèi will have no Xū or Dùnqiū.
Attack by land, and Hénèi will be struck;
attack by water, and Dàliáng will be destroyed.'
Wèi considered this true,
and thus served Qín.
Qín wished to attack Ānyì,
but feared Qí would rescue it,
so it entrusted Sòng to Qí,
saying:
'The King of Sòng is without virtue.
He made a wooden figure to resemble me
and shot at its face.
My lands are cut off and my troops are far away, so I cannot attack.
If you, King, can destroy Sòng and possess it,
it will be as if I myself have obtained it.'
After obtaining Ānyì,
and blocking Nǚjǐ,
it then used the destruction of Sòng as a crime against Qí.
Qín wished to attack Qí,
but feared the world would rescue it,
so it entrusted Qí to the world, saying:
'The King of Qí made four agreements with me,
and deceived me four times.
Three times he mustered the world to attack me.
If there is Qí, there is no Qín;
if there is no Qí, there is Qín.
I must attack it,
I must destroy it!'
After obtaining Yíyáng and Shǎoqū,
and reaching Lìn and Shí,
it then used the destruction of Qí as a crime against the world.
Qín wished to attack Wèi but valued Chǔ,
so it entrusted Nányáng to Chǔ, saying:
'I am determined to break with Hán!
Devastate Jūnlíng,
block Mèng'ài.
If it benefits Chǔ,
it will be as if I myself possess it.'
Wèi abandoned its allies and allied with Qín,
and then Qín used the blocking of Mèng'ài as a crime against Chǔ.
When the army was trapped in the woods,
Qin valued Yān and Zhào,
entrusting Jiāodōng to Yān,
and entrusting Jīxī to Zhào.
When Zhào reached an agreement with Wèi,
up to Gōngzǐ Yán,
Qin relied on Xīshǒu to lead troops and attack Zhào.
When the army was wounded at Líshí,
and suffered defeat at Mǎlíng,
and valued Wèi,
then it entrusted Yè and Cài to Wèi.
Once an agreement was reached with Zhào,
Qin then coerced Wèi,
but Wèi refused to cede territory.
When in distress, Qin sent the Queen Dowager and Ránghóu to make peace,
but when victorious, it deceived both its uncle and mother.
To those sent to Yān, it was said:
'Entrust Jiāodōng.'
To those sent to Zhào, it was said:
'Entrust Jīxī.'
To those sent to Wèi, it was said:
'Entrust Yè and Cài.'
To those sent to Chǔ, it was said:
'Block the Mèng'ài Pass.'
To those sent to Qí, it was said:
'Entrust Sòng.'
This inevitably makes their words circulate like a cycle,
and their use of troops as effortless as embroidering,
so that the mother cannot control them,
and the uncle cannot restrain them.
In the battles of Lóng Jiǎ,
Ànmén,
Fēnglù,
Gāoshāng,
and Zhào Zhuāng,
Qin killed millions of people from the Three Jìn.
Now those who survive,
are all orphans of those killed by Qín.
The lands west of the Yellow River, Shàngluò, and Sānchuān,
the calamities of Jìn,
are half of the Three Jìn.
The calamity brought by Qín is so great,
yet those in Yān and Zhào who serve Qín,
all compete to serve Qín and persuade their rulers,
this is what I greatly worry about."
Yān Zhāowáng did not act,
and Sū Dài regained importance in Yān.
Yān then formed alliances with the various states for vertical cooperation,
as in the time of Sū Qín,
some joined while others did not,
and the world thus revered the Sū family's vertical alliance.
Dài and Lì both died of old age,
and their fame spread among the feudal lords.
Sū Dài persuaded Fèngyáng Jūn in Zhào to attack Qí on behalf of Yān,
but Fèngyáng Jūn did not listen.
He then entered Qí to turn it against Zhào,
causing Qí to break off relations with Zhào.
After Qí had broken off relations with Zhào,
he went to Yān,
and said to Zhāowáng:
"Hán Wèi said to me:
'Someone told Fèngyáng Jūn:
The one who made Qí distrust Zhào,
is Master Sū;
now the King of Qí summoned Shǔzi to stop attacking Sòng,
it was Master Sū;
the one who plotted with the King of Qí to ally with Qín to scheme against Zhào,
is Master Sū;
the one who ordered Qí to guard Zhào's hostage with armor,
is also Master Sū.
I ask to inform you that if you request Qí,
and indeed guard Zhào's hostage with armor,
I will certainly guard you with armor.'
His words are malicious.
Nevertheless,
Your Majesty need not worry.
I knew beforehand that entering Qí would bring trouble from Zhào.
I acted to achieve what I desired,
and even if I die and Qí becomes greatly hostile to Zhào,
I would still feel as if alive.
If Qí and Zhào break off relations,
great chaos can be created.
If I were not Zhāng Mèngtán,
but if I were like Zhāng Mèngtán, then Qí and Zhào would surely have someone like Zhì Bó."
Fèngyáng Jūn told Zhū Huān and Zhào Zú:
"The King of Qí sent Gōngwáng Yuē to deliver a message, saying:
He would certainly not recall Hán Mín,
but now he has summoned him.
He would certainly not entrust Master Sū with any affairs,
but now he has enfeoffed him and made him chancellor.
He said he would not ally with Yān,
but now he treats Yān as his closest ally.
What I relied on was Shùn,
but now his words have changed even more than his father's,
and Shùn initially became an enemy of Master Sū.
When I met him, I knew he was not Lì,
but now he honors him and treats him as an equal,
it is over,
I have lost Qí!"
Fèngyáng Jūn was extremely angry.
If the King of Qí does not trust Zhào,
and I, a petty man, serve Fèngyáng Jūn,
I will betray him because of this.
If we do not create great chaos now,
and they reconcile and reunite,
then later nothing can be done.
Therefore, if the alliance between Qí and Zhào can be maintained,
death is not enough to worry me;
escape is not enough to shame me;
becoming a feudal lord is not enough to bring me glory;
letting my hair down and painting myself with lacquer to appear disfigured,
is not enough to bring me disgrace.
However, I do have a worry:
if I die and Qí and Zhào do not maintain their alliance,
and hostility is divided because of me,
and they later imitate each other,
that is my worry.
If after my death they must attack each other,
I will certainly strive for it and seek death.
Yáo and Shùn were virtuous and died,
Yǔ and Tāng were wise and died,
Mèng Bēn was brave and died,
Wū Huò was strong and died,
is there anything among living things that does not die?
Using inevitable things to achieve what is desired,
why should Your Majesty doubt?
I think it is better to escape and leave.
I will have Hán and Wèi follow Qí from within,
and for them ally with Qín,
deeply bonding with Zhào to strengthen it.
In this way, they will be close to attacking each other.
Although I will cause trouble for Yān because of this,
Fèngyáng Jūn told Zhū Huān:
'Master Sū is angry because the King of Yān did not make me chancellor,
nor did he give me a ministerial position,
nor did he make me a high official,
I fear Yān is lost.'
His suspicion has reached this point,
so although I act, I will not trouble Yān,
nor do I wish to trouble Your Majesty.
Yī Yǐn twice fled from Tāng to Jié,
and twice fled from Jié to Tāng,
and indeed fought in the Battle of Míngtiáo,
making Tāng the Son of Heaven.
Wǔ Zǐxū fled from Chǔ to Wú,
and indeed fought in the Battle of Bó Jǔ,
avenging his father's enemy.
Now if I flee and create chaos between Qí and Zhào,
it can be recorded in the Spring and Autumn Annals.
Moreover, those who undertake great affairs,
who does not flee?
During Duke Huán's troubles,
Guǎn Zhòng fled to Lǔ;
during Yáng Hǔ's troubles,
Confucius fled to Wèi;
Zhāng Yí fled to Chǔ;
Bái Guī fled to Qín;
when Wàngzhū was chancellor of Zhōngshān and sent to Zhào,
Zhào coerced him to demand territory,
Wàngzhū attacked the pass and fled;
during the trouble of the grandson,
Xuē Gōng released the carriage and fled through the pass,
and the Three Jìn praised him as a scholar.
Therefore, in undertaking great affairs,
escape is not enough to bring disgrace."
In the end, Qí broke off relations with Zhào,
and Zhào allied with Yān to attack Qí,
defeating it.
Sū Dài persuaded Qí on behalf of Yān,
before meeting the King of Qí,
he first persuaded Chúnyú Kūn, saying:
"There was a man who wanted to sell a fine horse,
for three mornings he stood in the market,
but no one recognized it.
He went to see Bó Lè and said:
'I have a fine horse,
and wish to sell it,
for three mornings I have stood in the market,
but no one has spoken to me,
I hope you will come and look at it,
and when leaving, look back at it,
I will offer you the earnings of one morning.'
Bó Lè then came and looked at it,
and when leaving, looked back at it,
and in one morning the horse's price increased tenfold.
Now I wish to present my fine horse to the king,
but there is no one to introduce me,
would you be willing to be my Bó Lè?
I offer a pair of white jade discs,
and a thousand yì of gold,
as fodder for the horse."
Chúnyú Kūn said: "I respectfully heed your command."
He entered and spoke to the king, who then received him,
and the King of Qí was greatly pleased with Master Sū.
Sū Dài, from Qí, sent someone to tell King Zhāo of Yān:
"I have heard that Qí and Zhào are estranged,
and Qí and Zhào are already isolated.
Why does Your Majesty not send troops to attack Qí?
I beg to weaken it for Your Majesty."
Yān then attacked Qí and assaulted Jìn.
He had someone tell King Mǐn:
"Yān's attack on Qí
is intended to recover its ancient territory.
Yān's troops are at Jìn and do not advance,
which shows their forces are weak and their plans hesitant.
Why does Your Majesty not order Master Sū to command and respond to Yān?
With Master Sū's worthiness,
commanding to respond to weak Yān,
Yān will surely be defeated.
If Yān is defeated, Zhào will not dare disobey,
thus Your Majesty defeats Yān and subdues Zhào."
King Mǐn said: "Good."
He then told Master Sū:
"Yān's troops are at Jìn,
now I am sending troops to respond to them.
I wish you to command them for me."
He replied: "As for me with troops,
how could I be adequate to take command?
Your Majesty should change your appointment.
If Your Majesty employs me,
it will ruin Your Majesty's troops
and deliver me to Yān.
If the battle is not won,
it cannot be recovered."
The king said: "Go ahead, I know you."
Master Sū then took command
and fought with the Yān people below Jìn.
The Qí army was defeated.
Yān obtained twenty thousand armored heads.
Master Sū gathered his remaining troops
to defend Yángchéng
and reported to King Mǐn:
"Your Majesty erred in appointing,
ordering me to respond to Yān.
Now the army is defeated, losing twenty thousand men.
I have the crime deserving axe and block.
I beg to surrender myself to the officials for execution."
King Mǐn said: "This is my fault.
Do not consider it your crime."
The next day, he again had Yān attack Yángchéng and Lí.
He again had someone tell King Mǐn:
"Previously Qí did not win below Jìn.
This was not the fault of the troops.
Qí had misfortune while Yān had heaven's fortune.
Now Yān again attacks Yángchéng and Lí,
thus taking heaven's fortune as their own achievement.
If Your Majesty again sends Master Sū to respond,
Master Sū, having first defeated Your Majesty's troops,
will afterward surely strive to repay Your Majesty with victory."
The king said: "Good."
He then again sent Master Sū.
Master Sū firmly declined,
but the king would not listen.
He then took command to fight with Yān at Yángchéng.
The Yān people won a great victory, obtaining thirty thousand heads.
The Qí ruler and ministers were not close,
and the common people were alienated.
Yān then sent Yuè Yì to raise a great army to attack Qí
and defeated it.
Sū Dài, from Qí, presented a letter to the King of Yān:
"When I departed,
I certainly knew there would be matters of slander.
Therefore I presented a letter to the royal carriage and departed,
saying:
'If I am esteemed in Qí,
the Yān great officers will not trust me;
if I am lowly,
they will despise me;
if I am employed,
they will have great expectations of me;
if Qí has any misdeeds,
they will blame me;
if the world does not attack Qí,
they will say I am good at planning for Qí;
if the world attacks Qí,
they will join with Qí to sell me out.
My position is like piled eggs.'
Your Majesty said to me:
'I certainly will not listen to the many mouths and slanderous words.
I trust you,
like cutting grass.
At best, you can gain employment in Qí;
next, you can gain trust below.
If you do not die,
there is nothing you cannot do.
With your self-confidence, it is acceptable.'
And you said to me:
'Leaving Yān for Qí is acceptable;
the goal is to accomplish the task.'
I received the order to serve in Qí,
and it has been five years.
Qí has repeatedly sent out troops,
but never plotted against Yān.
The relations between Qí and Zhào,
sometimes united, sometimes estranged.
If the King of Yān did not plot with Qí against Zhào,
then he plotted with Zhào against Qí.
Qí's trust in Yān
went so far as to empty its northern territories to deploy its troops.
Now Your Majesty trusts Tián Fá and the words of Cān and Qùjí,
and moreover attacks Qí,
making Qí like dogs and horses yet not speaking of Yān.
Now Your Majesty again sends Qìng to order me:
'I wish to employ those I consider good.'
If Your Majesty truly wishes to employ them,
then I beg to serve them for Your Majesty.
If Your Majesty wishes to release me and fully employ those you consider good,
then I beg to return and be released from service.
If I can get to see you,
then my wishes will be fulfilled."
Chén Cuì united Qí and Yān
and was about to have the King of Yān's younger brother go as a hostage to Qí.
The King of Yān agreed.
The queen dowager heard this and was greatly angered, saying:
"Lord Chén cannot serve others' states,
that is all.
How can there be one who separates mother and child?
This old woman wishes to have her way."
Chén Cuì wished to see the queen dowager.
The king said:
"The queen dowager is currently angry with you.
You should wait."
Chén Cuì said: "It is harmless."
He then entered to see the queen dowager, saying:
"Why are you so thin?"
The queen dowager said:
"I rely on the leftover food of the wild geese and ducks of the former king.
I should not be thin.
Being thin
is from worrying that the young prince is about to be a hostage in Qí."
Chén Cuì said: "A ruler's love for his children
is not as deep as that of commoners.
Not only does he not love his children,
he especially does not love his sons."
The queen dowager said:
"Why?"
He replied:
"When the queen dowager married her daughter to a feudal lord,
you presented her with a thousand pieces of gold
and bestowed a hundred lǐ of land,
considering it the end of her life.
Now the king wishes to enfeoff the young prince.
The officials hold to their duties;
the ministers offer loyalty, saying:
'The young prince has no merit and should not be enfeoffed.'
Now the king is having the young prince go as a hostage
in order to consider it the young prince's merit and enfeoff him.
If the queen dowager does not listen,
I therefore know that a ruler especially does not love his sons.
Moreover, while the queen dowager and the king are fortunately alive,
the young prince is noble;
after the queen dowager's passing and the king abandoning the state,
and the crown prince ascending the throne,
the young prince will be lower than a commoner.
Therefore, if he is not enfeoffed by the queen dowager and the king,
then the young prince will never be enfeoffed in his lifetime!"
The queen dowager said: "This old woman did not know the elder's plan."
She then ordered the young prince to prepare carriages, make clothes, and prepare for the journey.
King Zhāo of Yān was about to join the world in attacking Qí,
and there was a man of Qí serving in Yān.
King Zhāo summoned him and said:
"I am about to join the world in attacking Qí.
I will issue the order morning or evening.
You must oppose it.
If you oppose it and I do not listen,
you should then leave and go to Qí.
I may sometimes again seek reconciliation,
and will thereby rely on you to serve Qí."
At this time,
Yān and Qí could not coexist,
yet he constantly alone desired to have the intention to restore relations like this.
Yān was suffering famine,
and Zhào was about to attack it.
Chǔ sent a general to Yān.
Passing through Wèi,
he saw Zhào Huī.
Zhào Huī said:
"To eliminate calamity before it arrives
is easier than rescuing from calamity.
Wǔ Zǐxū and Gōng Zhīqí were not employed;
Zhú Zhīwǔ and Zhāng Mèngtán received great rewards.
Therefore, strategists all engage in the way of eliminating calamity,
and first make eliminating calamity before it arrives a priority."
Now, if I were to send you off with a hundred gold pieces,
it would not be as good as giving you words.
If you listen to my words and persuade the King of Zhào, saying:
'In the past, Wú attacked Qí,
because Qí was suffering from famine.
Attacking Qí might not necessarily lead to victory,
yet weak Yuè took advantage of its exhaustion to become hegemonic.
Now, Your Majesty's attack on Yān
is also because Yān is suffering from famine.
Attacking it might not necessarily lead to victory,
while powerful Qín will send troops to press upon Your Majesty's western borders.
This would place weak Zhào in the position of strong Wú,
and allow powerful Qín to occupy the role that weak Yuè used to become hegemonic.
I hope Your Majesty will carefully consider this.'"
The messenger then used these words to persuade the King of Zhào,
and the King of Zhào was greatly pleased,
so he stopped the attack.
When King Zhāo of Yān heard of this,
he enfeoffed the messenger with land.
Lord Chāngguó, Yuè Yì, assembled the armies of five states for King Zhāo of Yān and attacked Qí,
capturing over seventy cities,
and establishing them all as commanderies and counties under Yān's control.
Three cities remained uncaptured
when King Zhāo of Yān died.
King Huì succeeded to the throne,
and, influenced by Qí's use of counterintrigue,
he became suspicious of Yuè Yì
and sent Qí Jié to replace him as commander.
Yuè Yì fled to Zhào,
where he was enfeoffed as Lord Wàngzhū.
Tián Dān of Qí deceived Qí Jié,
and ultimately defeated the Yān army,
recovering the seventy cities and restoring Qí.
The King of Yān regretted this,
fearing that Zhào would use Yuè Yì to take advantage of Yān's exhaustion and attack Yān.
The King of Yān then sent a messenger to reproach Yuè Yì,
and also apologized to him, saying:
"The late king entrusted the entire state to you, General.
You, General, defeated Qí for Yān,
avenging the late king's enmity.
The whole world was shaken by this.
How could I dare forget your achievements for even a single day?
It happened that the late king passed away,
and I had just ascended the throne.
My attendants misled me.
The reason I sent Qí Jié to replace you, General,
was because you had long been exposed to the hardships of the field,
so I summoned you back to rest and discuss affairs.
You, General, misunderstood,
and, thinking there was a rift between us,
abandoned Yān and returned to Zhào.
If you, General, acted for your own sake, that is acceptable,
but how does this repay the late king's intentions in treating you so well?"
Lord Wàngzhū then sent a messenger to present a letter in reply to the King of Yān, saying:
"I am not talented,
and unable to uphold the late king's teachings,
or to comply with the wishes of your attendants.
Fearing I might incur the crime of execution,
and thereby tarnish the late king's wisdom,
and also harm Your Majesty's righteousness,
I fled and escaped to Zhào.
Bearing the guilt of my unworthiness,
I did not dare to offer any explanation.
Now that Your Majesty has sent a messenger to enumerate my crimes,
I fear that Your Majesty's attendants may not understand the reasons why the late king favored and trusted me,
nor may they be clear about my intentions in serving the late king.
Therefore, I dare to reply with this letter.
I have heard that wise and sagacious rulers
do not bestow emoluments privately upon their relatives,
but grant them to those with great achievements;
they do not appoint officials based on personal favor,
but place those who are capable in positions.
Thus, those who examine ability and confer office accordingly
are rulers who achieve success;
those who judge conduct and form friendships accordingly
are men who establish their reputations.
From what I have learned, I observe
that the late king's actions and decisions
showed a mind surpassing the age.
Thus, he borrowed credentials from the King of Wèi
and personally came to observe Yān.
The late king, in his excessive regard,
raised me from among the guests,
and placed me above the other ministers,
without consulting his elder relatives,
and appointed me as Assistant Minister.
I believed that by obeying orders and accepting instructions,
I could hope to avoid offense,
so I accepted the command without declining.
The late king commanded me, saying:
'I have deep-seated grievances and profound anger against Qí.
Despite our own weakness,
I wish to make Qí our objective.'
I replied: 'Qí inherits the remaining teachings of a hegemonic state,
and the legacy of repeated victories.
They are skilled in warfare,
and experienced in battle.
If Your Majesty wishes to attack them,
you must unite the world to plan against them.
To unite the world and plan against them,
there is no quicker way than to ally with Zhào.
Moreover, the lands of Huáiběi and Sòng
are equally desired by Chǔ and Wèi.
If Zhào agrees,
we can make a pact with Chǔ and Wèi,
and Sòng will exert its full strength.
With the four states attacking together,
Qí can be utterly defeated.'
The late king said: 'Excellent.'
I then received his oral command,
prepared the credentials,
and went south as an envoy to Zhào.
Upon returning to report,
troops were raised and followed to attack Qí.
By the way of Heaven,
and the spirit of the late king,
the lands north of the Yellow River
were all taken by the late king up to the Jì River.
The army at the Jì River, obeying orders to attack Qí,
achieved a great victory.
With light troops and sharp soldiers,
we drove straight to the capital.
The King of Qí fled and escaped to Jǔ,
barely saving his own life.
Pearls, jade, treasures, and wealth,
chariots, armor, and precious vessels,
were all taken into Yān.
The great bell Dàlǚ was displayed in Yuányīng,
the old tripods were returned to the Lìshì,
and Qí's vessels were placed in Níngtái.
What was planted at Jìqiū
was transplanted to Wénhuáng.
Since the time of the Five Hegemons,
no achievement has matched that of the late king.
The late king, considering his ambitions satisfied,
and regarding me as not having failed his command,
divided the land and enfeoffed me,
allowing me to rank with the lords of small states.
I am not talented,
but I believed that by obeying orders and accepting instructions,
I could hope to avoid offense,
so I accepted the command without declining.
I have heard that wise and enlightened rulers,
once they establish achievements, do not let them go to waste,
and thus they are recorded in the annals; men of foresight,
once they achieve fame, do not let it be destroyed,
and thus they are praised by later generations.
As for the late king's repayment of grievances and washing away of shame,
subduing the powerful state of ten thousand chariots,
and seizing the accumulations of eight hundred years—
up to the day he left his ministers behind,
the remaining decrees and the righteous legacy he bequeathed to his successors,
the ministers in charge of administration and affairs,
their ability to follow laws and commands,
to manage the collateral branches,
and to extend benefits to the common people—
all can serve as instruction for later generations.
I have heard that those who are good at starting
are not necessarily good at finishing;
those who are good at beginnings
are not necessarily good at endings.
In the past, Wǔ Zǐxū's advice was heeded by Hé Lǘ,
so the King of Wú left his traces as far as Yǐng.
Fū Chāi did not approve of this,
and gave him a leather sack to float in the river.
Thus, King Fū Chāi of Wú did not realize that following earlier advice could lead to achievement,
so he drowned Zǐxū without regret.
Zǐxū did not foresee early on that his lord's capacity was different,
so he entered the river without changing.
To preserve myself and complete my achievements,
and to clarify the late king's deeds—
this is my best plan.
To incur the fault of slander and disgrace,
and to ruin the late king's name—
this is what I greatly fear.
To face immeasurable crimes,
and to seek profit from misfortune—
is something righteousness does not permit.
I have heard that noble men of old,
even when ending a friendship, did not speak ill;
loyal ministers, when leaving,
do not try to clear their names.
Though I am not talented,
I have often received teachings from noble men.
I fear that Your Majesty's attendants may heed the words of those close to you,
and not examine the conduct of one who is distant.
Therefore, I dare to reply with this letter,
hoping that Your Majesty will consider it carefully."
Someone presented a letter to the King of Yān:
"If Your Majesty cannot rely on yourself,
do not disdain a lowly reputation to serve a strong power,
for serving a strong power
can ensure the state's security and long-lasting stability,
a wise strategy for ten thousand generations.
If serving a strong power cannot secure ten thousand generations,
then it is better to unite the weak.
But how can the weak unite if they cannot act as one?
This is what troubles me about the states east of the mountains.
The flounder fish,
if they do not come together, cannot swim;
thus the ancients praised them,
for they unite two into one.
Now the weak states east of the mountains unite but cannot act as one,
showing their wisdom is inferior to that of fish.
Again, take the example of men pulling a cart:
three men cannot move it,
but add two more,
and with five men the cart moves.
Now three weak states east of the mountains cannot resist Qín;
add two more states,
and they can defeat Qín.
Yet the states east of the mountains do not know to seek each other out,
their wisdom is truly inferior to that of cart-pullers.
The Hú and Yuè peoples,
whose languages are mutually unintelligible,
whose thoughts and intentions are not communicated,
yet when crossing waves in the same boat,
they assist each other as one.
Now the states east of the mountains,
though they are like crossing in the same boat,
when Qín's troops arrive,
cannot assist each other as one,
their wisdom is again inferior to that of the Hú and Yuè peoples.
These three examples
are things men can accomplish,
yet the rulers east of the mountains still do not realize this,
this is what troubles me about the states east of the mountains.
I hope Your Majesty will consider this carefully.
If the states east of the mountains unite,
their rulers will not have lowly reputations,
their states can long endure,
and their soldiers can be sent to garrison the western borders of Hán and Liáng.
This is the best strategy for Yān.
If this is not urgently done,
the state will surely be in danger,
and the ruler will surely face great worry.
Now Hán, Liáng, and Zhào have already united;
when Qín sees the solidarity of the three Jìn states,
it will surely campaign south against Chǔ.
When Zhào sees Qín campaigning against Chǔ,
it will surely attack north against Yān.
It is often the case that circumstances differ but disasters are the same.
Qín long campaigned against Hán,
hence Zhōngshān perished;
now if it long campaigns against Chǔ,
Yān will surely perish.
I privately plan for Your Majesty: it would be better to lead troops south to unite with the three Jìn states,
and agree to garrison the western borders of Hán and Liáng.
If the states east of the mountains cannot firmly do this,
they will all surely perish."
Yān indeed led troops south to unite with the three Jìn states.
A guest said to the King of Yān:
"Qí has defeated Chǔ in the south,
subdued Qín in the west,
using the troops of Hán and Wèi,
and the masses of Yān and Zhào,
as if wielding a whip.
If Qí were to campaign north against Yān,
even five Yān could not withstand it.
Why does Your Majesty not secretly send envoys,
disperse wandering scholars,
wear down Qí's troops,
exhaust its masses,
so that for generations there will be no worry?"
The King of Yān said:
"Give me five years,
and I will achieve my aim."
Sūzǐ said:
"I ask to give the king ten years."
The King of Yān was pleased,
provided Sūzǐ with fifty chariots,
and sent him south as an envoy to Qí.
He said to the King of Qí:
"Qí has defeated Chǔ in the south,
subdued Qín in the west,
using the troops of Hán and Wèi,
and the masses of Yān and Zhào,
as if wielding a whip.
I have heard that a true king of the age
must punish the violent and rectify disorder,
overthrow the unprincipled,
and attack the unjust.
Now the King of Sòng shoots at heaven and whips the earth,
casts statues of the feudal lords,
has them stand by screens and latrines,
stretches out their arms,
and flicks their noses.
This is the height of unprincipled and unjust behavior in the world,
yet Your Majesty does not campaign against him;
Your Majesty's name will never be established.
Moreover, Sòng
is a fertile land in the central plains,
where neighboring people dwell.
Rather than gaining a hundred lǐ from Yān,
it is better to gain ten lǐ from Sòng.
Campaigning against it is righteous in name,
and beneficial in reality;
why does Your Majesty not do it?"
The King of Qí said: "Good."
Thereupon he raised troops to campaign against Sòng,
thrice defeated Sòng,
and Sòng was then overthrown.
The King of Yān heard of this,
severed relations with Qí,
led the troops of the world to campaign against Qí,
fought one great battle,
and two smaller ones,
wore down the state of Qí,
and established his name.
Therefore it is said:
By exploiting its strength to make it stronger,
it can be broken;
by exploiting its expanse to make it vaster,
it can be diminished.
Zhào was about to campaign against Yān.
Sū Dài, on behalf of Yān, said to King Huì:
"Now as I came here,
crossing the Yìshuǐ River,
a clam had just emerged to sun itself,
and a snipe pecked at its flesh.
The clam closed its shell and clamped the snipe's beak.
The snipe said: 'If it does not rain today,
and does not rain tomorrow,
there will be a dead clam.'
The clam also said to the snipe: 'If you do not come out today,
and do not come out tomorrow,
there will be a dead snipe.'
Neither was willing to let go of the other,
and a fisherman caught them both.
Now Zhào is about to campaign against Yān.
If Yān and Zhào long contend with each other,
exhausting their masses,
I fear the strong state of Qín will become the fisherman.
Therefore, I hope Your Majesty will consider this carefully."
King Huì said: "Good."
Thereupon he stopped.
Qí and Wèi vied for Yān's allegiance.
Qí said to the King of Yān:
"I have gained Zhào."
Wèi also said to the King of Yān:
"I have gained Zhào."
Yān had no way to decide,
and had not yet inclined to either.
Sūzǐ said to the Yān chancellor:
"I have heard that those whose words are humble but gifts heavy
are losing the world;
those whose words are arrogant but gifts light
are gaining the world.
Now Wèi's words are arrogant and gifts light."
Yān thereupon allied with Wèi,
gained Zhào,
and Qí was then defeated.
Qí, Hán, and Wèi together attacked Yān.
Yān sent the crown prince to request aid from Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ sent Jǐng Yáng to lead troops and rescue them.
At evening encampment,
