he ordered the left and right marshals each to set up camp and mark the ground,
and after they finished,
planted markers.
Jǐng Yáng angrily said:
"The places you have camped,
the water will rise and submerge the markers.
How can we encamp here!"
Thereupon he ordered them to move.
The next day there was heavy rain,
mountain waters greatly rose,
and the places they had camped,
the water submerged the markers.
The officers then were convinced.
Thereupon he did not rescue Yān,
but attacked Wèi's Yōngqiū,
captured it, and gave it to Sòng.
The three states were afraid,
and then withdrew their troops.
The Wèi army was to the west,
the Qí army to the east,
and the Chǔ army wanted to return but could not.
Jǐng Yáng then opened the western peace gate,
by day with chariots and cavalry,
by night with torches visible, and communicated with Wèi.
The Qí army found this strange,
thinking that Yān and Chǔ were plotting with Wèi,
so they led their troops and withdrew.
After the Qí troops had left,
Wèi lost its allied state,
and had no one to jointly attack Chǔ with,
so they fled under cover of night.
The Chǔ army then returned.
Zhāng Chǒu was serving as a hostage in Yān,
and the King of Yān wanted to kill him.
As he was fleeing and about to cross the border,
the border official captured Chǒu.
Chǒu said: "The reason the King of Yān is about to kill me
is that someone said I possess a precious pearl,
and the king wants to obtain it.
Now I have already lost it,
yet the King of Yān does not believe me.
If you now hand me over,
I will say that you seized my pearl and swallowed it.
The King of Yān will certainly kill you,
cutting open your belly and your intestines.
A ruler who desires something
cannot be persuaded with profit.
I will die anyway,
but your intestines will also be cut into pieces."
The border official, terrified, released him.
King Xǐ of Yān sent Lì Fù with a hundred pieces of gold to offer longevity wishes to King Xiàochéng of Zhào.
After three days of feasting,
he returned and reported:
"The strong men among the Zhào people have all died at Chángpíng,
and their orphans are not yet grown;
we can attack them."
The king then summoned Lord Chāngguó, Yuè Jiān, and asked:
"What do you think?"
He replied: "Zhào
is a state accessible from all directions;
its people are all skilled in warfare,
and we cannot fight them."
The king said: "What if I attack with double their forces?
Is that feasible?"
He said:
"No."
The king said:
"What about with triple their forces?"
He said:
"No."
The king was greatly angered.
His attendants all believed Zhào could be attacked,
so he hastily raised an army of six hundred thousand to attack Zhào.
He ordered Lì Fù to lead four hundred thousand to attack
Hào, and sent Qìng Qín with two hundred thousand to attack Dài.
Zhào sent Lián Pō with eighty thousand to confront Lì Fù at Hào,
and sent Yuè Chéng with fifty thousand to confront Qìng Qín at Dài.
The Yān army was utterly defeated.
Yuè Jiān fled to Zhào.
The King of Yān sent a letter to apologize,
saying:
"I, your unworthy ruler,
was unable to comply with your wishes,
so you abandoned the state and left.
Thus, my incompetence is clear.
I dared to state my sincere wish,
but you were unwilling to listen,
so I have sent a messenger to convey my foolish thoughts.
Please consider them carefully.
It is said:
'The benevolent do not lightly sever ties,
the wise do not lightly harbor resentment.'
Your relationship with the former king
is well known to all.
I had hoped that if I erred, you would cover for me,
not that you would openly condemn me;
I hoped that if I made mistakes, you would instruct me,
not that you would openly condemn me.
Moreover, my faults
are known to all in the state,
and heard of throughout the world.
You secretly left and openly expressed resentment, abandoning me;
I must indeed be at fault.
Even so,
I fear you have not acted with full generosity.
A proverb says:
'The generous do not slander others to benefit themselves;
the benevolent do not endanger others to seek fame.'
Therefore, covering up others' faults
is the way of the generous;
saving others from their errors
is the path of the benevolent.
In this world, who but you would I hope
to cover my faults and
save me from my errors?
Now you generously received your position from the former king, achieving honor,
yet lightly abandoned me to satisfy your heart.
Thus, covering faults and saving from errors
are hard to expect from you.
Moreover, the world may treat one poorly, yet one should still act generously;
conduct may be flawed, yet one should still show kindness.
Now, if I bear the blame for incompetence,
and you bear the burden of lacking generosity,
in choosing a course for you,
there is nothing to gain.
A state has borders,
just as a home has walls,
to foster harmony and conceal faults.
If family members cannot live in harmony,
and speak to the neighbors about it,
that is not a wise plan.
To openly abandon someone before resentment and hatred appear
is not fully generous.
Though I may be incompetent,
I am not as chaotic as King Zhòu of Yīn;
though you may be discontent,
you are not as burdened as Shāng Róng or Jīzǐ.
Yet you did not cover for me internally
but openly expressed resentment externally.
I fear this may only damage your lofty reputation and diminish your conduct,
unless it is not so.
If it can clarify your righteousness
and complete your loftiness,
even bearing a bad reputation,
I would not find it difficult to accept.
If your intent was to expose my shortcomings,
yet you do not gain generosity;
if you publicize my disgrace,
yet you do not gain honor,
this is one act with two losses.
The righteous do not harm others to benefit themselves,
let alone harm others to their own detriment!
I hope you will not let my incompetence
tarnish the beauty of past affairs.
In the past,
Liǔxià Huì served as an official in Lǔ,
and was dismissed three times but did not leave.
Someone said to him:
'You may leave.'
Liǔxià Huì said:
'If I am at odds with others,
where can I go without being dismissed?
Since I would be dismissed anyway,
I would rather stay in my homeland.'
Liǔxià Huì did not let three dismissals burden him,
so he did not forget his former achievements;
he did not take leaving to heart,
so near and far, none criticized him.
Now, my faults
are unknown to the people of the state,
yet those who criticize me are everywhere under heaven.
It is said:
'Discourse should not trouble the heart,
debate should not burden things,
the benevolent do not lightly sever ties,
the wise do not neglect achievements.'
To abandon great achievements
is to stop halfway;
to lightly sever ties for substantial gain
is resentment.
To stop halfway and abandon them,
to resent and burden them—
this should apply to distant matters,
not something I would expect from you.
Now, since I am without fault,
how could you resent me?
I hope you will cast aside resentment,
reflect on the former king,
and once again instruct me!
I imagine you saying,
'I will harbor hidden intentions to complete your errors,
disregarding the former king to expose your faults,
so that you can neither advance to cultivate achievements
nor retreat to correct errors.'
This is what you surmise;
please consider it carefully!
This is my foolish intent.
I respectfully present it in this letter."
Yuè Jiān and Yuè Chéng resented that their advice was not followed, and both eventually remained in Zhào,
without replying.
When Qín annexed Zhào,
it turned north to confront Yān.
The King of Yān heard of this
and sent someone to congratulate the King of Qín.
The envoy passed through Zhào,
and the King of Zhào detained him.
The envoy said: "If Qín and Zhào unite,
the world will submit.
The reason Yān submits to Zhào
is for Qín's sake.
Now I am on a mission to Qín,
and Zhào detains me;
this means Qín and Zhào have a rift.
If Qín and Zhào have a rift,
the world will certainly not submit,
and Yān will not accept orders.
Moreover, my mission to Qín
does not hinder Zhào's attack on Yān."
The King of Zhào found this reasonable
and released him.
The envoy appeared before the King of Qín and said:
"The King of Yān has privately heard that Qín has annexed Zhào,
and the King of Yān has sent an envoy to present a thousand pieces of gold in congratulations."
The King of Qín said:
"Yān is without virtue,
I have caused Zhào to possess it,
why do you congratulate me?"
The envoy said:
"I have heard that when Zhào was whole,
its southern neighbor was Qín,
and its northern Xiàqūyáng was Yān.
Zhào was three hundred lǐ in breadth,
and for over fifty years it stood against Qín.
The reason it could not turn the tables and defeat Qín
was that its state was small and its territory offered nothing to seize.
Now if Your Majesty causes Zhào to annex Yān in the north,
Yān and Zhào will join forces,
and will certainly no longer submit to Qín.
I am deeply concerned for Your Majesty."
The King of Qín considered this reasonable,
and raised troops to rescue Yān.
The Crown Prince of Yān, Dān, was a hostage in Qín,
and fled back home.
Seeing that Qín was about to destroy the six states,
with troops approaching the Yì River,
he feared disaster was imminent.
Crown Prince Dān was troubled by this,
and said to his Grand Tutor Jū Wǔ:
"Yān and Qín cannot coexist,
I hope the Grand Tutor will consider this carefully."
Wǔ replied:
"Qín's territory spans the world,
threatening Hán, Wèi, and Zhào.
As for the area north of the Yì River,
its fate is not yet determined.
How can you, because of the resentment from being humiliated,
wish to strike against its scales?"
The Crown Prince said:
"Then what should be done?"
The Grand Tutor said:
"Allow me to retire,
and consider it."
After some time had passed,
General Fán fled from Qín to Yān,
and the Crown Prince gave him shelter.
Grand Tutor Jū Wǔ remonstrated:
"This cannot be.
The King of Qín is tyrannical,
and already harbors deep resentment toward Yān,
which is enough to chill the heart,
let alone if he hears that General Fán is here!
This is like throwing meat onto the path of a starving tiger;
disaster will surely be unavoidable!
Even with Guǎn or Yàn,
no plan could be devised.
I urge the Crown Prince to quickly send General Fán into the Xiōngnú to eliminate the evidence.
Let us ally with the Three Jìn in the west,
connect with Qí and Chǔ in the south,
and negotiate with the Chányú in the north.
Only then can we devise a plan."
Crown Prince Dān said:
"The Grand Tutor's plan
would take a long, drawn-out time.
My heart is anxious,
and I fear I cannot wait even a moment.
Moreover, this is not the only issue.
General Fán is destitute in the world,
and has entrusted himself to me, Dān.
I, Dān, will never be pressured by a powerful Qín
to abandon a pitiful friend and cast him into the Xiōngnú.
That would be the time of my destined end.
I ask the Grand Tutor to reconsider."
Jū Wǔ said:
"In Yān there is a Master Tián Guāng.
His wisdom is profound,
and his courage is deep.
You may consult with him."
The Crown Prince said:
"May I, through the Grand Tutor, be introduced to Master Tián? Is that acceptable?"
Jū Wǔ said:
"Respectfully, yes."
He went out to see Tián Guāng,
and conveyed the Crown Prince's words:
"He wishes to consult with you, Sir, on matters of state."
Tián Guāng said:
"I respectfully accept the instruction."
Then he went to visit.
The Crown Prince knelt to welcome him,
walked backward to guide the way,
and knelt to dust off the mat.
After Master Tián was seated,
with no attendants around,
the Crown Prince left his mat and requested:
"Yān and Qín cannot coexist,
I hope you, Sir, will give this your attention."
Tián Guāng said:
"I have heard that when the fine steed is in its prime,
it can gallop a thousand lǐ in a day.
When it declines,
even a nag can outrun it.
Now the Crown Prince has heard of me from my prime,
but does not know that my vigor has already faded.
Nevertheless,
I dare not neglect matters of state.
My good friend Jīng Kē
can be employed."
The Crown Prince said:
"May I, through you, Sir, be introduced to Jīng Kē?
Is that acceptable?"
Tián Guāng said:
"Respectfully, yes."
He immediately rose and hurried out.
The Crown Prince escorted him to the gate,
and said:
"What I have reported,
and what you, Sir, have discussed,
are matters of great importance to the state.
I hope you, Sir, will not divulge them."
Tián Guāng bowed his head and smiled:
"Yes."
Hunched over, he went to see Jīng Kē,
and said:
"Guāng and you are close friends;
everyone in Yān knows it.
Now the Crown Prince has heard of me from my prime,
but does not know that my body is no longer up to it.
He graciously instructed me:
'Yān and Qín cannot coexist,
I hope you, Sir, will give this your attention.'
Guāng, considering myself not an outsider,
recommended you to the Crown Prince.
I hope you will visit the Crown Prince at the palace."
Jīng Kē said:
"I respectfully accept the instruction."
Tián Guāng said:
"Guāng has heard that the conduct of a worthy man
does not give others cause to doubt him.
Now the Crown Prince made a pact with me:
'What is discussed
are matters of great importance to the state.
I hope you, Sir, will not divulge them.'
This means the Crown Prince doubts Guāng.
To act in a way that makes others doubt you
is not the behavior of a principled knight-errant."
He wished to kill himself to inspire Jīng Kē,
and said:
"I hope you will quickly visit the Crown Prince,
and tell him that Guāng is already dead,
to show that I did not speak."
Thereupon he cut his own throat and died.
Kē went to see the Crown Prince,
and said that Tián Guāng was dead,
to show that he had not spoken.
The Crown Prince bowed twice and knelt,
tears streaming down as he moved on his knees.
After a while, he said:
"When I asked Master Tián not to speak,
it was to ensure the success of a great plan.
Now Master Tián has died to prove he did not divulge the words;
how could this have been my intention?"
After Jīng Kē was seated,
the Crown Prince left his mat, kowtowed, and said:
"Master Tián did not know that I am unworthy,
and allowed me to come before you.
I wish to explain something.
This is Heaven taking pity on Yān and not abandoning its orphan.
Now Qín has a greedy and insatiable heart,
and its desires cannot be satisfied.
Unless it exhausts all the land under heaven,
and makes the kings within the seas its subjects,
its ambition will not be sated.
Now Qín has already captured the King of Hán,
and taken all his territory.
It has also raised troops to campaign against Chǔ in the south,
and approaches Zhào in the north.
Wáng Jiǎn leads several hundred thousand troops to the Zhāng and Yè regions,
while Lǐ Xìn advances from Tàiyuán
and Yúnzhōng.
If Zhào cannot withstand Qín,
it will surely submit as a vassal.
Once it submits,
disaster will reach Yān.
Yān is small and weak,
and has repeatedly suffered from warfare.
Now, by my reckoning, even mobilizing the entire state would be insufficient to oppose Qín.
The other feudal lords submit to Qín,
and none dare form alliances.
My personal plan,
foolish as it may be, is that if we could truly obtain a brave warrior of the world,
and send him to Qín,
to tempt them with great profit,
the King of Qín, greedy for the offering,
would surely grant our wish.
After a long time,
Jīng Kē said:
"This is a matter of great importance for the state.
I am but a humble and lowly servant,
and fear I am not fit for such a mission."
The Crown Prince stepped forward and bowed his head to the ground,
insistently urging him not to decline.
Only then did Jīng Kē give his consent.
Thereupon, the Crown Prince honored Jīng Kē as a High Minister,
lodged him in the finest quarters,
and visited him daily to inquire after his needs,
providing him with the finest sacrificial meats and rare delicacies,
and occasionally presenting him with carriages, horses, and beautiful women,
indulging all of Jīng Kē's desires,
in order to please and satisfy him.
After a long time,
Jīng Kē still showed no intention of setting out.
The Qín general Wáng Jiǎn had defeated Zhào,
captured the King of Zhào,
and seized all of its territory.
He then advanced his troops northward to seize more land,
reaching the southern border of Yān.
Crown Prince Dān, filled with fear and dread,
then entreated Jīng Kē, saying:
"The Qín army will cross the Yì Shuǐ any day now.
Even if I wished to continue serving you for a long time,
how could it be possible?"
Jīng Kē said: "Even without Your Highness's words,
I intended to request an audience with you about this.
But if I go now without something to gain their trust,
then I will not be able to get close to the King of Qín.
Now, regarding General Fán,
the King of Qín has offered a thousand catties of gold
and a fief of ten thousand households for his capture.
If we could truly obtain General Fán's head,
and present it along with the map of Yān's Dūkàng region to the King of Qín, the King of Qín would certainly be pleased to grant me an audience.
Then I would have a means to repay Your Highness."
The Crown Prince said: "General Fán came to me in his dire straits and distress.
I cannot bear, for the sake of my own private affairs,
to harm the feelings of an honorable man.
I wish you would consider another plan."
Knowing the Crown Prince could not bear to do it,
Jīng Kē then went privately to see Fán Wūqī and said:
"The way Qín has treated you, General,
can be said to be utterly ruthless.
Your parents and entire clan
have all been executed or enslaved.
Now I hear they are offering for your head
a thousand catties of gold
and a fief of ten thousand households.
What do you intend to do?"
General Fán looked up to heaven, heaved a deep sigh, and wept, saying:
"Every time I think of it,
the pain pierces me to the marrow of my bones.
But I can only look for a plan, not knowing where to begin."
Jīng Kē said: "Now I have a single proposal
that can resolve the threat to Yān
and avenge the wrongs done to you, General.
What would you think of that?"
Fán Wūqī stepped forward and said:
"What must be done?"
Jīng Kē said:
"I wish to obtain your head to present to Qín.
The King of Qín will surely be delighted and grant me a favorable audience.
With my left hand I will seize his sleeve,
and with my right hand I will stab him in the chest.
Then, General, your wrongs will be avenged,
and the shame of Yān's humiliation will be wiped away.
Would you be willing, General?"
Fán Wūqī bared one shoulder, gripped his wrist, and stepped forward, saying:
"This is what I have gnashed my teeth and beaten my breast over day and night.
Only today have I received your instruction."
Thereupon, he cut his own throat.
When the Crown Prince heard of this, he rushed there,
prostrated himself over the corpse and wept,
overwhelmed with grief.
After it was done,
with no other recourse,
he then had Fán Wūqī's head collected and placed in a container,
and sealed it in a box.
Thereupon,
the Crown Prince sought in advance the sharpest dagger in the land,
and obtained the dagger of Xú Fūrén, a man of Zhào.
He paid a hundred catties of gold for it,
and had a craftsman temper it with poison.
When tested on a person,
if it drew even a thread-like trickle of blood,
the person would invariably die instantly.
He then prepared the baggage and sent Jīng Kē off.
In Yān there was a brave warrior named Qín Wǔyáng,
who at the age of twelve
had killed a man,
and people dared not look at him defiantly.
He was then ordered to serve as Jīng Kē's assistant.
Jīng Kē was waiting for someone,
wishing to go together with him.
That man lived far away and had not yet arrived,
so Jīng Kē delayed, waiting for him.
A short time passed, and he still had not departed.
The Crown Prince grew impatient with the delay,
suspecting that Jīng Kē had changed his mind and regretted his decision.
He then went to urge him again, saying:
"The days have run out.
Could it be that you have no intention of going, Jīng Kē?
I request that we send Qín Wǔyáng ahead first." Jīng Kē grew angry,
and rebuked the Crown Prince, saying:
"To go today and not return—that is the act of a fool!
Now I am to take a single dagger into the unpredictable and powerful state of Qín.
The reason I have delayed
is to wait for my companion to go with me.
Since Your Highness now finds me tardy,
I request to take my leave now!"
Thereupon, he set out.
The Crown Prince and those guests who knew of the affair
all dressed in white mourning clothes and caps to see him off.
When they reached the banks of the Yì Shuǐ,
after the farewell sacrifices were performed
and the road was taken,
Gāo Jiànlí struck the zhù (a stringed instrument),
and Jīng Kē harmonized with it in song,
singing in the biànzhǐ mode.
All the assembled men shed tears and wept.
Then he stepped forward and sang:
"The wind sighs and sighs, oh, the Yì Shuǐ is cold.
The brave man, once gone, oh, will never return!"
He then sang again in the impassioned yǔ mode.
All the men glared with wide eyes,
their hair standing on end, lifting their caps.
Thereupon, Jīng Kē mounted his carriage and departed,
and never once looked back.
After arriving in Qín,
he took gifts worth a thousand catties of gold,
and lavishly presented them to Méng Jiā, the King of Qín's favored attendant, a Gentleman of the Palace.
Méng Jiā spoke on his behalf to the King of Qín beforehand, saying:
"The King of Yān truly trembles in awe and admiration of Your Majesty's might,
and dares not raise troops to resist Your Majesty.
He wishes to submit his entire state as an inner vassal,
to be ranked among the other feudal lords,
to render tribute and service like a commandery or county,
and thus be allowed to preserve and maintain the ancestral temples of his former kings.
In his fear and trepidation, he dared not state this himself.
He has respectfully cut off Fán Wūqī's head,
and presents along with it the map of Yān's Dūkàng region,
sealed in a box.
The King of Yān performed a bowing farewell in his court,
and sent an envoy to inform Your Majesty.
It is for Your Majesty to command."
When the King of Qín heard this, he was greatly pleased.
He then donned his court robes,
arranged the ceremony of the Nine Guests of Honor,
and received the Yān envoy in the Xiányáng Palace.
Jīng Kē carried the box containing Fán Wūqī's head,
and Qín Wǔyáng carried the case containing the map.
They advanced in order until they reached the foot of the throne dais.
Qín Wǔyáng's face changed color, and he trembled with fear.
The assembled ministers found this strange.
Jīng Kē looked back at Wǔyáng with a laugh,
stepped forward, and apologized, saying:
"He is an uncultured man from the northern barbarian regions,
who has never before seen the Son of Heaven.
Therefore he is trembling with terror.
I beg Your Majesty to bear with him a little,
and allow him to complete his mission before you."
The King of Qín said to Jīng Kē:
"Rise, and bring the map that Wǔyáng is holding."
After Jīng Kē took the map and presented it,
he unrolled the map,
and when the map was fully unrolled, the dagger was revealed.
Thereupon, with his left hand he seized the King of Qín's sleeve,
and with his right hand he grasped the dagger and stabbed at him.
Before it reached his body,
the King of Qín, startled,
jerked himself back and rose,
tearing off his sleeve.
He tried to draw his sword,
but the sword was long,
and he grasped only the scabbard.
In that moment of panic and urgency,
the sword was firmly lodged,
so he could not draw it out immediately.
Jīng Kē pursued the King of Qín,
and the King of Qín fled, circling around a pillar.
The assembled ministers were shocked and dumbfounded.
The suddenness of the attack,
caused them all to lose their composure.
Moreover, according to Qín law,
ministers attending in the palace hall
were not permitted to carry any weapons, even a foot long.
All the palace guards who carried weapons
were arrayed below the hall,
and without a command they were not permitted to ascend.
In the midst of the emergency,
there was no time to summon the guards below.
For this reason, Jīng Kē pursued the King of Qín,
and in their extreme panic and haste they had nothing with which to strike Jīng Kē,
and so they used their bare hands to grapple with him together.
At that time,
the court physician Xià Wúqiē
used the medicine bag he was carrying to strike at Kē.
The King of Qín was just then circling a pillar in flight,
in a state of panic and urgency, not knowing what to do,
when his attendants said:
"Your Majesty, put your sword on your back!
Your Majesty, put your sword on your back!"
He then drew it and struck Jīng Kē,
cutting off his left thigh.
Jīng Kē, disabled,
then raised his dagger
and threw it at the King of Qín,
but missed,
hitting the pillar instead.
The King of Qín struck Kē again,
inflicting eight wounds.
Kē knew that his mission had failed,
leaned against the pillar and laughed,
sprawled out and cursed, saying:
"The reason the affair did not succeed
was that I wanted to capture him alive,
to surely obtain a treaty to report to the Crown Prince."
The attendants then came forward and killed Jīng Kē,
and the King of Qín was dizzy for a long time.
He then discussed merits, rewarding the ministers and those who should be punished,
each according to their degree.
He bestowed upon Xià Wúqiē two hundred yì of gold,
saying: "Wúqiē loved me,
and thus used his medicine bag to strike Kē."
Thereupon, Qín was greatly angered at Yān,
increased the troops sent to Zhào,
and ordered Wáng Jiǎn's army to attack Yān.
In the tenth month, they captured Yān's capital city of Jì.
King Xǐ of Yān, Crown Prince Dān, and others,
all led their elite troops east to defend in Liáodōng.
The Qín general Lǐ Xìn pursued and attacked the King of Yān,
and the King, in urgency,
adopted the plan of King Jiā of Dài,
killed Crown Prince Dān,
and wished to offer him to Qín.
Qín again advanced troops to attack.
After five years, they finally destroyed the state of Yān,
and captured King Xǐ of Yān.
Qín unified the world.
Later, Jīng Kē's friend Gāo Jiànlí, by playing the zhù, gained an audience with the Qín emperor,
and then used the zhù to strike the Qín emperor,
seeking to avenge Yān,
but missed and died.
Qí attacked Sòng,
and Sòng sent Zāngzǐ to seek aid from Jīng.
The King of Jīng was greatly pleased,
and promised aid very earnestly.
Zāngzǐ returned worried.
His charioteer said: "You sought aid and obtained it,
why do you have a worried expression?"
Zāngzǐ said: "Sòng is small and Qí is large.
To aid small Sòng and earn the enmity of large Qí,
this is what the King should worry about;
yet the King of Jīng is very pleased,
he must be intending to strengthen us.
If we are strengthened and Qí is weakened,
it is to Jīng's benefit."
Zāngzǐ then returned.
The King of Qí indeed attacked,
captured five cities of Sòng,
and the King of Jīng did not come.
Gōngshū Bān devised machines for Chǔ,
intending to attack Sòng.
Mòzǐ heard of this,
traveled a hundred stages with calloused feet,
went to see Gōngshū Bān,
and said to him: "I have heard of you from Sòng.
I wish to borrow your help to kill the King."
Gōngshū Bān said: "I am righteous and do not kill kings."
Mòzǐ said:
"I hear you are making cloud ladders,
to attack Sòng.
What crime has Sòng committed?
It is righteous not to kill a king, yet you attack a state;
this is not killing few but killing many.
May I ask, what righteousness is there in attacking Sòng?"
Gōngshū Bān was convinced,
and asked to see the King for him.
Mòzǐ saw the King of Chǔ and said:
"Suppose there is a man here,
who abandons his ornate carriage,
and desires to steal his neighbor's broken cart;
abandons his embroidered finery,
and desires to steal his neighbor's coarse short robe;
abandons his fine grain and meat,
and desires to steal his neighbor's dregs and husks.
What kind of person is this?"
The King said: "He must have a stealing sickness."
Mòzǐ said: "The land of Jīng is five thousand lǐ square,
Sòng is five hundred lǐ square,
this is like the ornate carriage compared to the broken cart.
Jīng has Yúnmèng,
filled with rhinoceroses, sì, deer, and elk,
the rivers and lakes abound with fish, turtles, yuán, and tuó, the richest in the world,
while Sòng is said to have no pheasants, rabbits, or bream,
this is like fine grain and meat compared to dregs and husks.
Jīng has tall pines, patterned zǐ, pián, nán, and yùzhāng trees,
while Sòng has no tall trees,
this is like embroidered finery compared to coarse short robes.
I find that Your Majesty's officials attacking Sòng
is of the same kind."
The King said: "Well said!
Let us not attack Sòng."
Xīshǒu attacked Huáng,
passed through Wèi,
and sent a man to tell the Lord of Wèi:
"The army of my humble state passes by the suburbs of your great state,
is there not a single envoy to inquire after us?
I dare to ask what crime we have committed.
Now Huáng city is about to fall,
and after that,
we will move the army to arrive beneath the walls of your great state."
The Lord of Wèi was afraid,
prepared three hundred bundles of silk ribbons,
three hundred yì of gold,
to follow the envoy.
Nán Wénzǐ stopped him, saying:
"If he defeats Huáng city,
he certainly will not dare to come;
if he does not defeat it,
he also will not dare to come.
If he defeats Huáng city,
then his merit will be great and his name glorious,
and he will preside over his peers at court.
Those at court dislike being presided over,
and will discuss the matter.
Bearing a great name,
carrying a great achievement,
sitting in court awaiting the discussions of those at court,
even if Xīshǒu is foolish,
he certainly will not do it.
If he does not defeat Huáng city,
he will be broken-hearted and flee back,
fearing he cannot escape punishment!
How would he dare to attack Wèi to compound the crime of his defeat?"
He indeed defeated Huáng city,
led the army back,
and did not dare to pass through Wèi.
The King of Liáng attacked Hándān,
and demanded troops from Sòng.
The Lord of Sòng sent an envoy to request of the King of Zhào:
"The troops of Liáng are strong and their authority weighty,
now they demand troops from my humble state.
If my humble state does not comply,
then I fear it will endanger the altars of soil and grain;
if I assist Liáng in attacking Zhào,
to harm the state of Zhào,
then I cannot bear it.
I hope Your Majesty has some command for my humble state."
The King of Zhào said: "Indeed.
That Sòng is insufficient to match Liáng,
I know.
To weaken Zhào and strengthen Liáng,
certainly does not benefit Sòng.
Then what can I tell you that would be acceptable?"
The envoy said:
"I request to receive a border city,
delay the attack and prolong the days,
to wait until your officials have a city, that is all."
The King of Zhào said: "Good."
The people of Sòng then raised troops and entered Zhào territory,
and besieged a city.
The King of Liáng was very pleased,
saying:
"The people of Sòng are helping me attack."
The King of Zhào was also pleased, saying:
"The people of Sòng will stop here."
Thus the troops withdrew and the difficulty was resolved,
favor was bestowed upon Liáng without incurring resentment from Zhào.
Therefore, fame was increased and substance was gained.
He said to the Grand Minister:
"The lord grows older daily,
if he himself knows governance,
then you, sir, will have no affairs.
You, sir, should have Chǔ congratulate the lord on his filial piety,
then the lord will not seize the affairs of the queen dowager,
and you, sir, will long be employed in Sòng."
Sòng and Chǔ were like brothers.
Qí attacked Sòng,
and the King of Chǔ declared he would rescue Sòng.
Sòng then betrayed Chǔ’s importance to seek peace with Qí,
but Qí did not listen.
Sū Qín, on behalf of Sòng, said to the Prime Minister of Qí:
"It would be better to agree with them,
to make clear that Sòng has betrayed Chǔ’s importance to Qí.
Chǔ will be angered,
and will certainly break with Sòng and serve Qí.
When Qí and Chǔ unite,
then attacking Sòng will be easy."
The crown prince of Wèi personally led an army,
passing by Wàihuáng in Sòng.
A man of Wàihuáng, Master Xú, said:
"I have a strategy for winning a hundred battles out of a hundred.
Can Your Highness listen to me?"
The crown prince said: "I wish to hear it."
The guest said: "I sincerely wish to offer it.
Now Your Highness personally leads an attack against Qí.
If you achieve a great victory and annex Jǔ,
your wealth will not exceed possessing Wèi,
and your nobility will not increase beyond being king.
If the battle is not won,
then for ten thousand generations you will have no Wèi.
This is my strategy for winning a hundred battles out of a hundred."
The crown prince said: "Yes.
I will certainly follow your words and return."
The guest said: "Although Your Highness wishes to return,
it will not be possible.
Those who benefit from Your Highness’s warfare,
and wish to satisfy their ambitions are many.
Although Your Highness wishes to return,
I fear it will not be possible."
The crown prince mounted his chariot and requested to return.
His charioteer said: "To set out and then return
is the same as defeat.
It would be better to proceed."
So they proceeded.
They fought with the men of Qí and died,
and in the end did not gain Wèi.
During the time of King Kāng of Sòng,
a sparrow gave birth to a zhān (a type of hawk) in a corner of the city wall.
He had a historian divine it,
who said:
"The small giving birth to the great
means you will certainly dominate the world."
King Kāng was greatly pleased.
Thereupon he destroyed Téng, attacked Xuē,
and seized lands north of the Huái River.
He then became even more self-confident,
wishing his domination to be quickly achieved.
Therefore he shot at the heavens and whipped the earth,
chopped up the altars of soil and grain and burned them,
saying:
"My power subdues the ghosts and spirits of the world."
He cursed the elderly ministers who remonstrated,
wore a crown without a brim,
to display his courage.
He split the backs of hunchbacks,
chopped off the shins of those who waded in the morning,
and the people of the state were greatly terrified.
Qí heard of this and attacked him.
The people scattered,
and the city could not be defended.
The king then fled to the residence of the Marquis of Ní,
where he was captured and died.
To see an auspicious omen and not treat it as auspicious,
but instead bring about calamity.
Zhì Bó wished to attack Wèi,
and sent Lord Wèi four hundred wild horses
and one white jade disc.
Lord Wèi was greatly pleased,
and all his ministers congratulated him,
but Nán Wénzǐ had a worried expression.
Lord Wèi said: "A great state shows great favor,
why do you have a worried expression?"
Wénzǐ said: "Rewards without merit,
courtesy without effort,
must be examined.
Four hundred wild horses,
one hundred jade discs,
this is the courtesy of a small state,
yet a great state presents it.
My lord, please consider this."
Lord Wèi relayed his words to the border.
Zhì Bó indeed raised troops to surprise attack Wèi,
but upon reaching the border turned back, saying:
"Wèi has a worthy man,
who knew my plan in advance."
Zhì Bó wished to surprise attack Wèi,
so he pretended that his crown prince had fled,
and had him run to Wèi.
Nán Wénzǐ said:
"Crown Prince Yán is a gentleman,
deeply loved and favored.
If he flees without a great crime,
there must be a reason."
He sent someone to meet him at the border,
saying:
"If the chariots exceed five,
be careful not to admit them."
Zhì Bó heard of this,
and stopped.
Qín attacked Pú of Wèi.
Hú Yǎn said to Chūlǐ Jí:
"Your attack on Pú,
is it for Qín’s sake?
Or for Wèi’s sake?
If it is for Wèi, then it is good;
if it is for Qín, then it is not beneficial.
The reason Wèi remains Wèi
is because it has Pú.
Now if Pú falls to Wèi,
Wèi will certainly be subjugated by Wèi.
Wèi lost the lands west of the Hé River,
and has been unable to retake them,
because it is weak.
Now if Wèi annexes Wèi,
Wèi will certainly become strong.
When Wèi becomes strong,
the lands west of the Hé River will certainly be in danger.
Moreover, the King of Qín will also observe your actions.
Harming Qín to benefit Wèi,
the King of Qín will certainly resent you."
Chūlǐ Jí said: "What should be done?"
Hú Yǎn said: "You, sir, should abandon Pú and not attack it.
I request to enter Pú on your behalf to warn its defender,
and thereby show virtue to Lord Wèi."
Chūlǐ Jí said: "Good."
Hú Yǎn then entered Pú,
and said to its defender:
"Chūlǐzǐ knows the weakness of Pú,
and he says:
'I will certainly take Pú.'
Now I can make him abandon Pú and not attack."
The defender of Pú bowed twice,
and thereupon presented three hundred yì of gold,
saying:
"If the Qín troops truly withdraw,
I will request Lord Wèi to richly reward you."
Hú Yǎn took the gold from Pú,
thereby gaining weight in Wèi.
Chūlǐzǐ also obtained three hundred jin of gold and returned,
and also showed virtue to Lord Wèi.
Wèi sent an envoy to serve Wèi,
but for three years he could not get an audience.
The Wèi envoy was troubled by this,
and went to see Master Wúxià,
promising him a hundred jin of gold.
Master Wúxià said: "Yes."
He then went to see the King of Wèi, saying:
"I hear Qín is sending out troops,
but do not know where they are headed.
The relations between Qín and Wèi have not been cultivated for a long time.
I hope Your Majesty will broadly serve Qín,
without any other plans."
The King of Wèi said: "Yes."
The guest hurried out,
but upon reaching the palace gate turned back and said:
"I fear Your Majesty is too late in serving Qín."
The king said: "Why?"
The master said: "People are overly hasty in matters concerning themselves,
and overly slow in matters concerning others.
Now Your Majesty is slow in matters concerning yourself,
how can you be hasty in matters concerning others?"
"How do you know this?"
"The Wèi envoy said
he has served Your Majesty for three years without an audience.
I therefore know Your Majesty is slow."
The King of Wèi hurriedly granted an audience to the Wèi envoy.
Lord Sì of Wèi was ill.
Fù Shù said to Yīn Shùnqiě:
"If you listen to my words to persuade the lord,
without adding or subtracting,
the lord will certainly treat you well.
What a person does in life
differs from the intentions at death.
Initially, what the lord practiced in the world
was to enjoy luxury;
those he employed
were Xiè Cuò and Rú Bó.
All the ministers believed the lord despised the state and loved luxury,
so certainly none would discuss state affairs with the lord.
You should tell the lord: 'What you practice in the world is very mistaken.
Xiè Cuò monopolizes decisions in the state,
and Rú Bó assists him.
From now on,
the Gōngsūn clan will certainly not have its sacrifices continued.'"
The lord said:
"Excellent."
He gave him his seal,
saying:
"When I die,
you shall govern."
When the succeeding lord died,
Yīn Shùnqiě, in accordance with the lord's order, assisted Gōngqī.
The clans of Xiè Cuò
and Rú Bó were all expelled.
During the time of Wèi's Lord Sì,
a convict escaped to Wèi,
and Wèi offered a hundred catties of gold to ransom him,
but they refused.
They then requested to use Zuǒshì.
The ministers advised, saying:
"Using land worth a hundred catties of gold
to ransom a single convict—
is that not inappropriate?"
The lord said: "In governance, nothing is too small;
in chaos, nothing is too great.
If the people are enlightened through education,
a city of three hundred households
is sufficient for good governance.
If the people lack integrity and shame,
even if you had ten Zuǒshì,
how could you make use of them?"
A man from Wèi was welcoming a new bride.
As the bride boarded the carriage,
she asked:
"The outer horses—
whose horses are they?"
The driver said: "They are borrowed."
The new bride said to the servant:
"Pat the outer horses,
do not whip the inner ones."
When the carriage arrived at the gate,
she was helped down and instructed the escorting matron:
"Put out the stove fire,
or there will be a blaze."
Entering the house and seeing the mortar,
she said:
"Move it under the window,
so it doesn't obstruct passersby."
The host laughed at her.
These three remarks
were all pertinent,
yet she could not avoid being laughed at—
it was because the timing was off.
Wèi Wénhóu wanted to destroy Zhōngshān.
Cháng Zhuāngtán said to Zhào Xiāngzǐ:
"If Wèi annexes Zhōngshān,
Zhào will surely be next.
Why don't you request Qīng, the daughter of the lord, to be your principal wife,
and enfeoff her in Zhōngshān?
That would restore Zhōngshān."
Xīshǒu established five kings,
and Zhōngshān was the last to hold the title.
Qí said to Zhào and Wèi:
"I am ashamed to be king alongside Zhōngshān.
I wish to join the great states in attacking it,
to abolish its kingship."
When Zhōngshān heard this,
it was greatly alarmed.
It summoned Zhāng Dēng and told him:
"I am about to become king,
but Qí told Zhào and Wèi
that it is ashamed to be king alongside me
and wishes to attack me.
I fear the loss of my state,
not the pursuit of kingship.
No one but you can save me."
Dēng replied: "If my lord provides me with many carriages and generous gifts,
I will request an audience with Tián Yīng."
The lord of Zhōngshān sent him to Qí.
He met with Yīngzǐ and said:
"I have heard that you wish to abolish Zhōngshān's kingship,
and plan to join Zhào and Wèi in attacking it.
This is a mistake.
Given Zhōngshān's small size,
if three states attack it,
even if Zhōngshān were to further renounce kingship,
it would still comply.
Moreover, Zhōngshān, in fear,
would certainly renounce kingship for Zhào and Wèi and attach itself to them.
This would be you herding sheep for Zhào and Wèi—
not to Qí's benefit.
Would it not be better for Zhōngshān to renounce kingship and serve Qí?"
Tián Yīng said: "How?"
Zhāng Dēng said: "If you now summon Zhōngshān,
meet with it and promise it kingship,
Zhōngshān will surely be pleased and break with Zhào and Wèi.
Zhào and Wèi, angered, will attack Zhōngshān.
Zhōngshān, in dire straits, will find it difficult to maintain kingship for you,
and will certainly fear,
renouncing kingship to serve Qí.
They fear the loss of their state.
Thus, you would make them renounce kingship and lose their state—
better than herding sheep for Zhào and Wèi."
Tián Yīng said: "Agreed."
Zhāng Chǒu said: "No.
I have heard that
those with the same desires resent each other,
while those with the same worries bond.
Now five states have become kings together,
but the coastal state is not among them.
This means all desire to be kings,
but worry lies with the coastal state.
If you now summon Zhōngshān,
meet with it and promise it kingship,
you would be taking from the five states to benefit the coastal state.
Bringing Zhōngshān close and alienating the four states
will chill their hearts.
You should first grant it kingship and deliberately befriend it—
this would be you gaining Zhōngshān but losing the four states.
Moreover, Zhāng Dēng's character
has long been skilled at subtly advising the lord of Zhōngshān;
it is hard to trust that this is to our benefit."
Tián Yīng did not listen.
He indeed summoned the lord of Zhōngshān and promised him kingship.
Zhāng Dēng then said to Zhào and Wèi:
"Qí wishes to attack Hédōng.
How do I know?
Qí is deeply ashamed to be king alongside Zhōngshān.
Now it summons Zhōngshān,
meets with it and promises it kingship—
this is to use its troops.
Would it not be better for the great states to first grant it kingship,
to stop the meeting?"
Zhào and Wèi agreed,
and indeed granted Zhōngshān kingship and befriended it.
Zhōngshān indeed broke with Qí and followed Zhào and Wèi.
When Zhōngshān became king alongside Yān and Zhào,
Qí closed its borders and did not receive envoys from Zhōngshān,
saying:
"I am a state of ten thousand chariots;
Zhōngshān is a state of a thousand chariots.
How can it share the title with me?"
It wished to cede Píngyì to bribe Yān and Zhào,
and send troops to attack Zhōngshān.
Lánzhūjūn was troubled by this.
Zhāng Dēng said to Lánzhūjūn:
"Why are you troubled by Qí?"
Lánzhūjūn said: "Qí is strong,
a state of ten thousand chariots.
It is ashamed to share the title with Zhōngshān,
and does not hesitate to cede land to bribe Yān and Zhào,
and send troops to attack Zhōngshān.
Yān and Zhào value their positions and covet land;
I fear they will not support us.
At worst, our state will be endangered; at best, our kingship abolished.
How can I not be troubled?"
Zhāng Dēng said:
"Allow me to have Yān
and Zhào firmly assist Zhōngshān in establishing its kingship; once accomplished, the matter will be settled.
Do you desire this?"
Lánzhūjūn said: "This is what I desire."
He said:
"Allow me to treat you as the king of Qí, and I will attempt to persuade you.
If it works, then proceed."
Lánzhūjūn said: "I wish to hear your persuasion."
Dēng said:
"The reason Your Majesty does not hesitate to cede land to bribe Yān and Zhào,
and send troops to attack Zhōngshān,
is truly to abolish Zhōngshān's kingship.
The king says: 'Yes.'
Then Your Majesty's actions are costly and risky.
To cede land to bribe Yān and Zhào
strengthens enemies;
to send troops to attack Zhōngshān
initiates conflict.
If Your Majesty does both,
the desired outcome regarding Zhōngshān may not be achieved.
If Your Majesty employs my method,
land will not be lost and troops will not be used,
yet Zhōngshān's kingship can be abolished.
Your Majesty will surely ask: 'What is your method?'"
Lánzhūjūn said: "Then what is your method?"
Zhāng Dēng said: "Your Majesty sends an important envoy
to tell the lord of Zhōngshān: 'The reason I closed my borders and did not receive your envoys
is because Zhōngshān alone became king with Yān and Zhào,
and I was not informed,
so I obstructed it.
If you would deign to come see me,
I will also assist you.'
Zhōngshān fears that Yān and Zhào will not support it;
now if Qí's message says 'I will assist the king,'
Zhōngshān will certainly abandon Yān and Zhào
to meet with Your Majesty.
When Yān and Zhào hear of this,
they will angrily break with it,
The king will also sever ties with it,
leaving Zhōngshān isolated,
and how could an isolated state avoid being deposed?
If we present this argument to the King of Qí,
will the King of Qí listen?"
Lánzhūjūn said: "In that case, he will certainly listen.
This is the reason for deposing it;
how could there be any grounds for preserving it?"
Zhāng Dēng said: "This is precisely why the king should preserve it.
If Qí sends such a demand,
we can use it to inform Yān and Zhào and refuse to go,
thereby deepening our ties with Yān and Zhào.
Yān and Zhào will surely say:
'The reason Qí wants to cede Píngyì to bribe us
is not because it wishes to depose the king of Zhōngshān;
it merely wants to alienate us from Zhōngshān
so that it can draw closer to Zhōngshān itself.'
Even if it were a hundred Píngyì,
Yān and Zhào would certainly not accept it."
Lánzhūjūn said: "Excellent."
He sent Zhāng Dēng to go,
and indeed, Qí made such a demand.
Zhōngshān then informed Yān and
Zhào and refused to go,
and Yān and Zhào indeed both supported Zhōngshān and allowed its king to remain.
The matter was thus settled.
Sīmǎ Xǐ was sent to Zhào
to seek the position of chancellor of Zhōngshān for himself.
Gōngsūn Hóng secretly learned of this.
When the Lord of Zhōngshān went out,
Sīmǎ Xǐ drove the carriage,
and Gōngsūn Hóng rode as an attendant.
Gōngsūn Hóng said: "For a minister
to invoke the might of a great state
to seek the chancellorship for himself—
what does Your Lordship think of this?"
The lord said: "I would eat his flesh
and not share it with anyone."
Sīmǎ Xǐ bowed his head to the carriage rail and said:
"Your servant knows death is upon him!"
The lord said: "Why?"
"Your servant deserves punishment."
The lord said: "Go on,
I understand."
After a short while,
an envoy from Zhào arrived
to request the chancellorship for Sīmǎ Xǐ.
The Lord of Zhōngshān grew highly suspicious of Gōngsūn Hóng,
and Gōngsūn Hóng fled.
Sīmǎ Xǐ served three times as chancellor of Zhōngshān,
and Yīn Jiǎn opposed him.
Tián Jiǎn said to Sīmǎ Xǐ:
"The Zhào envoy has come to listen;
why not speak of Yīn Jiǎn's beauty?
Zhào will surely request her,
and if the lord gives her,
then you will have no internal troubles.
If the lord does not give her to Zhào,
you can then advise the lord to make her his principal wife.
Yīn Jiǎn's gratitude toward you
will be boundless."
Indeed, he had Zhào make the request,
and the lord refused.
Sīmǎ Xǐ said:
"If you do not give her to Zhào,
the King of Zhào will surely be enraged;
if he is enraged, Your Lordship will be in danger.
Therefore, make her your wife,
for surely no one resents another for not giving away his own wife."
Tián Jiǎn believed that by taking charge of the mission,
he could benefit Sīmǎ Xǐ,
benefit Yīn Jiǎn,
and cause Zhào not to make the request.
Consort Yīn and Consort Jiāng vied to become queen.
Sīmǎ Xǐ said to Consort Yīn's father:
"If this succeeds,
you will gain land and subjects;
if it fails, I fear you will lose your life.
If you wish to succeed,
why not consult me?"
Consort Yīn's father bowed and said: "Indeed, as you say,
but how can such matters be spoken of in advance?"
Sīmǎ Xǐ then submitted a memorial to the King of Zhōngshān, saying:
"Your servant has heard of weakening Zhào and strengthening Zhōngshān."
The King of Zhōngshān, pleased, received him and said:
"I wish to hear your plan for weakening Zhào and strengthening Zhōngshān."
Sīmǎ Xǐ said: "Your servant wishes to go to Zhào
to observe its terrain and strategic points,
the wealth and poverty of its people,
the worthiness or unworthiness of its ruler and ministers,
and assess the enemy's resources.
I cannot yet present a detailed plan."
The King of Zhōngshān sent him.
He met the King of Zhào and said:
"Your servant has heard that Zhào
is renowned throughout the land for music
and is the home of beautiful women.
Now,
as I came to the border
and entered the capital, observing the customs and songs of the people,
their features and complexions,
I found none particularly beautiful or lovely.
Having traveled extensively,
roaming everywhere without restriction,
I have never seen anyone like Consort Yīn of Zhōngshān.
Those who do not know her
would think her divine,
beyond the power of words to describe.
Her features and complexion
already surpass ordinary people.
As for her eyebrows, eyes, nose, forehead, and facial proportions,
like rhinoceros horn and the crescent moon,
she is fit to be an empress,
not merely a consort of a feudal lord."
The King of Zhào's interest was stirred,
and he said with great delight:
"I wish to request her.
What do you think?"
Sīmǎ Xǐ said: "Your servant privately observed her beauty
and could not help speaking of it.
If you wish to request her,
that is not something your servant dares to discuss.
I hope Your Majesty will not reveal this."
Sīmǎ Xǐ took his leave
and returned to report to the King of Zhōngshān:
"The King of Zhào is not a worthy ruler.
He does not care for virtue and morality
but delights in music and women;
he does not care for benevolence and righteousness
but delights in bravery and strength.
Your servant heard that he intends to request the so-called Consort Yīn."
The King of Zhōngshān flushed with anger and displeasure.
Sīmǎ Xǐ said: "Zhào is a powerful state,
and it will certainly make the request.
If you do not give her,
the state will be in danger; if you give her,
you will be laughed at by the feudal lords."
The King of Zhōngshān said: "What should I do?"
Sīmǎ Xǐ said: "Make her your queen,
to cut off the King of Zhào's desire.
No one in the world requests another's queen.
Even if he wished to request her,
neighboring states would not permit it."
The King of Zhōngshān then made her queen,
and the King of Zhào made no request.
Zhǔfù wished to attack Zhōngshān
and sent Lǐ Cī to observe it.
Lǐ Cī said: "It can be attacked.
If you do not attack it now,
I fear you will fall behind others."
Zhǔfù said: "Why?"
He replied: "The ruler of Zhōngshān
has visited seventy scholars in narrow alleys and poor lanes,
leaning from his carriage to pay respects."
Zhǔfù said: "This is a worthy ruler;
how can he be attacked?"
Lǐ Cī said: "Not so.
Promoting scholars
causes the people to pursue fame and neglect fundamentals;
honoring the worthy
makes farmers lazy and soldiers cowardly.
A state like this that does not perish
has never existed."
The Lord of Zhōngshān feasted the scholars of the capital,
and Minister Sīmǎ Zǐqī was present.
The mutton soup was not served to everyone,
and Sīmǎ Zǐqī angrily fled to Chǔ, persuading the King of Chǔ to attack Zhōngshān.
The Lord of Zhōngshān fled into exile.
Two men followed him, carrying spears.
The Lord of Zhōngshān turned to them and said:
"Why are you following me?"
The two replied: "We had a father
who once was starving and near death,
and you gave him a pot of food to eat.
Before our father died,
he said:
'If Zhōngshān faces trouble,
you must die for it.'
So we have come to die for you."
The Lord of Zhōngshān sighed deeply and looked up, saying:
"Gratitude does not depend on quantity
but on timely aid in distress;
resentment does not depend on depth
but on hurting the heart.
I lost my state over a cup of mutton soup,
and gained two loyal followers with a pot of food."
Yuè Yáng served as a general of Wèi,
attacking Zhōngshān.
At that time, his son was in Zhōngshān,
and the lord of Zhōngshān had him boiled,
made into a soup, and sent it to Yuè Yáng.
Yuè Yáng ate it.
Throughout the ages, it has been said:
Yuè Yáng ate his son to demonstrate his loyalty,
making clear the harm to a father in pursuit of the law.
King Zhāo, having allowed the people to rest and repaired the weapons,
again wished to attack Zhào.
Lord Wǔ'ān said:
"It cannot be done."
The king said: "In previous years, the state was empty and the people were starving,
yet you did not consider the strength of the common people,
seeking to increase military provisions to destroy Zhào.
Now I have allowed the people to rest in order to nurture the soldiers,
stored up grain and food,
the salaries of the three armies are double what they were before,
and yet you say 'it cannot be done'—
what is your reasoning?"
Lord Wǔ'ān said: "In the affair of Chángpíng,
the Qín army achieved a great victory,
and the Zhào army was utterly defeated;
the people of Qín rejoiced,
while the people of Zhào were terrified.
In Qín, the dead were buried with lavish funerals,
the wounded were generously cared for,
the laborers feasted together,
eating and drinking were provided,
thus squandering their wealth;
in Zhào, the dead could not be gathered,
the wounded could not be treated,
they wept and mourned together,
joined forces in shared sorrow,
plowed the fields and worked diligently,
to generate their wealth.
Now if Your Majesty sends out the army,
even if it is double what it was before,
I estimate that Zhào's defensive preparations
have also increased tenfold. Since Chángpíng,
the ruler and ministers of Zhào have been anxious and fearful,
holding court early and retiring late,
using humble words and heavy bribes,
sending out marriages in all directions,
forming alliances with Yān and Wèi,
establishing friendly relations with Qí and Chǔ,
concentrating their thoughts and uniting their hearts,
making preparation against Qín their priority.
Their domestic affairs are solid,
their foreign relations are successful.
At this time,
Zhào cannot be attacked."
The king said: "I have already raised the army."
Then he sent the five-colonel commander Wáng Líng to lead the attack against Zhào.
Líng's battle ended in defeat,
and he lost the five colonels.
The king wished to send Lord Wǔ'ān,
but Lord Wǔ'ān pleaded illness and would not go.
The king then sent Lord Yìnghóu to see Lord Wǔ'ān,
reproaching him, saying: "Chǔ,
with a territory of five thousand lǐ,
held a million halberd-bearing soldiers.
You previously led a force of several tens of thousands into Chǔ,
captured Yān and Yǐng,
burned their ancestral temples,
advanced east to Jìnglíng,
the people of Chǔ were shaken with fear,
moved east and did not dare to look westward.
Hán and Wèi joined forces,
raising a very large army,
the troops you commanded were not half of theirs,
yet you fought them at Yīquē,
utterly defeated the armies of the two states,
blood flowed and floated shields,
beheading two hundred and forty thousand.
Because of this, Hán and Wèi to this day are called the eastern vassals.
These are your achievements,
known throughout the world.
Now the Zhào soldiers who died at Chángpíng already number seven or eight out of ten,
their state is weakened,
therefore I have raised a large army,
with numbers several times greater than Zhào's forces,
and I wish to have you lead it,
determined to destroy them.
You have previously attacked many with few,
achieving victory as if by divine power,
how much more so when attacking the weak with the strong,
and the few with the many?"
Lord Wǔ'ān said:
"At that time, the king of Chǔ relied on the size of his state,
did not attend to his governance,
and his ministers were jealous of each other's achievements,
flatterers held power,
good ministers were ostracized and kept at a distance,
the hearts of the people were alienated,
city walls and moats were not repaired,
there were neither good ministers,
nor defensive preparations.
Therefore, I was able to lead troops deep into their territory,
doubling the number of cities,
destroying bridges and burning boats to concentrate the people,
plundering the countryside,
to supply the army's food.
At that time,
the soldiers in the Qín army
regarded the army as their home,
the generals as their parents,
they became close without needing agreement,
trusted each other without needing consultation,
united in heart and purpose,
they would die without turning back.
The people of Chǔ fought on their own land,
all concerned for their homes,
each with a scattered heart,
none with the will to fight.
Therefore, I was able to achieve success.
In the battle of Yīquē,
Hán, isolated, looked to Wèi,
not wanting to use its troops first.
Wèi relied on Hán's sharpness,
wanting to push them to the front.
The two armies contended for advantage, their strength not united,
therefore I was able to set up decoy troops,
to face Hán's formation,
concentrating the army and its sharpness,
striking Wèi by surprise.
Once the Wèi army was defeated,
the Hán army collapsed on its own,
and we pursued the defeated northward,
for these reasons I was able to achieve merit.
All were calculations based on advantages and circumstances,
the natural course of events,
what divine power was there in it!
Now Qín defeated the Zhào army at Chángpíng,
but did not seize the moment to take advantage of their shock and fear to destroy them,
instead, out of fear, released them,
allowing them to farm and increase their stores,
nurture orphans and raise the young
to increase their population,
repair weapons and armor to increase their strength,
raise city walls and deepen moats to increase their fortifications.
The ruler humbles himself to treat his ministers with respect,
the ministers devote themselves to treat the brave soldiers with respect.
As for those like Lord Píngyuán,
all have their wives and concubines mending clothes within the ranks.
The subjects are of one heart, superiors and inferiors unite their strength,
just like when Gōu Jiàn was trapped at Kuàijī.
If we join to attack them,
Zhào will certainly hold firm in defense.
If we challenge their army to battle,
they will certainly not come out.
If we besiege their capital,
it certainly cannot be taken.
If we attack their other cities,
they certainly cannot be captured.
If we plunder their countryside,
we will certainly gain nothing.
If the army sets out without achieving success,
the other feudal lords will have other thoughts,
and external rescue will certainly arrive.
I see the harm in this,
and do not perceive the benefit.
Moreover, I am ill,
and cannot go."
Yìng Hóu withdrew in shame,
and reported this to the king.
The king said:
"Without Bái Qǐ,
am I incapable of annihilating Zhào?"
He dispatched additional troops,
and sent Wáng Hé to replace Wáng Líng in attacking Zhào.
After besieging Hándān for eight or nine months,
casualties were heavy,
yet the city remained unconquered.
The king of Zhào sent out light, elite forces to harass their rear,
and Qín suffered several setbacks.
Lord Wǔ'ān said:
"They did not heed my counsel,
and now what has come to pass?"
When the king heard this, he was enraged.
He summoned Lord Wǔ'ān,
insisting he rise from his sickbed,
and said:
"Although you are ill,
force yourself to command the army for me even from your bed.
If you achieve merit,
it is my wish
to bestow greater honors upon you.
If you refuse to go,
I shall hold a grudge against you."
Lord Wǔ'ān kowtowed and said:
"I know that if I go, even without achieving merit,
I may escape punishment.
If I do not go, though I am not guilty,
I will not avoid execution.
Nevertheless, I earnestly hope Your Majesty will consider my humble counsel:
withdraw from Zhào and nurture the people,
awaiting changes among the feudal lords.
Pacify those who are fearful,
attack those who are arrogant,
exterminate those without virtue,
and command the feudal lords.
Then the world can be pacified.
Why must Zhào be the first priority? This is what is called 'yielding to one minister to conquer the world.'
If Your Majesty does not consider my humble counsel,
but insists on satisfying your desire regarding Zhào,
thereby condemning me for my fault,
this would be what is called 'conquering one minister but yielding to the world.'
Which is more imposing:
the authority to conquer one minister,
or the majesty to conquer the world?
I have heard that an enlightened ruler cherishes his state,
and a loyal minister cherishes his reputation.
A destroyed state cannot be restored to wholeness,
and dead soldiers cannot be brought back to life.
I would rather submit to severe punishment and die,
than bear the disgrace of being a defeated general.
I beg Your Majesty to consider this."
